Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
This bill extends death and disability benefits under the Public Safety Officers’ Benefits (PSOB) program to certain retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled as a direct and proximate result of a personal injury from a targeted attack based on the retired officer’s law enforcement service.

label: S. 97
title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department's SelectUSA program to gather input from state economic development groups and report to Congress on how to attract more foreign investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, using no new money.
summary: This bill tells SelectUSA, a Commerce Department program that tries to attract business investment to the United States, to study how to bring more foreign investment into making computer chips (semiconductors) here. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, SelectUSA's leader must ask state-level economic development organizations for comments. They would be asked what the federal government can do, what barriers exist, what opportunities states have found, and what resource gaps hold them back. They would also be asked for ideas on how SelectUSA can help and how to work with allied countries so that "foreign adversaries" do not benefit from the effort. Within two years, SelectUSA must send a report to the Senate and House commerce committees. The report would review the comments, describe what SelectUSA is already doing, and assess strategies it could use. The bill does not create new grants, tax breaks, or rules, and it does not authorize new money. SelectUSA must do the work with funds it already has. The bill passed the Senate on May 20, 2025, and is now waiting in the House. The text does not say anything about environmental, water, or air standards, or about public input beyond state organizations.

who: SelectUSA staff and the Commerce Department

Could encourage coordination with allied countries, which may strengthen supply chain security.
Costs no new federal money and creates no new mandates, so it may be a low-impact step.
concerns: Because the bill only requires a study and report, it may not lead to any direct change in chip investment or supply chain security.
Input is limited to state economic development organizations, so views from other groups, such as workers, local communities, or industry, may not be gathered under this bill.
Relying on existing SelectUSA funds may limit how much work can be done, which could affect the quality of the study.

label: S. 99
title: Strengthening Support for American Manufacturing Act
short_title: Strengthening Support for American Manufacturing Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department to hire an outside expert group to review its manufacturing and supply-chain offices and recommend ways to make them work better, with a report to Congress.
summary: This bill is a study bill. It does not create new programs, give out money, or change any rules for businesses. It tells the Secretary of Commerce to produce a report within one year of the bill becoming law. The report must list which Commerce Department offices and bureaus work on two things: keeping key supply chains strong (for example in defense, health, communications, energy, transportation, and farm supplies), and helping U.S. manufacturers and manufacturing workers with research, resources, or policy. For each office, the report must describe its duties and programs, its legal authority, and how well and how efficiently it works. It must also point out overlap or gaps between offices doing similar work. Finally, it must recommend ways to improve operations and coordination, including with other federal agencies. The Secretary must work with the National Academy of Public Administration, an independent, congressionally chartered group, to produce the report. Within 180 days after finishing the report, the Secretary must send it to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The Secretary must also send suggested legislative changes and the Department's own response to the recommendations. The bill text does not say how much the study would cost or where the money would come from.

who: Department of Commerce offices and bureaus involved in manufacturing and supply chains

label: S. 1353
title: A bill to extend the authority for modifications to the Second Division Memorial in the District of Columbia.
one: Gives more time for additions or engravings to be made to the Second Division Memorial in Washington, DC, which honors Second Infantry Division members who died in service.
summary:
The Second Division Memorial is in President's Park in Washington, DC. It honors members of the Army's Second Infantry Division who died serving the country. A 2017 defense law (section 352 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018) gave permission for changes to the memorial. That permission has a time limit. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the permission lets a veterans' group, the Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation, add commemorative elements or engravings on the memorial's raised platform or stonework.

This bill is very short. It says the 2017 permission keeps applying, even though a general rule in federal law (40 U.S.C. 8903(e)) would normally end it. The bill's text sets the new end date as September 30, 2033. The CRS summary says September 30, 2032. The two sources disagree, and the bill text is what would become law. The bill does not create new spending, new rules, or new powers beyond extending the existing deadline. The text I was given does not say who pays for the changes or what the approval process is. Those details would be in the earlier 2017 law, which I could not see.

Overrides the normal time limit in 40 U.S.C. 8903(e) for this authority.
Sets the new end date as September 30, 2033 in the bill text (the CRS summary says 2032).
Per CRS, lets the foundation keep adding commemorative elements or engravings on the platform or stonework honoring fallen Second Infantry Division members.
who: Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation
Families and veterans of the Second Infantry Division

National Park Service and other federal bodies that oversee memorials in DC (their role is not described in the text provided)

benefits: Lets the memorial be updated to honor more fallen service members over a longer period.
Keeps a long-planned, veteran-led project from lapsing because of a deadline.
Very small change with little risk.
concerns: The CRS summary (2032) and the bill text (2033) give different end dates, which could cause confusion.
The text provided does not describe approval steps or public review for changes to the memorial.
imp.cost: The bill text does not provide funding or give a cost estimate. It only extends an existing authority. How the modifications are paid for is set in the earlier 2017 law, which I could not see.
unknowns: Who pays for the additions and engravings.
What review or approval process applies to design changes.
Whether the end date is meant to be 2032 or 2033.
How many additions are planned.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to extend, for a set period, the existing authority under section 352 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018 to modify the Second Division Memorial in President's Park in Washington, DC. Per the Congressional Research Service summary, that authority lets the Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation add commemorative elements or engravings honoring Second Infantry Division members who died in service. The bill overrides the normal time limit in 40 U.S.C. 8903(e) so the authority does not lapse. The bill text sets the new end date as September 30, 2033, while the CRS summary says September 30, 2032.

oppose: The bill text sets the end date as September 30, 2033, but the CRS summary says 2032. Asking the sponsor's office to confirm the correct date would avoid confusion about how long the authority lasts.

The bill does not describe how changes to the memorial would be approved or whether the public gets a chance to comment. You could ask whether the approval process from the 2017 law is adequate for a memorial in a national park.

support: The bill keeps in place a veteran-led effort to honor Second Infantry Division members who died in service, so the project does not lapse because of a deadline.
The change is very short and only extends an existing authority. It does not appear to create new spending or new powers, according to the CRS summary.
Extending the window gives the foundation more time to add engravings or commemorative elements that recognize more fallen service members.

Specifically, it extends the authority of the Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation to place additional commemorative elements or engravings on the raised platform or stone work to honor the members of the Second Infantry Division who have given their lives in service to the United States.

label: S. 2434
title: A bill to amend the Dayton Aviation Heritage Preservation Act of 1992 to adjust the boundary of the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park, and for other purposes.
short_title: Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park Boundary Adjustment
one: The bill adds about one acre of land in Dayton, Ohio, to the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park by changing the park's legal boundary.
summary:
This bill makes a small change to the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park in Dayton, Ohio. The park honors the history of the Wright brothers and other aviation pioneers. Right now, the park's legal boundary covers certain listed sites. The bill adds one more piece of land, about one acre, to that boundary. The land is shown as "Proposed Addition" on a map titled "Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park Proposed Boundary Addition," dated February 2023.

The bill itself only changes the boundary line in the law. It does not say how the land would be bought, who owns it now, how much it would cost, or how it would be used. It also does not say whether the land would be donated, purchased, or managed through an agreement. The text does not mention any new spending. Because the bill is so short, many practical details would be worked out later by the National Park Service. The bill passed the Senate on November 10, 2026, and still needs House approval and the President's signature to become law.

label: S. 2887
title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
short_title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
one: Adds Route 66, about 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, to the National Trails System as a National Historic Trail, with strong limits on land acquisition, buffer zones, new permits, and any interference with energy projects.
summary:
This bill would officially name Route 66 a National Historic Trail. The trail would include every path U.S. Highway 66 followed between 1926 and 1985. It runs about 2,400 miles from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California. The Secretary of the Interior would run the trail in a way that keeps its quirky, one-of-a-kind character. Before taking actions that would strongly affect Indian Tribes, the Secretary would have to consult with them.

The bill also sets many limits. The federal government could not take land by eminent domain, which is the power to force a sale. Outside federal areas, it could only get land from owners who agree. It could not acquire land more than an average of a quarter mile on either side of the trail. The bill says the trail creates no "buffer zone." Activities that can be seen or heard from the trail could not be limited because of it. Nothing about the trail could block, hinder, or disrupt energy development or transport, such as pipelines and power lines. The designation would not add new permit requirements and would not change who can grant easements or rights-of-way (permission to cross land). It would also keep the trail from being treated as National Park System land under a pipeline law.

The text does not list any money amounts. It passed the Senate on November 12, 2026, and now goes to the House. The text does not say whether Congress would set aside money, and a CRS summary was not available.

label: S. 3296
title: Improving Access to Workers’ Compensation for Injured Federal Workers Act of 2025
short_title: Improving Access to Workers' Compensation for Injured Federal Workers Act
one: The bill would let nurse practitioners and physician assistants treat injured federal employees and make decisions in the federal workers' compensation system, roles now limited mostly to physicians.
summary: Federal employees hurt on the job can get benefits through a program called the Federal Employees' Compensation Act (FECA). Right now, the law mostly counts doctors (physicians and similar practitioners) as the providers whose care and opinions count in that program. This bill adds nurse practitioners and physician assistants, called "other eligible providers," to the law. They would count only for what they are allowed to do under their own state's law. The bill changes several sections so that these providers can be used where the law now says "physician." For example, an injured worker could choose one of them for treatment. Their reports could also count when deciding a claim. One change involves disputes. If the government's doctor and the worker's doctor disagree, a "third physician" now settles it. The bill changes that to "an additional physician." The bill gives the Secretary of Labor six months after it becomes law to finish the rules needed to carry it out. The bill text does not include a cost estimate or new funding. The Senate passed it without changes by unanimous consent. The House has not yet acted, based on the information provided.

label: S. 3493
title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
short_title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
one: The bill gives Carson City, Nevada about 1,270 acres and a small road parcel of federal land for free, orders the sale of other federal parcels to bidders, and updates a 2009 land law, with sale money going into a local account for costs and buying sensitive land.
summary: This bill adjusts how federal land around Carson City, Nevada, is handled under a 2009 law. First, the federal government would give Carson City about 1,270 acres for free. The city must use it for public purposes such as recreation and flood control, and the land can go back to the federal government if it stops being used that way. Second, about half an acre would go to the city for free to build a street connector. The city must add a crosswalk on South Curry Street near the Forest Service office within 2 years. Third, the Bureau of Land Management would sell about 356 acres to qualified bidders. The city would keep certain water line, drainage, and other existing rights. Fourth, the city could offer back about 45 acres to the federal government, which must accept. About 21 of those acres would then be sold. Sale money would go into a Carson City Special Account. It could pay for sale-related costs, including environmental reviews, and for buying environmentally sensitive land in the city. The bill also lets the city make agreements with outside parties, including for-profit ones, to run places like the Capitol City Gun Club, Centennial Park, and Eagle Valley Golf Course, without an appraisal. It sets a one-year deadline to offer certain lands for sale if there is a qualified bidder. The bill does not require the federal government or the city to clean up existing contamination on the conveyed lands.

label: S. 3589
title: RISE Act
short_title: RISE Act (Respond, Innovate, Succeed, and Empower Act)
one: Requires colleges that take federal student aid to accept common disability records as proof of disability, publish how they decide on accommodations, and report anonymized counts of students with disabilities, and authorizes $10 million for a national technical-assistance center.
summary: This bill changes the Higher Education Act, the main federal law covering colleges that receive federal student aid. First, colleges would have to accept several kinds of existing paperwork as enough proof that a student has a disability. These include a high school IEP (a special education plan) or a Section 504 plan used at any point in high school, a record from another college, a record from a licensed professional, a service record under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or documentation of a disability from military service. Colleges could still choose rules that are easier than these. Second, colleges would have to clearly explain how they decide who gets accommodations. They would need to share this with students, parents, and faculty, including at orientation and on a public website. Third, colleges would report yearly numbers to the federal data system (IPEDS): how many students are registered with disability services, how many get accommodations, what share of students that is, and how many degrees or certificates they earn. Colleges would not report numbers when doing so could identify a single student. Fourth, it authorizes up to $10 million over fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for a national center that helps colleges support students with disabilities. Authorizing money does not itself spend it; Congress must still appropriate it. The bill says it does not change the meaning of rights under the ADA or Section 504.

Exempts reporting when small numbers could reveal a student's identity.
Authorizes $10 million for FY2027-2031 for the National Center for Information and Technical Support for Postsecondary Students with Disabilities.

summary: This bill does not create a new national trail. It only asks the federal government to study whether it should. The bill adds the Bay Area Ridge Trail to the list of trails the Secretary of the Interior may study under the National Trails System Act. The trail is described as a multi-use path about 550 miles long. It runs along the ridgelines of the hills and mountains around the San Francisco Bay Area in northern California and links more than 75 parks and open spaces. The bill says the study must be done in consultation with state, tribal, and local government agencies and other interested groups, including the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council. The bill text does not say how long the study will take, how much it will cost, or what happens afterward. Any actual designation as a national scenic trail would need a separate act of Congress. label: S. 3923
title: Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews and greatly expands NOAA's weather, tsunami, hurricane, tornado, wildfire, heat, drought and alert programs for fiscal years 2027–2031, with new reporting rules, more use of private-sector data, and several new spending authorizations.
summary:
This bill renews and expands a 2017 law that guides how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) researches and forecasts weather. It authorizes about $167–174 million a year for weather research. It also sets up or renews programs for tornadoes, hurricanes, tsunamis, precipitation, atmospheric rivers, coastal flooding, extreme heat, drought, and wildfire weather.

The bill pushes NOAA to improve how warnings reach people. It would modernize NOAA Weather Radio, with $100 million for upgrades in 2027 and $25 million a year for operations. It bars buying upgrade equipment from companies based in foreign countries of concern. It orders studies of how people understand and act on alerts, with extra attention to rural areas, Tribes, older adults, people with disabilities, and non-English speakers.

It also leans more on commercial data, such as private satellites, radar, aircraft and ocean vessels. It adds rules for open data sharing, cost comparisons, and reports to Congress. It creates a "Fire Ready Nation" program with incident meteorologists, a fire weather testbed, and a temporary premium-pay waiver for wildland fire workers in 2027. It also lets NOAA transfer excess satellites to other agencies and keep the reimbursements. Finally, it requires annual unfunded-priority lists and capital plans. These are authorizations, meaning they allow spending but don't provide the money. Congress would still have to appropriate it.

Rewrites tornado (VORTEX-USA), hurricane, and new precipitation and atmospheric river programs, with annual reports and budget proposals.
Reauthorizes tsunami warning, research, and mitigation work at $30M a year, adds Tribal consultation, and orders alert and terminology reviews and a GAO report.
Creates a Radar Next program to replace NEXRAD radar by 2037 at the latest, and allows contracts with outside entities to fill radar gaps.
Expands the Commercial Data Program and pushes NOAA to buy private weather data, use multiyear contracts, and share data with the weather enterprise.
Sets up heat-health programs ($2.7M a year), aviation weather ($10M a year), aerial snow surveys, and drought and subseasonal forecasting ($40M and $15–17M a year).
Modernizes NOAA Weather Radio ($25M a year plus $100M in 2027), bars foreign-adversary equipment, and orders alert standards and a GAO report on alert IT.
Creates a Fire Ready Nation program: fire weather services, a testbed, an Incident Meteorologist Service, a rating-system review, and a working group.
Waives premium pay caps for certain wildland fire employees for 2027 and requires a hiring plan.
Lets NOAA transfer excess satellites to other agencies outside normal property rules, keep reimbursements in a special account, and notify Congress 60 days ahead.
Requires annual unfunded priorities lists, capital investment plans, and public stock assessment schedules.
Allows Arctic observation networks, Pacific Island technical help, and international weather partnerships.

label: S. 432
title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Establishment Act
short_title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Act
one: The bill would create a new National Park Service site at Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York, to preserve and tell the story of 982 World War II refugees housed there from 1944 to 1946, once enough land has been acquired.
summary:
This bill would set up a new national historical park in New York State at Fort Ontario. During World War II, 982 refugees, mostly Jewish people who had fled the Holocaust, were housed there from August 1944 to February 1946. The park's purpose is to preserve and teach about their stories for future generations.

The park would not start right away. The Secretary of the Interior must first decide that enough land, or interests in land, has been acquired inside the "Proposed Boundary" on a September 2024 map to make a manageable park. Within 30 days after that decision, the Secretary must announce the park in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice.

The National Park Service could get land by donation, by purchase with donated or taxpayer-appropriated money, or by exchange. Land owned by the State or a local government could be obtained only by donation. The Secretary could sign agreements with the State and with public or private groups to provide education and interpretation. The Secretary could also make agreements to restore important historic resources on non-federal land in or near the park. Any such agreement that helps non-federal land must allow reasonable public access. Within 3 fiscal years after funding becomes available, the Secretary must finish a general management plan in consultation with the State. The bill text does not give a dollar amount or say how much land is involved.

label: S. 433
title: National Manufacturing Advisory Council Act
one: Creates a Commerce Department advisory council of up to 30 industry, labor and academic members to advise on manufacturing policy and send Congress a yearly strategic plan, with no new money.
summary: This bill would set up a National Manufacturing Advisory Council inside the Department of Commerce within 180 days of becoming law. The council would have up to 30 members chosen by the Commerce Secretary. They would come from private industry (including small and mid-sized makers), colleges and universities, and labor unions. The Secretary must also take public suggestions for who to appoint, when practical. It would take over the work of the existing U.S. Manufacturing Council. The council would meet at least every 180 days under federal open-advisory-committee rules. It would advise Commerce on things like worker training, apprenticeships, new technology, supply chain problems, jobs for low-income people and new workers, and employee ownership of companies. It would collect input from rural areas, economically distressed areas, and places hit by factory layoffs. It would also look for federal, state or other regulations that cause unnecessary supply chain disruption, higher prices or costly burdens, and suggest fixes. Every year it would send a national strategic plan and a report of its activities to the Secretary and congressional committees. The bill gives it no new funding. The council would end on September 30 of the fifth year after its first meeting. The council only gives advice; it cannot make rules or spend money.

title: Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument Establishment Act

one: Creates a National Park System unit in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to preserve and teach the history of the Greenwood District, Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, with a mostly descendant-led advisory commission.
summary: This bill would create the Historic Greenwood District–Black Wall Street National Monument in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of the National Park System. Its purpose is to preserve and explain the history of the Greenwood District, the thriving Black business community known as Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre. The monument would not officially exist until the Interior Secretary decides enough land has been acquired to make a manageable park. The Secretary could get land inside the mapped boundary only by donation, by buying from a willing seller, or by swapping land. The bill says it does not affect the rights of private property owners inside or next to the monument. The Secretary could also sign agreements with public or private groups for education, interpretation, and technical help. The National Park Service would run the site under normal park laws and write a management plan within 3 years after money is first made available. The bill also creates an 11-member advisory commission. Seven members would be descendants of people who lived or worked in Greenwood in 1921, three would have historic preservation expertise, and one would be recommended by Tulsa's mayor. Members serve without pay, though travel costs are covered. The commission would end 10 years after the monument is established. The bill exempts the commission from a federal advisory committee law (FACA), which normally sets open-meeting and record rules. It does not give a dollar amount.

label: S. 1377
title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
short_title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
one: Requires the Interior Department to keep a genetically diverse herd of at least 150 horses in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, limits when horses can be removed, and requires yearly public reporting on the herd.
summary:
This bill would change the 1947 law that governs Theodore Roosevelt National Park in North Dakota. It would require the Secretary of the Interior to keep a herd of horses in the park's South Unit. The herd must be genetically diverse, meaning varied enough to stay healthy over time, and must have at least 150 horses.

Within 120 days of becoming law, Interior must write a plan for managing the horses. The plan must be cost-effective and must make sure the park's natural resources, such as grasslands and wildlife habitat, are not harmed.

The bill also limits removing horses from federal land in the park. Removal is allowed only as part of a plan to keep the herd genetically diverse, in an emergency, or to protect public health and safety. As written, the text joins these conditions in a slightly unusual way, so how they fit together could be a question for the agency or courts.

Finally, each year Interior must monitor the herd and publish what it finds about the herd's size, makeup, and health. The bill does not add money. It does not say how many horses is too many, or what happens if the herd and the park's plants and wildlife come into conflict. The bill passed the Senate on June 11, 2026, and is now in the House Natural Resources Committee.

label: H.R. 1013
title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act of 2025
short_title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act
one: The bill changes federal securities laws so 403(b) retirement plans, used by public school staff, charity workers, and church employees, can invest in pooled bank trust funds and insurance company separate accounts, as 401(k) plans already can.
summary:
Many teachers, nurses at nonprofit hospitals, charity workers, and church employees save for retirement in 403(b) plans. Today, federal securities rules mostly limit these plans to mutual funds and annuities. Larger 401(k) plans can also use other pooled investment options, such as collective investment trusts (CITs). A CIT is a pooled fund run by a bank or trust company. 401(k) plans can also use insurance company "separate accounts," which are investment accounts an insurer keeps apart from its other money. These options often have lower fees.

This bill would update three securities laws: the Investment Company Act of 1940, the Securities Act of 1933, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. After that, 403(b) plans could invest in CITs and insurance company separate accounts without those products having to follow the full registration and disclosure rules that apply to mutual funds.

The bill sets conditions. A plan must be covered by ERISA (the main federal private-pension law), or the employer must agree to act as a fiduciary for choosing the plan's investment options. A fiduciary has a legal duty to act in participants' best interest. Government plans would need the employer or another responsible person to review and approve each investment option before it is offered. The bill does not say when it would take effect. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Banking Committee.

For governmental 403(b) plans, requires the employer, a fiduciary, or someone acting for the employer to review and approve each investment option before it is offered.
Makes matching changes in the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, including broker and registration rules.

Reduced registration and disclosure requirements could make these products easier and cheaper for providers to offer.
concerns: Products that do not follow mutual fund registration and disclosure rules may give workers less standardized information to compare options.
Employers acting as fiduciaries may face legal responsibility for investment choices, which could be hard for smaller organizations to manage.
Plans not covered by ERISA rely on the employer's fiduciary role, so protections may vary from plan to plan.

label: H.R. 10238
title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
short_title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to create and share cybersecurity guidance with small businesses, including information on Defense Department cybersecurity certification for federal contractors, and to report yearly to Congress.
summary:
This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to help small businesses protect themselves from hackers and online threats. The SBA would work with two other federal agencies that focus on cybersecurity, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Together they would develop and share guides and resources on good cybersecurity habits.

The bill also covers small businesses that want to work as contractors or subcontractors for the federal government. The SBA, working with the Department of Defense and other agencies, would give them information about the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC). This is a set of cybersecurity standards for Defense Department contractors. The SBA would draw on existing Defense Department resources, including a small business office, a program created in the 2026 defense bill, and the APEX Accelerator program. The SBA would post this information on its website and in its outreach.

Each year the SBA would also consult its Office of Advocacy on the best ways to share other cybersecurity information. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, and every year after that, the SBA would send Congress a report. The report would give the number and a description of small businesses that contacted the SBA about cybersecurity. The bill does not set aside new money, and it does not create new penalties or requirements for businesses.

one: Requires the Small Business Administration to create, share, and yearly update educational materials that help small businesses spot and protect themselves from harmful conduct by foreign adversaries, such as hacking, IP theft, forced labor, and fraud.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to build and share guides that teach small businesses about harm that can come from foreign adversaries, meaning governments or companies tied to countries the U.S. treats as threats. The SBA must work with other agencies, including Homeland Security, State, the FBI, Treasury, Commerce, and the Trade Representative. The guides must explain what this harmful conduct looks like and how it hurts small businesses. Examples in the bill are stealing trade secrets, hacking, forced labor in supply chains, counterfeit goods and customs fraud, and unfair investment practices. The guides must also give best practices for protecting intellectual property, private business information, and supply chains. They must give cybersecurity and data protection tips, warn about risks in foreign investments, joint ventures, and licensing deals with adversary-linked entities, and point to federal help. They must also advise on protecting business interests abroad without needlessly limiting lawful business. The SBA would share the materials through its district offices and other programs. Starting October 1, 2027, it must review and update them every year. If the SBA decides a new type of activity poses a significant national or economic security risk, it must tell the House and Senate small business committees what the activity is and why. The bill creates no new penalties, rules, or grants. It does not give a cost estimate, and I could not see one in the text.

title: SBIC Reporting Modernization Act of 2026
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to post a public quarterly report on the Small Business Investment Company program, including licensing numbers, government-backed debt issued, and jobs created or sustained.
summary:
This bill would change the law that governs Small Business Investment Companies (SBICs). SBICs are privately owned investment firms licensed by the Small Business Administration (SBA). They invest in small businesses and can borrow money that the federal government guarantees. The bill would not change who can get that money or how much. It only adds a reporting duty.

Starting 90 days after the bill becomes law, the SBA would have to post a report on its website every three months. The report would include the same information the SBA already puts in its yearly report on this program, such as how many SBICs are licensed and how much government-backed financing each has received. It would also list how many applicants were approved to move to the final licensing stage. It would list how many of those applicants went on to meet the legal requirements for a license. It would give the dollar value of debentures issued, which are loans the government backs. Finally, it would give the number of jobs created or sustained because of SBIC investments.

The bill passed the House on November 11, 2026. It is now in the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee. The text does not say how the SBA would count jobs.

label: H.R. 10375
title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026
short_title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act
one: This bill loosens and updates rules for the SBA 504 loan program, which helps small businesses finance buildings and equipment, with changes aimed at small manufacturers, workforce training, disaster recovery, and faster loan closings.
summary:
The SBA 504 loan program helps small businesses buy or build property and equipment. A nonprofit-style lender called a certified development company (CDC) works with a bank and the SBA to make these loans. This bill changes the program in several ways, mostly for loans made on or after October 1, 2027.

First, it adds new goals that can qualify a project for help: job training programs of at least 12 weeks, helping areas recover after a declared disaster (generally for five years, with one-year extensions), and expanding businesses with 10 or fewer employees.

Second, it lets certain top-rated CDCs fix typos, move up to 10% of project costs between categories, and add or change guarantors and co-borrowers at closing. It also shifts some file-review duties from SBA district lawyers to the SBA's Office of Credit Risk Management, and sets requirements for approved closing attorneys.

Third, it changes leasing rules. Borrowers may lease out part of a building to other tenants. Small manufacturers building new facilities may occupy as little as 50% instead of 60%. For existing buildings, a business that has been in place 12 months may lease up to 66%, with yearly checks and "anti-investor" certifications to keep out real estate developers.

Fourth, it requires an SBA marketing plan and a report to Congress within five years. It also removes the "credit elsewhere" test, which asks whether a borrower could not get credit elsewhere, for CDC-related financings.

Moves file-review duties for loans closed by designated attorneys from SBA district counsels to the Office of Credit Risk Management.
Sets requirements for designated closing attorneys: licensed, malpractice insurance, and SBA-approved training.
Requires SBA to create a marketing and outreach plan, possibly with resource partners.

Changes leasing limits: new facilities may lease up to 20% (small manufacturers need to occupy only 50%); existing buildings may lease up to 50%, or up to 66% with conditions, annual or biennial checks, and an anti-investor certification.
Caps residential leases at 1 year and commercial leases at 5 years under these rules.
Requires an SBA report to Congress within 5 years on how the leasing changes affect access to capital.
Exempts CDC loans and financings under the Small Business Investment Act from the 'credit elsewhere' test.
Applies to loans made or guaranteed on or after October 1, 2027.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to modernize the SBA 504 loan program, which helps small businesses finance expansion or modernization of property and equipment through certified development companies. 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026
This bill generally expands the Small Business Administration (SBA) 504 Loan Program to include additional objectives and flexibilities (e.g., new economic development objectives that may be used to qualify for assistance under the program). The program provides a small business with SBA financing—through a certified development company intermediary—for expansion or modernization.
Specifically, the bill expands the public policy goals that allow an intermediary to qualify for assistance to include additional objectives. These include (1) workforce development through work-based or work-integrated training, and (2) aiding the revitalization of an area for which a disaster has been declared or determined.
The bill also authorizes an intermediary to take specified actions to facilitate the closing of 504 loans, such as correcting borrower or lender information on loan documents or reallocating up to 10% of the cost of a project.
Further, the bill allows small businesses to lease a larger portion of renovated buildings that are financed with 504 loans to other tenants in certain circumstances. In the case of a project to renovate or reconstruct an existing building, a small business may lease a maximum of 66% of the building to commercial or residential tenants if certain conditions are met. For example, the small business must have occupied the building for 12 consecutive months prior to the project.
Additionally, the bill exempts intermediaries from the requirement to demonstrate they are unable to obtain credit elsewhere to receive 504 loans.

label: H.R. 1047
title: GRID Power Act
one: Requires FERC to write a rule letting grid operators move "dispatchable" power plants (like gas, coal, and other on-demand generators) ahead of other projects in the line to connect to the electric grid.
summary: Before a new power plant can send electricity into the high-voltage grid, it has to wait in a line called the interconnection queue. This bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the agency that oversees the interstate power grid, to change the rules for that line. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, FERC must start a rulemaking. Within 180 days, it must finish a final rule. The rule must let grid operators (called transmission providers) ask FERC for permission to move "dispatchable" projects higher in the line. Dispatchable means a power source that can be turned up or down on demand and provides predictable supply. The bill does not name specific fuels. The official summary gives fossil fuel plants as examples. Grid operators who make such a request must show why it is needed and explain how it will improve grid reliability or resilience. They must also hold public comment and stakeholder engagement before sending the request to FERC. They must report regularly to FERC on grid reliability and resilience. FERC then has 60 days to approve or deny each request. FERC must review the rule at least every five years. The bill does not say what happens to projects that get bumped down the line. It also does not mention clean energy, cost limits, or environmental review.
does: Orders FERC to start a rulemaking within 90 days of enactment and finish a final rule within 180 days.
Directs FERC to address delays and inefficiency in processing grid connection requests so new dispatchable projects can connect quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.
Changes the standard large-generator connection procedures and agreement so grid operators may propose moving dispatchable projects higher in the queue.
Requires each proposal to show a need and explain how it improves grid reliability or resilience.
Requires public comment and stakeholder engagement before a proposal goes to FERC.
Requires grid operators to report regularly to FERC on grid reliability and resilience and on actions taken under the Act.
Requires FERC to approve or deny each proposal within 60 days.
Requires FERC to review and update the rule at least every five years.
who: Developers of dispatchable plants (such as gas, coal, nuclear, hydro, or storage, depending on how FERC defines the term)
Developers of wind, solar, and other variable generation waiting in connection queues
Grid operators, regional transmission organizations, and utilities
FERC staff and commissioners
Electricity customers and ratepayers
Communities near new power plants

benefits: Dispatchable projects that can be turned up or down on demand could help grid operators keep supply steady, according to the bill's stated goal of improving reliability and resource adequacy.
The required showing and public comment steps may give the public and regulators a way to review queue changes before they take effect.
Faster interconnection for dispatchable projects could possibly help add capacity sooner where it is needed.
concerns: Projects moved down the queue could face longer waits, and the bill does not say what happens to them.
The bill does not mention clean energy, cost limits, or environmental review, so its effects on costs, emissions, and renewable projects are not addressed.
Giving priority to one category of generation could change which projects get built and how quickly, which could affect competition among developers.
The 60-day FERC review period is short, and the bill does not describe how FERC would judge whether a proposal is sound.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state any cost, funding amount, or budget impact for this bill."]
unknowns: What happens to projects that are moved lower in the interconnection queue, including whether they lose their place or face new costs.
Whether the bill would change electricity prices or costs for consumers.
How FERC would define or measure 'reliability' or 'resilience' when deciding requests.
Whether the change would affect emissions or environmental review, since the bill does not address these topics.
How much the rule would speed up interconnection for any project type.
Whether the bill will pass the second chamber, since its latest action is in Senate committee.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by making sure new dispatchable power projects, which can supply electricity on demand and with predictable timing, can connect to the high-voltage grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. It addresses the problem that new power plants must wait in an interconnection queue before connecting, by directing FERC to revise the rules so grid operators can propose moving dispatchable projects higher in that queue.

oppose: The bill does not mention clean energy, cost limits, or environmental review, so it does not say how it would affect electricity costs, emissions, or renewable projects. You could ask your member how those effects would be measured.

Moving dispatchable projects up the queue could push other projects, including renewable ones, to wait longer. The bill does not say what happens to projects that are moved down, and you could ask for that to be spelled out.

FERC would have only 60 days to approve or deny each queue proposal, and the bill does not describe how FERC should judge whether a proposal is sound. You could ask how that review would work and whether it allows enough time for public input.
support: The bill's stated goal is to help keep the grid reliable by letting dispatchable power, which can be turned up or down on demand, connect sooner where it is needed. You could ask your member how this would work during periods of high demand.

The bill requires grid operators to show a need for each queue change and explain how it improves reliability or resilience, and to hold public comment before sending a proposal to FERC. You could say these steps help keep the process transparent.

The bill requires FERC to approve or deny each proposal within 60 days and to review the rule at least every five years. You could say these deadlines keep the process moving and allow the rule to be updated over time.

crs:
Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable Power Act or the GRID Power Act

This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue and periodically review a rule that revises the approval process for interconnection requests of generating units that produce electricity to prioritize dispatchable power projects (e.g., certain fossil fuel projects). 
Under the bill, 
dispatchable power
 generally refers to an electric energy generation resource, such as a generating unit that produces electricity from fossil fuels, capable of providing known and forecastable electric supply in time intervals necessary to ensure grid reliability. Currently, FERC receives interconnection requests from those projects and other generating units, such as units that produce electricity from renewable energy. Interconnection requests are requests from generating units to connect to the high voltage transmission lines of the electric grid.
First, the rule must address the efficiency and effectiveness of the existing procedures for processing interconnection requests to ensure that new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can interconnect to the electric grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. 
Second, the rule must revise the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement as appropriate, to authorize transmission providers to submit proposals to FERC to prioritize new dispatchable power projects that will improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by assigning those projects higher positions in the interconnection queue of the provider. FERC must review and approve or deny such proposals within 60 days after the proposal is submitted.

life.reason: Prioritizing fossil fuel plants in the queue could speed fossil generation and its pollution-related health and ecological harms, with no environmental review required.

water.reason: Fast-tracking fossil plants may increase cooling-water withdrawals and discharges from thermal plants, and the bill has no water protections.

air.reason: Moving fossil fuel plants ahead of clean generators in the queue would likely increase emissions of air pollutants and greenhouse gases, and the bill has no environmental review.

transparency.reason: Grid operators must hold public comment and stakeholder engagement and file regular public-facing reliability reports with FERC before proposals are sent.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill speeds access to the grid for favored dispatchable projects, which mainly benefits developers' schedules and returns, while wind and solar developers would be pushed back without cost or ratepayer protections.

local_say.reason: The bill includes a public comment step but does not give communities a real veto or say over siting, so the effect is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide direct subsidies or tax breaks, though it does not address who bears costs of reprioritizing the queue.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill is neither clearly honest nor dishonest and does not touch on kindness in a clear way.

votes.question: On Passage

news.overall: Only one Lean Left headline names the GRID Power Act directly, and the rest address related energy topics. The evidence is thin, so this summary describes only one outlet group and cannot compare it with other perspectives. Within the group, coverage presents the bill as part of a larger debate about speeding up energy permits and grid capacity amid affordability concerns.

label: H.R. 1453
title: Clean Energy Demonstration Transparency Act of 2025
one: Requires the Department of Energy to publish, at least twice a year, contracts, milestone status, and major changes for clean energy demonstration projects it funds or manages.
summary: This bill adds a reporting rule to the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. It covers clean energy demonstration projects, which are pilot-scale projects the Department of Energy (DOE) funds to test new energy technology. Starting six months after the bill becomes law, and at least every six months after that, the Energy Secretary must send a report to key House and Senate committees. The report must also be posted online for the public. For each project, the report must include a copy of the first contracts or financial assistance agreements between DOE and the award recipient, along with related documents the Secretary thinks are appropriate. It must list technical, material, or financial milestones that were met or missed. It must also describe major changes to the project's scope, schedule, funding (including cost-share requirements, meaning the share the recipient pays), partners, or budget. DOE may combine these reports with other required reports, where practical, to avoid duplicating work. The bill does not add money, change which projects get funded, or set penalties for missing the deadlines. The bill passed the House on May 19, 2025, and is now in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

who: Department of Energy and its Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (new reporting work)

Allowing reports to be combined with other required reports may reduce extra paperwork for DOE.

Because the bill sets no penalties for missed deadlines, DOE could submit late reports without direct consequences.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to increase transparency about clean energy demonstration projects that the Department of Energy's Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations manages or supports. label: H.R. 1455
title: ITS Codification Act
one: The bill writes into federal law the existing federal telecom research lab (the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences) and orders it to start an effort to develop tools for finding people trapped in mines, collapsed buildings, and similar places.
summary:
The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) is a lab inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), part of the Commerce Department. It already exists, but this bill would put it into federal law so its role is official. The bill says ITS would be the main executive-branch lab for studying radio signals, how they travel, and how they interfere with each other. It would also test technology that lets federal agencies and private companies share radio spectrum (the airwaves used for phones, radar, and more), and help make federal spectrum more available to non-federal users. The bill lets ITS make research and technology agreements with outside parties under several existing laws.

The bill also requires ITS to start an initiative to help develop emergency communication and tracking tools. These would help find people trapped in places where regular radios don't work well, such as underground mines, high-rise buildings, or collapsed structures. ITS would work with private companies and federal agencies to assess needs and help develop technical standards. Within 18 months, the NTIA head would have to send Congress, and post publicly, a report on that needs assessment. The bill does not state a dollar amount or create new funding. I could not see any budget numbers in the text.
does: Adds a new section 106 to the NTIA Organization Act that makes ITS an official, permanent test center.
Names ITS the primary executive-branch lab for studying radio emissions, interference, and how signals travel.
Directs ITS to test spectrum-sharing technology and promote access to federal spectrum for non-federal users.
Lets the Assistant Secretary hand ITS other NTIA duties.

label: H.R. 197
title: Lake Winnibigoshish Land Exchange Act of 2025
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to swap about 17.5 acres of federal land in Chippewa National Forest for about 36.7 acres owned by Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC, if the company offers the swap.
summary:
This bill covers a small land swap in Itasca County, Minnesota, near Lake Winnibigoshish (often called Lake Winnie). The swap involves the Chippewa National Forest. If a private company, Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC (BWLT), offers to give the U.S. about 36.7 acres, the Forest Service must accept the offer within one year. In return, the Forest Service must give BWLT about 17.5 acres of federal land. The federal government would keep a right of way (an easement) so people can still reach national forest land west of the federal parcel.

The swap is supposed to be equal in value. If the federal land is worth more, BWLT pays the difference in cash. If the company's land is worth more, the government does not have to pay the difference, and the extra value counts as a donation from BWLT. Before the government accepts the company's land, the company must complete a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment. This is a records review and site check for signs of contamination. The company must also show clear title to the land. BWLT pays all closing costs, including survey, title, and environmental study costs. Land the government gets would become part of the Chippewa National Forest and be managed under normal national forest rules. The map and legal descriptions would be finalized after the bill passes and kept open for public viewing at Forest Service offices.

label: H.R. 2600
title: ASCEND Act
short_title: ASCEND Act (NASA Commercial Satellite Data Program)
one: The bill makes NASA's program for buying Earth-imaging data from commercial satellite companies a permanent part of federal law, with rules protecting scientific publication, wider data use, a preference for U.S. vendors, and yearly reports to Congress.
summary:
This bill would write into federal law a NASA program that buys satellite pictures and data of Earth from private companies. NASA started this as a pilot in 2019 and says it worked well. Scientists use this kind of data to study land, water, weather, and climate.

Under the bill, NASA would run the program inside its Earth Science Division. NASA could buy data from commercial companies and could set or change license terms so that more people than just NASA-funded researchers can use the data. The contracts could not block scientists from publishing the data for scientific purposes, or from publishing new information made from it. NASA would have to buy from U.S. companies as much as practical.

Starting 180 days after the bill becomes law, and every year after, NASA would send Congress a report. It would list the agreements, the license terms, how each one helps science (including National Academies priorities), and whether federal workers, contractors, or the public can use the data.

The bill does not give a specific dollar amount. It does not say how much NASA must spend. The bill has passed the House and is waiting on the Senate calendar.

This bill provides statutory authority for the Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition (CSDA) program run by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Remote sensing

label: H.R. 2659
title: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
short_title: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
one: Creates a temporary CISA-led, FBI-co-led task force to coordinate federal agencies against Chinese state-sponsored hackers like Volt Typhoon, with yearly classified reports to Congress and public unclassified summaries.
summary: This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security, through its cybersecurity agency (CISA), to set up a joint task force within 120 days of becoming law. The task force would help federal agencies that oversee key industries (like energy, defense, and agriculture) work together against hacking by groups tied to the Chinese government, including one known as Volt Typhoon. That group has been reported to hide inside U.S. critical systems such as power, water, and transportation. CISA's director would lead the task force and the FBI director would be vice chair. Other agencies must share relevant information, following existing laws and security-clearance rules. The task force would send Congress a first report within 540 days, then yearly reports for five more years. Reports would assess risks to critical systems, what extra resources or legal powers agencies need, what could happen in a major crisis or conflict, how hacking could slow U.S. military movement, and the economic and social effects of disruptions. They would also include a one-time plan for an awareness campaign for owners and operators of critical infrastructure. Reports are mostly classified, but an unclassified executive summary may be posted on a DHS website. The task force ends 60 days after its final briefing. It is exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act and the Paperwork Reduction Act. The bill does not give a dollar amount.

crs:
Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
The bill creates a joint interagency task force to facilitate agency collaboration on efforts to respond to Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors, including Volt Typhoon. 
The task force must be established and led by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), an agency within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The task force must facilitate collaboration and coordination among the Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs) specified in the President's National Security Memorandum- 22 (e.g., the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, and the Department of Agriculture) to detect, analyze, and respond to Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors by ensuring that such agencies’ actions are aligned and mutually reinforcing.
The bill directs DHS, CISA, the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and specified SRMAs to provide the task force with analysis, inspections, audits, and other relevant information necessary for the task force to carry out its responsibilities. The production and use of information must comply with all applicable statutes, regulations, and executive orders, and task force members must have appropriate security clearances to access classified information.
The task force must provide annual reports and briefings to Congress detailing its assessment of cyber threats and recommendations to improve the detection and mitigation of the cybersecurity threat posed by Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors.
The first report must be provided no later than 540 days after the establishment of the task force, and additional reports must be provided annually thereafter for six years.

water.reason: The task force targets Volt Typhoon-style intrusions into water systems and aims to improve federal coordination on defending them, which somewhat advances safe water supply protection.

transparency.reason: Reports go to Congress and an unclassified executive summary must be posted publicly, which helps transparency, but most content is classified and the task force is exempted from FACA public-meeting rules, which offsets the gain.

label: H.R. 2768
title: Benton MacKaye National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act of 2026
short_title: Benton MacKaye National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act
one: Requires the Agriculture Department to study, within two years, whether the 287-mile Benton MacKaye Trail in Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina should become a national scenic trail.
summary:
This bill does not create a new national trail. It only orders a study. The Benton MacKaye Trail is a hiking-only (nonmotorized) trail about 287 miles long that runs through Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina. The bill adds the trail to the list of routes in the National Trails System Act that the government must study for possible national scenic trail status.

The Secretary of Agriculture, who oversees the U.S. Forest Service, would have two years from the date the bill becomes law to finish the study and send it to Congress. The Secretary must talk with interested groups, including the Benton MacKaye Trail Association, while doing the work.

The bill does not say what the study must examine, such as land ownership, environmental effects, or cost. It does not give money for the study, and it does not say how the public or local landowners and communities would be able to weigh in beyond the "interested organizations" the agency must consult. Making the trail a national scenic trail would need a separate act of Congress later. The bill passed the House on June 2, 2026, and is waiting on the Senate calendar.

This bill requires the Department of Agriculture to study the feasibility of designating the Benton MacKaye Trail (located in Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina) as a national scenic trail.

transparency.reason: The bill requires a published feasibility study sent to Congress and requires consultation with interested organizations, which modestly increases public visibility into a federal land decision.

local_say.reason: It requires consultation with named interested groups, but it does not create a formal role for local landowners or communities, so the effect on local say is unclear.

label: H.R. 2876
title: University of Utah Research Park Act
short_title: University of Utah Research Park Act
one: The bill confirms that the University of Utah's use of about 593 acres of formerly federal land in Salt Lake City as a research park, including student housing and a transit hub, counts as a valid public purpose under federal law.
summary: In 1968 the federal government gave about 593.54 acres of land in Salt Lake City to the University of Utah under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act. That law lets public bodies get federal land for public uses like schools and parks. The University has used the land as a research park, and the Interior Department approved that plan in a 1970 letter. This bill says that use, and any later changes the Interior Department approved before the bill becomes law, is a valid public purpose under that 1926 law. It also says other uses are valid if they fit a research park and related university purposes. The bill names student housing and a transit hub as examples. The earlier terms and conditions in the 1970 letter and approvals still apply to the approved plan. The bill does not give out new land or spend money. It appears to clear up legal doubt about whether the land's current and future uses fit the original grant. The bill text does not say what happens if the land is used for something else. It also does not say whether private companies that lease space in the park are covered, or whether the public gets a say in future changes. The House passed it on December 15, 2025. It is now on the Senate calendar.
does: Confirms the University of Utah's research park use of about 593.54 acres in Salt Lake City as a valid public purpose under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act.
Covers the plan approved by the Interior Department in a December 10, 1970 letter and any changes the Department approved before the bill becomes law.
Confirms other uses consistent with a research park and related university purposes, including student housing and a transit hub.
Keeps the terms and conditions of the 1970 letter and earlier approvals in place.
Describes the land as tracts D (minus parcels 1-5), G, and J, conveyed by patent 43-99-0012 dated October 18, 1968.
who: University of Utah, its students and staff
Companies and organizations that lease or operate in the research park
Salt Lake City residents and nearby neighborhoods
Transit users in the area
The Interior Department / Bureau of Land Management

benefits: The bill may reduce legal doubt about whether the land's current and future uses fit the original 1968 federal grant.
The University may have more certainty when planning research park uses, student housing, and a transit hub.
concerns: The bill text does not say what happens if the land is used for something other than the approved purposes.
The bill does not say whether private companies that lease space in the park are covered by its terms.
The bill does not say whether the public gets a say in future changes to the land's use.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state any cost or funding amount. The bill does not provide new land or spend money, according to the summary provided."]
unknowns: It is not stated what would happen if the land were used for something not covered by the bill.
It is not stated whether private tenants in the research park are covered.
It is not stated whether the public would have a role in approving future changes.
It is not stated what specific student housing or transit hub projects are planned.

stage.last_action: Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 717.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to confirm that the University of Utah's use of about 593 acres of federal-granted land in Salt Lake City as a research park, and related university purposes such as student housing and a transit hub, is a valid public purpose under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act. According to the bill summary, this addresses legal doubt about whether the land's current and future uses fit the original 1968 grant. The bill does not provide new land or funding.

oppose: The bill does not say what happens if the land is used for something other than the approved purposes, so it may leave a gap in accountability for future uses.
The bill does not say whether private companies that lease space in the research park are covered, which could extend a public-purpose designation to private tenants without clear limits.
The bill does not give the public a clear role in future changes to how the land is used, so residents may have little say in decisions about this public land.
support: The bill may reduce legal uncertainty about whether the land's current and planned uses fit the original 1968 federal grant, which could help the University plan with more confidence.
The bill names student housing and a transit hub as related university purposes, which could support housing and transportation goals for the campus and nearby community.
The bill does not give out new land or spend federal money, and it keeps the conditions of the 1970 Interior Department approval in place.

crs:
University of Utah Research Park Act
This bill confirms the use by the University of Utah of approximately 593 acres of specified nonfederal land in Salt Lake City, Utah, as a university research park and for related university purposes (including development of student housing and a transit hub) as a valid public purpose.

transparency.reason: The bill settles legal questions about future land uses without requiring public notice, hearings, or disclosure of future changes, and it leaves unclear whether the public gets any say.

people_over_profit.reason: It blesses a research park whose private tenants may be covered, and it does not clearly limit leases or commercial uses that could benefit companies over public purposes.

local_say.reason: It locks in the approved plan and validates later uses without giving Salt Lake City residents or neighbors a formal role in future changes.

news.overall: Both groups have only one headline each, with no descriptions, so the evidence is thin. The Lean Left piece frames data centers as a federal public-lands issue pushed by Democrats, while the Center piece frames it as a Utah state transparency concern. Neither headline mentions the University of Utah Research Park Act directly, so it is unclear from this coverage how either article relates to that bill.
