label: H.R. 3029
title: To amend the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act to support nucleic acid screening, and for other purposes.
short_title: Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act
one: Directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to research and help set voluntary-style best practices and technical standards for screening synthetic DNA/RNA orders to prevent misuse, and to address risks from engineering biology and AI, with $5 million a year authorized for 2027–2031.
summary: This bill updates an existing 2022 science law. It tells NIST, a federal agency that develops measurement standards, to do research that supports better safety checks for companies that make custom DNA and RNA. These materials are used to make medicines and farm products, but they could also be misused to create dangerous biological agents, either on purpose or by accident. The research would cover how to test whether screening actually works, how to keep the databases of "sequences of concern" secure, how to put screening into practice, and how to check that companies follow standards. NIST would also set up a group of industry, universities, nonprofits, and customers to agree on priorities and best practices and to map out future work. Within 18 months of that group's first meeting, NIST must send a report on its findings to the House and Senate science committees. The bill also adds risk-management standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including risks tied to artificial intelligence. It authorizes $5 million each year from 2027 through 2031. "Authorizes" means Congress allows that spending, but a separate vote is needed to actually provide the money. The bill text does not say that the standards are mandatory, and it does not create new penalties.
does: Requires NIST to carry out measurement research supporting best practices and technical standards for biosecurity in nucleic acid synthesis.

Covers testing of screening accuracy and reliability, security of sequence-of-concern databases, technical implementation guidance, conformity assessment (checking that standards are met), and ways to measure effectiveness.

Requires NIST to convene a consortium of industry, universities, nonprofits, and customers to develop and update consensus best practices for screening synthetic nucleic acid orders and to create roadmaps.
Requires a report summarizing the consortium's findings to the Senate Commerce and House Science committees within 18 months of its first meeting.
Adds best practices and standards for risk management in engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including AI-related risks, to NIST's existing duties.
Authorizes $5 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, drawn from NIST's existing research funding authorization.
who: NIST and other federal agencies it consults
Companies that make synthetic DNA/RNA and biotechnology and biomanufacturing firms
University and nonprofit researchers who buy or use synthetic nucleic acids
Customers of synthetic nucleic acid providers
The general public, through biosecurity and public health protection
Congress, which receives the report

benefits: Research and standards could make it easier to detect orders for dangerous biological materials, which may reduce misuse risk.
A shared stakeholder group could help align industry and other groups on common screening practices.
Testing and conformity assessment could give customers and regulators a way to check that providers meet standards.
Risk-management guidance for biomanufacturing and AI-related risks could help organizations plan for new threats.
concerns: The bill does not say the standards will be mandatory, so companies may not be required to adopt them.
With no new penalties, there may be little incentive for companies that ignore the standards.
Keeping databases of sequences of concern secure is a stated goal, but the bill does not describe how this would be done.
Voluntary standards may not cover providers outside the stakeholder group.
imp.cost: ["The bill authorizes $5 million per year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031. Authorization means Congress permits this spending, but a separate appropriations vote is needed to provide the money.", "The material does not state the total cost beyond the authorized amounts."]
unknowns: Whether the standards developed under this bill will become mandatory for providers is not stated.
How the stakeholder group will be selected and how its members will be chosen is not stated.
What specific screening methods or thresholds NIST will recommend is not stated.
Whether Congress will provide the authorized funding is not known.
How this bill would interact with the 2023 AI executive order's ongoing NIST work is not stated.
The bill's current status is listed as in Senate committee; whether it will pass is unknown.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to support better biosecurity for nucleic acid synthesis, the process of designing and creating custom DNA and RNA used in medicines and farm products, which could also be misused to create dangerous biological agents. It directs NIST to conduct measurement research and help develop best practices and technical standards for synthesis screening, and it also adds risk-management standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including AI-related risks.

oppose: The bill does not say the standards will be mandatory, so it is unclear whether companies would be required to follow them at all.
The bill creates no new penalties, so companies that ignore the standards would face no clear consequence under this bill.
The bill says databases of sequences of concern must be kept secure but does not explain how that would be done, which leaves a key safeguard undefined.
Voluntary standards might not reach providers outside the stakeholder group, so some companies could stay outside the system.
The bill authorizes $5 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, paid from NIST's existing research funding, so it would take up part of an existing budget.
support: The bill would have NIST develop measurement research and technical standards that could make it easier to detect orders for dangerous biological materials, which may reduce misuse risk.
A consortium of industry, universities, nonprofits, and customers could agree on shared screening practices, which may help providers apply consistent safety checks.
Testing and conformity assessment could give customers and regulators a practical way to check that providers meet the standards.
The bill adds risk-management guidance for biomanufacturing and AI-related risks, which could help organizations plan for new threats.
The bill requires a report to the Senate Commerce and House Science committees within 18 months of the consortium's first meeting, which gives Congress information to guide future decisions.

cost_flag: The bill authorizes $5 million per year from fiscal years 2027 through 2031. Authorization means Congress permits this spending, but a separate appropriations vote is needed to provide the money. The material does not state the total cost beyond the authorized amounts.
crs:
Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act
This bill explicitly requires the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support the development of best practices and technical standards for nucleic acid synthesis.
Nucleic acids, including deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA), carry genetic information within cells. Nucleic acid synthesis is the process of designing and creating custom nucleic acids; it is used in the development of medications and agricultural products. However, this technology also poses a risk of misuse (e.g., the intentional or unintentional creation of dangerous biological agents).
The bill requires NIST to carry out measurement research to support the development and improvement of biosecurity best practices and technical standards related to nucleic acid synthesis. This effort must address specified topics including nucleic acid synthesis screening, operational security, and conformity assessment. (A 2023 executive order titled 
Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
 directed NIST to develop and refine similar specifications and best practices for use by synthetic nucleic acid providers. NIST's work on this topic is ongoing.)
In carrying out this effort, NIST must convene stakeholders to develop and periodically update consensus priorities and best practices for synthetic nucleic acid screening mechanisms. Within a specified period, NIST must submit a summary of the stakeholder group’s findings to Congress.
NIST must also take steps to advance risk management best practices and technical standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including with respect to risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence.

life.reason: Research and standards for screening synthetic DNA/RNA orders aim to reduce the risk of dangerous biological agents being created, which protects human, animal, and plant life, though the bill is non-mandatory and only funds research and consensus work.

transparency.reason: Requires NIST to convene a multi-stakeholder consortium and submit a findings report to the Senate Commerce and House Science committees, making the standards work more open to congressional oversight.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill sets voluntary consensus best practices and research; it neither clearly favors nor burdens corporate profit margins.

no_bailouts.reason: It authorizes $5 million per year in NIST research funding without creating corporate subsidies or tax breaks.

label: H.R. 3187
title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to convey a parcel of property of the Forest Service to Perry County, Arkansas, and for other purposes.
short_title: Perry County, Arkansas Forest Service Land Conveyance
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to give a roughly 0.81-acre parcel in Perryville, Arkansas, to Perry County for public uses like education and youth development, with the land returning to the federal government if it stops being used that way.
summary: This bill would make the U.S. Forest Service hand over a small piece of land, about 0.81 acres, to Perry County, Arkansas. The land is at 1069 Fourche Avenue in Perryville and includes any buildings on it. The county has to ask for it in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The county would not pay for the land itself, but it would have to pay all the costs of the transfer. That includes a survey, any required environmental review, and any review required by the National Historic Preservation Act. The county must use the land only for public purposes, such as education and youth development. If the county stops using it that way, the land can go back to the United States, but only if the Forest Service chooses to take it back. The land is handed over "as is" through a quitclaim deed, which means the government makes no promises about the title. The Forest Service also would not have to give the usual promise about cleaning up hazardous contamination. Existing rights, such as easements held by others, would stay in place. The House passed the bill on December 15, 2025. It is now on the Senate calendar and has not yet had a Senate vote.
does: Requires the Forest Service to convey about 0.81 acres (parcel 850-10555-001, 1069 Fourche Avenue, Perryville, AR) to Perry County if the county asks in writing within 180 days of enactment.
who: Perry County government and residents of Perryville, Arkansas

benefits: The county could gain a property of about 0.81 acres with buildings for public uses such as education and youth programs.
The Forest Service would no longer need to manage a small parcel that it may not need, and the transfer would be made at no cost to the government for the land itself.
Requiring the county to use the land for public purposes may help keep it in public service.
concerns: Because the transfer is "as is" with no title promises or contamination warranty, the county could face unknown title problems or cleanup needs after the transfer.
The county would bear all transfer costs, which could be significant depending on survey, environmental, and historic review needs; the amounts are not stated.
The reversion right depends on the Forest Service choosing to take the land back, so the enforcement of the public-use requirement is not guaranteed.
The bill does not describe the condition of the buildings or the current use of the property.
imp.cost: ["The county would receive the land without paying for it, but it would have to pay all costs of the conveyance, including a survey, any required environmental analysis or resources survey, and any National Historic Preservation Act review. The bill does not state the amount of these costs or any federal funding. The bill does not give a cost estimate from the Congressional Budget Office."]
unknowns: The bill does not say what the land is currently used for or what condition the buildings are in.
The bill does not say whether the land has any known contamination or existing easements beyond the general statement that valid existing rights stay in place.
The total cost to the county for the survey and reviews is not stated.
It is not stated how the Forest Service would decide whether to use its option to take the land back.
The bill does not say how the land's public purpose would be monitored after the transfer.
The bill is on the Senate calendar and has not had a Senate vote; whether it will pass the Senate is unknown.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 295.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to transfer a small Forest Service parcel of about 0.81 acres (about one acre per the CRS summary), with any buildings on it, to Perry County, Arkansas, so the county can use it for public purposes such as education and youth development. The bill's official title describes it as a conveyance of Forest Service property to the county.

oppose: The bill transfers the land 'as is' by quitclaim deed with no title promises and no warranty about contamination, so the county could inherit unknown title or cleanup problems.
The county would pay all costs of the transfer, including the survey, any environmental review, and any historic preservation review. The bill does not state how much these costs could be.
The bill does not describe the condition of the buildings or the current use of the property, so Congress may lack details needed to judge whether the transfer is appropriate.
The reversion requirement depends on the Forest Service choosing to take the land back if it stops serving public purposes, so enforcement of the public-use condition is not guaranteed.
support: The Forest Service would no longer have to manage a small parcel it may not need, which could reduce federal property responsibilities.
The county would receive a property with buildings that could support public uses such as education and youth programs, at no cost for the land itself.
The bill requires the county to use the land for public purposes and allows the land to revert to the United States if that use stops, which helps keep the property in public service.
The county must request the land in writing within 180 days and pay the transfer costs, so the local government takes on the responsibility of the transfer process.

crs:
This bill directs the Forest Service to convey approximately one acre of land to Perry County, Arkansas, upon the request of the county. The county must use the land for public purposes, such as supporting education and youth development. If it ceases to be used for such purposes, then the property must, at the discretion of the Forest Service, revert to the United States.
The exact acreage of land to be conveyed must be determined by a survey satisfactory to the Forest Service.
The conveyance must be subject to valid existing rights, made without consideration, made by quitclaim deed, and subject to other terms and conditions that the Forest Service considers to be appropriate to protect the interests of the United States.
As a condition of the conveyance, the county must pay costs associated with the conveyance, including the cost of a survey, any environmental analysis or resources survey required under federal law, and any analysis required to comply with the National Historic Preservation Act.
The bill prohibits the Forest Service from having to provide any covenant or warranty for the property and improvements conveyed to the county.

local_say.reason: Perry County gets to request and then hold and use the federal parcel for public purposes such as education and youth development, giving local government more control over that land.

no_bailouts.reason: The county receives the 0.81-acre federal parcel without paying for the land itself, a no-cost federal transfer, though the county pays transfer costs and the value is small.

label: H.R. 331
title: To amend the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to clarify a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes.
one: The bill lets holders of existing water-transport permits on Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land use them, on their own behalf or for a State, Tribe, or public entity, to recharge underground aquifers without a new federal authorization, after giving BLM 30 days' notice.
summary:
Some ditches, canals, and pipelines cross public land run by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). The people or groups who hold permits or rights-of-way for them can already move water across that land to refill underground water supplies, called aquifer recharge, as long as they don't expand or change how the permit is used. This bill widens that rule.

Under the bill, a permit holder could use the existing permit for aquifer recharge for itself or for a State, local government, Indian Tribe, or other public entity. It would not need new approval from the Interior Department. The bill says this use cannot be treated as an expansion, change, or major departure from the permit.

There are limits. The holder must give BLM written notice at least 30 days ahead. The notice must name who will use the permit, identify the permit, describe the plan, and include a copy of the agreement between the holder and the user. The bill also says it does not excuse anyone from federal laws or BLM policies. It also does not authorize building, changing, or expanding any infrastructure.

The CRS summary also mentions an exemption from extra BLM rent for non-profit uses. I could not find that language in the bill text I was given. It may come from the existing law. The summary also says the use would not count as a "major federal action", but the bill text I saw does not use that phrase.
does: Lets holders of existing BLM rights-of-way, easements, permits, or similar authorizations use them for aquifer recharge without new Interior Department authorization.
Allows that use on behalf of the holder or of a State, local government, Indian Tribe, or public entity.
Says such use is not an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation from the existing authorization.
Requires written notice to BLM at least 30 days before the use begins.
Requires the notice to name the user, identify the authorization, describe the intended use and scope, and attach the agreement between the holder and the user.
States that the law does not waive the holder's duty to follow all applicable federal laws and BLM policies.
States that the law gives no authority to build, modify, or expand existing infrastructure.
Makes small wording fixes, changing 'Act' to 'section' in parts of the existing law.
who: Holders of water rights-of-way, ditches, and canals across BLM land, such as irrigation districts and water companies
States, local governments, Indian Tribes, and public water entities that want to recharge aquifers
The Bureau of Land Management and the Interior Department
Farmers, ranchers, and communities in the West that depend on groundwater
People living near affected canals and public lands who may want input on new uses

benefits: Could make it easier for public entities to use existing water infrastructure on BLM land to refill underground water supplies without a new federal approval process.
The 30-day notice and agreement requirement may give BLM a record of who is using each authorization and why.
Keeping federal laws and BLM policies in place may limit how far the change reaches.
concerns: Because the bill says this use is not a major federal action, some people may worry that federal environmental review would not apply to these projects. The bill text provided does not state how NEPA would apply, so this is a possible concern, not a confirmed effect.
Allowing use on behalf of other entities could shift how existing permits are used over time, which some may see as a change in scope despite the bill's wording.
The 30-day notice may give BLM limited time to review or object, depending on how the notice is handled.
imp.cost: ["The bill text provided does not state a cost or funding amount. The CRS summary says holders would not pay additional BLM rent for these uses, except for-profit uses. The CRS summary's rent exemption language was not found in the bill text provided, so its effect on federal revenue cannot be confirmed from the material given."]
unknowns: Whether the rent exemption appears in the bill text or existing law. The source material conflicts on this point.
Whether the 'not a major federal action' wording in the CRS summary appears in the bill text, since the bill text provided does not use that phrase.
How BLM would respond to notices, and whether it could object or set conditions.
How the for-profit limit would be applied in practice.
How much water could be moved, and what effects this could have on land, wildlife, or other water users.
The bill's current status: it is in Senate committee, which is the second chamber.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify and expand the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act so that holders of existing BLM rights-of-way and similar authorizations can move water across public land to refill underground aquifers, including on behalf of states, Indian Tribes, or public entities, without getting new approval from the Department of the Interior.

oppose: The bill says this use is not an expansion, modification, major federal action, or substantial deviation. A constituent could ask the Congressman how this affects federal environmental review under NEPA, since the bill text does not explain it.

The bill lets permit holders act for states, Tribes, or other public entities without new federal approval. A constituent could ask how BLM would track changes in who uses each permit and whether the 30-day notice gives BLM enough time to review or object.

The bill allows use of existing infrastructure for aquifer recharge but does not authorize building or expanding it. A constituent could ask how the Congressman would make sure existing permits are not used in ways that change their original scope over time.
support: The bill would let existing ditches, canals, and pipelines on BLM land be used to refill underground water supplies without a new federal approval process. A constituent could say this helps communities use infrastructure already in place.

The bill requires holders to give BLM written notice at least 30 days ahead, naming the user, the permit, the plan, and the agreement between the parties. A constituent could say this gives BLM a record of how each permit is used.
The bill says it does not waive federal laws or BLM policies and does not authorize new construction. A constituent could say these limits keep the change narrow and in line with existing rules.

crs:
This bill modifies the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to expand provisions concerning authorizations (e.g., rights-of-way) to transport water across public land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for aquifer recharge purposes.
Under the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, the holder of existing rights-of-way, easements, permits, or other authorizations to transport water across BLM land may transport the water for aquifer recharge purposes without additional authorization from the Department of the Interior so long as the use does not expand or modify the operation of such authorizations across public land.
The bill allows the holders of such authorizations to act not only on behalf of themselves, but also on behalf of states, Indian Tribes, or public entities, to use the existing authorizations for aquifer recharge without additional authorization from the Department of the Interior. Further, the bill states that this use may not be considered an expansion, modification, major federal action, or substantial deviation.
Additionally, the bill exempts holders from paying additional rents to the BLM for any use of such authorizations; however, the exemption does not apply to for-profit uses of aquifer recharge or for-profit entities. 
Finally, holders of rights-of-way or other authorizations must provide notice to the BLM of the intended use of authorization as specified by the bill.

life.reason: Refilling aquifers can help sustain groundwater that supports people, animals, and plants in dry Western areas.

water.reason: Expanding aquifer recharge helps replenish groundwater supplies, though the bill does not set water quality standards.

local_say.reason: Permit holders can start new recharge uses for States, Tribes, or other entities without new Interior review, and the notice requirement does not give the public a chance to comment or object.

label: H.R. 3410
title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
one: Directs the FAA to change its rules so civil aircraft can fly faster than the speed of sound over U.S. land without special permission, as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground, and to set takeoff and landing noise limits for those aircraft.
summary: Right now, FAA rules ban civil (non-military) aircraft from flying faster than the speed of sound, called Mach 1, over U.S. land unless the FAA gives a special authorization. This bill would order the FAA to rewrite that rule within one year of the bill becoming law. Under the new rule, a civil aircraft could fly faster than Mach 1 in U.S. airspace with no special permission, as long as it is flown so that no sonic boom reaches the ground. The bill also requires the FAA to finish a rule by April 1, 2027, saying these aircraft cannot be louder at takeoff and landing than the most recent noise levels required for current subsonic (slower than sound) aircraft. The FAA must also set up a process to review and update those noise limits over time as quieter technology and related rules change. The bill does not mention fuel use, air pollution, climate effects, or public hearings. It also does not say how the "no boom reaches the ground" condition would be tested or enforced, and it doesn't give local governments or residents any role. The bill does not create new spending or subsidies. It passed the House on March 24, 2026, and is now in the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
does: Orders the FAA to issue or revise rules within 1 year of enactment so civil aircraft may fly above Mach 1 without special authorization.
Limits that permission to flights operated so that no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
Requires a final FAA noise rule by April 1, 2027, capping takeoff and landing noise at the most recent levels required for current subsonic aircraft.
Requires the FAA to set a process for periodically reviewing and updating the noise rule as technology and regulations change, as the FAA Administrator decides.
Points to the current rule (14 CFR 91.817) as an example of a regulation to change; today it bans such flights over land without special authorization.
who: Aerospace companies developing supersonic civil aircraft
Airlines and business-jet operators and their (likely high-paying) passengers
The FAA, which must write and enforce new rules on tight deadlines
People living under flight paths or near airports, who could experience noise
Wildlife and the general public, if emissions or noise change

benefits: Could allow faster civil air travel over U.S. land without case-by-case FAA authorization, which may reduce paperwork for supersonic aircraft makers and operators.
Setting noise limits tied to subsonic standards could mean supersonic aircraft are no louder at takeoff and landing than slower jets.
A required review process could let noise limits keep up with quieter technology over time.
concerns: The bill does not say how the 'no sonic boom reaches the ground' condition would be tested or enforced, so it is unclear whether the rule would hold up in practice.
Because the bill gives no role to local governments or residents and does not require public hearings, communities may have little say in how the rules are applied.
The bill does not address fuel use, air pollution, or climate effects, so these possible impacts are not covered.
Noise limits are set only for takeoff and landing; the bill does not address noise from flight over land at supersonic speeds beyond the sonic boom condition.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not create new spending or subsidies. The material does not state what the FAA would cost to carry out the rulemaking, reviews, or enforcement."]
unknowns: It is not stated how the FAA would measure or enforce the requirement that no sonic boom reaches the ground.
It is not stated whether the FAA's rule would set specific decibel or noise numbers beyond pointing to subsonic standards.
The material does not say what effects on fuel use, air quality, or climate could follow from more supersonic flight.
The material does not say whether the Senate will take up the bill or whether it will change.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to modernize U.S. aviation rules so civil aircraft can operate faster than Mach 1 over U.S. land without a special FAA authorization, provided no sonic boom reaches the ground. It also aims to set takeoff and landing noise limits for these aircraft, tied to the noise levels required for current subsonic aircraft, with a process to update those limits over time.

oppose: The bill does not explain how the 'no sonic boom reaches the ground' condition would be tested or enforced, so it is unclear whether the limit would work in practice.
The bill gives local governments and residents no formal role and does not require public hearings, so communities may have little say in how the new rules are applied.
The bill does not address fuel use, air pollution, or climate effects of faster civil flights, so these possible impacts would not be covered by the bill.
support: The bill would remove the requirement for case-by-case FAA special authorization for supersonic civil flights over U.S. land, which could reduce paperwork for aircraft makers and operators.

The bill requires noise limits for takeoff and landing that match the most recent levels required for current subsonic aircraft, so supersonic aircraft would be no louder at those times than slower jets.
The bill requires the FAA to set a process for periodically reviewing and updating the noise rules, so limits could keep pace with quieter aircraft technology over time.

crs:
Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to operate at speeds above Mach 1 (i.e., supersonic) over land in the United States under certain conditions. 
Specifically, the FAA must issue or revise regulations to allow for the operation of civil aircraft at speeds greater than Mach 1 in the national airspace system without a special authorization, so long as no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
The FAA must also issue a final rule to establish noise standards that prohibit civil aircraft operating at speeds greater than Mach 1 from exceeding takeoff and landing noise levels required for subsonic aircraft (i.e., aircraft that operate at speeds that do not exceed Mach 1). As part of the rule, the FAA must specify a process to periodically review and update the noise standards to reflect future advances in aircraft noise reduction technology and regulatory changes.
Current regulations prohibit civil aircraft from operating above Mach 1 speeds over land in the United States without a special flight authorization issued by the FAA.

life.reason: Allowing supersonic flight over land could increase noise exposure and wildlife disturbance, though the no-boom condition and takeoff/landing noise cap offset part of that risk.

air.reason: Supersonic flight is typically more fuel-intensive and emissions-heavy, and the bill is silent on emissions, so it likely works against clean air.

transparency.reason: The bill removes the FAA case-by-case authorization process and provides no public hearings, and it does not say how the no-boom condition would be tested or enforced.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly benefits aerospace companies and high-paying premium travelers by removing a permission requirement, while residents bear the noise risk.

local_say.reason: It removes the special authorization step and gives local governments and residents no role in decisions affecting their area.

label: H.R. 4922
title: D. C. Criminal Reforms to Immediately Make Everyone Safe Act of 2025
one: The bill would treat DC residents aged 18 to 24 as adults instead of "youth offenders," end judges' power to go below mandatory minimum sentences for youth offenders, bar DC's local government from changing existing criminal sentences, and require a public website of juvenile crime data.
summary:
This bill changes how criminal sentencing works in Washington, DC. Today, DC's Youth Rehabilitation Act lets judges treat people up to age 24 as "youth offenders." That can mean lighter or different sentences, such as probation instead of jail. The bill would cut that age limit so only people under 18 qualify. It would also remove a rule that lets judges give a youth offender a sentence below a mandatory minimum.

The bill's title and the CRS summary say it would also block the DC Council and other DC authorities from changing any criminal sentence that is in effect when the bill becomes law. The bill text provided to me does not include a section doing this, so I could not check its exact wording.

Finally, the bill would make the DC Attorney General build a public website within 180 days. It would show juvenile arrest and prosecution data, such as age, race, sex, type of crime, repeat arrests, cases declined, and sentence lengths. It would be updated monthly, kept as an archive, and offered in downloadable machine-readable form. It could not show any juvenile's personal information. Courts and police would have to share juvenile records with the Attorney General for this purpose. The bill passed the House on September 16, 2025, and is now in the Senate.
does: unused
who: People aged 18 to 24 charged with crimes in DC
DC judges, prosecutors, and defense lawyers
DC Council and DC residents, who vote for local lawmakers but lack full congressional representation
DC Attorney General's office, which must build and run the website
Crime victims and DC communities
Researchers, journalists, and the public who would use the data

benefits: The website could give the public clear, regularly updated, downloadable data on juvenile crime and how cases are handled.
Data broken down by age, race, and sex could help people spot patterns and unfairness.
Supporters say firmer sentences and mandatory minimums may deter crime and improve public safety.
The bill bars personal information about juveniles from the site.
concerns: It would limit the elected DC government's power over its own criminal sentencing laws, which cuts against local self-government.
Treating 18- to 24-year-olds as adults could mean harsher sentences for young people who may otherwise be rehabilitated.
Removing judges' discretion below mandatory minimums limits case-by-case decisions.
Congress would override local choices for DC residents who have no voting member of Congress.
The website definition of 'juvenile' ties to 'youth offender,' which would now cover only under-18s. That could make the data narrower than expected.
Requiring agencies to share sealed juvenile records raises privacy questions, even though names and personal details must be left off.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding was provided in the material I saw. The bill does not appear to give money for the website, so the DC Attorney General's office would probably pay from its existing budget. Longer sentences could raise corrections costs.
unknowns: The Home Rule Act section described in the title and CRS summary is not in the text I was given, so its exact wording and reach are unclear.
The text has a cross-reference mismatch: it adds section 16-2340a but the effective-date clause cites 16-2341. This looks like a drafting error.
The bill text says 'under 18' while the title says '18 or younger.'
It is unclear how many people would be affected or what would happen to current sentences.
It is unclear how the Senate will act.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to limit the District of Columbia government's authority over its criminal sentencing laws, and to narrow who qualifies as a "youth offender" under DC law (from under 24 to under 18). It also aims to make juvenile crime and case data publicly available through a regularly updated website. The bill's official title and the CRS summary describe these aims; the stated reasons for them come from the bill's own title and summary, not from the sponsor's private motives.

oppose: The bill would take away the DC government's power to change criminal sentences that are already in effect, which many residents see as a limit on local self-government.

Lowering the youth offender age from 24 to 18 would mean 18- to 24-year-olds could no longer get the youth sentencing options judges now have, such as probation instead of confinement. Critics say this could lead to harsher outcomes for young adults who could still be rehabilitated.
Removing judges' power to sentence a youth offender below a mandatory minimum takes away case-by-case discretion, which critics say can lead to rigid results in individual cases.
Requiring courts and police to share sealed juvenile records with the Attorney General raises privacy concerns, even though the bill bars names and personal details from the public website.
support: The bill would give the public regularly updated, downloadable data on juvenile arrests and prosecutions, including age, race, sex, type of crime, repeat arrests, declined cases, and sentence lengths, which could help residents see how cases are handled.
Supporters say firmer sentences and mandatory minimums may deter crime and improve public safety, and that narrowing youth protections to under-18s sets a clearer line for the justice system.
Supporters say the bill protects privacy by barring personal information about juveniles from the public website, while still giving the public useful aggregate information.
Supporters say that when a city's laws affect the whole country, including the federal capital, Congress has a role in setting certain sentencing rules for DC.

crs:
DC Criminal Reforms to Immediately Make Everyone Safe Act or the DC CRIMES Act
This bill limits the authority of the District of Columbia (DC) government over its criminal sentencing laws. 
The bill eliminates the DC government’s authority to enact any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of the bill's enactment.
The bill also (1) reduces the maximum age of a youth offender from 24 years to 18 years, and (2) repeals a provision that allows a DC criminal court to issue a sentence to a youth offender that is less than the mandatory minimum term otherwise required by law. A DC criminal court currently has the discretion to reduce or modify certain criminal sentences for a youth offender under specified circumstances. For example, a DC court may sentence a youth offender to probation in lieu of confinement. (However, this discretion does not apply to several specified violent crimes.) 
Additionally, the bill directs the Office of the Attorney General for DC to publish, and update monthly, certain youth offender crime data on a publicly accessible website.

transparency.reason: The bill requires the DC Attorney General to publish monthly, downloadable juvenile crime and case-handling data, giving the public more visibility into how youth cases are handled.

local_say.reason: It strips the DC Council and other DC authorities of power to change criminal sentences in effect when the bill becomes law and narrows local sentencing options for young adults, overriding residents' elected lawmakers.

honesty_kindness.reason: Removing youth-offender treatment for 18- to 24-year-olds and barring judges from going below mandatory minimums for young offenders points toward harsher, less individualized treatment of people who may be rehabilitated.

votes.question: On Passage

news.overall: Only one thin item was supplied, from a Lean Right outlet (Reason), and it concerns a PBS documentary on criminal justice history rather than the D.C. bill. No comparison across perspectives is possible from this evidence. Additional coverage from other perspectives and article descriptions would be needed to describe how the bill is framed.

label: H.R. 5549
title: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
one: The bill would let the Nuclear Regulatory Commission skip its end-of-process public hearing for nuclear power plant permits and licenses, and for uranium enrichment facility licenses, when no affected person asks for one.
summary:
Today, the Atomic Energy Act requires the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold a public hearing before it issues certain permits and licenses for nuclear power plants. This bill changes that. If no one whose interests may be affected asks for a hearing, the NRC could issue a construction permit, operating license, combined permit and license, or an amendment to one of these without holding a hearing. It would still have to give 30 days' notice in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice publication. For some amendments that pose no significant safety hazard, even that notice could be skipped, which the law already allows.

If a hearing is held, the NRC would have to use informal hearing procedures. These are usually simpler and less court-like than formal ones.

The bill also changes licensing of uranium enrichment facilities, which make nuclear reactor fuel. The NRC would hold a hearing only if an affected person requests one. It would also no longer have to hold that hearing "on the record," which is a formal, court-style process.

The changes would apply to applications already pending at the NRC when the bill becomes law. I could not see the full text of the old law that is being struck, so this summary relies on the bill's wording and the CRS summary.
does: Lets the NRC issue nuclear plant construction permits, operating licenses, combined licenses, and amendments without a hearing if no affected person requests one.
Requires 30 days' notice in the Federal Register before issuing a license without a hearing.
Keeps the NRC's ability to skip the 30-day notice for amendments that involve no significant hazards consideration.
Requires informal adjudicatory (less formal, less court-like) procedures for any hearing the NRC holds under this provision.
Changes the hearing rules in the existing law so they refer to informal procedures, and removes the "formal or informal" wording.
Makes hearings for uranium enrichment facility licenses happen only if an affected person asks, and removes the "on the record" requirement.
Applies the changes to all applications and proceedings pending at the NRC on or after the date the bill becomes law.
who: Nuclear power plant and enrichment facility applicants, who could get faster decisions
Residents and communities near proposed or existing nuclear and uranium enrichment sites
Environmental, safety, and watchdog groups that take part in NRC proceedings
The NRC and its staff
Electricity customers and the nuclear industry

benefits: Could speed up licensing for uncontested nuclear projects by skipping hearings no one asked for.
Could reduce NRC workload and time spent on routine or uncontested applications.
Informal hearing procedures, if used, may be simpler and less costly to run.
concerns: Members of the public may not know a licensing action is happening if they miss the Federal Register notice or if the notice is skipped for some amendments.
Requiring a request before a hearing can be held may make it harder for people to take part if they are unaware of their rights or deadlines.
Informal procedures may give affected parties fewer tools to examine evidence than formal, court-style hearings.
Dropping the "on the record" requirement for uranium enrichment facilities could change how evidence is gathered and reviewed in those cases.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state any cost, funding amount, or budget effect for the bill."]
unknowns: The full text of the existing law being changed was not available, so the exact wording being struck is not confirmed.
It is not stated how the NRC would define "affected person" or what the request process would look like.
It is not stated how much time or money the change would save the NRC or applicants.
It is not stated whether the informal procedures would differ in practice from current hearing procedures in a significant way.
The effect on safety review outcomes is not addressed in the material provided.
The bill is in the Senate committee stage, so the final wording could change.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make the NRC's licensing process for certain nuclear plant permits and licenses more efficient, as its title suggests. It addresses the requirement to hold a public hearing on uncontested applications, even when no one has asked for one. The bill aims to let the NRC issue these permits and licenses without a hearing when no affected person requests one, and to use simpler informal procedures when a hearing is held.

oppose: The bill would let the NRC issue nuclear plant construction permits and operating licenses without a hearing if no affected person requests one. Some people may not know a licensing action is happening or may miss the deadline to ask for a hearing.
For some amendments that involve no significant hazards consideration, the 30-day Federal Register notice could be skipped, so the public could get less advance warning of licensing decisions.
The bill would require informal, less court-like procedures for any hearing held, which may give affected people fewer tools to examine evidence than formal hearings do.
For uranium enrichment facilities, the bill removes the "on the record" requirement, which could change how evidence is gathered and reviewed in those cases.
stated_purpose_placeholder
support: The bill says its goal is to speed up licensing for projects no one has challenged, by skipping hearings that no affected person has asked for.
Because the NRC would not have to hold hearings nobody requested, it could reduce agency workload and time spent on routine or uncontested applications.
The bill still requires 30 days' notice in the Federal Register before a license is issued without a hearing, so the public would still be told about these decisions.
When a hearing is held, informal procedures are usually simpler and may cost less to run, which could make the process more efficient for everyone involved.

crs:
Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
This bill expedites the process of reviewing certain uncontested permits and licenses for nuclear power plants (e.g., construction permits and operating licenses) by removing a requirement for the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold a public hearing at the end of the process. The bill applies to the licenses and permits if a hearing has not been requested by a person whose interest may be affected. The bill also directs the NRC to use informal adjudicatory procedures if such a hearing is held.
Additionally, the bill directs the NRC to hold an adjudicatory hearing regarding the licensing of the construction and operation of a uranium enrichment facility only if the person whose interest may be affected by such construction and operation has requested the hearing.

life.reason: Removing mandatory public hearings for uncontested nuclear plant and enrichment licenses and switching to informal procedures could reduce scrutiny of safety reviews, slightly raising risk to life.

air.reason: The bill does not change emissions or air quality standards, so its effect on clean air is unclear.

transparency.reason: Eliminating mandatory public hearings, shifting to less formal procedures, and dropping the on-the-record requirement for enrichment licensing reduces public visibility into NRC decisions, though 30-day Federal Register notice is kept.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill speeds licensing for applicants and reduces procedural steps that could slow or challenge projects, favoring industry timelines over public review.

local_say.reason: Communities near proposed plants or enrichment sites lose the default right to a hearing unless they affirmatively request one, and hearings that are held become less formal.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide subsidies, bailouts, or ratepayer-funded tax breaks.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not directly address honesty or kindness in government or business conduct.

label: H.R. 5729
title: North Rim Restoration Act
one: The bill lets the National Park Service use fast-track emergency contracting to rebuild and restore the Grand Canyon North Rim after the Dragon Bravo Fire, and lets it hand some rebuilding contracts to the current North Rim concessioner without competitive bidding.
summary:
The Dragon Bravo Fire damaged parts of Grand Canyon National Park's North Rim. This bill would make it faster for the National Park Service (NPS) to hire contractors for the cleanup and rebuilding. It has two main parts.

First, it lets NPS use emergency buying rules, such as higher spending limits before full bidding rules apply, without waiting for a presidential disaster declaration. This covers forest restoration, rebuilding and designing damaged structures, improving grounds and buildings, and other recovery work in the burned area. The authority ends after 7 years or when the work is done, whichever comes first. If a new wildfire hits the area, NPS can ask Congress for a 12-month extension.

Second, it lets NPS sign contracts without competitive bidding for rebuilding or running things like employee housing, water and power systems, lodging, food service, and shops on the North Rim. NPS may do this only if it decides in writing that the current North Rim concessioner (the private company that runs visitor services there) is uniquely positioned to do the work and that skipping competition is needed for safety, resource protection, or continuity of services. These contracts cannot extend the company's existing concession contract or give it ownership-type rights. NPS may still choose to use competition.

NPS must also send Congress a report every 180 days on costs, overruns, contractors, conflicts of interest, and any waste, fraud, or abuse.
does: Allows NPS to use emergency acquisition rules (48 CFR part 18) in the burned area of Grand Canyon National Park without a presidential emergency or disaster declaration.
Covers forest restoration, rebuilding and design of fire-damaged structures, improvements to grounds and structures, and recovery work.

Lets NPS award noncompetitive (sole-source) contracts for North Rim assets such as employee housing, water, wastewater, power and communications systems, lodging, food service, retail, and transportation.
Requires a written finding by the Secretary that the current concessioner is uniquely positioned and that skipping competition is needed for safety, resource protection, or essential services.

Says these contracts do not change, extend, or add benefits (such as leasehold surrender interest) to the existing concession contract, and do not allow a concession contract to be awarded without following concession law.
Lets the Secretary still use competitive procedures if that is in the government's best interest.

Requires reports every 180 days to four congressional committees on expected cost, spending, overruns, contractors, conflicts of interest, waste, fraud, abuse, under-budget contracts, and completion timeline.

Ends both authorities after 7 years; the emergency authority ends sooner if recovery is finished. A 12-month extension can be requested if a new wildfire interferes, subject to congressional approval.
who: National Park Service and Grand Canyon National Park staff
The private company that currently holds the North Rim concession contract
Other contractors who might have bid on the work but could be shut out of sole-source contracts
Park visitors and people who depend on North Rim tourism, including nearby communities
North Rim employees who may rely on employee housing and facilities
Federal taxpayers who would pay for contracts
Congressional committees receiving the reports

benefits: Faster contracting could speed up forest restoration and rebuilding after the Dragon Bravo Fire.
Using the current concessioner may keep services running and reduce delays in reopening the North Rim.
Required 180-day reports could give Congress regular information to track spending and spot problems.
Time limits and bans on extending concession rights may limit how long the special rules last.
concerns: Skipping competitive bidding could possibly lead to higher costs or weaker contract terms, since fewer companies may compete.
Giving one concessioner first access to contracts could reduce fair competition and raise questions about favoritism.
The bill relies on NPS written determinations, and the bill text does not say how outside review of those decisions would work.
Emergency rules without a disaster declaration may reduce some normal checks on spending.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state the bill's cost or how much funding it would authorize. It also does not say where money would come from."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much the recovery work or noncompetitive contracts would cost.
It is not stated how much work would be done under the noncompetitive authority or which specific contracts would be used.
The material does not explain what standards NPS must use to decide whether the concessioner is 'uniquely positioned.'
It is unclear whether the 180-day reports would be public or how Congress would act on them.
The bill's effect on other North Rim concession arrangements after the seven-year period is not described.
The bill is in the Senate committee stage, so its final form and whether it will pass are not known.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help the National Park Service restore forests, rebuild structures, and reopen the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park after the Dragon Bravo Fire. It would do this by letting the Park Service use emergency contracting rules in the burned area without a presidential disaster declaration, and by allowing some noncompetitive contracts for North Rim visitor assets, subject to written determinations and congressional reporting.

oppose: Skipping competitive bidding for North Rim contracts could mean fewer companies compete, which may raise costs or weaken contract terms for taxpayers.
Giving the current North Rim concessioner first access to contracts could reduce fair competition and raise questions about favoritism toward one company.
The bill relies on the Park Service's own written determinations that skipping competition is needed, and the bill text does not explain how outside review of those decisions would work.
Using emergency buying rules without a presidential disaster declaration may reduce some normal spending checks, and I would like to see strong oversight kept in place.
support: Faster contracting could speed up forest restoration and rebuilding after the Dragon Bravo Fire, helping the North Rim reopen sooner.
Using the current concessioner could keep visitor services such as lodging, water, and power running and reduce delays for workers and visitors who depend on the North Rim.
The bill requires reports to Congress every 180 days on costs, overruns, contractors, conflicts of interest, and waste, fraud, or abuse, which gives lawmakers regular information to track spending.
The authorities end after seven years or when the recovery work is finished, and the bill does not allow the concessioner's existing contract to be extended or given ownership-type rights.

crs:
North Rim Restoration Act
This bill allows the National Park Service (NPS) to expedite the approval of contracts to restore forests, structures, and assets within areas of the Grand Canyon National Park impacted by the Dragon Bravo Fire in Arizona.
Specifically, the bill authorizes the NPS to use emergency acquisition flexibilities without a presidential emergency or disaster declaration to contract for the following services in such impacted areas: managing or restoring forests, rebuilding structures affected by the fire, improving grounds and structures, conducting recovery efforts, or other specified activities.
This authority expires on the date that is the earlier of the following: (1) seven years after the date of this bill's enactment, or (2) the date on which projects and recovery efforts within such area are completed. The NPS may request Congress extend such authority for 12 months if a new wildfire ignites within such area and impacts recovery efforts related to the Dragon Bravo Fire.
The bill also authorizes the NPS to enter into noncompetitive procurement contracts for rebuilding, rehabilitating, replacing, or operating assets, such as lodging or utilities, to support the recovery and reopening of the Grand Canyon National Park North Rim. This authority is conditioned upon the NPS making certain determinations regarding the North Rim concessioner and it terminates seven years after this bill's enactment.

life.reason: Faster fire-recovery work on forests, water and power systems, and fire-damaged structures could help restore habitat and protect people and infrastructure sooner.

water.reason: The bill mentions water systems among rebuildable assets, but it does not meaningfully change water quality or water protection rules.

air.reason: The bill does not address air quality or emissions.

transparency.reason: Sole-source contracts and emergency buying rules are awarded with less public competition, though the 180-day reports to Congress partly offset this.

people_over_profit.reason: Noncompetitive contracts to the incumbent concessioner can reduce price competition and favor that company's profits over taxpayer and other-bidder interests, though the bill bars extending its concession contract and requires findings.

local_say.reason: The bill does not change how local residents or communities participate in decisions about the North Rim, though it reduces competitive input from outside contractors.

no_bailouts.reason: Federal taxpayers would fund sole-source work that benefits one private concessioner, which resembles a special financial advantage to a single company, though it is not a classic bailout.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill requires reports on overruns, conflicts of interest, waste, fraud, and abuse, and it includes safeguards against the concessioner gaining ownership-type rights.

label: H.R. 617
title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
one: Directs the Commerce Department's tourism office to identify and promote music-related places and events (and sports events for international visitors) and to report to Congress every two years.
summary:
This bill changes an existing law called the Visit America Act. It tells the Commerce Department's top tourism official (the Assistant Secretary for Travel and Tourism) to find places and events in the U.S. that matter to music tourism and to promote travel to them. That covers music museums, studios, venues of all sizes, festivals, concerts, and other live music events. The bill asks for both domestic promotion (Americans traveling within the U.S.) and international promotion (foreign visitors coming here).

The bill also rewrites the section on international business and leisure travel. It keeps the focus on large meetings and conferences and on rural and other destinations rich in cultural heritage or ecological tourism. It adds a duty to promote international travel to sports and recreation events.

Finally, the tourism official must send Congress a report one year after the bill becomes law, then every two years. The report covers activities, findings, achievements, and "vulnerabilities" tied to the tourism goals. The reports go to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The bill adds a definition of "music tourism." It does not give a dollar amount, create new grants, or set new rules for businesses. It passed the House on April 28, 2025, and is waiting on the Senate calendar.
does: Requires the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism to identify U.S. places and events important to music tourism and promote domestic travel to them.
who: Commerce Department's National Travel and Tourism Office staff

benefits: Music-related sites and events could gain more visibility, which may help draw visitors to local music scenes.
Promoting both domestic and international travel may help spread tourism spending across different regions.
Regular reports to Congress could give lawmakers information on what the tourism office is doing and what is working.
The reports' focus on "vulnerabilities" may help identify problems that could slow tourism goals.
concerns: The bill does not set clear measures for success, so it is unclear how the promotion would be judged.
Choosing which music places and events to promote could favor some locations or businesses over others.
Adding new duties without new funding could strain an office that already has limited resources, though the bill does not say how much work it would require.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not give a dollar amount, does not create new grants, and does not state how the new duties would be funded. The cost is not stated in the material provided."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much money the tourism office would spend on music or sports promotion.
It is not stated how "vulnerabilities" would be defined or what the reports would have to include beyond the listed topics.
It is not stated whether the bill would change how the tourism office works with private music or sports groups.
The bill does not set new rules for businesses, so its effects would depend on how the tourism office carries out its promotion work.
The Senate has not acted on the bill yet, so it could change before becoming law. The bill passed the House on April 28, 2025, and its latest action is in Senate committee.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 59.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to promote tourism to U.S. music-related attractions and events, such as music festivals, concert venues, and other live music sites, and to expand the Commerce Department's existing duty to promote sports and recreation tourism to include international visitors. It also requires the Commerce Department's tourism office to report its activities and findings to Congress within one year of enactment and every two years after that.

oppose: The bill adds new promotion duties for the Commerce Department's tourism office but does not provide new funding, so it could strain an office that already has limited resources.
The bill does not set clear measures for success, so it may be hard to judge whether the promotion efforts work or are worth the cost.
Choosing which music venues and events to promote could favor some places or businesses over others, and the government may be picking winners in a private market.
support: The bill would direct federal tourism promotion toward music festivals, concert venues, and other live music sites, which could draw visitors to local music scenes across the country.
The bill covers both domestic travel by Americans and international travel by foreign visitors, which may help spread tourism spending to more regions.
The bill requires regular reports to Congress every two years, which would give lawmakers information on what the tourism office is doing, what is working, and what problems may slow progress.

crs:
American Music Tourism Act of 2025
This bill directs the National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO) of the Department of Commerce to promote tourism to music-related and sports attractions.
The bill requires NTTO to promote domestic and international travel and tourism to U.S. music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related attractions and locations. The bill also expands NTTO's current mandate to facilitate sports and recreation events and activities to include the promotion of international travel and tourism to such activities in the United States.
NTTO must report its activities and findings to Congress within one year after the bill's enactment and, thereafter, every two years.

transparency.reason: It requires the Commerce tourism office to report its activities, findings, achievements, and vulnerabilities to Congress one year after enactment and every two years after that.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill provides no dollar amounts, grants, or tax breaks.

label: H.R. 6329
title: Information Quality Assurance Act of 2025
one: Requires the White House budget office and federal agencies to update their information-quality rules so agencies use the best available evidence for major rules and guidance, and publish the key facts they relied on and let the public comment on them.
summary: This bill changes federal law so agencies have to show their work when they write rules and guidance. Within one year of becoming law, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which oversees how federal agencies operate, must update its existing information-quality guidelines. These cover "influential" information, meaning data an agency reasonably decides will have a clear and substantial impact on important public actions, policies, statements, or private-sector decisions. Agencies then have one year to update their own guidelines so they rely on the "best reasonably available" evidence that fits the purpose. The bill also tells OMB to direct agencies to put the critical facts they relied on into the public docket (the rule's file) or administrative record, along with citations to other sources. When an agency takes public comments on a rule or guidance, it must also let the public comment on those critical facts, and it must post any major later changes to them. Agencies can withhold material if a law bars release, and must then explain why and what they're doing to widen access. Agencies must follow the rules only "to the maximum extent feasible" considering cost. Existing ways to ask an agency to correct bad information stay available. The bill authorizes no new money.
does: see items
who: Federal agencies that write rules and guidance
Office of Management and Budget
Members of the public, researchers, and advocacy groups who comment on rules
Businesses and industries affected by federal rules
Communities affected by environmental, health, and safety regulation

benefits: Agencies may be required to show the key facts behind rules and guidance, which could make their reasoning easier to check.
The public may get a chance to comment on the critical facts, not just the final rule, which could improve transparency.
Posting major later changes to those facts could help people track how an agency's evidence shifts over time.
Existing correction processes remain available, so people still have a way to challenge inaccurate information.

The "to the maximum extent feasible" standard and cost consideration may leave room for agencies to apply the rules unevenly.
The bill does not define "best reasonably available" evidence in detail, so agencies may interpret it differently.
Withholding material under legal bars could limit public access to some facts, even with required explanations.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make federal agencies show the key facts behind the rules and guidance they write. It requires agencies to rely on the best reasonably available influential information, publish the critical factual material they used, and give the public a chance to comment on that material. The bill's findings and summary describe these steps as a way to improve the quality and openness of federal information.

oppose: The bill adds steps to rulemaking and guidance, such as public comment on critical facts and posting later changes. Opponents may say this could slow down agencies that need to act quickly on health, safety, or other urgent matters.

The phrase "to the maximum extent feasible," along with cost considerations, gives agencies room to decide how much to follow the rules. Opponents may worry this could lead to uneven application across agencies.

The term "best reasonably available" evidence is not defined in detail in the bill. Opponents may say agencies could interpret it differently, which could create uncertainty for the public and for businesses.
support: The bill requires agencies to publish the critical facts they relied on and cite other sources. Supporters may say this makes agency reasoning easier for the public and courts to check.
The public would get a chance to comment on the key facts behind a rule, not only on the final rule. Supporters may say this could improve transparency and lead to better decisions.
Posting major later changes to those facts would let people track how an agency's evidence shifts over time. Existing ways to ask an agency to correct inaccurate information would remain available.

Information Quality Assurance Act of 2025
This bill requires the Office of Management and Budget to revise the guidelines for federal agencies with respect to the dissemination or use of 
influential information or evidence
, which means information or evidence about which an agency can reasonably determine that reliance on or dissemination of has, or will have, a clear and substantial impact on important public actions, policies or statements, or on important private sector decisions.
The guidelines must ensure that federal agencies rely on the best reasonably available influential information and evidence that is appropriate for the purpose when developing, issuing, or informing the public about the rules and guidance of the agency.
An agency also must publish (1) the critical factual material relied on as part of the rulemaking or guidance development process, and (2) a citation to any other source used to inform the rulemaking or guidance development process.
The guidelines must also require an agency to provide certain opportunities for the public to comment on the critical factual material upon which the agency relied.

transparency.reason: It requires agencies to publish the critical factual material and sources behind influential rules and guidance, and to let the public comment on that material and post major later changes.

local_say.reason: The public gets a formal chance to comment on the critical facts underlying rules that affect their communities, though this is a procedural right rather than a new decision-making power.

honesty_kindness.reason: Requiring agencies to rely on the best reasonably available evidence and to disclose their sources promotes honest justification of government decisions.
