label: H.R. 7567
title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
short_title: Farm Bill 2026 (Farm, Food, and National Security Act)
one: A very large five-year farm bill that renews and changes USDA programs for crop support, conservation, trade and food aid, SNAP and other nutrition, farm credit, rural development, research, forestry, energy, and more, with a mix of conservation, water and nutrition gains and some reduced environmental or public-review safeguards.
summary:
This is the 2026 farm bill, a huge package that renews most Department of Agriculture programs through fiscal year 2031. I could see the digest for about nine of eleven parts. It stops partway through Section 10211, so the later pesticide, crop insurance, horticulture, livestock, and foreign farmland ownership parts named in the CRS summary are not covered here.

Commodities (Title I): It keeps the suspension of old permanent price-support law through 2031. It rebuilds tree disaster aid, creates a framework for direct payments to specialty crop growers hit by a market crisis, and lets disaster aid be given as block grants. It extends dairy programs and adds dairy cost reporting, covers propane storage loans, restores tobacco as a Commodity Credit Corporation commodity, and loosens proof rules for Mexican wolf livestock losses.

Conservation (Title II): It extends the Conservation Reserve Program, with a goal of at least 8.6 million acres in continuous enrollment, and the farmable wetland program. EQIP gets more flexibility. This includes higher payments for precision agriculture, composting as a practice, wildlife corridor payments, a higher organic payment cap, and a new Southern Border Initiative to repair farmland damage. A new state and Tribal soil health grant program gets $100 million a year. The bill sets conservation funding from $2.53 billion in FY2027 up to $3.255 billion in FY2031. It speeds up third-party technical help and practice standards. It reworks easement programs and creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program that replaces the Healthy Forests Reserve Program. It also changes the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, floodplain and watershed programs, and emergency conservation payments. Several studies are included.

Trade and food aid (Title III): Food for Peace moves from USAID to USDA. The bill sets spending floors for several food aid programs and requires at least $200 million a year for therapeutic foods in years of high child wasting, when funding is high enough. It funds market development and requires negotiation to protect "common" food names such as parmesan and feta in foreign markets. It creates a trade enforcement task force, including a plan to challenge India's price supports at the WTO. It requires reports on USMCA changes and on Argentine beef, and creates an overseas farm exchange program.

Nutrition (Title IV): SNAP appropriations are extended. States may contract out some SNAP work under limits. Hot rotisserie chicken becomes SNAP-eligible, and online purchasing becomes permanent. USDA must propose EBT card security rules and report on payment errors. It extends and changes the commodity programs for emergency food, seniors, and Tribes. School meals must buy 95 percent domestic food and may not buy poultry or seafood from China or Russia. Several incentive and local food programs are expanded, including a $200 million-a-year local food purchasing program.

Credit (Title V): Loan limits rise, for example direct farm ownership from $600,000 to $850,000. Experience rules relax, and there are new fast-approval and refinancing options. A new heirs property legal-aid program is authorized at $60 million a year. Farm Credit System lending powers expand, including rural community facilities, and the Farm Credit Administration is named sole regulator.

Rural development (Title VI): Broadband is renamed ReConnect, with a faster 50/25 Mbps standard and limits on overbuilding. Rural water gets new tools: zero-interest loans for distressed systems, a national circuit rider network, and decentralized household water grants. The bill also adds support for meat processing, rural childcare, health facilities, and a Rural Development Innovation Center, and extends many authorizations.

Research (Title VII): It extends dozens of research and education programs. It adds topics such as biochar, PFAS and microplastics in farmland, wildfire smoke and grapes, and mental health for farmers. It sets up a specialty crop automation program with at least $30 million a year, and organic transition research. It requires state matching funds for 1862 and 1890 institutions and creates a commission to modernize USDA farm statistics.

Forestry (Title VIII): It expands wildfire and forest tools. This includes larger categorical exclusions from environmental review for hazard trees and fuel work, no re-consultation under the Endangered Species Act when new species are listed, and exemptions from environmental and historic review for some communications sites. It also creates a "contain within 24 hours" wildfire standard, a Save Our Sequoias package, a white oak initiative, grazing changes, and timber loan guarantees. Data and reporting rules are added too.

Energy (Title IX): It changes biofuel and biorefinery support, rescinds $18 million, repeals the biodiesel education program, expands the Rural Energy for America Program, studies second-use EV batteries, and creates a $50 million-a-year tree planting grant program.

Horticulture and organics (Title X, partial): It extends specialty crop grants, urban agriculture, and organic programs. It rewrites hemp rules to count total THC and tighten reporting. It creates a pilot allowing up to 75 labs to move engineered microorganisms without permits. It makes big changes to pesticide law, which exempt plant biostimulants and some plant-incorporated protectants from FIFRA and increase USDA's role in EPA pesticide decisions.

Overall, many provisions strengthen water, soil, food access, and transparency reporting. Others reduce public review or regulatory oversight, or send public money to private businesses. Final costs are not stated in the digest, and the part of the text I could not see may matter.
does: Extends suspension of permanent price support law through 2031 and rewrites the Tree Assistance Program (120-day decisions, replant options, advance payments).
Creates a specialty crop emergency payment framework based on prior-year sales, with a payment cap of at least $900,000 for persons earning 75%+ of income from farming.
Lets the Secretary give disaster aid as block grants, only from newly appropriated funds.
Extends dairy indemnity and promotion, adds mandatory dairy processing cost reporting with a biennial public report, and replaces annual dairy reports.

Treats marketing assistance and sugar loan servicing as emergency work during shutdowns; extends storage loans to propane; restores tobacco as a CCC commodity; studies fertilizer storage loans; requires online disaster enrollment forms.
Requires USDA to accept proof of Mexican wolf livestock deaths that does not rely mainly on subcutaneous hemorrhaging.
Extends the Conservation Reserve Program and farmable wetlands through 2031, targets at least 8.6 million continuous acres, and caps CRP and wetland easements at 25% of county cropland.

Expands EQIP: precision agriculture (up to 90% of costs), composting, wildlife corridor payments, an organic cap of $200,000, a one-year Southern Border Initiative to repair farm damage, and allows EQIP together with conservation loans.
Creates a state and Tribal soil health grant program at $100 million per year for FY2027-2031 (capped at $5 million per recipient).
Sets CSP minimum annual payment of $4,000; sets annual CCC conservation funding from $2.53 billion (FY2027) to $3.255 billion (FY2031); $450 million per year for RCPP.

Speeds third-party technical assistance certification, requires frequent review of conservation practice standards, creates an Office of Conservation Innovation, direct hiring for NRCS, and farmer-to-farmer networks.

Reworks agricultural land easements (65% federal share, 90% for socially disadvantaged owners, a 25% lower-cost option, reduced oversight of experienced entities) and wetland reserve easements (stewardship funding, 15% for enhancement).

Creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program ($25-65 million per year) with a $500,000 cap on restoration assistance, limited subsurface mineral development, and repeals the Healthy Forests Reserve Program while honoring existing contracts.
Changes RCPP: 180-day agreement deadlines, 30-day partner payments, 10% cap on partner admin reimbursement, and added wildlife connectivity and flood or drought purposes.

Rewrites watershed rehabilitation (90% federal share, streamlined review) and emergency programs (advance payments up to 75%, floodplain easements with compatible uses); orders flood vulnerability and winter wheat cover crop studies.

Moves Food for Peace from USAID to USDA; extends food aid programs through 2031; caps non-commodity spending at 50%; requires at least $15 million per year for the international food relief partnership; requires at least $200 million per year for therapeutic foods in high child-wasting years.
Sets CCC market development funding at $255 million (FY2026), $500 million (FY2027), and $533 million per year (2028-2031); funds foreign cold-chain projects.

Defines food and wine 'common names' (feta, parmesan, gouda, and others) and directs USDA and USTR to negotiate to protect their use abroad; creates a seasonal fruit and vegetable trade working group.

Creates an Agricultural Trade Enforcement Task Force including a WTO plan against India's price supports; orders a GAO shrimp trade report, a USMCA impact report, and an Argentine beef quota report; creates a $10 million per year international farm cultural exchange.

Revises SNAP: removes a sunset on fee bans, allows limited contracting out of certification, requires reporting all payment errors, requires EBT security rules, adds animal protein as an incentive food, makes online purchasing permanent, makes hot rotisserie chicken eligible.

Extends TEFAP, FDPIR, CSFP, and the seniors farmers' market program (adding maple syrup and tree nuts); creates home delivery pilot for elderly CSFP participants ($10 million per year) and a Tribal CSFP demonstration.

Requires school meal purchases to be 95% domestic and bars buying Chinese or Russian poultry and seafood; expands nutrition incentive programs; dairy nutrition incentives raised to $50 million; creates the $200 million per year Local Farmers Feeding Our Communities program; raises the Healthy Food Financing Initiative to $135 million.

Raises farm loan limits (direct ownership $850,000, guaranteed ownership $3.5 million, direct operating $750,000, guaranteed operating $3 million, microloans $100,000), eases experience and ownership rules, adds refinancing and expedited approval pilots.
Authorizes $60 million per year for free legal help for underserved heirs property owners; extends the heirs relending program.

Expands Farm Credit System powers (rural community facilities capped at 15% of loans, aquatic business credit, export finance, waste, telecom and electricity financing), makes the FCA sole regulator, and lets FCA extend exam cycles for small institutions to 24 months.

Rebrands rural broadband as ReConnect (50/25 Mbps standard, $350 million per year, overbuild limits, no rate regulation), and adds satellite and innovative technology demonstrations and technical assistance grants.

Expands rural water tools: zero or 1% loans and forgiveness for distressed systems, a $25 million per year national circuit rider network, $20 million per year for household decentralized water systems, and reauthorizes grants through 2031.

Adds rural development programs: food supply chain loan guarantees up to $40 million, meat processing grants ($3 million per year), rural childcare priority, a Rural Development Innovation Center, rural health facility assistance, microentrepreneur and cooperative development changes, and guarantee fee caps of 3% and 0.75%.

Extends dozens of research and extension programs to 2031; boosts 1890 institution funding shares; adds topics (biochar, PFAS and microplastics, wildfire smoke, invasive species, farmer mental health); reserves at least $30 million per year for specialty crop automation; creates organic transition research ($7.5 million per year); requires state matching funds.

Creates a commission on NASS modernization, a veterans farming grant program ($3 million per year), an Aquaculture Advisory Committee, and a Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research reporting expansion.

Extends forestry programs, adds categorical NEPA exclusions (hazard trees up to 6,000 acres, utility rights-of-way, fuel projects up to 10,000 acres), raises collaborative project limits to 10,000 acres, and removes the need to reinitiate ESA consultation on forest plans when new species are listed.

Sets a 24-hour wildfire containment goal on certain lands, exempts some communications site approvals from NEPA and historic review, expands good neighbor authority and stewardship contracts (up to 20 years), and adds timber loan guarantees up to $220 million.

Creates Save Our Sequoias, white oak, nursery, wildfire technology, grazing-for-fire-risk, and forest data and carbon tracking provisions; adds a botanical products fee system and transparency rules for legacy road remediation.

Updates energy programs: adds sustainable aviation fuel, raises biorefinery guarantees to $400 million and rescinds $18 million, repeals biodiesel education, expands REAP (cap to $50 million, 10% reserve for underutilized technologies), and authorizes $50 million per year for tree planting to lower home energy use.

Extends specialty crop, urban agriculture, and organic programs; rewrites hemp rules (total THC, designations, lab accreditation); creates a pilot letting up to 75 parties move engineered plant microbes without permits; changes organic inspection rules.

Rewrites parts of pesticide law (FIFRA): exempts plant biostimulants and some plant-incorporated protectants, requires EPA coordination with USDA and ESA mitigation in interim decisions. The text I received stops partway through Section 10211, so remaining Title X, crop insurance, livestock, foreign farmland, and later titles are not summarized.

SNAP participants, seniors, Tribal food program participants, school children and school food authorities

label: H.R. 7618
title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
short_title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act
one: Extends National Park Service battlefield preservation grants through 2036 and orders studies of French and Indian War and Mexican-American War sites, subject to funding.
summary: This bill keeps alive a set of National Park Service grant programs that help protect and restore American battlefields. Right now, the acquisition grants (money to buy or protect battlefield land) are approved through 2028. The bill pushes that out to 2036. It also changes the rules for the other two grant programs, which pay for updating how battlefields are explained to visitors and for restoring battlefield sites. It sets one combined spending limit of $2 million per year through 2036 for those two programs, and it removes an older subsection of the interpretation grant law. The bill also asks the National Park Service to study sites linked to important events in the French and Indian War (1754–1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846–1848). The studies would list sites, rank how important they are, look at threats to them, and suggest ways to protect them. These could include making some a national park unit. Outside groups could do the studies, and the Park Service would check them. The studies only happen if Congress provides money. Finished studies go to House and Senate natural resources committees. Authorizing money does not itself spend it. Congress must still approve funds each year.
does: placeholder
who: National Park Service
Battlefield preservation groups such as the American Battlefield Trust

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep three National Park Service grant programs that help preserve, interpret, and restore American battlefields running through fiscal year 2036, instead of expiring after 2028. oppose: The bill uses federal tax dollars to extend grant programs for about eight more years. Someone who opposes this could argue that Congress should review the cost of these programs before extending them.

American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
This bill extends through FY2036 three National Park Service (NPS) grant programs that preserve U.S. battlefields and requires the NPS to study additional sites for potential preservation.
Specifically, the bill extends through FY2036 grant programs for the acquisition, interpretation modernization, and restoration of certain U.S. battlefields. (Under current law, the grants are authorized through FY2028.)
The bill also requires the NPS to prepare or certify studies of locations tied to significant events during the French and Indian War (1754-1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846-1848) for potential preservation.

label: H.R. 8800
title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA)
one: The yearly defense policy bill authorizes Pentagon programs, troop levels, weapons buying, military construction and nuclear-weapons programs for FY2027, and it carries hundreds of policy riders on pay, health care, contracting, and more.
summary:
What I could see: the digest covers Parts 1–15 of 32, through about Sec. 1089F in Title X. I could not see Parts 16–32. That includes the rest of Title X, the foreign-policy titles, cyber and space titles, the military construction details, the Energy Department and maritime titles, the funding tables, and Division E (the "SAVE America Act" voter-citizenship and photo-ID provisions). Everything below covers only what I could read. The headings for the unseen sections are noted where I know them.

Division A, Title I (Procurement): The bill authorizes buying aircraft, ships, vehicles and munitions. It allows multiyear contracts for Arleigh Burke destroyers, oilers, amphibious ships, E-2D aircraft, F-15EX and F-35 fighters, and armored vehicles. Some are capped or conditioned, such as a 5% savings certification for the F-35. It sets minimum inventories, including 1,800 fighters, 136 P-8A aircraft, and 1,524 Strykers. It bars retiring certain aircraft such as the F-22, MQ-9, E-11, and EA-18G. It bans buying humanoid robots from foreign adversaries and limits cut-flower purchases to U.S.-grown flowers.

Title II (Research): The bill adds many small funding lines, each offset by a cut elsewhere. It also sets up pilots on AI, quantum computing, drones, biotechnology, and secure data centers. It bars FY2027 funds for gain-of-function research on potential pandemic pathogens, with a waiver. It bars animal research with foreign countries of concern. It also directs a U.S.–Israel defense technology initiative.

Title III (Operations and Maintenance): The bill pushes nuclear energy into Pentagon energy policy. It requires a transportable microreactor in the Indo-Pacific by 2030. It orders reports on geothermal power, PFAS ("forever chemical") destruction, and a standard process for cleaning up old munitions sites. It sets up a Civil Reserve Industrial Base that can offer "other incentives." It also pushes 155mm shell production toward 100,000 per month, bans certain Chinese-linked connected vehicles on bases, and creates a secure registry for freight carriers.

Title IV–V (Personnel): The bill sets end strengths (for example, 469,000 in the Army). It bars enlistment by nationals of covered nations. It requires merit-only personnel decisions and bans hate symbols. It expands victim protections in the military justice system. This includes a death-penalty option for child rape under the military code, limits on appellate "factual sufficiency" review, and new offenses for retaliation and for sharing intimate images, including AI-forged ones. It also adds recruiter access to high schools, higher tuition assistance, and a Chaplains Modernization Act that protects chaplains' religious practice.

Title VI (Pay and benefits): The bill raises the death gratuity from $100,000 to $165,000. It increases leave accrual, adds bereavement leave for pregnancy loss, and improves housing allowances. It also adds a fuel discount at exchanges, a Survivor Benefit Plan change, a Marine Corps and Navy meal-charge ban, and a ban on Chinese seafood in military dining and commissaries.

Title VII (Health): The bill adds fertility care, a no-cost reserve dental plan, a year's supply of contraception, and required chaperones and sexual-assault examiners. It restores services at 41 military medical facilities and sets up many pilots. It bars TRICARE coverage of "gender-related medical treatment" with exceptions. It also bars funds for fertility steps such as artificial wombs and human cloning. The bill also contains autism-care, brain-injury, and suicide-prevention studies, and a GAO audit of TRICARE pharmacy payments.

Title VIII (Acquisition): The bill raises many contracting thresholds. The simplified buying limit goes from $250,000 to $500,000, and the cost-data threshold goes from $2 million to $10 million. It limits suspensions of progress payments. It reduces monitoring of contractor business systems. It makes government-purpose rights the default for technical data and software. It adds price-increase reporting on no-bid contracts and bars contracting with employers of people convicted of trafficking. It also bars certain solar equipment from foreign entities of concern.

Title IX–X (Organization and general provisions): The bill adds the Coast Guard Commandant to the Joint Chiefs. It allows $6 billion in transfers between accounts. It would cut DoD budgets by 0.5% each year it lacks a clean audit opinion. It also extends Guantanamo transfer and closure bars, limits detention authority to non-citizens, and requires a public report on the cost of operations in Iran since February 28, 2026. It adds ship-building and ship-maintenance rules and many reports.

Unseen: I could only read headings for the SAVE America Act (voter citizenship verification and photo ID), the maritime "SHIPs for America" provisions, a ban on funds for labs hosting certain foreign visitors, and a ban on reclassifying high-level nuclear waste. I did not judge those provisions.
does: Authorizes FY2027 procurement, research, operations, personnel, military construction and Energy Department national security programs by reference to funding tables (the tables themselves were not in the portion I could read).

Expands child care: grants for infant and toddler care, direct payments, au pair treatment (barring state or local extra conditions on military host families), and studies. Bars males from female sports at DoDEA schools and funds ballistic door systems in about 600 classrooms.

Prohibits and reverses listed service reductions at 41 military medical facilities, and requires numerous reports and pilots on brain injury, suicide prevention, autism care, and TRICARE pharmacy payments.

Raises contracting thresholds (simplified acquisition from $250,000 to $500,000; cost or pricing data from $2 million to $10 million), limits progress payment suspensions, and cuts review frequency of contractor business systems.

Establishes a Chief Acquisition Talent Officer and extends the acquisition workforce demonstration project to 130,000 to 143,000 people through 2035.

Requires a public, unclassified report on the cost of U.S. military operations in Iran since February 28, 2026, and costs of Operation Southern Spear.

Adds the Coast Guard Commandant to the Joint Chiefs and makes the National Guard Bureau chief eligible to chair them.

Repeals dozens of obsolete reporting requirements from earlier defense bills.
Includes Medal of Honor and other valor award authorizations for named individuals, and a requirement to give Congress an unredacted ground-combat effectiveness review within seven days.

label: H.R. 8880
title: Small Business Cybersecurity Assistance Evaluation Act of 2026
short_title: Small Business Cybersecurity Assistance Evaluation Act
one: Requires the Government Accountability Office to study and report on how well federal cybersecurity help for small businesses works and how to improve it, with no new money authorized.
summary: This bill asks the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's nonpartisan watchdog agency, to look at the federal programs, tools, and services meant to help small businesses with cybersecurity. The study would cover how these programs help owners spot cyber risks, check how ready they are, and plan for, limit, and recover from cyberattacks, scams, fraud, and social engineering (tricking people into giving up access or money). It would also look at programs that help owners find or get money to pay for these protections. The GAO would describe the most common attacks hitting small businesses, list the federal programs, and assess how well known and widely used they are, and why use differs. It would also assess how well the programs work together and how effective they are. It would point out basic cybersecurity ideas the programs leave out and recommend ways to make them more effective, better known, and better coordinated. The GAO would send the findings to the small business committees of the House and Senate. The bill does not create new programs, rules, or requirements for businesses. A section says no money is authorized to be appropriated for it, so the GAO would have to do the work with existing funds. The bill passed the House on June 23, 2026, and is now in a Senate committee.
does: Directs the GAO to study current federal cybersecurity programs, tools, and services for small businesses.
who: Small business owners and their employees and customers

benefits: A review could show which federal cybersecurity help for small businesses is useful and which is not well known.
Findings could point Congress toward better coordination among federal small business cybersecurity programs.
Because the bill imposes no new requirements on businesses, it would not add compliance duties for small firms.
concerns: The bill creates no new help for small businesses by itself; any improvements would depend on later action by Congress or agencies.
Because no funding is authorized, the study may be limited by GAO's existing budget and staff time.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not authorize any appropriation of money. GAO would have to complete the study using funds it already has. The bill's cost is not stated beyond this."]
unknowns: The material does not say how long GAO would have to finish the study or set a report deadline.
The material does not say how much GAO's work would cost or how many staff would be assigned.
The material does not name the specific federal programs that would be reviewed.
It is not stated whether the Senate will take up the bill or when.
The material does not say whether GAO's recommendations would be binding or what agencies must do in response.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the Government Accountability Office, Congress's nonpartisan watchdog, study federal cybersecurity programs, tools, and services that help small businesses identify and prepare for cyber threats and vulnerabilities. The study would describe the most common cyberattacks on small businesses and recommend ways to make federal help more effective, better known, and better coordinated. The bill does not itself create new programs or requirements for businesses.

oppose: The bill creates no new federal help for small businesses by itself, so it may spend time and money on a review without直接 changing what owners receive. (Note: the bill text is limited to a GAO study.)
The bill authorizes no new funding, so GAO would have to complete the study using its existing budget and staff time, which could limit how thorough it is.
Constituents could ask whether a federal study is the best use of resources when many small businesses may already be aware of current programs and need hands-on help rather than another report.

A study could help Congress improve coordination among many federal programs, so small business owners are not left trying to find help across several agencies.
The bill adds no new compliance rules or duties for small businesses, so it would not create extra paperwork or obligations for small firms.

label: H.R. 9613
title: Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act
one: Changes the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's independent reactor safety advisory panel so it can skip reviewing license applications it deems routine, caps its size at 15 members, and sets term limits.
summary: This bill changes the law that sets up the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, an expert panel that advises the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) on reactor safety. Today, the law says the panel must review certain license applications for nuclear facilities. Under this bill, the panel could decline to review an application if it decides the application has nothing unique, new, or noteworthy, or does not raise issues that warrant its review. The bill caps the panel at 15 members, appointed by the NRC, who should have varied technical expertise. Members could serve up to two 4-year terms, with more allowed if the NRC finds a compelling need. This applies to members appointed after the bill becomes law. The panel is told to focus, as far as practical, on issues tied to facility design that matter for safety, are new or noteworthy, and have not been handled before. The NRC must keep or change its policies so the panel acts efficiently and on time. Some old references in the Atomic Energy Act are cleaned up, and the rules for temporary operating licenses are adjusted so that the panel's report is needed only "if applicable." The bill does not set new spending amounts. Supporters would likely say it speeds up licensing; critics could worry it weakens independent safety review.
does: Lets the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards decline to review license applications it finds lack unique, novel, or noteworthy issues.
Caps the committee at 15 members appointed by the NRC, with diverse technical expertise.
Limits members to two 4-year terms, with exceptions if the NRC finds a compelling need.
Directs the committee to focus, where practical, on design-related, safety-significant, novel issues not previously addressed.
Requires the NRC to keep or change policies for efficient and timely committee action.
Keeps per diem pay and travel costs for members and the NRC-designated chairperson.
Makes conforming edits: removes a reference to a defunct General Advisory Committee, fixes section cross-references, and makes the committee's report 'if applicable' for temporary operating licenses.
who: Members of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission and its staff
Companies applying for nuclear reactor and other nuclear facility licenses
Communities near existing or proposed nuclear facilities
Medical and research users of nuclear materials and facilities
Electric utility customers

benefits: Could let the committee spend its time on novel, safety-significant issues rather than repetitive reviews.
Requires members to have diverse technical expertise.
Term limits could bring fresh perspectives.
Could shorten licensing timelines, including for medical and research uses.
concerns: Applications could be licensed without independent expert safety review, which could raise safety and environmental risks.
The bill sets no requirement to publicly explain or document a decision to decline review.
Emphasis on 'efficient and timely' action could create pressure to speed approvals over thoroughness.
Term limits with an NRC-decided exception, and NRC appointment of all members, could reduce independence and institutional knowledge.
Narrower focus on facility design could sideline issues like operations, environmental impacts, or waste.
Local communities get no new say.
imp.cost: No spending amounts are specified. Members keep existing per diem and travel pay; no cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: How often the committee would actually decline reviews.
Whether declined reviews would be publicly explained.
How 'unique, novel, or noteworthy' would be interpreted.
Whether the bill's 'facility' focus differs in practice from current 'reactor' focus.
Cost or time savings, as no estimate is available.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reform the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, the expert panel that advises the Nuclear Regulatory Commission on reactor safety. Its stated aims are to let the committee decline reviews of license applications that lack unique, novel, or noteworthy issues, to focus the committee on design-related, safety-significant, and new issues, and to direct the NRC to keep the committee's work efficient and timely.

oppose: The bill lets the committee decline to review license applications for commercial, industrial, medical, and research nuclear facilities if it finds no unique, novel, or noteworthy issues. Independent expert review of safety could be skipped for some applications, and I would ask that every reactor license keep a full safety review.

The bill does not require the committee or the NRC to publicly explain or document why a review was declined. I would ask that any decision to skip a review be written down and made public so the community can understand it.

The bill asks the NRC to pursue efficient and timely committee action, and it narrows the committee's focus to reactor design issues. I am concerned this could push approvals faster than thorough safety checks allow, and could leave out operations, environmental effects, and waste questions.
support: The bill lets the committee focus its limited time on new, safety-significant issues instead of repeating reviews that have already been done. I support using expert time where it matters most for safety.

The bill requires members to have diverse technical expertise relevant to the NRC's mission, which could strengthen the committee's range of knowledge. I support clear expertise requirements for advisory panels.

The bill sets two 4-year term limits for members, which could bring in fresh perspectives. It may also help shorten licensing timelines, including for medical and research uses that need faster decisions. I support efforts to make the licensing process more predictable and timely.

crs:
The following analysis is based on 
draft bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act
This bill modifies requirements governing the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), including by allowing the committee to decline to review certain license applications (e.g., applications for commercial nuclear power plants) issued by the NRC.
Specifically, the committee may decline to review license applications regarding certain commercial, industrial (e.g., utilization and production facilities), medical (e.g., therapy, such as radiation treatment), or research and development purposes if it determines that such applications do not (1) contain issues that are unique, novel, or noteworthy; or (2) raise issues that warrant review by the committee.
The bill also directs the committee to focus on issues that (1) directly relate to reactor design, (2) are safety significant, (3) are novel, and (4) have not been previously acted on by the committee.
In addition, it directs the NRC to maintain or modify policies to ensure efficient and timely action by the committee.
Finally, the bill requires the membership of the committee to reflect a diverse background of technical expertise relevant to the NRC's mission.

life.reason: Allowing independent safety review to be skipped for applications deemed routine could reduce a safety check on nuclear facilities.

transparency.reason: The committee could decline reviews with no stated requirement to publicly explain why, reducing visibility into safety vetting.

people_over_profit.reason: The emphasis on speed and skipping reviews mainly eases the path for license applicants, which may favor industry timelines over added public safety scrutiny.

label: H.R. 1318
title: United States Research Protection Act
one: Narrows and clarifies the federal ban on researchers joining "malign foreign talent recruitment programs" so it covers programs run by foreign countries of concern (such as China, Iran, North Korea and Russia), whether they pay or reward researchers directly or indirectly.
summary: A 2022 law (part of the CHIPS and Science Act) bars researchers who get federal research money from joining "malign foreign talent recruitment programs." These are programs where a foreign government offers pay or other rewards in ways that create conflicts of interest or involve unauthorized activity, like sharing protected information without permission. This bill makes a small wording fix to that definition. First, it says the programs covered are those tied to a "foreign country of concern," a term already defined in federal law, and the CRS summary says this includes China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. Second, it removes the older two-part structure of the definition and folds the list of covered activities into one list. The bill text does not show what the removed subparagraph (B) said, so I can't describe it. Third, it says the pay or rewards can come "directly or indirectly," which could catch money routed through middlemen. The bill adds no new money, no new agency, and no new penalties. Its effect is to define which foreign programs researchers who get federal funds must avoid. It passed the House on March 24, 2025, and is now with the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
does: Adds "of concern" after "foreign country" in the definition of a malign foreign talent recruitment program.
Removes a subparagraph (B) from the definition and merges the list of covered activities into a single list. The text does not show what (B) said.
Says the pay or incentives can be provided "directly or indirectly."
Changes no funding levels, and the bill text shows no new penalties.
who: Researchers and universities that receive federal research funding
Federal science agencies that enforce the restrictions
Foreign-born and international researchers, including those with ties to countries of concern
Foreign governments running talent recruitment programs
Could make the rules clearer for researchers and universities about which programs are barred.
Covering indirect payments could close loopholes that let foreign governments pay through intermediaries.
Could help protect publicly funded research and unpublished findings from unauthorized transfer.

benefits: By tying the definition to a term already in federal law, the bill may make the scope of covered programs clearer for researchers and institutions.
Covering indirect compensation may make it harder for foreign programs to avoid the rules by routing payments through middlemen.
concerns: Because the removed subparagraph's content is not described in the material, it is unclear whether any covered activities or programs were dropped by the change.
The phrase "directly or indirectly" is broad, so it could be read to reach a wide range of payments, which may create compliance questions for researchers.
imp.cost: ["The material states that the bill adds no new money, no new agency, and no new penalties. No cost estimate is given in the material provided."]
unknowns: How the removed subparagraph (B) affected the definition is not stated in the material.
Whether the change would alter which researchers or programs are covered in practice is not stated.
How federal agencies would enforce the revised definition is not described.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill or change it is not known; the bill is in Senate committee.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify the definition of a "malign foreign talent recruitment program" under the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which is part of the CHIPS and Science Act. The bill says the restrictions apply to programs sponsored by a "foreign country of concern," including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia, and that such programs may involve direct or indirect compensation or incentives. The CRS summary describes the law's aim as barring researchers who receive federal research funds from joining programs where foreign countries offer pay or rewards that create conflicts of interest or involve unauthorized activity.

oppose: The bill removes a subparagraph from the existing definition, and the bill text does not describe what it said. Opponents could ask whether any covered activities or programs were dropped, and ask for an explanation before the bill moves forward.

The phrase "directly or indirectly" is broad. A constituent could ask how researchers would know whether a payment routed through a third party counts, and whether the bill gives clear guidance to universities and labs.

The bill is a narrow wording change. A constituent could argue that Congress should first review how the existing 2022 law is working in practice, including whether researchers face confusion about compliance, before changing the definition.
support: The bill ties the definition to "foreign country of concern," a term already in federal law, which may make it clearer which programs researchers must avoid. A constituent could say this reduces uncertainty for universities and scientists.

Covering indirect compensation may close a gap. A constituent could say that without this language, foreign programs might avoid the rules by routing payments through middlemen, and this change addresses that risk.

The bill adds no new funding, no new agency, and no new penalties. A constituent could say it is a focused fix to protect federally funded research from undisclosed foreign influence, without creating new bureaucracy.

crs:
United States Research Protection Act
This bill clarifies the definition of a 
malign foreign talent recruitment program
 under the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act.

The Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which was included in the CHIPS and Science Act, prohibits researchers who receive federal funds from participating in malign foreign talent recruitment programs, in which foreign countries incentivize or compensate researchers for activities that present a conflict of interest for the researcher or that are otherwise unauthorized (e.g., sharing proprietary information without proper authorization).
The bill clarifies that these restrictions apply to programs that are sponsored by a foreign country of concern, including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia. The bill also clarifies that malign foreign talent recruitment programs may involve direct or indirect compensation or incentives from such countries.

news.overall: Evidence is thin: only five headlines from one perspective group, with no article descriptions and no mention of the bill by name. The headlines frame the surrounding topic as research security, China-linked espionage, international student flows, and Covid origins, but they do not show how these outlets characterize the bill itself. Comparison across perspectives is not possible from this input.

label: H.R. 10136
title: Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026
one: If Arkansas asks within 180 days, the Forest Service must hand the Crossett Experimental Forest and its research area and facilities to the state for free, on the condition that it stays a research and education forest tied to Arkansas universities.
summary: This bill would move the Crossett Experimental Forest in Arkansas from federal ownership to the State of Arkansas. The land includes the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area and related buildings and facilities. The state would have to ask in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The transfer would be free, by quitclaim deed (a deed that passes along whatever interest the government has, with no guarantees about the title). Arkansas would pay all transfer costs, such as surveys and paperwork. After the transfer, Arkansas must name it the Crossett Experimental State Forest and manage it under state forest laws. The state must keep using it for forest research, education, and demonstration, in line with its long research history. It must also work with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture and give them reasonable access. If the state fails to follow these rules and doesn't fix the problem within 180 days of written notice, the Secretary of Agriculture may take back all or part of the land. The Forest Service must also give the state copies of its research plans, plot data, measurement histories, and archives. Existing legal rights on the land would stay in place. The bill does not say how many acres are involved. It refers to a map dated May 1, 2026, which was not in the text I was given.
does: Requires the Forest Service to convey the forest to Arkansas if the state asks within 180 days of enactment.
Makes the transfer free, by quitclaim deed, and subject to valid existing rights.
Makes Arkansas pay all conveyance costs, including surveys.
Requires the state to designate it the Crossett Experimental State Forest and manage it under Arkansas state forest laws.
Requires use for forest research, education and demonstration, in coordination with two University of Arkansas entities, with reasonable access for them.
Lets the land revert to the United States, at the Secretary's discretion, if the state fails to comply and doesn't fix it within 180 days of notice.
Requires the Forest Service to give the state copies of all research plans, data, and archives, while keeping federal records laws in force.
Allows minor boundary and map corrections by mutual agreement.
who: State of Arkansas, which would gain land and facilities and take on management costs.
USDA Forest Service, which would lose a research site.
University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, researchers and students.
Local residents and nearby communities in southeast Arkansas, including those who use or live near the forest.
Federal taxpayers, who would no longer fund the site's upkeep.

benefits: Keeps the land in public ownership with a legal requirement for research, education and demonstration use.
Brings management closer to local and state institutions, including the state's universities.
Preserves decades of research data by passing copies to the state.
Gives no payment, land or break to a private company, and the state pays the transfer costs.
Reversion clause lets the federal government take the land back for non-compliance.
concerns: The bill does not say if timber sales, leasing, or other revenue activities are allowed, so land use could change in ways it doesn't spell out.
The Research Natural Area could lose some federal protections, and the bill doesn't say how it would be protected.
Reversion is at the Secretary's discretion, not automatic, so enforcement depends on the agency.
The bill has no public comment or local input step on the transfer itself.
The state will take on long-term upkeep costs, and the bill is silent on how it will pay.
imp.cost: No spending is authorized. Arkansas pays conveyance costs. The federal government gives up the land for no payment, and may save upkeep costs. No official cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: Acreage and exact boundaries, which depend on a map I could not see.
Whether Arkansas will request the transfer.
Whether the state's forest laws would allow logging, and how much.
How the Research Natural Area's protections would be kept.
How the state will fund ongoing operations.
Whether the public can still access the forest as they do now.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to transfer the Crossett Experimental Forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and related facilities from federal ownership to the State of Arkansas, if Arkansas requests it. It says the land must continue to be used for forest research, education, and demonstration in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, consistent with the forest's historic research mission.

oppose: The bill does not say whether timber sales, leasing, or other revenue-generating activities would be allowed on the forest, so land use could change in ways the text does not spell out. You could ask your representative what limits would apply.

The Research Natural Area could lose some federal protections, and the bill does not explain how it would be protected after the transfer. You could ask how the research area's long-term protection would be guaranteed.

The transfer has no public comment or local input step, and reversion to the federal government is at the Secretary's discretion rather than automatic. You could ask why the bill does not require public review before the land leaves federal ownership.
support: The bill keeps the forest in public ownership and requires it to be used for forest research, education, and demonstration, which protects its long research purpose in writing.

Management would move closer to Arkansas state institutions, including the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, which the bill requires to have reasonable access for research and teaching.

The transfer would be made without payment, and Arkansas would pay the conveyance costs, while the federal government keeps a reversion option if the state does not comply. The bill also gives the state copies of decades of research data and archives.

crs:
Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026
This bill directs the Forest Service, upon the request of the State of Arkansas, to convey the Crossett Experimental Forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and associated facilities to the state. 
Upon the conveyance, Arkansas must designate the land as the Crossett Experimental State Forest. In order to retain the land, Arkansas must
use the land for forest research, education, and demonstration purposes in a manner consistent with the historic research mission of the forest; and
use the forest in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, including by providing the universities with reasonable access to the forest for research and educational purposes.
The bill outlines the terms and conditions of the conveyance, including requiring the conveyance to be (1) subject to valid existing rights, (2) made without consideration (e.g., payment), and (3) made by quitclaim deed.
Arkansas must pay the costs of the conveyance, including costs for surveys and other administrative costs.

life.reason: Requires the land to stay a research forest, which helps keep the forest and its plants and animals studied and in public hands, though the bill has no explicit habitat protections.

transparency.reason: Research records pass to the state and federal records laws remain in force, though the bill has no public comment step.

local_say.reason: Moves control from the federal government to the state, which is closer to the people who live near the forest, though the bill has no direct local input process.

label: H.R. 2140
title: Diesel Emissions Reduction Act of 2025
one: Extends the EPA's diesel emissions reduction grant, rebate and loan program for five more years, through fiscal year 2029.
summary: This bill is very short. It changes one year in an existing law, the Energy Policy Act of 2005, from 2024 to 2029. That law lets the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) run a program that helps pay for cleaner diesel engines. Under the program, the EPA can give grants, rebates, or loans to owners of older diesel vehicles and equipment. The money helps them replace old engines or add pollution-control equipment to them. Examples include school buses, trucks, ports, and construction equipment, though the bill itself does not list them. The bill does not change how the program works, who can qualify, or the rules. It only keeps the program's legal authority to operate going through FY2029. The bill text shown does not give a dollar amount. The extension is only an authorization, so Congress would still have to approve actual spending in separate budget bills. Without the extension, the program's authority to receive funding would stay expired. The bill has passed the House and was placed on the Senate calendar, where it awaits a possible vote.
does: Changes the end date in Section 797(a) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 from 2024 to 2029.
Keeps the EPA's authority to fund diesel engine replacements and retrofits through FY2029.
Leaves the program's existing rules and eligibility unchanged.
who: Owners of older diesel vehicles and equipment, such as school districts, trucking firms, port operators and fleet operators
People living near highways, ports, rail yards and other diesel-heavy areas
Children riding diesel school buses
Engine and pollution-control technology makers
The EPA and federal taxpayers, who fund the grants

benefits: Could keep cutting harmful diesel exhaust such as fine particles and nitrogen oxides.
May improve health for children and for communities near freight corridors.
Gives school districts and small fleets a way to pay for cleaner engines.
Could also lower greenhouse gas emissions from some engines.
concerns: Uses taxpayer money to help private fleet owners with upgrades.
Extending the authorization does not guarantee any money will be appropriated.
The bill text does not say how funds are split between areas or how results are measured.
imp.cost: The bill text gives no dollar amount. It only extends the authorization through FY2029. The actual spending would be set later in appropriations bills, so the cost is not stated here.
unknowns: How much money Congress will actually provide each year.
Whether the Senate will vote on the bill and pass it.
How the program's rules and priorities may change under EPA management.
The exact cost, which the bill text does not state.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 624.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep the EPA's diesel emissions reduction program authorized by extending its end date from 2024 to 2029 under Section 797(a) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. The program provides grants, rebates, or loans to help replace diesel engines or add pollution control technology. The bill does not change the program's rules or eligibility.

oppose: The bill uses taxpayer money to help private fleet owners pay for engine upgrades, and you may question whether that is the best use of public funds.
The bill only extends the program's legal authority to 2029. It does not provide a dollar amount, so Congress would still need to decide future spending in separate budget bills.
The bill text does not say how funds would be divided among regions or how results would be measured, so you may want to ask how success would be tracked and whether the program is cost-effective.
support: The bill could help keep cutting harmful diesel exhaust, including fine particles and nitrogen oxides, which are linked to health problems.
Children and communities near busy freight routes may benefit from cleaner engines, and this program could help reduce their exposure to diesel pollution.

School districts and small fleet owners may have a hard time paying for cleaner engines on their own, and this program offers grants, rebates, or loans to help them. Some upgrades could also lower greenhouse gas emissions.

crs:
Diesel Emissions Reduction Act of 2025 
This bill reauthorizes through FY2029 a diesel emissions reduction program under which the Environmental Protection Agency provides grants, rebates, or loans for replacing diesel engines or retrofitting the engines with pollution control technologies.

life.reason: Less diesel exhaust can reduce illness and early deaths, and it may also lessen harm to wildlife and plants.

air.reason: It continues funding to replace or retrofit older diesel engines, which directly cuts soot and smog-forming pollution.

people_over_profit.reason: It puts public health benefits ahead of the lower cost of running older, dirtier engines, though the program also helps businesses pay for upgrades.
