label: H.R. 226
title: Eastern Band of Cherokee Historic Lands Reacquisition Act
short_title: Eastern Band of Cherokee Historic Lands Reacquisition Act
one: Puts about 76 acres of TVA-managed land, plus two trail easements, on the Tellico Reservoir in Monroe County, Tennessee, into federal trust for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians for memorials, a museum, and recreation, while keeping TVA's flood and water-control powers and banning gaming.
summary:
This bill would move certain federal land now managed by the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) into "trust" for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians. Trust means the United States holds the land for the tribe's benefit. The land is on the shore of Tellico Reservoir in Monroe County, Tennessee. It includes about 46 acres around the Sequoyah Museum, about 11.9 acres of support land, and about 18.2 acres around the Chota and Tanasi memorials. The tribe would also get two permanent trail easements (rights to use land below the 820-foot elevation line) totaling about 20 acres. The tribe would own the memorials and other improvements on the land.

The land would be used mainly to honor and teach Cherokee history and culture, for recreation and trails, and for the reburial of Cherokee remains returned under federal law. The support land could hold classrooms, offices, and temporary guest housing.

TVA keeps strong powers. It can temporarily flood the lower parts of the land, raise and lower reservoir levels, and enter the land for flood control, public health, and navigation work. Building near the water needs TVA's written consent. Future development must compensate TVA for lost hydropower capacity unless TVA agrees otherwise. The U.S. would not be liable for flooding or wave damage. TVA stays responsible for cleaning up any hazardous substances and must assess the land before the transfer. Gambling on the land is banned.
does: Declares about 76 acres of TVA land on or above the 820-foot elevation line to be held in trust for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
Creates two permanent trail easements below the 820-foot line, about 8.5 acres at the Chota peninsula and 11.4 acres between the Chota and Tanasi memorials.
Makes the memorials and other improvements on the land the tribe's property.
Directs the land to be used mainly for memorials, the Sequoyah museum, reburial of remains, interpreting the Trail of Tears, recreation, and tribal programs.
Lets TVA temporarily flood land below 824 feet, change reservoir levels, permanently flood adjacent land below 815 feet, and enter the land for river control, flood control, and public health work.
Requires TVA's written consent for water-use facilities and certain structures near the shoreline.
Requires compensation to TVA for lost hydropower capacity from future development, unless TVA agrees otherwise.
Shields the United States from liability for flooding, wave action, and water-level changes.
Makes TVA solely responsible for environmental cleanup and for a hazardous substance assessment before the transfer.
Requires TVA to send revised maps to Congress within a year of the transfer.
Bans Class II and Class III gaming on the lands.
who: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and other Cherokee tribes
Tennessee Valley Authority
Residents and visitors of Monroe County, Tennessee, and users of Tellico Reservoir
Visitors to the Sequoyah Museum and Chota and Tanasi memorials
Electricity customers of TVA (indirectly, through hydropower and flood control)

benefits: Returns historically important Cherokee sites to tribal control and protects them for memorial and educational use.
Supports a respectful place for reburial of ancestral remains returned under federal law.
Requires TVA to assess hazardous substances, tell the tribe and Interior, and pay for required cleanup.
Keeps public benefit uses such as trails, education, and recreation.
Preserves TVA's flood control and river management, protecting downstream safety.
The gaming ban limits commercial development concerns.
concerns: The tribe would bear flood, wave, and water-level risks with no U.S. liability.
TVA's broad entry rights, including applying larvicides and chemicals and dredging, could affect the memorial setting, although the bill requires that it not unreasonably interfere.
Hydropower compensation for future development could limit what the tribe can build or raise its costs.
The gaming ban limits the tribe's future economic options on these lands.
Taking land into trust removes it from local property tax and state and local regulation, which some local officials may object to.
imp.cost: No cost estimate is provided in the material. The bill makes TVA responsible for cleanup costs, and TVA is funded by power revenue rather than regular taxpayer appropriations. It authorizes no new spending. Future development would require compensation to TVA for lost hydropower capacity.
unknowns: Results of the hazardous substance assessment and any cleanup costs.
The amount of any hydropower compensation under the TVA guideline.
The effect on local property tax revenue in Monroe County.
Timing of the transfer after enactment.
Whether the 2015 maps need corrections.

stage.last_action: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to take certain Tennessee Valley Authority lands and easements along Tellico Reservoir in Monroe County, Tennessee, into trust for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians. According to its summary, the land includes the Sequoyah Museum, the Chota and Tanasi memorials, and support land for cultural programs, and the bill aims to keep these sites for memorial, educational, and tribal use. The bill also says TVA keeps its river control and flood management powers on the land.

oppose: The tribe would carry flood, wave, and water-level risks on these lands, and the United States would not be liable for resulting damage, which some constituents may see as an unfair shift of risk.

TVA would keep broad entry rights, including applying larvicides and chemicals and dredging, which could affect the setting of the memorials even though the bill says this work must not unreasonably interfere with the sites.
Taking the land into trust removes it from local property tax rolls and from state and local regulation, a concern some local officials have raised about county revenue and local control.
support: The bill would return historically important Cherokee sites, including the Sequoyah Museum and the Chota and Tanasi memorials, to tribal control and protect them for memorial and educational use.
The bill supports a respectful place for reburial of ancestral remains returned under federal law, and it keeps public uses such as trails, education, and recreation.

The bill requires TVA to assess hazardous substances before the transfer, tell the tribe and the Interior Department about them, and pay for required cleanup, and it keeps TVA's flood control and river management in place to protect downstream safety.

crs:
Eastern Band of Cherokee Historic Lands Reacquisition Act

This bill takes specified lands and easements in Monroe County, Tennessee, into trust for the use and benefit of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians. These lands include the Sequoyah Museum, the Chota Memorial, the Tanasi Memorial, and land to provide support for these properties and cultural programs.

The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) maintains its right to carry out river control and development on these lands, including temporarily and intermittently flooding certain lands. The bill specifies the structures that may be constructed with the TVA's written consent on certain lands subject to flooding. Additionally, the TVA must be compensated for lost hydropower capacity from future development of these lands.

Further, the bill specifies that the United States is not liable for loss or damage resulting from certain activities, such as the permanent flooding of adjacent lands.

In addition, the bill outlines the TVA's continuing responsibilities, including those related to environmental remediation.
 Finally, the bill prohibits gaming on these lands.

life.reason: It protects burial and reburial sites for human remains and requires hazardous substance assessment and cleanup.

water.reason: TVA must assess and fund cleanup of hazardous substances on shoreline land, which could protect reservoir water quality, though TVA retains the right to apply chemicals and larvicides.

transparency.reason: TVA must disclose hazardous substance findings to the tribe and Interior and give revised maps to congressional committees.

people_over_profit.reason: It puts culturally important public-interest land under tribal stewardship for memorial and educational use and bars gaming, rather than treating it for commercial value, though TVA keeps hydropower compensation rights.

label: H.R. 2306
title: Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act
one: The bill gives the Adams Memorial Commission more time (through 2032) to build a John Adams memorial in Washington, DC, and sets where it can go.
summary: This bill deals with a planned memorial in Washington, DC, honoring President John Adams. A group called the Adams Memorial Commission is in charge of setting it up. Its legal authority was due to run out in 2025. The bill pushes that deadline to 2032, and treats the extension as if it took effect on December 1, 2025. It also changes related older laws so the memorial's approval period runs to 2032. The bill picks the memorial's location. It must go in an area shown on a February 25, 2025 map made by the Commission. That area is south of the White House, near Ellipse Road, Pennsylvania Avenue, and 15th Street NW. If the Commission decides that spot won't work because of physical or security problems, the memorial must go in "the Reserve." The Reserve is the central National Mall area, from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and from the White House to the Jefferson Memorial. The bill says the site can be chosen despite a section of federal law (40 U.S.C. 8908(c)) that normally limits building in the Reserve. It also repeals two sections of an older law (Public Law 107-315). The text provided shows parts marked as struck out, so I could not tell exactly which wording is final. The bill does not give a cost figure or new money.
does: Extends the Adams Memorial Commission's authority from 2025 to 2032, effective as if enacted December 1, 2025.
Extends the time limit on the memorial's establishment under Public Law 107-62 to 2032.
Requires the memorial to be sited in the area on the Commission's February 25, 2025 map, south of the White House near Ellipse Road.
Allows the Reserve (central National Mall area) as a fallback if the Commission finds the first site unsuitable or infeasible for physical or security reasons.
Overrides the normal restriction on new memorials in the Reserve (40 U.S.C. 8908(c)) for this site choice.
Repeals sections 2 and 3 of Public Law 107-315.
who: Adams Memorial Commission members and staff
National Park Service and agencies that review DC memorials
Visitors and residents of Washington, DC
Supporters of honoring John Adams and U.S. history
Federal taxpayers, if public money is ever used

benefits: Keeps the effort to honor John Adams alive instead of letting its authority lapse.
Gives a clear first-choice site and a clear fallback.
Gives more time to raise funds and complete design.
concerns: Waives the normal Reserve rule (40 U.S.C. 8908(c)), which could reduce the usual review of National Mall development.
Allows the Commission itself to decide that the first site is unsuitable, and the bill does not say how that is made public.
Fixing the site in law could limit input from DC residents and planning bodies.
Could affect green space near the White House and the Mall.
imp.cost: The bill gives no cost estimate and appropriates no money. Earlier law behind the Commission generally relies on private donations, but I could not confirm that from the text given.
unknowns: Final cost and funding source for the memorial.
How the Commission would decide, and report, that the first site is unsuitable.
What review by planning and design bodies would still apply.
Exact effect of the repealed sections of Public Law 107-315, which are not shown.
The environmental effect of building at either site.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep the effort to build a permanent memorial in Washington, DC, honoring President John Adams from lapsing. It extends the Adams Memorial Commission's authority through 2032 and sets a site for the memorial, with a backup location if the first site is found unsuitable or infeasible.

oppose: The bill waives the normal rule in 40 U.S.C. 8908(c) that limits new memorials in the Reserve, which could reduce the usual review of development on the National Mall.

The bill fixes the memorial's site in law and lets the Commission decide the first site is unsuitable, and it does not say how that decision would be made public. This could limit input from DC residents and planning bodies.
The memorial could affect green space near the White House and the Mall, and the summary does not describe a full review of those impacts.
support: The bill keeps the Adams Memorial Commission active through 2032 instead of letting its authority expire in 2025, so the effort to honor John Adams can continue.
The bill names a clear first-choice site and a clear backup, which gives the Commission certainty about where the memorial would go.
The extra time gives the Commission more room to raise funds and complete its design.

crs:
The Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act
This bill extends through 2032 the Adams Memorial Commission, whose purpose is to establish a permanent memorial in Washington, DC, to honor John Adams and his legacy.
The bill specifies that the Adams Memorial shall be located within the area specified by the 
Adams Memorial Commission in a February 25, 2025 map
 (i.e., south of the White House, adjacent to Ellipse Road and near Pennsylvania Avenue and 15th Street, Northwest).
If the Commission determines that this location is not suitable or feasible due to physical or security constraints, the bill requires that the memorial be located in 
the Reserve
, an area which generally extends from the United States Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial, and from the White House to the Jefferson Memorial.

transparency.reason: It sets the site in law and waives a standard Reserve rule, which may bypass some of the usual public review steps.

local_say.reason: Congress would choose the site and waive a general rule, which could limit DC residents' input on use of local public land.

label: H.R. 2916
title: To authorize, ratify, and confirm the Agreement of Settlement and Compromise to Resolve the Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim in the State of New York, and for other purposes.
short_title: Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim Settlement Act
one: Congress would approve a negotiated settlement of a decades-old Mohawk land claim in northern New York and treat certain tribe-owned land in set areas as "Indian country."
summary: This bill would put Congress's approval on a settlement agreement that ends a long-running land dispute in northern New York. The Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne, New York State, Franklin and St. Lawrence Counties, the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay, and the New York Power Authority all signed it. The tribe had brought court claims saying land, rights-of-way and easements were taken improperly. Under the bill, Congress would also approve any land transfers that are the subject of three named court cases. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the settlement itself restores some land rights and access to land for the tribe, gives tuition help to tribal members at certain colleges, and requires the Power Authority to make yearly payments to the tribe. The bill text itself does not list those terms; they are in the agreement, which I could not see. The bill also says land the tribe owns now, or buys later, inside the "Settlement Acquisition Areas" counts as "Indian country." That is a legal term that mainly affects which government handles criminal cases on the land. This status is subject to the settlement's terms, conditions and limits. The bill does not say how much money is involved or when payments start.
does: Authorizes, ratifies and confirms the Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim settlement agreement.
Approves any land, right-of-way or easement transfer that is the subject of three named federal court cases.
Treats land owned by the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe in the Settlement Acquisition Areas as Indian country, both land owned at the agreement's effective date and land acquired later.
Makes that Indian country status subject to the settlement's terms, conditions and limits.
who: Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and its members
Mohawk Council of Akwesasne
State of New York
Franklin and St. Lawrence Counties and the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay
New York Power Authority and its electricity customers (ratepayers)
Landowners and residents near the settlement areas

benefits: Could end decades of litigation and uncertainty over land title.
Could restore land rights and access for the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe.
Could provide tuition help to tribal members.
Settlement was agreed by local governments and the state, not imposed.
concerns: Annual Power Authority payments could affect its finances and might be passed on to electricity customers; this is not stated.
Indian country status could change which government handles criminal cases and regulation on that land, which some neighbors may worry about.
Ratifying past transfers extinguishes claims in the named cases, so some parties lose legal options.
imp.cost: No cost estimate was given. Per CRS, the New York Power Authority would make annual payments to the tribe. Amounts and funding source are in the settlement agreement, which I could not see.
unknowns: Dollar amounts of payments and how long they last.
How the Power Authority would fund payments and whether ratepayers would bear them.
Exact size and location of the Settlement Acquisition Areas.
Environmental or land-use rules that apply to the land.
Federal cost, if any.

stage.last_action: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to approve, or "ratify and confirm," a settlement agreement that resolves the Akwesasne Mohawk land claim in northern New York. Under the settlement, the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and other parties agree to end their disputes over land, rights-of-way, and easements. According to the Congressional Research Service, the settlement restores some land rights and access for the tribe, provides tuition assistance for tribal members, and requires the New York Power Authority to make annual payments to the tribe. The bill itself does not list those terms, and it does not state the amount of money or when payments begin.

oppose: The bill approves past land, right-of-way, and easement transfers in three named court cases, which may end legal options for some parties who have claims in those cases.

The bill would treat tribal land in the Settlement Acquisition Areas as Indian country, which could change which government handles criminal cases and regulation on that land. You could ask how local residents and officials would be affected.

The bill does not state how much money the Power Authority will pay each year or whether those costs could be passed on to electricity customers. You could ask for these figures to be made public before Congress acts.
support: The settlement was reached by the tribe, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne, New York State, local counties and towns, and the Power Authority, so it resolves the dispute through agreement rather than imposing a result.
The bill could end decades of litigation and uncertainty over land title, giving landowners and governments more certainty about who holds the land.

The settlement, as described by the Congressional Research Service, would restore some land rights and access for the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and provide tuition help to tribal members at certain colleges.

crs:
This bill recognizes and settles the Akwesasne land claim in northern New York. (Akwesasne is a Mohawk territory that extends into the United States and Canada, specifically New York, Ontario, and Quebec.)
The bill authorizes, ratifies, and confirms a specified settlement agreement entered into by the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe (SRMT), the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne, the State of New York, Franklin and Saint Lawrence Counties in New York, the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay in New York, and the New York Power Authority. (Among its provisions, the settlement agreement restores land rights and provides access to land to SRMT, provides tuition assistance for tribal members to certain postsecondary institutions, and requires the New York Power Authority to make annual payments to SRMT.)
Additionally, the bill authorizes, ratifies, and confirms any transfer of land, right-of-way, or easement that is the subject of claims in specified court cases.
The bill also recognizes as 
Indian country
 any land owned or subsequently acquired by SRMT within the settlement acquisition areas. (The term 
Indian country
, for purposes of criminal jurisdiction, generally refers to all lands within a tribal reservation, dependent Indian communities, and tribal allotments.)

people_over_profit.reason: It resolves a claim by people against a state power utility and local governments, with land rights, tuition help and payments going to the tribe.

local_say.reason: It ratifies an agreement negotiated by the tribe, state, counties and towns, and restores tribal land access, though it also extinguishes some claims.

honesty_kindness.reason: It aims to settle a long-standing grievance through negotiated, mutually agreed terms and gives the tribe some redress.

label: H.R. 3978
title: Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act
one: The bill would let the NRC license future spent-nuclear-fuel recycling plants under the shorter "special nuclear material" process instead of the longer process used for reactors and similar facilities.
summary: This bill changes one definition in the Atomic Energy Act. Today, certain nuclear facilities are called "production facilities" and go through a longer, more detailed licensing process with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). The bill says that a plant that recycles (reprocesses) used nuclear fuel, as long as it does so in a way that does not separate out pure plutonium, would not count as a "production facility." Instead, the NRC would license it under the rules for "special nuclear material," which the Congressional Research Service says has fewer steps. No commercial recycling plants operate in the U.S. today, so this would apply only to future plants. Recycling turns used fuel into material that can be burned again to make electricity, which could reduce the amount of waste needing disposal. The bill does not itself fund anything, build anything, or change safety standards in writing. It also does not say what safety, environmental review, public hearing, or waste-handling requirements would apply under the alternate path. Supporters would likely say it speeds up a clean-energy and waste-management option and removes a regulatory mismatch. Critics could worry that a lighter process gives less review and less public input for facilities that handle highly radioactive material, with possible risks to nearby water, air, and communities.
does: Amends the definition of 'production facility' in Section 11(v) of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954.
Excludes facilities that reprocess spent nuclear fuel in a way that does not isolate plutonium from that definition.
Results in such facilities being licensed under the special nuclear material rules, which have fewer steps, per CRS.
Applies to future domestic recycling facilities; none are commercially operating now.
who: Companies that might build nuclear fuel recycling plants
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission
Communities near any future reprocessing site
Nuclear utilities and electricity customers
Environmental and public-interest groups that take part in licensing proceedings

benefits: Could reduce the amount of spent fuel needing long-term disposal by reusing it.
Could give a clearer, more predictable licensing path for recycling plants.
May support nuclear fuel supply and low-emission electricity.
No direct spending in the bill.
concerns: Fewer licensing steps could mean less scrutiny and fewer chances for public participation.
Reprocessing facilities handle highly radioactive material, with possible risks to nearby water, air, and people if poorly regulated.
The 'does not isolate plutonium' standard is a narrow definition and its proliferation and security implications are not addressed in the text.
Local communities could have less say over siting.
imp.cost: The bill authorizes no spending and has no stated cost. Any future costs would depend on private projects or later government support, which the bill does not address.
unknowns: Exactly which environmental review and public hearing requirements would apply under the special nuclear material path.
Whether NRC would add new rules for reprocessing safety.
Whether any company would actually build a plant and who would bear costs and risks.
How the bill treats waste from reprocessing and plutonium security.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 695.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to create a clearer, more efficient licensing path for future facilities that recycle (reprocess) used nuclear fuel without isolating plutonium. It does this by amending the Atomic Energy Act's definition of "production facility" so that these recycling plants would be licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission under the rules for special nuclear material, which the Congressional Research Service describes as having fewer steps. The bill's title describes the aim as recycling fuel efficiently through expedited licensing.

oppose: The bill moves future fuel recycling plants out of the 'production facility' licensing rules and into a path with fewer steps, which could mean less federal review of facilities that handle highly radioactive material.

The bill does not spell out what safety, environmental review, public hearing, or waste-handling requirements would apply under the new path, so constituents cannot easily confirm how nearby water, air, and communities would be protected.
The bill's 'does not isolate plutonium' standard is narrow, and the text does not address proliferation or security concerns linked to plutonium handling.
Local communities could have fewer chances to comment on or influence where these plants are sited.
support: The bill would give future recycling plants a clearer and more predictable licensing path by using the special nuclear material rules, which CRS says have fewer steps.
Recycling used fuel could reduce the amount of spent fuel that needs long-term disposal, which could ease waste-management challenges.
Reusing recycled material as fuel could support the domestic nuclear fuel supply and low-emission electricity generation.
The bill itself carries no direct federal spending, and it only changes one statutory definition rather than creating a new program.

crs:
The following analysis is based on 
draft bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act
This bill directs the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to license future recycling facilities that reprocess certain spent nuclear fuel (i.e., radioactive waste) under 
regulations
 for special nuclear material rather than 
regulations
 for production and utilization facilities. The bill applies to domestic facilities that reprocess spent nuclear fuel in a manner that does not isolate plutonium. Generally, such recycling facilities reprocess spent nuclear fuel into materials that may be reused as nuclear fuel for electricity.
While there are no commercial reprocessing facilities currently operating in the United States, the bill specifies which regulatory framework the NRC must use when issuing licenses to future facilities by excluding such facilities from the statutory definition of 
production facility
. The licensing process under regulations for special nuclear material has fewer steps than the licensing process under regulations for production and utilization facilities.

life.reason: Lighter licensing for facilities handling highly radioactive material could reduce safety review, though recycling might also reduce waste.

water.reason: Reprocessing plants carry contamination risks, and fewer licensing steps could mean less scrutiny of those risks.

transparency.reason: A shorter licensing process may offer fewer public review and comment opportunities.

local_say.reason: Fewer licensing steps could limit chances for nearby communities to weigh in on siting of reprocessing plants.

label: H.R. 4463
title: To amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993.
one: The bill removes a 1993 federal limit on who can be a Catawba tribal member, leaving membership decisions to the tribe itself.
summary: In 1993, Congress passed a law settling a land claim between the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina and the government. That law included a rule saying the tribe could only enroll new members if they were direct descendants of someone on the tribe's final base membership roll (the official list of original members) and had kept up "political relations" with the tribe. This bill deletes that rule. It is a single short edit to one section of the 1993 law. If it passes, the Catawba Nation would decide its own membership requirements, as most tribes do. The Congressional Research Service notes that the tribe already uses three base rolls and requires anyone applying to prove they descend from someone on one of those rolls. The bill does not give money, change land, or change the rest of the 1993 settlement. The text does not say what new membership rules the tribe would adopt, so any changes would come from the tribe's own decisions later. The Senate Committee on Indian Affairs has ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment.
does: Strikes the clause in Section 7(d) of the 1993 Catawba Land Claims Settlement Act that limits future enrollment to lineal descendants of people on the final base roll who kept political relations with the tribe.
Leaves the tribe free to set its own membership criteria.
Makes no other changes to the 1993 settlement.
who: Members of the Catawba Indian Nation and people seeking enrollment
Tribal government leaders who set membership rules
Federal agencies that deal with the tribe under the 1993 settlement

benefits: Gives the tribe self-governance over its own membership.
Removes a federal rule that may be out of step with how the tribe operates.
Has no stated federal cost.
concerns: Without the federal limit, the tribe could change enrollment rules in ways that affect who receives tribal benefits, and some people may disagree with those choices.
Possible effects on benefits tied to the 1993 settlement are not addressed in the text.
imp.cost: No funding provided or authorized in the text. No cost estimate was provided in the material; direct costs appear negligible.
unknowns: What new membership rules, if any, the tribe would adopt.
Whether the change would affect distribution of settlement benefits or services.
Whether the state of South Carolina or other parties to the 1993 settlement have any objections.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 so the tribe can decide its own membership rules. The 1993 law limited future enrollment to lineal descendants of people on the final base membership roll who kept political relations with the tribe. The bill removes that federal limit, leaving the tribe free to set its own membership criteria.

oppose: The 1993 settlement set clear federal limits on who can join the Catawba Nation. Removing them could change who qualifies for tribal membership and benefits that are linked to the settlement.
The bill does not say what new membership rules the tribe would adopt. Constituents may want to know those rules before Congress removes the existing ones.
The bill does not address how changes to membership could affect benefits tied to the 1993 settlement. Constituents may ask Congress to clarify this before acting.
support: The bill would give the Catawba Nation control over its own membership, as most tribes already have. Supporters say tribes should decide who belongs to their community.

The tribe already uses three base membership rolls and requires applicants to prove descent from someone on them. Supporters say the tribe's current process is already based on lineal descent, so the bill mainly removes a federal rule that may not match how the tribe operates.
The bill is a single, short edit to one section of the 1993 law. It does not change land, provide money, or alter the rest of the settlement, and it has no stated federal cost.

crs:
This bill revises tribal membership requirements for the Catawba Indian Nation (a tribe in South Carolina).
The Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 explicitly restricted the tribe’s future membership to lineal descendants of people on the final base membership roll who maintained continuous political relations with the tribe. This bill removes these membership criteria and allows the tribe to determine its membership. (The tribe uses three base membership rolls and anyone who wants to be enrolled must prove lineal descent from someone listed on one of these base membership rolls.)

local_say.reason: It lets the Catawba community decide its own membership rather than having Congress fix the rules.

label: H.R. 5682
title: To take certain land in the State of California into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians, and for other purposes.
short_title: Pechanga Band Land Into Trust Bill
one: Moves about 860 acres of federal land in Riverside County, California, into trust for the Pechanga Band of Indians, to be kept as open space with no gaming.
summary: This bill would move about 860 acres of public land in Riverside County, California, from the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to the Pechanga Band of Indians. The land would be held "in trust," meaning the federal government keeps legal title but the tribe benefits from it and manages it. The land would become part of the tribe's reservation. The bill sets firm limits on how it can be used. It must stay open space. It can only be used for things that fit with open space and for protecting and maintaining the archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources there. Utilities or structures are allowed only if they fit open space and serve those protection goals. Gaming such as casinos is banned on the land. Existing rights, such as easements, rights-of-way, leases, and permits, would stay in place. Existing water rights and water service agreements would not change. The map showing the parcel would be kept on file for public viewing at BLM offices. The text mentions no spending and no new money. The Senate Committee on Indian Affairs has approved it without changes. The bill does not say when the transfer would take effect beyond becoming law.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to take about 860 acres of land in Riverside County, California, now administered by the Bureau of Land Management, into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians. The bill says the land would become part of the tribe's reservation and be kept as open space to protect its archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources.

The bill would let the Pechanga Band of Indians protect and manage cultural and archaeological resources on the land, which the bill identifies as a goal.

crs:
This bill takes approximately 860 acres of land in Riverside County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians. The land is currently administered by the Bureau of Land Management.
The land taken into trust shall be (1) part of the tribe's reservation; (2) maintained as an open space; and (3) used only for purposes consistent with the maintenance of the land as open space and for the protection, preservation, and maintenance of the archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources on the land. Further, the bill prohibits gaming on the land.

life.reason: Requires open space and protection of wildlife resources on the land.

people_over_profit.reason: Bans gaming and limits commercial use, keeping the land for conservation and cultural purposes.

local_say.reason: Gives a tribal community authority over land in its homeland area, though broader local input is not addressed.

label: H.R. 8195
title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
short_title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act
one: Requires the Fish and Wildlife Service to set up regional rules, with state, tribal and flyway council input, for managing and lethally controlling double-crested cormorants until 2034.
summary: This bill tells the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to write rules within one year for managing double-crested cormorants, a native waterbird. Fish farmers and anglers often complain that these birds eat fish. The rules would be built region by region with the four Flyway Councils, which are groups that coordinate bird management across states. Each regional plan must keep breeding populations at a level that protects the species and keep total killing of the birds within a sustainable limit. Each plan must also say how birds may be killed, when, and who may do it. That could include state and tribal wildlife agencies, lake managers and pond managers. Plans must require public yearly reports on how many birds were killed, including birds that were not the target. They must include steps to avoid harming other species and list non-lethal methods that must be used. Plans must weigh the birds' effects on fisheries, plants, other birds, human health, water quality and endangered species. They must also include recommendations for National Wildlife Refuges. The agency must survey cormorant numbers and update the plans every five years. Within 90 days it must report to Congress on whether hunting licenses for cormorants are feasible. The bill expires January 1, 2034. The text does not give a dollar cost.
does: unused

Refuge recommendations could weaken refuge protection for birds, though they must fit refuge purposes.
imp.cost: No funding or cost estimate is in the bill text. Costs for rulemaking, surveys and reporting would fall on the Fish and Wildlife Service, so on taxpayers, subject to appropriations.
unknowns: How many birds could be killed.
How much the bill would cost and who would pay.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to require the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to set up regional management frameworks for double-crested cormorants, a native waterbird. According to the bill's title and CRS summary, the aim is to manage regional populations responsibly while keeping breeding populations at a level that ensures conservation. The bill's findings and summary describe the concern as the birds' effects on fisheries and other resources, which the frameworks must consider. The requirements end on January 1, 2034.

oppose: The bill allows lethal control of a native, protected bird, and opponents worry that this could lead to large numbers of birds being killed.
Private lake and pond managers could be allowed to take birds, which may mean less government oversight of who kills them and how.
Non-target birds and species protected under the Endangered Species Act could be harmed by mistake, and the bill's safeguards for them may not be strong enough.
The bill does not clearly require public comment beyond normal rulemaking, so the public may have limited say in how the frameworks are written.
support: The bill requires management based on the best available science and sets sustainability limits on how many birds can be taken.
The bill requires public annual reports on all birds killed, including non-target birds, which adds transparency.
The bill requires non-lethal measures and habitat restoration best practices to be part of the plans.
Fish farmers, anglers, and pond owners say cormorants harm fisheries, and the bill would require regional plans that consider these documented effects, with states and tribes given a role.

crs:
Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
This bill requires the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to develop frameworks to manage regional populations of double-crested cormorants (a type of waterbird native to North America).
Specifically, FWS must coordinate with the four Regional Flyway Councils to develop regional management frameworks for double-crested cormorants. Among other elements, each framework must (1) ensure the breeding population is managed at a sufficient level to ensure conservation, (2) include parameters regarding the taking (e.g., capturing or hunting) of double-crested cormorants, and (3) consider any documented effects of double-crested cormorants in the region (e.g., impacts on fisheries). 
In developing each framework, FWS must also work with state and tribal game and fish agencies and the applicable Regional Flyway Council to make recommendations for managing double-crested cormorants within the National Wildlife Refuge System. 
FWS must coordinate with the Regional Flyway Councils every five years to survey the population of double-crested cormorants. Additionally, each framework must be reviewed and updated every five years, incorporating results of the most recent population survey. FWS must also report to Congress on the feasibility of issuing hunting licenses to manage double-crested cormorants in accordance with the frameworks.
The requirements of this bill terminate on January 1, 2034.

life.reason: It authorizes killing a native protected bird and could harm non-target birds, though it adds sustainability limits, non-lethal measures and habitat restoration.

transparency.reason: It requires public annual reports on all birds killed, including non-target birds, and regular population surveys.

local_say.reason: It gives states, tribes and regional councils a role in setting plans for their areas, though there is no explicit public input step.

honesty_kindness.reason: Expanding lethal control of animals is less kind to wildlife, though it requires non-lethal methods to be identified.

label: H.R. 9084
title: Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act
short_title: Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act
one: Requires the Department of Energy to post online, within 72 hours, its nuclear facility authorizations, safety-standard changes, and safety analyses, and to send Congress a yearly report.
summary: This bill would make the Department of Energy (DOE) tell the public quickly about key decisions on its higher-risk nuclear facilities. These are facilities ranked Hazard Category 1, 2, or 3, which are ranked by how much radioactive material they hold and how badly an accident could hurt the public, workers, or the environment. The bill covers only facilities where the Secretary of Energy has authority under the Atomic Energy Act. Within 72 hours, DOE would have to post on a public website: (1) any change to a DOE directive or safety standard for these facilities, with a summary of what changed; (2) any safety analysis it issues, whether preliminary (for new or majorly modified facilities) or final, including the analysis itself; and (3) any agreement authorizing such a facility, including conditions attached to it. DOE could edit the safety analyses only to remove commercially sensitive information, classified information, or controlled nuclear or unclassified information. The bill does not say how DOE should show what was removed. Each year by January 31, DOE would also have to send a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on what it did to authorize these facilities in the prior year. The bill does not add money or change the safety rules themselves. It only requires public posting and reporting.
does: Requires a public website post within 72 hours of any change to a directive or safety standard for covered nuclear facilities, with a summary of the change.
Requires posting of any preliminary or final documented safety analysis within 72 hours of issuance.
Allows DOE to edit those analyses only to remove commercially sensitive, classified, or controlled information.
Requires a post within 72 hours of any agreement authorizing a covered facility, including its conditions.
Requires an annual report by January 31 to House and Senate energy committees on authorization activities.
Defines covered facilities as Hazard Category 1, 2, and 3 DOE nuclear facilities under the Secretary's authority.

Communities near DOE nuclear facilities
DOE nuclear facility workers
Companies that build or operate DOE-authorized nuclear facilities or seek authorization
Congressional energy committees
Journalists, watchdog groups and researchers

benefits: Communities, workers and the press could learn quickly about approvals and safety rule changes at high-hazard sites.
Public posting could discourage weakening of safety standards without notice.
The yearly report gives Congress a regular way to oversee DOE authorizations.
Public safety analyses could allow independent experts to review them.
concerns: The 'commercially sensitive information' exception could be used broadly to hide important content, and the bill does not require marking redactions.
The bill only requires posting after the fact; it does not give the public a chance to comment before decisions.
A 72-hour deadline could add paperwork burden for DOE, though the bill gives no funding.
It covers only DOE-authorized facilities, not those licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
imp.cost: The bill provides no new funding and no cost estimate was given. Costs would be limited to DOE staff time for posting and reporting, paid from existing appropriations.
unknowns: How broadly DOE would define commercially sensitive or controlled information when redacting.
Whether DOE would need extra resources to meet the 72-hour deadline.
How many facilities and actions would be covered each year.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill; it is in committee now.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make the Department of Energy tell the public quickly about key decisions on its higher-risk nuclear facilities (Hazard Category 1, 2, or 3). It would require DOE to post, within 72 hours, agreements authorizing these facilities, changes to related directives or safety standards, and safety analyses, and to send Congress an annual report on its authorization activities. The bill's title and summary describe this as a transparency measure; the summary does not state a specific incident or problem that prompted it.

oppose: The bill's exception for 'commercially sensitive information' is broad, and the bill does not require DOE to mark where material was removed, so the public may not be able to tell how much was withheld.
The bill requires posting only after decisions are made, so it gives the public no chance to comment before DOE authorizes a high-hazard facility.
A 72-hour posting deadline could add paperwork for DOE, and the bill provides no added funding to meet it.
The bill covers only DOE-authorized facilities and does not reach facilities licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, so it leaves some nuclear sites outside its rules.
support: The bill would let communities, workers, and the press learn quickly about approvals and safety rule changes at high-hazard DOE nuclear sites.
Public posting of changes to safety standards could make it harder to weaken those standards without anyone noticing.
Making safety analyses public could allow independent experts to review them and raise concerns.
The annual report to the House and Senate energy committees gives Congress a regular way to oversee DOE's authorization of these facilities.

crs:
The following analysis is based on 
draft bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act
This bill directs the Department of Energy (DOE) to report actions related to its authorization of DOE nuclear facilities and other related DOE actions on a public website within 72 hours of those authorizations or actions occurring. 
Specifically, DOE must post information about agreements to authorize nuclear facilities that fall under Hazard Category 1, 2, or 3. Hazard categories are based on the radioactive material inventories of the facilities and the potential consequences to the public, workers, and the environment. Hazard Category 1 represents the highest potential consequence.
DOE must also post a summary of any actions it took to alter a directive or safety standard relating to such facilities.
Further, DOE must post any preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis that it issues for such facilities. A 
preliminary documented safety analysis 
means documentation prepared in connection with the design and construction of a new Hazard Category 1, 2, or 3 DOE nuclear facility or a major modification to such nuclear facility already in existence that provides a reasonable basis for the preliminary conclusion that the nuclear facility can be operated safely through the consideration of certain factors. A 
documented safety analysis
 means a documented analysis of the extent to which a nuclear facility can be operated safely with respect to workers, the public, and the environment.
DOE must also issue an annual report detailing any activities it took to authorize such DOE nuclear facilities during the previous year.

life.reason: Public posting of safety analyses and standard changes could make high-hazard nuclear sites safer for people and ecosystems, though the bill sets no new safety rules.

transparency.reason: It requires DOE to post nuclear authorizations, safety standard changes and safety analyses within 72 hours and to report yearly to Congress.

people_over_profit.reason: It puts public access to safety information ahead of secrecy, though it still lets DOE withhold commercially sensitive information.

local_say.reason: Timely information lets nearby communities understand and respond to nuclear decisions, but the bill creates no formal comment or approval role.

honesty_kindness.reason: It promotes openness and honest public disclosure by the government about risky facilities.

label: H.R. 9269
title: Renewing the African American Civil Rights Network Act
short_title: Renewing the African American Civil Rights Network Act
one: Restarts and extends for seven years a National Park Service program that recognizes and supports historic sites and resources tied to the African American civil rights movement.
summary: The African American Civil Rights Network is a National Park Service (NPS) program. It links together historic sites, facilities, and educational resources connected to the African American civil rights movement. The program's legal authority ran out on January 8, 2025. This bill would renew it for seven years, counted from the date the new law is enacted. The bill changes one line in existing law and does nothing else. It does not create new sites, set a dollar amount, or add new rules. Under the program, places in the network can use the network's logo and can get technical help from the NPS. Technical help usually means advice on things like preservation and education. The bill text does not describe this in detail, and the CRS summary only says it exists. The bill does not say how much money would be spent. Any money would have to come through separate budget decisions. The bill has passed the House and is now in the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
does: Changes the program's end date in section 308404 of title 54 of the U.S. Code to seven years after this new law is enacted.
Keeps the African American Civil Rights Network running as an NPS program after its January 8, 2025 lapse.
Keeps in place existing benefits: use of the network logo and NPS technical support for included sites.
Adds no new funding amount, new sites, or new requirements in the text provided.
who: Historic sites, museums, and educational programs in the network
National Park Service staff who run the program
Local communities and visitors near civil rights sites
Students, teachers, and researchers of civil rights history
Federal taxpayers, to the extent NPS spends money on the program

benefits: Restores official recognition and the NPS support network for civil rights sites.
Could help local sites draw visitors and educational interest.
Supports public learning about civil rights history.
Simple and low-risk: only an end date changes.
concerns: The bill sets no funding level, so the program's real strength depends on later budget decisions.
Any NPS spending on the program could compete with other park needs.
imp.cost: The bill text states no dollar amounts. The cost is probably small, limited to NPS staff time and technical help, but the text and CRS summary give no estimate.
unknowns: No cost estimate was provided.
The text does not say how many sites are in the network or how much NPS support they receive.
It is unclear when or whether the Senate will act.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to renew the African American Civil Rights Network, a National Park Service program that links historic sites, facilities, and educational resources connected to the African American civil rights movement. The program's legal authority expired on January 8, 2025, and the bill would extend it for seven years after the new law is enacted.

oppose: The bill sets no funding level, so it is unclear how much federal money would be spent on the program, and any spending would depend on later budget decisions.
Any National Park Service time and money spent on this network could compete with other park needs, such as maintenance and preservation at existing parks.
The bill does not add new rules or accountability measures, and the text does not describe in detail what the NPS technical support includes, so you may want to ask how success would be measured.
support: The bill restores official recognition for civil rights sites that were part of the network before its authority lapsed on January 8, 2025.
Places in the network can use the network logo and receive NPS technical help with things like preservation and education, which could help local sites serve visitors and students.
The bill is simple: it changes only the end date in existing law, so it keeps a working program in place for seven years without creating new sites or new rules.

crs:
Renewing the African American Civil Rights Network Act
This bill reauthorizes for seven years the African American Civil Rights Network. The network is a National Park Service (NPS) program that designates historical sites and educational resources that are connected to the African American civil rights movement. The program expired on January 8, 2025.
Locations, facilities, and resources included in the network are eligible to use the network logo and receive technical support from the NPS.

transparency.reason: Keeping a public program that documents and shares civil rights history helps people learn an accurate record of how government treated its citizens.

honesty_kindness.reason: Honoring civil rights struggles and preserving truthful history supports honesty about the past and respect for those who were harmed.

label: H.R. 9612
title: American Enrichment Deployment Act
one: Lets companies start building uranium enrichment plants before the NRC has issued a license, at their own risk, while keeping the NRC's power to deny the license and keeping environmental review and public hearing rights.
summary: Today, a company must get a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) before it starts building a uranium enrichment facility. Enrichment is the step that raises the share of the fuel-grade uranium atoms in uranium so it can power reactors. This bill would change that. Enrichment plants could be built before the license is issued, under the same terms that already apply to other nuclear fuel plants, such as those that convert uranium or make fuel. The bill calls this "at-risk construction." The company would be building at its own risk, because the NRC could still turn down the license if the company didn't meet the rules. The bill says it does not change the NRC's power to deny a license. It also says it does not change three things: the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review that applies to the license, the right of affected people to request a hearing, and the NRC's power to inspect enrichment plants. The NRC would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to write or update its rules. The bill text doesn't say who pays for construction, and it doesn't say what limits would apply to early construction. Those limits would depend on the rules for other fuel facilities and on the NRC's new rules. The bill has passed the House and is now in a Senate committee.
does: placeholder
who: Companies that want to build uranium enrichment plants
Communities near proposed enrichment sites
Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff, who must write rules within 180 days
Nuclear power operators and fuel buyers
Environmental and public interest groups that take part in licensing hearings

benefits: Could speed up domestic uranium enrichment and reduce dependence on foreign fuel supply.
Could cut project delays and costs for companies, and may bring jobs.
Keeps NEPA review, hearing rights, inspection authority and the NRC's power to deny a license.
Matches how other nuclear fuel plants are already treated.
concerns: Construction before a license could limit how much public comment and review can change a project.
Money already spent could create pressure to approve a license.
Site disturbance could harm land, water or wildlife before environmental review is done.
The 180-day rulemaking leaves key limits to the NRC, which the bill does not spell out.
imp.cost: The bill gives no funding and no cost estimate. The bill text doesn't say who would pay for construction or for losses if a license is denied. The NRC would need staff time to write rules within 180 days.
unknowns: What limits would apply to early construction, such as safety-related work.
Whether the NRC could require environmental review to be done before construction starts.
Who bears the costs if a plant is built and the license is denied.
How the NRC would write its rules and how much public input it would take.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to allow uranium enrichment facilities to be built before the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issues a license, under the same terms that already apply to other nuclear fuel cycle facilities such as uranium conversion and fuel fabrication plants. Based on the bill's summary, the problem it addresses is the timing of licensing for enrichment plants, and it aims to support building domestic enrichment capacity. The bill says companies would build at their own risk, since the NRC could still deny a license.

oppose: Building an enrichment plant before a license is issued could make it harder for public comments and environmental review to change the project, since much of the money would already be spent.
The bill's summary notes that money already spent could create pressure to approve a license, even if concerns come up later.
Site work could disturb land, water, or wildlife before the environmental review under NEPA is finished.
The bill gives the NRC 180 days to write rules but does not spell out the limits on early construction, so key protections would be left to future agency decisions.
support: The bill could help the U.S. build its own uranium enrichment capacity, which may reduce reliance on foreign fuel supplies.
Allowing early construction could cut project delays and costs for companies, which may create jobs.
The bill keeps the NRC's power to deny a license, the NEPA review, the right to request a hearing, and the NRC's inspection authority.
The bill would treat enrichment plants the same way other nuclear fuel facilities, such as conversion and fuel fabrication plants, are already treated.

The following analysis is based on 
draft bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
American Enrichment Deployment Act
This bill allows for the construction of a uranium enrichment facility before a license is issued by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).
Under current law, a license is required from the NRC prior to the construction of a uranium enrichment facility. Under the bill, uranium enrichment facilities are allowed to be constructed under the same terms and conditions applicable to other fuel cycle facilities (i.e., uranium conversion and fuel fabrication facilities). Such facilities must be licensed by the NRC to process and handle special nuclear material and source material.
NRC must issue or revise regulations to carry out this bill not later than 180 days after enactment.

life.reason: Allowing construction before safety and environmental licensing is finished could increase risk to people, wildlife and plants, though inspections and license denial remain.

water.reason: Early site work before licensing could disturb land and water resources before the review is complete.

transparency.reason: Starting construction early could reduce how much public review shapes a project, even though NEPA and hearing rights are kept.

people_over_profit.reason: It lets companies move faster on projects, which could put schedule and cost savings ahead of finishing the review first.

local_say.reason: Nearby communities could face a plant that is already partly built by the time they can weigh in, although hearing rights are preserved.

label: H.R. 9614
title: NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act
one: Lets the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Chairman pay senior career executives up to 10% above the normal top Senior Executive Service pay cap, with added reporting.
summary: This bill changes the Atomic Energy Act so the head of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), the federal agency that oversees nuclear power plants and nuclear materials, can pay certain senior career employees more. These are "career appointees," meaning senior executives who hold top jobs and got them through the civil service rather than as political picks. Today, pay for these executives is capped at the top rate for the Senior Executive Service (SES), the federal government's top management pay system. Under the bill, the Chairman could set pay up to 110% of that cap, which is 10% higher. The authority applies no matter when the executive was hired. The bill says using this power cannot affect the government's approval of the NRC's performance appraisal system. It also adds a reporting requirement: the NRC's existing reports on its special pay authorities would have to include how many career appointees are being paid under this new power. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's watchdog agency, would also include this authority in its review under the 2024 ADVANCE Act. The bill gives no dollar estimate, and the text doesn't say how many people it covers or how much it would cost. It passed the House and was sent to the Senate Homeland Security committee.
does: Lets the NRC Chairman set pay for career appointees up to 110% of the top Senior Executive Service pay rate at the NRC.
Applies to career appointees regardless of when they were hired.
Says using this power cannot affect certification of the NRC's performance appraisal system.
Adds the number of career appointees paid under this power to the NRC's required reports.
Extends the existing GAO report under the ADVANCE Act of 2024 to cover this new authority.
Applies existing rules and limits on the NRC's other pay authorities to this one, through conforming edits.
who: Senior career executives at the NRC
NRC Chairman and agency management
Companies and communities regulated by or near nuclear facilities, indirectly through staffing and oversight
Taxpayers and NRC fee payers, who fund the agency (NRC is largely funded by fees on licensees)
GAO and Congress, which receive added reporting

benefits: Could help the NRC hire and keep experienced safety and technical leaders, which may support strong nuclear oversight.
Adds the number of executives paid under this power to existing reports, and GAO review covers it, giving some transparency.
Narrow in scope: limited to career appointees, not political appointees.
concerns: Allows pay above the normal Senior Executive Service cap, with 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' language that overrides other limits.
Reports only give a total count, not names, amounts or reasons.
Higher pay could raise costs for taxpayers or fee payers if no offsets are found.
Pay-setting power sits with the Chairman, so how it is used depends on one official's discretion.
imp.cost: No cost estimate is provided in the material. NRC is largely funded by fees charged to the industry it regulates, but the bill text does not state the funding source for these pay increases.
unknowns: How many career appointees would receive higher pay and by how much.
Total cost and whether it would be paid from fees or appropriations.
Whether higher pay would actually improve hiring and retention.
Whether the authority has a sunset date or other limits; the text shows none.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let the Nuclear Regulatory Commission set higher pay for certain senior career appointees, up to 10% above the normal top Senior Executive Service pay rate, so the agency can hire and keep experienced leaders. The bill's text and summary describe this as a pay-alignment change for NRC staff; they do not state the sponsor's private reasons.

oppose: The bill lets the NRC Chairman set pay for career appointees up to 110% of the top Senior Executive Service rate, going beyond the normal cap, and it uses 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' language that can override other pay limits.
The bill gives no dollar estimate and does not say how many people it would cover or what it would cost. Higher pay could raise costs for taxpayers or fee payers if no offsets are found.
Reporting under the bill would only give a total count of executives paid under this power, not names, amounts, or reasons, so the public would have limited visibility into how the authority is used.
Pay decisions would rest with one official, the Chairman, so how the authority is applied would depend on that person's judgment.
support: The bill would let the NRC pay certain senior career executives up to 10% above the normal Senior Executive Service cap, which could help the agency hire and keep experienced safety and technical leaders.
Experienced staff are central to nuclear safety oversight, so the bill may help the NRC retain people with the expertise needed to oversee nuclear power plants and nuclear materials.
The authority is narrow: it covers only career appointees, not political appointees, and it is subject to reporting requirements and a GAO review under the 2024 ADVANCE Act.
The reporting requirement and GAO review add some transparency, since the number of executives paid under this power must be included in NRC reports and GAO's review will cover it.
