The following analysis is based on 
draft bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act
This bill allows the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to increase the annual compensation of a career appointee. Specifically, NRC may set such compensation at a rate that is up to 10% over the maximum annual rate of basic pay for a Senior Executive Service position within the NRC. This authority applies regardless of when the career appointee was appointed.

life.reason: Better retention of senior nuclear safety executives could modestly support safe oversight of nuclear facilities, though the effect is indirect.

transparency.reason: It adds a count of career appointees paid under this power to the NRC's reports and to the GAO review, though it doesn't require names or amounts.

label: H.R. 9615
title: BRACE Act
one: The bill would let facilities that store lithium-ion batteries before recycling them follow lighter "universal waste" rules instead of stricter hazardous-waste rules, and would order the EPA to write a permanent rule within 18 months.
summary: Right now, many used lithium-ion batteries are treated under federal rules that can require recycling facilities to get a hazardous waste storage permit if they store the batteries before recycling them. This bill would change that. Until the EPA finishes a new rule, recycling facilities that store these batteries would follow the "large quantity handler of universal waste" rules. Universal waste is a lighter set of rules for common items like batteries, lamps and some pesticides. Those rules cover things like labeling, employee training, handling releases, and tracking shipments. Under the bill, facilities could store these batteries without the special permit. The bill also gives the EPA 18 months to write a permanent rule on managing lithium-ion batteries as universal waste. The EPA must consider battery-specific requirements, parts of the interim rules, other changes to support recycling and recovering critical minerals while protecting health and the environment, and extra safety rules to fill gaps. The bill does not limit future EPA rulemaking on these batteries. It also makes a technical fix to an older battery law so that it points to the current federal regulations (40 CFR part 273) instead of a 1995 notice. The bill does not give any funding. Supporters say it could make recycling easier and cut reliance on imported minerals. Critics could worry about fire and pollution risks at storage sites with less oversight.
does: Lets destination facilities (recyclers) that store lithium-ion batteries before recycling follow large-quantity universal waste rules instead of the stricter hazardous waste storage rules, until the EPA issues a final rule.
Removes the need for a special hazardous waste storage permit for that storage, per the CRS summary.
Requires the EPA to issue a rule on managing lithium-ion batteries as universal waste within 18 months of enactment.

Tells the EPA to consider battery-specific requirements, parts of the interim rules, other recycling and critical mineral recovery changes that protect health and environment, and added safety requirements.
Says the bill does not limit future EPA rulemaking on lithium-ion batteries.
Updates the Mercury-Containing and Rechargeable Battery Management Act to refer to current federal regulations (40 CFR part 273) instead of a 1995 notice.
who: Battery recycling companies and other destination facilities
Battery makers, electric vehicle and electronics industries that need recycled critical minerals
Communities near battery storage and recycling sites
Firefighters and emergency responders
The Environmental Protection Agency
Consumers and businesses that dispose of used lithium-ion batteries

benefits: Could make it cheaper and faster to recycle lithium-ion batteries, keeping them out of landfills.
Could boost domestic recovery of critical minerals like lithium, cobalt and nickel.
Requires the EPA to write a permanent rule through public notice and comment.
Requires the EPA to consider extra safety requirements and to maintain health and environmental protections.
Interim universal waste rules still include training, labeling, release response and tracking requirements.
concerns: Removing the hazardous waste storage permit could mean less oversight, inspection and public input for sites storing many batteries.
Lithium-ion batteries can catch fire; large storage sites could pose fire, air and runoff risks to nearby communities.
The interim rules apply right away, before the EPA finishes its safety review.
The EPA only has to 'consider' added safety rules, not adopt them.
Communities lose the permit process that gives neighbors a say on hazardous waste storage.
imp.cost: No funding or cost estimate is given in the text. Facilities may save on permitting costs. The EPA would bear the cost of the rulemaking from existing resources, though the bill doesn't say so.
unknowns: What the EPA's final rule would require, and whether it would add safety rules.
How many facilities would use the interim rules and how much battery volume they would store.
Whether fire and environmental incidents would rise or fall.
How states with stricter rules would respond. I could not tell from the text whether state rules are preempted.
The cost to the EPA of the rulemaking.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make it easier to recycle lithium-ion batteries and recover critical minerals (per its title, the "Battery Recycling for America's Competitive Economy Act," and the CRS summary). It does this by letting facilities that store these batteries before recycling follow the lighter large-quantity universal waste rules instead of the stricter hazardous waste storage rules, so they can store batteries without a special permit until the EPA finishes a permanent rule. The bill also gives the EPA 18 months to write that rule.

oppose: Removing the hazardous waste storage permit could mean less oversight, inspection, and public input for recycling sites that store large numbers of lithium-ion batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries can catch fire. Large storage sites could pose fire, air, and runoff risks to nearby communities, and the bill would apply the lighter rules right away, before the EPA finishes its safety review.
The bill says the EPA must only 'consider' extra safety requirements, not adopt them, so safety gaps could remain in the final rule.
support: Recycling lithium-ion batteries can be costly under current hazardous waste rules. This bill could make recycling cheaper and faster, which may keep batteries out of landfills.
Recovering minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries could reduce reliance on imported materials and support domestic supply.

The bill keeps protections in place. Interim universal waste rules still require training, labeling, release response, and shipment tracking, and the EPA must write a permanent rule through public notice and comment within 18 months, while considering health, environmental, and safety requirements.

crs:
Battery Recycling for America’s Competitive Economy Act or the BRACE Act
This bill modifies the regulation of lithium-ion batteries under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act in order to facilitate the recycling of lithium-ion batteries and the recovery of critical minerals. Specifically, the bill directs certain facilities that store lithium-ion batteries prior to recycling them to follow regulations for large quantity handlers of universal waste instead of following the more stringent hazardous waste regulations that currently apply, thereby allowing these facilities to store lithium-ion batteries without needing a special permit.

life.reason: Better recycling could reduce toxic battery waste and mining pressure, but lighter storage rules could raise fire and exposure risks, with a slight net benefit due to the required health protections.

local_say.reason: Removing the hazardous waste storage permit for these facilities could reduce the permit process through which neighbors can weigh in.

label: H.R. 9785
title: South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
short_title: South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
one: Directs the Interior Department to study whether three Missouri River water supply projects serving rural and municipal areas in South Dakota and neighboring states are feasible, with the federal share of each study capped at $10 million and 50%.
summary: This bill does not build anything. It pays for studies. It tells the Secretary of the Interior to look at whether three proposed projects could bring drinking and other water from the Missouri River to communities, farms, and businesses. The three are the Western Dakota Regional Water System, an expansion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System (Iowa, Minnesota, South Dakota), and the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System (South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, Minnesota). Each is run by a nonprofit group that would share the study work and costs. The federal government could pay no more than half of each study and no more than $10 million per study. For the first two projects, Interior must finish by writing a report that recommends whether Congress should approve construction and how costs should be split, with locals paying at least 25% of construction. That report goes to the House and Senate natural resources committees and must be posted publicly with the study documents. Interior must also consult federal, state, tribal, regional, and local authorities. The Dakota Mainstem study is optional ("may") and has no public-report or tribal-consultation requirement in the text. Authority for each study ends after 7 years. The bill does not approve construction or provide construction money, and it does not say where the study money would come from.
does: Orders Interior to study feasibility of a Missouri River water project for the Western Dakota Regional Water System.
Orders Interior to study feasibility of expanding the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System in Iowa, Minnesota, and South Dakota.
Allows (but does not require) Interior to study a Dakota Mainstem water supply project in South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, and Minnesota.
Caps the federal share of each study at $10 million and 50% of study cost.
Requires reports for the first two studies recommending whether to build and setting a local construction cost share of at least 25%.
Requires those reports and study documents to be sent to congressional committees and made public.
Requires consultation with federal, state, tribal, regional, and local authorities on the first two studies.
Ends each study authority 7 years after enactment.
who: Rural and small-town residents and businesses in South Dakota, Iowa, Minnesota, and Nebraska who need water supplies
The three nonprofit regional water systems named in the bill
Department of the Interior (Bureau of Reclamation)
Tribal nations and local governments in the study areas, who would be consulted on the first two studies
Federal taxpayers, who would cover up to half of study costs
Communities and ecosystems along the Missouri River

benefits: Could help communities with unreliable or poor-quality water plan safe, steady supplies.
Reports for two studies must be public and go to Congress.
Local nonprofits help shape the studies, and tribal, state, and local authorities are consulted on two of them.
Spending is limited: $10 million and 50% federal caps per study, with a 7-year sunset.
Requires a local share of at least 25% of any later construction costs in two of the reports.
concerns: Studies could lead to large later taxpayer-funded construction projects.
Taking more water from the Missouri River could affect river ecosystems, fish and wildlife, and other users, and the text does not mention environmental review.
The Dakota Mainstem study has no public-report requirement, no stated recommendation on local cost share, and no required tribal consultation.
'Industrial' water supply could benefit businesses, and rural ratepayers may eventually bear local costs.
Federal study costs fall on taxpayers, up to $10 million per study.
imp.cost: Federal share of each of the three studies is capped at $10 million and 50% of that study's cost (up to $30 million total). The bill does not say where the money comes from, and no money is appropriated in the text. Local nonprofits would cover the rest. Future construction would need separate approval, with at least 25% local share recommended for two of the projects.
unknowns: Actual study costs and whether Congress will fund them.
Whether the projects will be found feasible or ever be built.
How much water would be taken and its effects on the Missouri River and on tribal water rights or interests.
Who would use the 'industrial' water and how costs would be passed on to ratepayers.
Whether the Dakota Mainstem study will be done, since it is optional.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the Department of the Interior study whether water projects drawing from the Missouri River could supply municipal, rural, and industrial water in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, and South Dakota. It names three systems: the Western Dakota Regional Water System, the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System, and the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System. The bill does not build anything or provide construction money. It addresses the problem of communities needing reliable, good-quality water supplies, according to its findings and summary.

oppose: The bill pays for studies that could lead to large later construction projects. Since the bill does not set construction costs, you could ask your member how much taxpayers might eventually pay.

Taking more water from the Missouri River could affect river ecosystems, fish, wildlife, and other water users. The bill's text does not mention environmental review, so you could ask how these effects would be checked before any project moves forward.

The Dakota Mainstem study is optional, has no public-report requirement, and has no required tribal consultation. You could ask why the bill's transparency and consultation rules apply to only two of the three studies.
support: The bill pays for feasibility studies only. It does not build anything or provide construction money, so Congress would see the findings before any later decision.

Two of the studies must produce public reports sent to the House and Senate natural resources committees. Local, state, and tribal authorities are consulted on those studies, which gives communities a voice in the process.

The bill limits spending. Federal money is capped at 50% of each study's cost and $10 million per study, and each study authority ends after 7 years. Any later construction would require local cost sharing of at least 25% under the reports' recommendations.

cost_flag: Federal share of each of the three studies is capped at $10 million and 50% of that study's cost (up to $30 million total). The bill does not say where the money comes from, and no money is appropriated in the text. Local nonprofits would cover the rest. Future construction would need separate approval, with at least 25% local share recommended for two of the projects.
crs:
South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
This bill directs the Department of the Interior to study the feasibility of constructing projects to supply municipal, rural, and industrial water from the Missouri River in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, and South Dakota. Specifically, the bill requires studies on projects to supply water to the (1) Western Dakota Regional Water System; (2) Lewis and Clark Regional Water System, Inc.; and (3) Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System.

life.reason: Safe, reliable water supplies could support human health in rural communities, though possible river effects on wildlife are not addressed.

water.reason: The studies examine bringing reliable water to rural and small-town communities, but only as studies, with no guaranteed result or quality standards.

transparency.reason: Two of the three studies require public reports and study documents, though the third has no such requirement.

people_over_profit.reason: The projects are run by nonprofits and focus on community water needs, though 'industrial' use could also benefit businesses.

local_say.reason: Locally run nonprofit water systems partner on the studies, and two require consulting tribal, state, and local authorities.

news.overall: Only two headlines from one outlet (Christian Science Monitor, Center) were provided, and neither addresses the South Dakota bill directly. The evidence is limited to a single perspective with no article descriptions, so no comparison across perspectives is possible. The coverage that is present concerns Western reservoir and Colorado River conditions rather than the state-level water feasibility legislation.

label: H.R. 5490
title: Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
one: Creates a White House–led task force to shut down foreign online scam compounds (mainly in Southeast Asia) that use trafficked workers to steal from Americans, requires sanctions review of named people and companies, and funds help for trafficking victims.
summary:
This bill targets large criminal "scam compounds" in places like Burma, Cambodia, and Laos. Many of these use trafficked people, forced to run online scams such as "pig butchering" (fake romance or crypto investment cons). The bill says Americans lost at least $10 billion to these scams in 2024.

Within 30 days of becoming law, the President must set up a task force led by the Secretary of State. It would include State, Justice, Homeland Security, and Treasury, and could include the SEC, FTC, FCC, and others. Within 180 days it must write a strategy to close scam centers, go after the criminals and corrupt officials, build up foreign police partners, recover stolen money, and work with banks, social media, crypto exchanges, and phone companies. The strategy also lists "offensive cyber" tools and pushing for international financial watchlisting of countries such as Cambodia.

The President must decide, within 180 days, whether about 50 named people and companies should be sanctioned (frozen assets, visa bans). If someone isn't sanctioned, the President must explain why. The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons after notifying Congress. Trafficking victims are exempt from sanctions.

The State Department may fund care, shelter, and reintegration help for trafficking victims. The bill authorizes $30 million per year for 2026 and 2027. The task force ends after seven years and must report to Congress yearly.
does: Requires the President to create a task force, chaired by the Secretary of State, within 30 days of enactment.
Requires a government-wide strategy within 180 days to shut down scam centers, stop trafficking into them, and hold corrupt officials accountable.
Requires the President to decide whether about 50 named individuals and companies (e.g., Prince Group, Huione Group) meet sanctions criteria, and to impose sanctions if so.
Requires a written justification to Congress for any named person who is not sanctioned; allows a national-security waiver with 15 days' notice.
Exempts people the President finds to be trafficking victims from sanctions.

Directs agencies to fully share data and plans with the task force, and to consult state and local police, anti-trafficking groups, and private companies like banks, social media, and crypto exchanges.

Lists strategy goals including investigating Chinese and Burmese military involvement, building foreign law enforcement capacity, using offensive cyber tools, recovering stolen assets, and urging Financial Action Task Force listing of countries like Cambodia.
Authorizes State Department programs for trauma-informed care, shelter, and reintegration of trafficking victims in scam centers.
Requires annual unclassified reports to Congress (with possible classified annex) for five years on sanctions, losses, recovered funds, victims, and known scam centers.
Authorizes $30 million for each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027, and ends the task force after seven years.
who: Americans targeted by online investment and romance scams, especially older adults and people who lose savings
Trafficking victims forced to work in scam compounds
Named foreign individuals and companies, and officials in Cambodia, Laos, and Burma
Federal agencies (State, Justice, DHS, Treasury, and possibly SEC, FTC, FCC)
Banks, crypto exchanges, social media, dating apps, and telecom firms asked to partner
State and local law enforcement
U.S. taxpayers, who fund the $30 million per year

benefits: The bill may help disrupt large criminal scam networks that target Americans.
Trafficking victims may receive care, shelter, and help returning to normal life.
Trafficking victims are exempt from sanctions, which may protect them from penalties tied to the scam operations.
A single coordinated task force may bring several agencies together on the problem.
Sanctions and international financial watchlisting could make it harder for scam operators to move and hide money.
Required yearly reports to Congress may give lawmakers ongoing information about the effort.
concerns: The 'offensive cyber' tools listed in the strategy are not described in the material, so their scope and risks are unclear.
The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons, which may limit how firmly the sanctions are applied.
Sanctions on foreign government officials could affect diplomatic relations with the countries involved, though the material does not discuss this.
Requiring banks, social media firms, and phone companies to work with the government may raise privacy questions, which the material does not address.
The task force has a fixed seven-year life, so its work may not continue if the problem lasts longer.
imp.cost: ["The bill authorizes $30 million per year for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 for the State Department to provide trafficking victim support. The material does not say how the rest of the task force and strategy would be funded, and it does not state a total cost estimate."]
unknowns: The material does not say how the 'offensive cyber' tools would be used or what legal limits would apply.
It is not stated which specific 50 people and companies are named or which may be sanctioned.
The effect on scam operations in Burma, Cambodia, and Laos is not predicted in the material.
It is not stated how the bill would affect Americans' privacy when banks and phone companies work with the government.
The bill's current status is 'out of committee' and on the House calendar; whether it will pass is not stated.
The material is based on draft text, which may differ from the introduced bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to shut down criminal syndicates that run mass online scams against Americans, especially scam compounds in Southeast Asia that use trafficked people to carry out financial fraud such as "pig butchering" schemes. It aims to do this through a federal task force, a government-wide strategy, sanctions on named individuals and companies and their supporters, and help for trafficking victims. The bill states that Americans lost at least $10 billion to these scams in 2024.

oppose: The strategy lists 'offensive cyber' tools without describing what they are, so a constituent may ask what limits would apply and how these tools would be overseen.
The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons after giving Congress 15 days' notice, which a constituent may feel weakens how firmly the sanctions are enforced.
The bill would require banks, social media companies, and phone companies to work with the government, which raises privacy questions the bill's summary does not address.
Sanctions on foreign government officials could strain diplomatic relationships with countries such as Burma, Cambodia, and Laos, and the bill does not discuss this risk.
support: Americans lost at least $10 billion to these scams in 2024, according to the bill, and a coordinated federal task force could bring several agencies together on the problem.
The bill authorizes sanctions that freeze assets and block visas for people and companies that run or support scam compounds, which could make it harder for scam operators to move and hide money.
Trafficking victims are exempt from sanctions and may receive trauma-informed care, shelter, and help returning to normal life, which addresses the human cost of the scam centers.
Yearly unclassified reports to Congress for five years would give lawmakers ongoing information on sanctions, losses, recovered funds, and victims, supporting oversight of the effort.

cost_flag: The bill authorizes $30 million per year for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 for the State Department to provide trafficking victim support. The material does not say how the rest of the task force and strategy would be funded, and it does not state a total cost estimate.
crs:
The following analysis is based on draft 
bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
This bill establishes an interagency task force to shut down criminal syndicates perpetuating mass online scams. This bill also explicitly authorizes sanctions against foreign individuals or entities operating or providing support to scam compounds. (Scam compounds target individuals for financial fraud and are concentrated in Southeast Asia.)  
The President must establish an interagency task force to shut down transnational criminal syndicates that use large scam centers and forced labor of trafficked persons to perpetuate mass online scams against Americans. The task force must submit to Congress and oversee implementation of a strategy to combat scam centers, dismantle the criminal elements involved with them, and hold corrupt officials accountable. The task force must periodically report to Congress, including a list of foreign persons sanctioned by the United States for their involvement with online financial scams from Southeast Asia against U.S. nationals.
The President is explicitly authorized to impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on (1) any foreign individual or entity that owns, controls, directs, or provides significant support to a significant scam compound operation or an enabling service; and (2) foreign government officials who knowingly enable or benefit from scam compound operations within their jurisdiction.
The Department of State is authorized to provide (1) trauma-informed care and other support services for trafficked persons within online scam centers, and (2) high-resolution satellite imagery to nongovernmental organizations and research institutions for the purposes of monitoring and documenting human rights abuses related to online scam centers in Southeast Asia.

label: H.R. 7934
title: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
short_title: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
one: Requires federal agencies to publish a searchable public online database of major settlement agreements (large payments, monitors, or state/local government parties), with exceptions for confidential or FOIA-exempt material.
summary: This bill would make federal agencies put information about their larger settlement agreements on a public website. A settlement agreement here includes consent decrees and deferred prosecution agreements that resolve alleged violations of federal law. An agreement is covered if it requires at least $10 million in payments, involves a special master or monitor (an outside overseer), involves a state, tribal, or local government, or meets other criteria set by the White House budget office (OMB). Each agency would have two years to set up a searchable database. It would list whether the case is civil or criminal, the date signed, the laws allegedly broken, attorneys' fees, payments to or from the government, fines and penalties, how long the deal lasts, and any governments named. A copy of the agreement would also be posted. Some things are left out: personnel cases, non-prosecution agreements and plea bargains, tax matters, and Bankruptcy Trustee matters. Information under a court-ordered confidentiality or that could be withheld under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) also need not be posted, nor must classified information. Agencies must report yearly on how many agreements they kept hidden and why. The bill would apply to new agreements and, where practical, to ones signed since January 1, 2015 that are still active. Posting would not change the terms of any deal or create new legal rights.
does: Requires each agency with a covered settlement to create a public, searchable online database within 2 years.
Covers settlements of $10M+ in obligated payments, those with a special master or monitor, those involving state, tribal or local governments, and others OMB designates.
Requires posting of a copy of each agreement plus key details such as payments, penalties, attorneys' fees, alleged violations, and duration.
Directs OMB, with the Attorney General, to issue guidance within 1 year on dates, data standards, and a common web address format like agencyname.gov/settlements.
Exempts material under confidentiality provisions or court orders, FOIA-exempt material, and classified information.
Excludes personnel actions, non-prosecution agreements, plea bargains, tax matters, Bankruptcy Trustee matters, and certain chapter 46 of title 18 matters.
Requires an annual public report to Congress on how many covered agreements were fully withheld and under which exemptions.
Applies to new agreements and, where practicable, to active ones signed since January 1, 2015.
who: Federal agencies that enter settlements (they must build and maintain databases)
Companies and other parties that settle with the federal government
State, local, and tribal governments named in settlements
Journalists, researchers, watchdog groups, and the general public
Congress and OMB, which gain oversight information and issue guidance
Communities affected by settlements, such as environmental or consent decree cases

benefits: Public could see settlement terms, payments, penalties, and monitors in one searchable place.
Standardized, machine-readable data helps journalists, researchers, and watchdogs spot patterns.
Annual report on withheld agreements shows how often secrecy is used.
State, local, and tribal governments and communities can more easily see agreements that affect them.
Retroactive coverage back to 2015 (where practicable) extends visibility to ongoing agreements.
concerns: Agreements under confidentiality clauses or court orders, or FOIA-exempt material, can be withheld, which may leave major gaps.
'To the extent practicable' language and retroactivity limits may lead to uneven compliance.
The bill creates no right to enforce or challenge omissions.
Smaller settlements under $10M with no monitor or government party may not be covered unless OMB designates them.
Excluded categories such as plea bargains, non-prosecution agreements, and tax matters stay out of view.
Agencies bear new compliance work and costs.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is provided in the text I was given. Agencies would have to cover the cost of building and maintaining databases, likely from existing budgets.
unknowns: Actual cost to agencies and any CBO estimate.
How many agreements would be withheld under confidentiality or FOIA exemptions.
What additional criteria OMB would set to designate covered agreements.
How fully agencies would cover pre-enactment agreements.
Whether Senate action or changes would occur; the bill has passed the House.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make federal settlement agreements easier for the public to find and understand by requiring agencies to post covered agreements and key details (such as payments, penalties, attorneys' fees, alleged violations, and duration) in a searchable online database. The bill's findings and CRS summary describe this as a way to increase public visibility into larger government settlements, including those involving monitors, state, local, or tribal governments, or large payments.

oppose: The bill would require agencies to build and maintain new searchable databases within 2 years, which adds compliance work and costs for agencies that already have limited resources.

Many agreements can still be withheld. The bill exempts material under court-ordered confidentiality, material that FOIA allows agencies to withhold, and classified information, so the database may have major gaps.
The 'to the extent practicable' language and limits on retroactive coverage could lead to uneven compliance, and the bill creates no right to enforce or challenge missing information.
Some kinds of agreements, such as non-prosecution agreements, plea bargains, and tax matters, are excluded entirely, which could limit how complete the public picture is.
support: The bill would put settlement terms, payments, penalties, attorneys' fees, and court-appointed monitors in one public, searchable place, so citizens can see how their government resolves claims.
Posting standardized, machine-readable data would help journalists, researchers, and watchdog groups spot patterns across agencies and track large agreements over time.
The annual report to Congress on withheld agreements would show how often agencies use secrecy exemptions, giving lawmakers and the public a way to check that practice.

Covering agreements that involve state, tribal, or local governments would help communities see deals that directly affect them, and retroactive coverage back to 2015 would extend visibility to agreements still in effect.

crs:
Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
This bill requires federal agencies to publish a searchable, online database of information about certain settlement agreements entered into by the agency. The database must include
a copy of each settlement agreement,
whether the agreement resolves a civil or criminal claim (or both),
the date the agreement was executed,
any alleged statutory violations,
the amount of attorneys fees provided by or to the United States,
any payment made to or by the federal government,
the projected duration of the agreement, and
any unit of government that is identified by the terms of the agreement.
In general, the bill applies to settlement agreements that
require at least $10 million in payments by a settling party;
involve the appointment of a special master or monitor;
involve a party that is a state, county, or local government; or
meet other criteria as determined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
The bill excludes several types of settlement agreements from the database, including agreements related to a federal employee personnel action, a non-prosecution agreement or plea bargain, or the Internal Revenue Code.
To extent practicable, the bill also applies retroactively to covered settlement agreements that were entered into on or after January 1, 2015, and remain in effect on or after the date of enactment.
The OMB must issue guidance to implement the bill.

transparency.reason: It requires public, searchable databases of settlement terms and payments and an annual report on what is withheld.

people_over_profit.reason: Public visibility into corporate settlements and penalties could improve accountability, though exemptions limit the effect.

local_say.reason: Listing state, local, and tribal governments named in settlements helps communities see and respond to agreements affecting them.

no_bailouts.reason: Making payments and terms public could help people see where settlement money goes, though it does not directly block bailouts or tax breaks.

honesty_kindness.reason: It promotes openness and honest disclosure by agencies, including reporting on what they choose not to disclose.

label: H.R. 9640
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the U.S. Geological Survey's Earth Mapping Resources Initiative through fiscal 2031 with $84 million, adds new data sources and technologies, and requires contractor ownership disclosure with a preference for U.S.-owned firms.
summary:
This bill keeps alive a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program called the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, often called Earth MRI. The program maps what is under U.S. ground, especially critical minerals such as lithium and titanium, and the bill's text also names geothermal and geologic hydrogen resources. The bill would authorize $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. "Authorize" means Congress says the money may be spent. A separate spending law must actually provide it.

The bill also updates how the mapping is done. It says the program may use newer tools such as airborne gravity gradiometry (measuring tiny changes in gravity from aircraft), digital chemical analysis, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis. It adds the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps U.S. water features, to the data sources the program must combine.

Finally, the bill sets new rules for contracts. Any company that wants a contract under the program must disclose who owns the main contractor and each subcontractor. The USGS must also, when practical, prefer companies that are owned and controlled in the United States, while still considering specialized expertise it needs.
does: placeholder
who: USGS and its scientists
Mining, minerals, geothermal and hydrogen exploration companies that use public maps
Contractors and subcontractors bidding for USGS mapping work, especially foreign-owned firms
State geological surveys and universities that work with USGS data
Taxpayers, who fund the program
Communities near areas that may be mapped and later explored for resources

benefits: Public ownership disclosure for contractors and subcontractors adds transparency about who does government work.
Combining water mapping data could improve public knowledge of water resources.
Publicly funded geologic maps can help communities, researchers and regulators, and can reduce duplicate private surveys.
Bipartisan sponsorship, including Rep. Dingell, suggests broad support.
concerns: Better mineral maps could speed mining and exploration, which can harm water, air, land, wildlife and local communities if not carefully regulated.
The bill does not add any public input or local consent steps for areas that may later be explored or developed.
The U.S.-owned preference could limit competition or access to specialized expertise, though the bill says expertise must still be considered.
The disclosure requirement does not say whether the ownership information will be public.
imp.cost: Authorizes $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. This is taxpayer money from general federal funds, and it only gets spent if Congress separately appropriates it. The text does not give a CBO cost estimate.
unknowns: Whether Congress will actually appropriate the full $84 million.
Whether contractor ownership disclosures will be published or kept internal.
How much preference U.S.-owned firms will get in practice, since it applies only 'to the extent practicable'.
How the mapping results will later be used for leasing or mining decisions, which this bill does not address.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reauthorize the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, a USGS program that maps U.S. natural resources with a focus on critical minerals such as lithium and titanium, through fiscal year 2031. According to the CRS summary, it also expands the program's data integration, adds the USGS 3D Hydrography Program data, allows newer sensing technologies, and sets rules on contractor ownership and preference for U.S.-owned contractors.

oppose: Better mineral maps could make mining and exploration faster. If those projects are not carefully regulated, they can harm water, air, land, wildlife, and nearby communities, so you could ask how the bill protects these areas.
The bill does not add public input or local consent steps for areas that may later be explored or developed. You could ask the member whether residents would have a say before work begins.

The preference for U.S.-owned contractors could narrow the pool of companies and limit access to specialized expertise. The bill says expertise must still be considered, and you could ask how that balance will be applied in practice.
The ownership disclosure requirement does not say whether the information will be public. You could ask the member to make it clear that the public can see who is doing government-funded work.
support: The bill extends a USGS mapping program through 2031. Modern geologic maps of critical minerals such as lithium and titanium can help the country plan supply chains and reduce reliance on foreign sources.
Publicly funded maps can help communities, researchers, and regulators, and can reduce duplicate private surveys. You could say this is a good use of federal science dollars.

Adding USGS 3D Hydrography Program data would combine water resource mapping with geologic data, which could improve public knowledge of water resources. The bill also requires ownership disclosure for contractors and subcontractors, which adds transparency about who does government work.

The bill has bipartisan sponsorship, including Rep. Dingell, which suggests broad support. The U.S.-owned contractor preference applies only where practical and still allows for specialized expertise the program needs.

cost_flag: Authorizes $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. This is taxpayer money from general federal funds, and it only gets spent if Congress separately appropriates it. The text does not give a CBO cost estimate.
crs:
Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program charged with integrating and modernizing the mapping of U.S. natural resources, with a focus on critical mineral resources such as lithium and titanium. The bill also expands the initiative’s data integration functions and requires the USGS to give preference to U.S. contractors under the initiative.
Specifically, the bill requires entities contracting with the USGS pursuant to the initiative to disclose the ownership of the primary contractor and each subcontractor carrying out a part of the contract. To the extent practicable, the USGS must give preference to entities owned and controlled in the United States when entering contracts under the initiative, while giving appropriate consideration to specialized expertise essential to the objectives of the initiative.
Further, under current law, the initiative is required to provide certain types of integrated mapping, including geologic, geophysical, and topographical mapping. Under the bill, the initiative must include data from the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps U.S. water resources. The bill also explicitly allows the initiative’s integrated mapping to include data from modern sensing technologies, including real-time data acquisition systems and data-driven analytical methods.

water.reason: It adds the USGS 3D Hydrography Program water mapping data to the initiative, which could improve knowledge of water resources.

transparency.reason: It requires contractors to disclose ownership of the primary contractor and subcontractors, though public release is not specified.

local_say.reason: It speeds up mapping of resources that could lead to development in local areas without adding any community input.

label: H.R. 2102
title: Major Richard Star Act
one: The bill would let certain medically retired veterans with combat-related disabilities and fewer than 20 years of service keep their full military retired pay while also receiving their VA disability compensation, instead of having one reduced by the other.
summary:
Today, many veterans who retire from the military and also get VA disability pay see their military retired pay cut by the amount of the disability pay. This is called an "offset." Some veterans who served 20 or more years have had that offset removed over time. But veterans who were medically retired because of injury or illness (under "chapter 61" of the law) with fewer than 20 years of service are still hit by the offset, even when their disability came from combat.

This bill would end the offset for that group. If a veteran was medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service and is eligible for combat-related special compensation (a separate payment for combat-related disabilities), their retired pay could no longer be reduced because of their VA disability pay. They would receive both in full.

The bill also cleans up the law. It changes a section title and deletes old language about a phase-in period that has already ended. The changes would start on the first day of the first month after the bill becomes law. They would apply to payments for months from that date on. The bill does not say it pays back money withheld in the past. It also does not state a cost. The House has passed it, and it now goes to the Senate Armed Services Committee.
does: Stops the reduction of military retired pay for combat-related disabled veterans who retired for medical reasons (chapter 61) with fewer than 20 years of service.
Applies to those veterans who are eligible for combat-related special compensation.
Changes the title of section 1414 of title 10 to refer to "concurrent receipt" of retired pay and VA disability compensation.
Removes outdated phase-in language that no longer applies.
Takes effect the first day of the first month after enactment, covering payments from then on.
who: Veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service who have combat-related disabilities
Families and survivors who depend on those veterans' income
The Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs, which administer the payments
Federal taxpayers, because the government would pay out more

benefits: Veterans with combat-related disabilities in this group could receive their full retired pay and full VA disability pay.
Could reduce financial strain for veterans whose retired pay was previously cut by the offset.
The bill removes an outdated phase-in provision, which may make the law easier to read.
concerns: The bill does not pay back money withheld in the past, so veterans who lost pay before the change may not get that money back.
Because the change applies only to this group, veterans with other disabilities or other service lengths may still face the offset.
The material does not describe how the change fits with other concurrent-receipt rules.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state a cost or a funding source. The material does not give an estimate of how much more the government would pay out in retired pay."]
unknowns: How many veterans would be affected.
The total cost to the government and how it would be funded.
Whether the Senate will pass the bill in its current form.
Whether any back pay will be considered in the future.
The exact meaning of the section title change, since the material does not give the new title.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to stop the reduction of military retired pay for certain veterans with combat-related disabilities who were medically retired (under chapter 61 of title 10) with fewer than 20 years of service, so they can receive both their retired pay and VA disability compensation in full. The bill also updates the title of section 1414 of title 10 to refer to "concurrent receipt" and removes outdated phase-in language that no longer applies.

oppose: The bill does not pay back money that was withheld from veterans in the past, so veterans who already lost retired pay under the offset would not get that money back.

The bill covers only one group: combat-related disabled veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service. Veterans with other disabilities or other service lengths would still face the offset, which some may see as an uneven result.

The summary does not explain how this change fits with other concurrent-receipt rules, and it does not state a cost, so Congress would need to review the budget impact and related rules before acting.
support: The bill would let eligible veterans with combat-related disabilities receive their full military retired pay and full VA disability pay, without the offset that cuts retired pay today.
The offset currently applies to veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service even when their disability came from combat, and this bill would end that reduction for that group.
The bill removes an outdated phase-in provision and updates a section title, which may make the law clearer for veterans and the agencies that apply it.

crs:
Major Richard Star Act
This bill allows a veteran with a combat-related disability to receive retirement pay, without reduction, concurrently with their disability compensation. This includes veterans with a combat-related disability and fewer than 20 years of creditable service. (Currently, veterans who receive combat-related special compensation and retirement pay are subject to an offset in retirement pay for concurrent receipt of such benefits.)

people_over_profit.reason: Veterans with combat-related disabilities keep their full retired pay instead of having it reduced by VA disability pay, which favors individual people's income over government payment limits, though it is not a corporate profit issue.

no_bailouts.reason: It increases federal payouts to a specific group without offsetting funding, and the bill states no cost, so it adds to federal spending that taxpayers fund.

honesty_kindness.reason: Ending the offset for combat-disabled veterans who were medically retired treats them more fairly and compassionately, and the bill also cleans up outdated language.

label: H.R. 7954
title: Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act
one: Directs the Interior Department to help Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations own, restore, and manage buffalo herds and habitat on Indian land, through contracts, grants, technical help, consultation, and transfer of surplus federal buffalo, for seven years.
summary: This bill would tell the Department of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations so they can own and manage buffalo (bison) and the land where buffalo live on Indian land. Interior would have to sign contracts and cooperative agreements and give grants to Tribes and qualifying Tribal groups. The money could pay for buffalo restoration or management programs, commercial activities tied to buffalo or buffalo products, mobile Tribal meat processing facilities, and other related work. Interior would also have to give technical help. Within one year, and then on an ongoing basis, Interior would have to consult with Tribes on Interior actions that affect buffalo, including efforts to contain or wipe out diseased buffalo. It would also write a policy for managing buffalo and habitat on Indian land that follows Tribal-approved plans and Tribal laws. Information that Tribes label as culturally sensitive, proprietary, or confidential could not be shared by Interior. Interior could also, but is not required to, sign agreements to move surplus buffalo from federal land onto Indian land, and could waive charges for them. The bill says it does not weaken federal or state laws on diseased buffalo or buffalo that escape Indian land, and it does not change treaty rights. The authority ends seven years after the bill becomes law. The bill does not set a dollar amount.

crs:
Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act
This bill directs the Department of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and tribal organizations to develop and promote tribal ownership and management of buffalo and buffalo habitat on Indian lands.
Specifically, the bill requires Interior to (1) enter into contracts, award grants, and provide technical assistance to Tribes and tribal organizations for activities related to buffalo restoration or management; (2) consult with Tribes and tribal organizations on initiatives that affect buffalo or buffalo habitat, including efforts to contain or eradicate diseased buffalo; and (3) develop a policy related to buffalo and buffalo habitat management activities on Indian land.

The authority provided by the bill sunsets seven years after enactment.

honesty_kindness.reason: It acknowledges the historical harm of near-extermination of buffalo and supports Tribal cultural and food needs while protecting treaty rights.

label: H.R. 8483
title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
one: Moves about 847 acres of federal land in San Diego County into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians, keeps public access and fire-response access, and bans casino gaming on it.
summary:
This bill would take three pieces of federal land in San Diego County, California, totaling about 847 acres, and place them in trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. "In trust" means the United States holds the land for the Tribe, and it becomes part of the Tribe's reservation. One piece (about 164 acres) is now managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The other two (about 683 acres) are now managed by the Forest Service, and control of those would move to the Interior Department.

The transfer comes with conditions. Existing rights such as easements, leases, permits and road rights-of-way would stay in place. The public would keep access for recreation, scenery, science and conservation, including existing roads and trails, under the rules in effect when the bill is enacted. Federal employees would keep access for search and rescue, wildfire fighting, evacuations and land management. Federal agencies could still do fuel-reduction work in consultation with the Tribe. The Tribe must maintain the fuel break (a cleared strip meant to slow wildfire) on the two Forest Service parcels to Forest Service standards. The land cannot be used for casino-style gaming. Existing water rights and service agreements would not be changed. The Interior and Agriculture departments must prepare an official map available for public inspection. The bill text gives no cost estimate.

Transfers administrative control of the two Forest Service parcels (about 683 acres) to the Interior Department.
Keeps existing liens, rights-of-way, leases, permits and easements in place.
Keeps public access for recreation, scenic, scientific and conservation uses, plus existing roads and trails, under current rules.

Lets federal agencies do fuels reduction and restoration work in consultation with the Tribe.
Requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break on the two Forest Service parcels to Forest Service standards.
Bans class II and class III gaming (casino-style gaming) on the land.
Says existing water rights and service agreements are not altered.
Requires an official map to be prepared and kept open for public inspection.

Nearby residents and recreational users of the trails and roads in San Diego County
Bureau of Land Management, Forest Service and Interior Department staff
Holders of existing permits, leases, easements and rights-of-way on the land

benefits: Gives the Barona Tribe more control over land next to its reservation.
Keeps public recreation access and existing trails and roads.
Guarantees firefighters and rescuers access and keeps fuel-break upkeep in place.
Bans casino-style gaming on the land.
Leaves existing water rights and service agreements unchanged.
Requires a public map.
concerns: Federal public land would leave the national forest and BLM system and become tribal trust land, which some people may see as a loss of public land.
Public access is tied to the rules in effect at enactment, and later tribal management could differ.
Tribe takes on fuel break maintenance costs with no funding stated.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to take three parcels of federal land in San Diego County, California (about 847 acres) into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians, making them part of the Tribe's reservation. The bill's summary says it also transfers administrative control of two Forest Service parcels to the Interior Department and sets conditions to keep existing rights, public access, and firefighting access in place.

oppose: The bill would move about 847 acres of federal public land out of the Forest Service and BLM systems and into tribal trust status, so the public would lose the broader federal management that now applies to these parcels.

Public access is tied to the rules in effect on the date of enactment. Later tribal decisions could change how the land is used, and a constituent may want firm, long-term guarantees that recreation and trail access will continue.

The Tribe would take on fuel break maintenance on two parcels to Forest Service standards, but the bill does not state any funding for this work. A constituent may ask how this cost will be covered and whether wildfire risk to nearby communities is adequately addressed.

Minor boundary adjustments can be made by agreement between agencies, and the public may not see these changes in advance. A constituent may ask for more public notice and comment before boundaries change.
support: The bill would give the Barona Tribe land next to its existing reservation, which could support its governance and its use of land it considers important to its community.

The bill keeps public recreation, scenic, scientific and conservation access, including existing roads and trails, so current visitors would still be able to use these areas under the rules in place at enactment.

The bill guarantees that BLM and Forest Service staff can reach the land for search and rescue, wildfire suppression, evacuations and land management, and it requires the Tribe to keep the fuel break maintained to Forest Service standards.
The bill bans casino-style gaming on the transferred land and states that existing water rights and service agreements are not changed.

Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
This bill takes three parcels of specified federal land (approximately 847 acres) in San Diego County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians of the Barona Reservation, California. The land taken into trust shall be part of the Tribe's reservation.
One parcel (approximately 164 acres) is currently administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), and two parcels (approximately 683 acres) are currently administered by the Forest Service. The bill requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break within two of the parcels in accordance with applicable Forest Service standards.
The bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

transparency.reason: Requires an official map on file for public inspection, though minor adjustments can be made by agency agreement.

people_over_profit.reason: Bans gaming and keeps public access, so the land is not opened to commercial gaming profits.

local_say.reason: Gives the Tribe greater control over land next to its reservation while keeping existing public access.

label: H.R. 9237
title: Take Care of America's Veterans Act
short_title: Take Care of America's Veterans Act
one: A very large veterans' package that expands pay and benefits, mental health and suicide-prevention care, and survivor support, tightens VA oversight and reporting, authorizes major VA building projects, and also changes how sleep apnea and tinnitus are rated.
summary: This is a huge veterans bill that touches almost every part of the VA. It would let more retired veterans collect both military retired pay and VA disability pay, and let remarried surviving spouses keep certain benefits. It would raise survivor payments, add a monthly extra payment for veterans who need daily help, and make it easier to get Guard and Reserve home loans (with higher fees in some cases). VA could no longer deny a claim only because a veteran missed an exam. The bill expands mental health and suicide-prevention programs, starts a naloxone (overdose rescue drug) pilot, a service dog grant pilot, and a program for veterans with spinal injuries. It adds protections and better notices for survivors of military sexual trauma, and requires lactation rooms at VA hospitals. It orders many studies and public reports, creates an outside advisory commission, and gives Congress stronger access to VA records. It authorizes billions for new VA medical centers in Manchester, San Antonio and Indianapolis. It also orders VA to rewrite ratings for sleep apnea and tinnitus; for new claims these changes could lower some ratings, though current awards are protected. Parts of the bill text were not visible to me, so some details are missing.
does: Allows concurrent receipt of military retired pay and VA disability pay for certain retirees with combat-related disabilities (Major Richard Star Act).

Take Care of America's Veterans Act
This bill addresses veterans’ benefits, health care, counseling, Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) personnel, VA infrastructure, and the Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP).

revises VA disability ratings for sleep apnea and tinnitus;
expands eligibility for a memorial headstone or marker for the spouse, surviving spouse, child, or dependent of a veteran or member of the Armed Forces;
addresses the administration of the VCCP and codifies the eligibility standards;
establishes a standardized screening process for priority or routine admission to certain mental health care programs; and
addresses VA personnel, hiring, and infrastructure matters.

label: H.R. 9600
title: Common Sense 250 Act of 2026
short_title: Common Sense 250 Act (Thomas Paine monument location)
one: The bill approves placing the already-authorized Thomas Paine monument in Area I of the National Mall, the zone reserved for works of preeminent historical significance.
summary: Congress already authorized a monument to Thomas Paine in a 2023 spending law. Paine was the writer whose pamphlet "Common Sense" argued for American independence. This bill does one narrow thing: it decides where that monument can go. Normally, the Commemorative Works Act (the law that controls memorials in Washington, DC) sets strict rules for putting a memorial in Area I, the most prestigious part of the National Mall and its surroundings. Area I is saved for works of preeminent and lasting importance to the nation. This bill says "notwithstanding" those rules, which means it skips the normal requirements. It approves the location for the Paine monument within Area I, as shown on a 2003 National Capital Planning map, and requires the monument be built there. The bill does not say how much the monument would cost, who would pay, or exactly which spot inside Area I. It does not appear to provide federal money. Since the bill text skips the usual approval steps for Area I, the usual review by planning and design bodies and public input may be shortened. The bill text itself does not describe those review steps, so that is a possible consequence, not a stated provision.
does: placeholder
who: Visitors to the National Mall and Washington, DC
The group or sponsors building the Thomas Paine memorial
National Park Service and DC planning and review bodies
Taxpayers, if any federal costs arise (none stated in the bill)

Gives clarity on location so planning and fundraising can move ahead.
Narrow bill with no stated new spending.
concerns: Skips the normal Area I requirements, which could shorten the usual review and public input.
Sets a precedent for Congress to bypass the Commemorative Works Act case by case.
Placement on the Mall's prime area could limit other uses of the space and affect open space.
imp.cost: The bill contains no appropriation or cost estimate. Funding for the monument is not addressed in the text I was given. Under the Commemorative Works Act, memorials are generally privately funded, but the text here does not state that.

Total cost and who pays for building and maintenance.
Which of the normal Area I requirements would be skipped in practice and what review would still happen.
Whether the Senate will act on it.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to place the already-authorized Thomas Paine monument in Area I of the National Mall, an area reserved for commemorative works of preeminent and lasting historical significance. According to the CRS summary, Paine wrote "Common Sense," which argued for American independence from Great Britain. The bill's stated aim is to set the monument's location, and it does this by setting aside the normal Commemorative Works Act rules for Area I.

oppose: The bill says "notwithstanding" the Commemorative Works Act, so it skips the normal Area I requirements that are meant to limit Area I to works of preeminent and lasting national importance.

Skipping those steps may shorten the usual review by planning and design bodies and reduce opportunities for public input. The bill text does not itself describe those review steps, so this is a possible effect rather than a stated provision.
Congress would be setting a location for a memorial directly, which could become a precedent for bypassing the Commemorative Works Act case by case.
Placing a monument in the Mall's most prominent area could limit other future uses of that space and affect its open character.
support: Congress already authorized this monument in a 2023 spending law, and this bill only settles where it goes, which could help planning move forward.
The bill would honor Thomas Paine, whose pamphlet "Common Sense" argued for American independence, in the year of the 250th anniversary.
The bill is narrow: it names a location within Area I shown on a 2003 National Capital Planning Commission map and does not state new federal spending.
Supporters could argue that a figure central to the nation's founding deserves a prominent place on the Mall, and that Area I is appropriate for that kind of work.

label: H.R. 4464
title: Preventive Health Savings Act
one: Lets key congressional leaders ask the Congressional Budget Office to estimate long-term (10–30 years out) spending savings from preventive health care in a bill, shown as an extra estimate that cannot be used for budget enforcement.
summary: Right now, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) mostly estimates what bills cost over 10 years. That can make prevention look like a bad deal, because the savings from preventing disease often show up many years later. This bill changes the rules for one narrow situation. If the top Republican and Democrat on the Budget Committee and on the main committee handling a bill (in either the House or Senate) ask for it, CBO must decide whether the bill would cut government spending in later years by using preventive health care. "Later years" means the two 10-year periods that start 10 years from now, so roughly years 11 through 30. If CBO finds net savings, it must include in its estimate a description and number for those savings and explain how it got them. CBO may then produce projections covering those longer periods. These longer-term numbers are only extra information. They cannot be used to decide whether a bill follows the Congressional Budget Act or other budget rules, such as spending limits or pay-for requirements. Preventive health care is defined as actions that protect and promote health and prevent disease, disability, and early death. The definition includes approaches backed by public, credible evidence such as clinical trials and long-term studies. The bill spends no money and does not create any new health programs.
does: Lets the budget and main committee chairs and ranking members (of the House or Senate) jointly ask CBO to check if a bill would cut spending in later years through preventive health care.
Defines the later years as the two 10-year periods starting 10 years from now (about years 11 to 30).
Requires CBO to include a description and estimate of the savings, and the basis for them, if it finds net savings.
Allows CBO to project beyond the usual time periods.
Says the estimate is supplementary only and cannot be used for budget enforcement or compliance under the Budget Act.
Defines preventive health care as actions that protect health and prevent disease, disability, and early death, including interventions backed by credible, public evidence.
who: Members of Congress and budget/committee leaders
Congressional Budget Office staff
Patients and the public, indirectly if prevention-focused policies become easier to pass
Health care providers and public health programs
Taxpayers, indirectly

benefits: Could give lawmakers a fuller picture of long-term savings from prevention, which short 10-year scoring tends to hide.
Could make it easier to support disease prevention, which may save lives and reduce suffering.
Requires CBO to explain its basis, which supports transparency about how estimates are made.
Requires both the majority and minority leaders of the committees to join the request, so it is bipartisan by design, and it has bipartisan cosponsors.
concerns: Long-range estimates (up to 30 years) are uncertain and could be overly optimistic or be used to promote favored programs.
Because the estimates cannot be used for budget enforcement, they may have limited direct effect on whether bills pass.
Could add to CBO workload, and the bill does not provide extra funding for it.
Only leaders of the committees can request the analysis, so rank-and-file members and the public cannot trigger it.
imp.cost: The bill authorizes no new spending. CBO may have some extra administrative workload; no cost estimate or CRS cost figure was provided in the material I was given.
unknowns: How often leaders would make requests and how CBO would model 11–30 year effects.
Whether the supplementary estimates would change how Congress votes in practice.
How CBO would treat the evidence standards in the definition.
No final CBO cost estimate was included in the material I saw.

stage.last_action: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let Congress see the longer-term budget effects of preventive health care. Under current practice, CBO mainly estimates costs over 10 years, and the savings from preventing disease often arrive later, so prevention can look less worthwhile. The bill lets certain committee leaders ask CBO to look at savings in years 11 through 30 and report them as supplementary information only.

oppose: Long-range estimates covering up to 30 years are highly uncertain, and small changes in assumptions can produce large differences in projected savings.
The bill says these estimates cannot be used for budget enforcement or Budget Act compliance, so they may carry little weight in deciding whether bills pass, while still shaping debate.
CBO would take on new analytical work without any added funding in the bill, which could strain its existing workload.
Only the chairs and ranking members of the budget committee and the main committee of a bill can request the analysis, so rank-and-file lawmakers and the public cannot trigger it.
support: Ten-year budget scores can make prevention look like a poor investment because its savings often come years later, and this bill lets Congress see those longer-term effects.
Preventive care aims to reduce disease, disability, and early death, so a clearer view of its benefits could support programs that help people stay healthy.
The bill requires CBO to explain the basis for any savings it reports, which supports transparency about how estimates are made.
The request requires agreement from both the majority and minority leaders of the relevant committees, and the bill has bipartisan cosponsors.

crs:
Preventive Health Savings Act
This bill requires the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), upon receiving a request from Congress, to determine if proposed legislation would reduce spending outside of the 10-year budget window through the use of preventive health care.
Under the bill, the term 
preventive health care
 generally refers to an action that focuses on the health of the public, individuals, and defined populations in order to protect, promote, and maintain health and wellness and prevent disease, disability, and premature death.
If CBO determines that the proposed legislation would result in net reductions in budget outlays from the use of preventive health care, any CBO projection regarding the legislation must include (1) a description and estimate of the reductions in outlays, and (2) a description of the basis for these conclusions. 
Any estimate provided by CBO pursuant to this bill must be used as a supplementary estimate and may not be used to determine compliance with the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 or any other budgetary enforcement controls.

life.reason: It could make disease-prevention policies easier to justify, which may save lives, though the effect is indirect.

transparency.reason: CBO must describe and explain the basis for long-term savings estimates, giving Congress and the public more information.

label: S. 4784
title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA)
one: The annual Senate defense policy bill sets what the Pentagon and the Energy Department's nuclear weapons programs may buy, build, and do in fiscal year 2027, with a mix of spending authority, policy rules, and a few safeguards on artificial intelligence.
summary:
This is the yearly bill that gives the Department of Defense (DOD) and the nuclear weapons programs of the Department of Energy permission to spend money and sets rules for how they operate. It does not itself hand out the cash. A separate spending bill does that. The bill covers buying ships, aircraft, and vehicles, how many troops the services may have, military health care and pay, and construction on bases. It also covers cyber operations, artificial intelligence (AI), and DOD dealings with other countries.

Parts I could read include approval for multiyear contracts to buy Infantry Squad Vehicles, longer authorities for amphibious ship building, and a plan to bring the Army National Guard into Arctic planning. They also include a rule that DOD must review a facility's services before downsizing military medical facilities. Another part has limits on AI and autonomous weapons. Those limits bar AI from deciding to launch a nuclear weapon, bar AI from tracking people believed to be in the U.S. where the law does not allow it, and bar lethal force by autonomous weapons without suitable human judgment. DOD would also have to set up an incident reporting system and send yearly reports to Congress. The CRS summary adds that DOD's Office of Strategic Capital could buy ownership stakes in private companies working on batteries and critical minerals. It also says DOD must review materials such as boron carbide, copper foil, and synthetic diamond.

Important limit: much of the supplied bill text was blank or cut off, so I could not see many sections, including environmental, base cleanup, and most contracting rules.
does: Authorizes fiscal year 2027 funding levels for procurement, research, operations, military construction, and Energy Department defense programs through funding tables.
Allows multiyear contracts for Army Infantry Squad Vehicles, for up to five fiscal years, with savings and termination protections required.
Extends and widens Navy amphibious ship buying authorities (advance construction, bulk long-lead purchases, spare parts) to September 30, 2030.
Extends the time for funding the refueling overhauls of USS John C. Stennis and USS Harry S. Truman from six years to eight.
Requires the Army to bring the National Guard fully into its Arctic strategy, with a report due June 30, 2027.
Keeps the minimum C-130 aircraft inventory and the ban on cutting Guard C-130s through fiscal year 2028.
Transfers three retired F-14D Tomcats at no cost to the U.S. Space & Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama, with the recipient paying all costs.
Bars AI from nuclear launch decisions, from unlawful tracking or targeting of people believed to be in the U.S., and from lethal autonomous force without appropriate human judgment.
Requires testing of AI and autonomous weapons, a working group on AI safety, an incident repository, and annual reports to Congress through January 2037.
Requires a review before reducing services at a military medical facility (the text was cut off, so details are unknown).
Per CRS: requires DOD to review boron carbide, copper foil, and synthetic diamond supply, and lets the Office of Strategic Capital make equity investments in battery and critical-mineral firms.
Authorizes the National Nuclear Security Administration and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.

benefits: AI safeguards could reduce the risk of unlawful domestic surveillance and of machines making lethal or nuclear decisions without human control.
An AI incident repository and annual reports could give Congress and, in unclassified form, the public more visibility.
Review before downsizing military medical facilities could protect care access for service members and families.

Supply chain reviews could reduce reliance on foreign sources of key materials.
concerns: Large authorizations may flow mainly to defense contractors, and multiyear contracts could lock in spending.
Government equity investments in private battery and mineral firms could expose taxpayers to losses or favor some companies.
Classified annexes may limit public oversight of some plans and reports.
AI limits include exceptions (other statutes, and crisis, conflict, or war) that could weaken them.
Nuclear weapons and base activities can carry environmental and health risks, and I could not see any related provisions.

The F-14 transfer is at no cost to the Navy, with the recipient paying.
