label: H.R. 3495
title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
short_title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
one: Says that direct sellers (like people who sell products through home-party or network sales companies) and qualified real estate agents are not "employees" under the federal wage-and-hour law, so minimum wage and overtime rules would not apply to them.
summary:
This bill changes the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), the main federal law that sets the minimum wage and overtime pay. It adds one sentence to the law's definition of "employee." Under that sentence, anyone who counts as a "direct seller" or a "qualified real estate agent" would not be an employee under the FLSA. Those two terms are not defined in the bill itself. Instead, it points to section 3508(b) of the tax code, which already treats these groups as independent contractors for federal tax purposes. That tax rule generally covers people paid based on sales or output, not hours worked, who work under a written contract saying they are not employees for tax purposes.

In practice, a company that works with these sellers or agents would not have to pay them the federal minimum wage or overtime under the FLSA. The bill supporters call it "harmonizing" labor law with tax law so the two match. The bill does not say what happens under state wage laws, and it does not change any other federal worker protection laws, as far as the text shows. It does not include any spending. The House Rules Committee has set it for floor debate under a closed rule, meaning no floor amendments, with one hour of debate.
does: placeholder
who: Direct sellers (people who sell consumer products person-to-person, such as through home sales or network marketing companies)
Real estate agents who meet the tax code definition of a qualified real estate agent
Direct selling companies and real estate brokerages
Workers who might be misclassified or who work under unclear arrangements

benefits: Aligns federal labor-law and tax-law treatment, which could reduce confusion and legal disputes over classification.
Could keep the flexible, commission-based work arrangements many sellers and agents say they prefer.
Could lower legal and compliance risk for direct selling companies and brokerages, which may help small independent sellers keep access to the work.
concerns: Takes away federal minimum wage and overtime coverage from these workers, even if a particular worker is in practice controlled like an employee.
Could make it harder for workers to challenge misclassification under the FLSA, and might encourage companies to push more control over workers without paying wage protections.
Could shift risk and costs onto individual workers, and the exclusion is written to be broad rather than tied to actual independence.
imp.cost: The bill has no spending or funding provisions. Any cost would fall indirectly on workers (lost wage protections) or benefit businesses (lower labor costs). I could not see a Congressional Budget Office estimate in the material provided.
unknowns: How many workers would actually lose FLSA coverage today versus those already treated as contractors.
Whether state minimum wage and overtime laws would still apply to these workers.
How the tax-code definitions, which depend on written contracts and pay based on sales, would interact with real working conditions.
The text of the amendment is short, but the committee report and any floor changes were not available to me.

stage.last_action: Rules Committee Resolution H. Res. 1665 Reported to House. Rule provides for consideration of H.R. 3495 and H.R. 5267. The resolution provides for consideration of H.R. 3495 and H.R. 5267 under a closed rule with one hour of debate and one motion to recommit on each bill.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to harmonize federal labor law with federal tax law. It would add a sentence to the Fair Labor Standards Act's definition of "employee" so that direct sellers and qualified real estate agents, as defined in section 3508(b) of the tax code, are not treated as employees under that law. Supporters describe this as aligning the two laws so that workers classified as independent contractors for tax purposes are treated the same way under labor law.

oppose: The bill would remove federal minimum wage and overtime protections under the Fair Labor Standards Act from direct sellers and real estate agents, even if a worker is in practice controlled by a company the way an employee would be.

The bill's exclusion relies on a tax-code definition that covers people paid by sales or output rather than hours and who sign a contract calling them non-employees. Critics say this could be broad and does not test whether a worker is actually independent.

Critics worry the bill could make it harder for workers to challenge misclassification and could let companies shift costs and risks onto workers without paying wage protections. The bill's text does not address state wage laws, so protections there would be unchanged.
support: The bill would align federal labor law with federal tax law, which could reduce confusion and legal disputes over whether these sellers and agents are employees or independent contractors.
Supporters say many direct sellers and real estate agents prefer flexible, commission-based work and want to keep control over their schedules, and this bill would keep that arrangement in place.
Supporters argue that lowering legal and compliance risk for direct selling companies and brokerages could help small independent sellers keep access to these opportunities.

Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
This bill excludes a real estate agent or a direct seller of consumer products from the definition of an 
employee
 for the purpose of applying the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA). Workers who are considered employees under the FLSA must be paid the minimum wage and are generally eligible to receive overtime compensation for hours worked in excess of a 40-hour workweek.

people_over_profit.reason: It removes federal minimum wage and overtime protections for these workers, which could shift costs from companies to individuals, though many are commission-paid and may value flexibility.

label: H.R. 5267
title: American Franchise Act
one: The bill would write into federal law a narrow test for when a franchisor (the parent brand) counts as a joint employer of a franchisee's workers, so brands would be responsible only if they directly and regularly control things like pay, hiring, firing, or schedules.
summary:
Many fast-food, hotel, and retail brands are franchises. A local owner (the franchisee) runs the business under the parent company's (the franchisor's) name and rules. A long-running legal question is whether the parent company is also a "joint employer" of the local workers. If it is, it can be held responsible for labor-law violations and may have to bargain with a union.

This bill says a franchisor can be a joint employer only if it actually has and uses "substantial, direct, and immediate control" over at least one essential job term. Those terms are wages, benefits, hours, hiring, firing, discipline, supervision, and direction of work. The control must be regular or continuous, not occasional or minor. The bill applies this test to both the National Labor Relations Act (union and collective bargaining rights) and the Fair Labor Standards Act (minimum wage and overtime).

The bill lists things that do NOT count as control. Examples are setting store operating hours, setting minimum staffing levels, setting brand standards, offering training materials, setting minimum hiring standards, and telling a franchisee about worker misconduct. It would not apply to cases that began before the bill becomes law. It essentially puts into law a 2020 National Labor Relations Board rule that the board brought back in 2026, and it extends that approach to wage-and-hour law.
does: placeholder
who: Workers at franchise businesses (about 8.4 million, per the bill's findings)
Franchisors (national brands)
Franchisees (local owners)
Unions trying to organize or bargain at franchise locations
Federal labor agencies and courts

benefits: Gives franchisees and franchisors a clear, stable rule instead of shifting standards.
May protect small local franchise owners from being swept up with large brands in lawsuits.
Could reduce legal costs, which supporters say helps keep franchising, and its jobs, viable.
Local owners keep independence over their own hiring and labor relations.
concerns: Could make it harder for franchise workers to unionize or bargain with the brand that has real power over their jobs.
Could limit who can be held liable for wage theft or overtime violations, leaving workers to pursue only a possibly under-resourced local owner.
Lists many brand controls (hours, staffing levels, training, brand standards) as not counting, even though they can shape working conditions.
Locks in the standard by statute so future agencies cannot change it.
Applies to FLSA wage-and-hour cases too, going beyond the NLRB rule.
imp.cost: No spending or funding is provided. No cost estimate was in the material I was given. The effects would fall mostly on private parties through who is legally responsible for labor-law compliance.
unknowns: How courts would apply terms like 'regular or continuous consequential effect.'
How many workers would actually lose the ability to bargain with or sue the franchisor.
Whether the Senate would take up the bill and whether it could pass.
Whether the NLRB's 2026 reinstatement of the 2020 rule might change again without this law.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify when a franchisor (the parent company) counts as a "joint employer" of a franchisee's workers under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. It would treat a franchisor as a joint employer only if it regularly exercises direct and immediate control over essential job terms, such as wages, hours, hiring, firing, discipline, and supervision. The bill also aims to give franchisors and franchisees a clear, stable standard, and it puts into statute a 2020 National Labor Relations Board rule that the board reinstated in 2026.

oppose: The bill says a franchisor is a joint employer only if it has substantial, direct, and immediate control over essential job terms. Workers may argue that brand rules on hours, staffing, and training shape their jobs in ways this test ignores, and the bill lists those controls as not counting.

Because the bill covers the Fair Labor Standards Act as well as the NLRA, it could limit who can be held responsible for overtime or minimum wage violations. Workers could be left to seek back pay only from a local owner who may have few resources.

The bill writes the 2020 NLRB standard into law, so future agencies could not change it through regulation. Opponents may say this removes the ability to adjust the rule as workplaces and franchise models change.

The bill gives franchise owners and parent companies a clear, consistent test for when a parent is a joint employer. Supporters say this reduces confusion and lawsuit risk that come from shifting standards.
Supporters say the bill protects small, locally owned franchisees from being treated as if they were the large brand, so local owners keep control over their own hiring and labor relations.

crs:
American Franchise Act
This bill explicitly states that, for purposes of requirements under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), franchisors are only considered to be joint employers with their franchisees if they regularly exercise direct and immediate control over the terms and conditions of employment for a franchisee's employees (e.g., directly hiring or firing employees on a regular basis). (The NLRA provides for collective bargaining rights in the private sector. The FLSA provides for a minimum wage, overtime pay, and other standards for employment.)
Specifically, the bill provides statutory authority for a 2020 
rule 
by the National Labor Relations Board, particularly in relation to franchisors and franchisees. Under this rule, an entity is considered a joint employer of a separate employer's employees under the NLRA only if the entity exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over one or more essential terms or conditions of employment. 
Essential terms or conditions of employment
 are defined to mean wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. (In 2026, the board reinstated the 2020 rule as the applicable standard.) 
The bill explicitly applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees and additionally specifies conduct that does and does not meet this standard (e.g., a franchisor setting a franchisee's operating hours does not sufficiently indicate direct and immediate control over the hours of work of a franchisee's employees). The bill also applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees under the FLSA.

people_over_profit.reason: It narrows when large brands can be held responsible for workers' pay and bargaining rights, though it also gives small franchise owners clearer rules.

honesty_kindness.reason: It could leave franchise workers with fewer parties to hold accountable for unfair treatment, though supporters argue it protects small owners from unfair liability.

label: H.R. 2323
title: Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act
short_title: Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act
one: Lets the Interior Secretary add about 6,100 acres next to Big Bend National Park in Texas, but only through donation or land swap, never by forced taking.
summary: This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior bring about 6,100 acres of land into Big Bend National Park in Texas. The land is marked on a map titled "Big Bend National Park, Proposed Boundary Adjustment," dated November 2022. The government could get the land only by donation (someone gives it) or exchange (a land swap). It could not buy the land under this bill, because the bill only authorizes donation or exchange. It also bars the government from using eminent domain or condemnation, which means forcing a landowner to sell. Once the government gets any of the land, the Secretary must move the park boundary to include it and manage it like the rest of the park under existing laws and rules. The map has to be kept on file where the public can look at it, at National Park Service offices. The bill does not say how much an exchange might cost, who the current owners are, or what the land is used for today. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. The bill text is complete, but the map itself was not included in the material I reviewed.
does: unused
who: Owners of the roughly 6,100 acres shown on the map, who could choose to donate or swap land
Visitors to Big Bend National Park
National Park Service staff who would manage the added land
Nearby communities and local businesses in the Texas Big Bend region
Wildlife and plants living on the added land

benefits: Could protect more habitat for wildlife and plants by placing the land under park management.
Because it is voluntary, landowners keep the choice to take part.
Bans eminent domain, protecting landowners from forced takings.
The map must be publicly available, which supports openness.
Could improve park management by tidying up boundaries, though the bill does not say this is the goal.
concerns: Added land could raise park upkeep and staffing costs, and the bill does not say who pays.
Land exchanges could trade away federal land; the bill does not say what land might be given up.
Neighbors or local governments may lose some local land use or tax base once land becomes federal; the bill does not address this.
Landowners may feel pressure to sell or donate even without condemnation; the bill does not discuss this.
imp.cost: The bill does not authorize any specific money and no cost estimate was provided. Donations would cost little up front, but managing the land could create future costs for the National Park Service.
unknowns: Who owns the 6,100 acres and whether they support the plan
Current uses of the land, such as grazing, and whether they would continue
Cost of managing the additional land
What federal land might be offered in exchanges
No CRS summary or cost estimate was available
I did not see the map itself

purpose: The bill says it would allow the Secretary of the Interior to bring about 6,100 acres of land into Big Bend National Park in Texas, as shown on a map dated November 2022. The land could be added only through donation or exchange, not purchase or condemnation, and once acquired it would be managed as part of the park under existing laws. The bill's text does not spell out a broader problem it is meant to solve; its stated aim is to change the park's boundary to include this land.

oppose: The bill does not say who would pay for managing the added land, so park upkeep and staffing costs could fall on the federal budget.
Land exchanges could give up federal land, but the bill does not say which federal land would be traded away.
Once land becomes federal, neighboring communities and local governments may lose some tax revenue and local land-use options, and the bill does not address this.
support: The bill would add about 6,100 acres of land that could protect more habitat for wildlife and plants inside Big Bend National Park.
The bill is voluntary: land would come into the park only by donation or exchange, and landowners keep the choice to take part.
The bill bans eminent domain and condemnation, so landowners cannot be forced to sell, and the map must be available to the public at National Park Service offices.

life.reason: Adding land to the park could extend habitat protection for wildlife and plants, though the bill does not state specific conservation goals.

transparency.reason: The map must be on file and open to public inspection at National Park Service offices.

local_say.reason: Only voluntary donations or exchanges are allowed and eminent domain is barred, so landowners keep control.

label: H.R. 2116
title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
short_title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
one: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to run a public awareness campaign about foreign governments harassing or threatening people in the U.S., and to research tools to help law enforcement counter it.
summary: This bill adds a new section to the Homeland Security Act. It tells the Secretary of Homeland Security to have the department's Office of Partnership and Engagement run a public service announcement campaign. The campaign would teach the public and U.S. international allies about "transnational repression." That term means a foreign government, or someone acting under its control, trying to scare, harass, coerce, or hurt people in the U.S. or U.S. persons abroad. It includes threats against family members, efforts to silence people's First Amendment rights, and extrajudicial killings (killings outside any legal process). The campaign must also explain what help is available to victims and how to anonymously report suspected cases to the FBI. It should be run in languages the Secretary finds relevant. Within one year, and "to the extent practicable," DHS must also research and test technologies and methods to better support federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials in countering this kind of repression and related terrorism threats. That work must follow constitutional, privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties protections. The bill sets no dollar amount and does not create new crimes or new police powers. It does not say where the money comes from. The bill is out of committee and on the House calendar.

The bill does not create new crimes or new police powers, according to the summary provided.

Anonymous reporting to the FBI may make it easier for victims to come forward without fear of exposure.
Multilingual outreach could reach communities that may be most at risk.
Research into new tools could help officials at all levels respond to these threats.
The bill requires that research follow privacy and civil liberties protections.

The research requirement is limited by 'to the extent practicable,' so the level of commitment is not firm.

It aims to do this by having DHS run a public education campaign so the public and international allies can recognize the threat and know where to get help, and by directing DHS to research tools that can help federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials respond to these threats.

crs:
Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to take actions to combat transnational repression against individuals inside the United States. The term 
transnational repression
 generally refers to actions of a foreign government or agent to harm, intimidate, threaten, harass, or coerce individuals in the United States.
Specifically, the bill requires DHS to direct the Office of Partnership and Engagement to conduct a public service announcement campaign to educate the public and international allies on the issue of transnational repression and related terrorism threats.
The bill also requires DHS to conduct research and development into technologies and techniques for enhancing its support to federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials in combating transnational repression and related terrorism threats.

life.reason: A public awareness campaign on transnational repression, including threats and extrajudicial killings, and R&D to help officials counter such threats, modestly advances protection of people from harm.

transparency.reason: The bill requires DHS to publicly educate people about a foreign-government threat and how to report it, which informs the public about government work on this issue.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill aims to protect people from threats, harassment, and intimidation and to inform victims of available help, which supports kindness toward those targeted.

label: H.R. 143
title: Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
one: Starting in fiscal year 2026, the bill automatically cuts the spending limits for federal programs whose congressional authorization has expired, by 10% and then 15% a year, and ends those programs after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them.
summary:
Congress usually works in two steps. First, it passes a law that "authorizes" a program, which means it permits the program to get money. Second, it passes yearly spending bills that actually fund it. Many programs keep getting money after their authorization runs out. This bill targets those programs.

Each year, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) publishes a list of programs whose authorizations have expired or will expire that year. Under the bill, every program on that list would face automatic cuts to its share of the spending ceiling set for the House and Senate Appropriations Committees. The first year after expiration, the ceiling drops by 10% of what the program got in its last authorized year. In the second and third years, it drops by 15% each year, if the program is still unauthorized.

If a program is still unauthorized after the third year of cuts, it ends on October 1 of the following year. Only already-made commitments could still be paid off. No new money could be committed unless Congress reauthorizes it for no more than three years.

If Congress reauthorizes a program in time, with a sunset of three years or less, the cuts are cancelled and any lost funding is restored. Programs that expired before 2026 and are funded in 2026 are treated as if they expire in 2026. The cycle repeats every three years.
does: Creates a repeating three-year cut cycle for unauthorized programs, starting in fiscal year 2026.
Defines an unauthorized program as one listed in CBO's 'Expired and Expiring Authorizations of Appropriations' report.
Treats programs that expired before fiscal 2026 and are funded in 2026 as expiring in 2026.
Cuts the spending ceiling by 10% of the program's last-authorized-year funding in the first year after expiration.
Cuts it by 15% in each of the second and third years if the program is still unauthorized.
Requires the House and Senate Budget Committee chairs to send the revised levels to the Appropriations chairs.
Terminates programs after the third reduction year, with funds left only to close out valid earlier obligations.
Bars new spending on a terminated program unless Congress reauthorizes it for three years or less.
Cancels and restores cuts if a program is reauthorized in time with a sunset of three years or less.
who: Recipients and workers of federal programs with expired authorizations
Federal agencies running those programs
House and Senate Appropriations and Budget Committees
State and local governments and nonprofits that depend on federal grants
Congressional authorizing committees, which would face deadlines
Taxpayers and the public served by affected programs

benefits: May push Congress to review and renew program authorizations on a regular schedule.
Could make the link between authorization and funding more visible to lawmakers and the public.
Could reduce funding for programs that have not been reviewed in a long time.
concerns: Programs could lose funding or end even if their work is still useful, if Congress does not act in time.
Automatic cuts could create uncertainty for people and organizations that depend on these programs.
Termination after three years could disrupt services, though existing commitments could still be paid.

The exact dollar effect is not stated."]
unknowns: How many programs CBO would list in a typical year, and how much total funding they receive, is not stated.
It is not stated how the reductions would be divided among specific programs within the appropriations committees' allocations.
It is not stated how the bill would treat programs whose authorization lapses for only a short time, or how it would apply to multi-year funding beyond what is described.
The bill's latest action is 'out of committee, on the House calendar'; whether it will pass is not stated.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reduce federal spending on programs that receive annual appropriations but have no current authorization of appropriations, and to push Congress to review and renew those authorizations. It targets programs listed in CBO's annual report of expired or expiring authorizations, cutting their funding ceilings over three years and ending them if they stay unauthorized.

oppose: Automatic cuts of 10% and then 15% a year could reduce funding for programs that are still doing useful work, simply because Congress has not renewed their authorization on time.
Terminating a program after three years could interrupt services that families, schools, or local organizations depend on, even though existing commitments could still be paid.

The bill relies on a CBO list to decide which programs are hit, so timing of expiration rather than program performance determines whether funding is cut, which may not reflect whether a program is effective.
support: The bill could encourage Congress to review and renew program authorizations on a regular schedule rather than letting programs run for years without a fresh look.
Linking authorization to funding makes it clearer to lawmakers and the public which programs have not been reviewed in a long time.
Requiring reauthorization every three years or less gives taxpayers a regular checkpoint to decide whether programs should continue and in what form.

crs:
Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
This bill reduces budgetary levels for certain federal programs that are funded through the annual appropriations process and do not have an authorization of appropriations.
Under the bill, 
budgetary levels
 are spending allocations provided to the congressional appropriations committees by a congressional budget resolution or a deeming resolution. The allocations are provided under the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 and are often referred to as 302(a) allocations.
The bill applies to programs included in the Congressional Budget Office's (CBO's) annual report listing programs that are funded through the appropriations process and have an authorization of appropriations that has either expired or will expire during the year. 
If a program is listed in the CBO report, the bill requires specified reductions to be implemented over a three-year period and terminates the unauthorized programs at the end of the third unauthorized year.

transparency.reason: Ties funding levels to a public CBO list of expired authorizations, making unauthorized spending more visible and pressuring Congress to reauthorize programs openly.

label: H.R. 1640
title: HEIRS Act of 2025
one: Lets HUD give grants to help families who inherited land or homes without a will (heirs' property) pay for the legal and title work needed to keep their property and protect it from forced sale.
summary:
When someone dies without a will, their home or land often passes to several relatives who all own it together, as "tenants in common." In many places, any one of those relatives, or an outsider who buys that person's share, can ask a court to force a sale of the whole property. This has caused many families, especially low-income and Black rural families, to lose land and homes that were passed down for generations.

This bill would let the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) run two grant programs. The first would give money to states, local governments, territories, and tribal governments that have adopted (or will adopt) the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act, a model law with protections against forced sales. They would use the money to help residents pay for things like title reports, land surveys, heirs searches, estate planning, filing fees, and legal fees. The second would give grants to HUD-approved housing counseling agencies, college legal clinics, and qualifying nonprofits to give counseling, legal help, and financial help to clear titles and keep homes. Housing counselors that already get HUD money would also have to explain heirs' property risks and point people to help. Both grant programs end seven years after the bill becomes law. The bill says HUD "may" create the programs and does not set a dollar amount.
does: Lets HUD create a grant program for states, localities, territories, and tribes that have adopted or later adopt the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (or something HUD finds substantially equivalent).
who: Families who own inherited land or homes without clear title, especially low- and moderate-income and rural families

benefits: Could help families pay for the paperwork and legal steps needed to prove and clear ownership of inherited property.
Could give heirs access to counseling and legal help before a forced sale happens.
Encourages states to adopt the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act, which includes protections against forced sales.
May help families keep land and homes that have been passed down for generations.
concerns: Grants depend on states and groups applying and on HUD choosing to run the programs, so help may be uneven across places.
The seven-year end date means the programs could stop before heirs' property problems are fully addressed.
Housing counselors who already receive HUD funds would take on a new duty to explain heirs' property risks, which could add work for them.
Because the bill sets no dollar amount, the actual reach of the help is uncertain.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state a dollar amount or appropriation for either grant program. The funding level is not stated in the material provided."]
unknowns: How much money Congress would provide, and therefore how many families could be served.
How quickly HUD would set up the programs, and what rules or application process it would use.
How many states have adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act or similar laws and would qualify for grants.
Whether the grants would actually reduce forced sales of inherited property.
Whether the bill would be enacted, since its latest action is that it is out of committee and on the House calendar.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help people who inherit property without a will deal with the legal steps needed to establish and clear ownership, so they can keep their homes and land. It responds to the problem that co-heirs can be forced to sell inherited property through partition lawsuits, which has caused many families to lose land passed down for generations. The bill would authorize HUD to fund state and local help with title and estate costs, and counseling and legal aid for heirs.

oppose: The bill authorizes grant programs but sets no dollar amount, so it is unclear how much money would actually be spent or how many families would be helped.
Grants depend on states, localities, and nonprofits applying and on HUD choosing to run the programs, so help could vary widely from place to place.
The programs end seven years after enactment, and the bill does not say what happens to heirs' property problems that remain after that date.
Housing counselors who already receive HUD funding would have to take on a new duty to explain heirs' property risks, which could add paperwork and workload for them.
support: Many families, especially low-income and rural families, lose inherited land and homes through forced sales that a single co-owner can request, and this bill would help them handle the paperwork needed to protect their claims.
The bill would help pay for costs such as title reports, land surveys, heirs searches, estate planning, and legal fees, which can be out of reach for families with limited incomes.
The bill encourages states to adopt the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act, which includes due process protections against forced sales of inherited property.
Access to housing counseling and legal help before a forced sale happens could let heirs keep land and homes that have been in their families for generations.

crs:
Heirs Estate Inheritance Resolution and Succession Act of 2025 or the HEIRS Act of 2025
This bill authorizes the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to provide grants to assist individuals with the legal processes associated with inheriting certain real property.
Under the first program, HUD may provide grants to states that have enacted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (UPHPA) (or similar state law). The UPHPA provides due process protections against forced property sales for individuals who inherit real property from a landowner without a will. Historically, state property laws have provided that recipients of such property become tenants-in-common, which permits a single tenant to exercise their right to partition and sell the property.
A state, tribe, or local government must use grant funds to assist residents in the jurisdiction with expenses related to establishing and documenting property ownership rights or settling a decedent's estate, including costs related to
obtaining title reports, title abstracts, copies of public records, and land surveys;
estate planning;
heirs searches or tracing services; and
recording and filing fees, notary fees, and legal fees and expenses.
Under the second program, HUD may provide grants to housing counseling agencies, legal services clinics at institutions of higher education, and qualified nonprofits. Such organizations must use grant funds to provide housing counseling, legal assistance, and financial assistance related to title clearing and home retention efforts for individuals who inherit property as tenants-in-common.
Both grant programs terminate seven years after the enactment of this bill.

life.reason: Helping families keep inherited homes and land protects housing stability and the wellbeing that comes with it, though the effect on life broadly is indirect.

transparency.reason: Requires HUD-funded housing counselors to explain heirs' property risks and points residents to help, and the grant programs are publicly administered, which modestly improves public understanding of their rights.

people_over_profit.reason: It shields families from forced sales that can be triggered by outside investors buying a single heir's share, putting household land retention ahead of investor gains from partition sales.

local_say.reason: It encourages states and localities to adopt the UPHPA, a local legal protection that limits forced sales and keeps decisions about family property with the owners and heirs.

no_bailouts.reason: It is a grant program for individuals and governments, not a corporate bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break, and the bill sets no dollar amount.

honesty_kindness.reason: It provides compassionate help to grieving families navigating complicated estate and title processes, and it is not contrary to honesty.

label: H.R. 2613
title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
short_title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
one: Sets up Department of Energy research, demonstration, and standards programs to develop better pipeline materials, leak sensors, and safety technology, funded by shifting money already authorized for other energy research.
summary: This bill would create several federal programs to research and test new pipeline technology. Pipelines covered include natural gas, liquid fuel, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and water lines, plus liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fuel storage sites. First, the Department of Energy (DOE) would run a demonstration program giving competitive grants to colleges, labs, nonprofits, and private companies. Projects could cover leak detection, stronger materials and coatings, sensors, robots, self-repairing pipe, cybersecurity, and tools to judge whether old pipelines can carry hydrogen or carbon dioxide. Projects that measurably reduce pipeline harm to air, water, or soil, especially in rural and underserved areas, get priority, as do projects with matching non-federal money. Second, DOE, the Department of Transportation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) would run a joint early-stage research program. Third, DOE would set up a National Pipeline Modernization Center with a university or similar partner, and it would help train federal and state pipeline safety inspectors. Fourth, NIST would run pipeline measurement and standards research. label: H.R. 5089
title: Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
one: Renews and expands NOAA's weather forecasting, warning, and research programs through FY2030, with more use of private-sector weather data, new radar, satellite, cloud and AI work, and better public alerts.
summary:
This bill renews a 2017 law that guides how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Weather Service forecast dangerous weather. It sets funding limits through FY2030 for weather research, tornado and hurricane forecasting, tsunami warning, and other programs. It adds new programs on atmospheric rivers (long bands of moisture that cause heavy rain), coastal flooding and storm surge, and precipitation forecasting. It also covers weather gaps in rural, urban, and offshore areas, and aviation weather such as turbulence and icing.

The bill pushes NOAA to buy more weather data from private companies through a Commercial Data Program, with up to $100 million a year authorized, and to pilot "radar-as-a-service" contracts. It directs a plan to replace the national NEXRAD radar network by 2040 and a move of NOAA's forecaster software to the cloud. It supports AI and supercomputing research and opens NOAA's models to public testing.

On public communication, it calls for clearer watches and warnings, research on how people respond to alerts, upgrades to NOAA Weather Radio (including rural areas and parks), and replacing NWS's chat tool. It asks for studies of forecaster hiring and shift-work health, and lets NWS name hydrologists at forecast offices. The bill authorizes spending limits, but Congress must still appropriate the money. I could not see the text of some partial sections.

Reauthorizes tsunami warning and research at $30 million a year, with standardized warning products and clearer alert levels.
Creates a Commercial Data Program ($100 million a year) and Pilot Program (at least 15% of that) to buy private weather data, with open competition, multiple providers, and an ombudsman.
Lets NOAA contract for radar data from third parties and plans to replace NEXRAD by Sept. 30, 2040.
Directs work to close weather data gaps in underserved, urban, offshore, and vulnerable areas, including a FEMA pilot and heat mapping.
Requires NOAA to make purchased data not under redistribution limits available to U.S. weather-sector users, and to archive commercial data publicly at NCEI.
Supports AI, cloud, and supercomputing research and a public NOAA Data Lake; allows multi-year computing contracts.
Funds aviation weather work, a satellite partnership program ($20 million a year), and moving AWIPS to the cloud by 2030.
Improves hazard communication, NOAA Weather Radio (including rural areas and parks), and replaces NWSChat by Oct. 1, 2027.
Requires staffing assessments, a shift-work health study, and allows service hydrologists; states it does not require new hires.
Authorizes $46 million a year for a water-focused center and requires a report on satellite transfers to other agencies.

Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2025 or the Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
This bill reauthorizes, revises, and establishes several programs related to weather forecasting, monitoring, and research. 
For example, the bill reauthorizes through FY2030 programs that are administered by the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), including the U.S. Weather Research Program. It also provides statutory authority for NOAA's Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes Experiment (known as VORTEX-USA).
The bill also requires NOAA to establish programs that support weather forecasting technology, including improvements to radar accuracy, weather forecasting in underserved areas, and coastal flooding forecasting. NOAA must also acquire weather-related data from the private sector and establish a pilot program to test the compatibility of this data with NOAA infrastructure. 
In addition, NOAA must improve weather-related communication systems, including those related to hazardous weather events, through system upgrades that use more modern technology (e.g., cloud-based services) and that allow for expanded coverage (e.g., in rural areas).
Finally, NOAA must administer programs that support weather forecasting for agricultural and water management, including pilot programs to improve precipitation forecasts in the western and central states and a soil moisture monitoring network.

label: H.R. 5276
title: Community Bank LIFT Act
one: Lowers the capital cushion required for simplified-rule community banks, raises the size cap for those banks from $10 billion to $15 billion in assets, and orders regulators to review and rewrite the rules.
summary: Banks must hold a certain amount of their own money, called capital, as a cushion against losses. Smaller "community banks" can use a simple version of this rule called the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR). Under current law, a bank can use it if it has under $10 billion in assets, and regulators must set the required ratio between 8% and 10%. This bill makes two changes. It raises the asset limit to $15 billion, so larger banks can use the simple rule. It also lowers the allowed range for the ratio to 6% to 8%, which would let regulators require less capital. The bill also tells the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days. The report must suggest ways to get more community banks to join, especially smaller ones, and to cut paperwork. It can cover how the ratio is calculated, how certain assets are treated, who qualifies, how banks opt in or out, and any needed law changes. Within 180 days regulators must propose rules, and within one year they must finalize rules carrying out the bill and the report's recommendations. The bill does not set a specific ratio. Regulators would pick one within the new range.

The simpler framework could reduce paperwork and compliance costs for eligible banks.
Banks in the newly added asset range could gain access to a simpler capital option.

Raising the asset limit could bring larger banks under the simpler rule, which some may see as weakening oversight of institutions with more risk.
Because the bill sets only a range, the actual requirement depends on later regulatory choices that are not yet made.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to relax requirements for the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR), a simpler capital standard for qualified community banks, so more eligible banks can use it. support: Lowering the allowed CBLR range to 6%-8% could let qualifying community banks hold less capital under a simpler rule, potentially freeing money for local lending.

Community Bank Leverage Improvement and Flexibility for Transparency Act or the Community Bank LIFT Act
This bill relaxes requirements related to the community bank leverage ratio, which is a simplified capital standard applicable to qualified community banks. Community banks qualify by having less than $10 billion in assets, along with meeting other criteria.
Specifically, the bill increases this asset limit to $15 billion. Additionally, it reduces the statutory range of the leverage ratio from 8%-10% to 6%-8%. (The specific rate is set by regulation. A reduction in the leverage ratio eases capital requirements.)
The Federal Reserve Board, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation must review and report on the leverage ratio and the rules issued to carry out its implementation. The report must include a consideration of how to modify the leverage ratio to encourage more participation in the community bank leverage ratio framework, with a focus on community banks with fewer assets and providing relief from regulatory compliance burdens.
After this report is issued, the participating agencies must propose and finalize rules to implement this bill and the recommendations contained in the report.

transparency.reason: The bill requires the Fed, OCC, and FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress, which gives lawmakers and the public a documented review of the rule's workings.

people_over_profit.reason: Lower capital requirements and a higher asset cap let banks hold less of a cushion and expand their use of a simplified rule, which mainly benefits bank shareholders and margins at the expense of added safety for depositors and the public.

no_bailouts.reason: Thinner capital cushions raise the chance that banks fail and need taxpayer-backed deposit insurance or emergency support, which is a form of implicit bailout exposure.

label: H.R. 7086
title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
short_title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
one: The bill reworks federal Charter Schools Program grants so states can get money to buy, lease, renovate and maintain charter school buildings. It also removes federal property-tracking rules for these funds and gives priority to states with certain local land-use limits.
summary: This bill changes parts of the federal Charter Schools Program, which gives money to help charter schools (publicly funded schools run independently of the regular district) open and grow. First, it replaces an existing facilities grant with a new competitive grant for state agencies and similar groups. The money would help pay up to 60 percent of the cost of buying, leasing, renovating, and maintaining charter school buildings. The rest must come from non-federal sources, including outside organizations. States get priority if they offer charter schools tax-exempt financing, treat charters like other public schools in land use rules, or stop local governments from putting deed restrictions on property (for example, limits on charters buying surplus public property). Second, it lets another existing grant pay for help finding buildings and one-time fixes to meet building codes. States could put up to 10 percent of those grants into a revolving loan fund. It also appears to lower the minimum share that must go out as subgrants from 90 to 80 percent. Third, it says federal money in this program does not create a "federal interest" in property. That means the usual federal recording and reporting rules for property would not apply. Fourth, groups that got credit enhancement grants would have to file annual reports for 10 years. The bill does not list a dollar amount. I could not see the text of the existing law it edits.

Caps the federal share at 60 percent of project costs and lets outside partner organizations cover any part of the non-federal share.

Allows grant money to fund charter building purchases, leases, renovations, ongoing facility costs, and "alternative ownership models."
Lets state entities keep up to 5 percent of the new grants for evaluation, technical help, and sharing information.
Requires applications to describe how the state will help charters in low-income and rural areas and narrow funding gaps with other public schools.

Declares that no funds under this part create a "federal interest" in property, so federal property recording and reporting rules would not apply.
Requires credit enhancement grant recipients to file annual reports for 10 years after the grant, including recipients from before the law.
Applies the changes only to grants awarded after the bill becomes law.

Priority rules that limit local control over surplus property or land use could raise concerns among local governments and communities.

crs:
Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
This bill expands and revises certain grant programs under the Charter Schools Program (CSP).
Currently, the CSP's State Charter School Facilities Incentive Grant (SFIG) program provides competitive grants to help states establish and enhance or administer per-pupil facilities aid for charter schools.
The bill replaces the SFIG program with a new grant program, which requires the Department of Education to (1) award competitive grants to state entities with the highest-quality applications for paying the federal share of acquiring and maintaining charter school facilities; and (2) give priority to certain state entities, such as those located in a state that has tax-exempt financing for charter schools. Further, the bill outlines program requirements (e.g., cost-sharing) and allowable uses of grants.
Currently, the CSP's State Entities (SE) program authorizes competitive grants to state entities and, through them, subgrants to eligible applicants to enable them to open and prepare for the operation of a new charter school or replicate or expand a charter school. 
The bill revises the SE program by allowing grants to be used for (1) providing assistance to charter schools with locating and accessing a facility, and (2) providing one-time assistance to ensure the facility complies with building codes. Further, state entities may reserve up to 10% of grant funds for a revolving loan fund.
The bill (1) specifies that no funds made available under the CSP create a federal interest in associated property, and (2) revises reporting requirements for the CSP's Credit Enhancement grants.

transparency.reason: Declaring that federal money creates no federal interest in property and exempts it from federal recording and reporting rules reduces public visibility into how federally funded charter buildings are held and used, though credit enhancement recipients must file annual reports for 10 years, which partly offsets this.

local_say.reason: Priority for states that ban local deed restrictions and require equal land-use treatment for charters limits local control over zoning and surplus public property decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill uses federal money to subsidize charter building purchases, leases, and maintenance, including tax-exempt financing support, and lets outside partners cover non-federal shares, which is a federally funded facilities subsidy for private-operated schools.

label: H.R. 8437
title: Geo POWER Act
one: Directs the Department of Energy to create a program that gives milestone-based financing to next-generation geothermal power demonstration projects in at least three states.
summary: This bill would change an existing 2007 energy law to set up a new Department of Energy program for "next-generation" geothermal power. These are projects in hot rock that is hard for water to flow through (called low-permeability or impermeable reservoirs), which older geothermal methods can't easily use. Within 180 days of becoming law, the Energy Secretary would have to start the Milestone-Based Geothermal Demonstration Program. Money would be awarded through a competition, and projects would get it as they hit set technical and financial goals. The Secretary would have to favor projects in places with little or no geothermal power now (including on or near tribal land), projects that share data publicly, projects aiming for at least 30 megawatts of power, and projects likely to draw private investment. The program must fund at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 different sponsors. "Innovative financing" can include tools like loans or loan guarantees the Department of Energy can already use. The bill also removes one paragraph from the existing law (subsection (d), paragraph 3) and authorizes "such sums as are necessary" to be appropriated for the program. It sets no dollar cap, so total cost is unknown and would depend on later spending decisions by Congress.

Awards 'innovative financing' competitively, tied to meeting technical and financial milestones.
Focuses on geothermal in low-permeability and impermeable reservoirs.
Prioritizes new regions, including on or near Indian land, public data sharing, projects of at least 30 MW, and projects that can attract private investment.
Requires awards to at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, to at least 3 different sponsors.
Requires DOE to keep enough staff to run the program.

Department of Energy staff

Electricity customers and taxpayers

purpose: The bill says it would create a Department of Energy program to help develop "next-generation" geothermal power in hot rock with low permeability, where older geothermal methods struggle to work. According to the bill's summary, the program aims to expand geothermal energy to new regions, including tribal areas, and to tie federal funding to technical and financial milestones. The Crs summary was not provided, so this description relies on the official title and the plain-English summary of the bill text.

oppose: The bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' with no dollar cap, so the total cost to taxpayers is unknown and would depend on future congressional spending decisions.
The bill provides federal financing to private companies, which puts taxpayer money at risk if projects fail to reach their goals.

The bill does not include explicit environmental review, water protection, or local consent requirements, and the summary notes that hard-rock geothermal drilling can involve large water use and induced earthquakes.
support: The bill would create a competitive program that pays out funds only as projects meet set technical and financial milestones, which ties federal money to results.
The bill would direct support toward regions with little or no geothermal power today, including on or near tribal land, which could bring new energy supply and jobs to those communities.

The bill requires projects to share data publicly and aims for projects of at least 30 megawatts, which could add to public knowledge and help geothermal power provide steady, low-emission electricity.

air.reason: Supports geothermal power, which gives off far less air pollution than fossil fuel plants, though the bill doesn't require that it replace them.

transparency.reason: Prioritizes projects that collect and share public data on new geothermal resources.

no_bailouts.reason: Uses taxpayer-backed federal financing for private developers with an uncapped authorization, though it is competitive and milestone-based rather than a bailout.

label: H.R. 9468
title: STAR Act
short_title: STAR Act (Saving Today's Acute-Care Resources Act)
one: The bill would let more very sick Medicare patients in long-term care hospitals qualify for the higher Medicare payment rate, while extending a payment cut on other long-term care hospital stays through fiscal year 2032.
summary:
Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) treat patients who are very sick and need hospital care for a long time. Medicare pays them one of two ways. Stays that meet certain rules get a higher, specialized rate. Stays that don't meet the rules get a lower "site-neutral" rate. That lower rate is based on what Medicare would pay a regular acute-care hospital, or the stay's cost if that is lower.

This bill would change who gets the higher rate. For stays ending on or after October 1, 2026, it adds a new "high acuity" test. A stay would qualify if the patient came straight from a regular hospital or a critical access hospital (a small rural hospital). The patient must also have a diagnosis group with a "relative weight" of 0.8 or more, a measure of how costly the case is. The diagnosis group must not be one assigned because of 96 or more hours on a ventilator. The LTCH must also have been enrolled, been in its qualifying period, been under construction, or had state approval before the bill became law. That limit blocks new LTCHs from using the exemption.

The bill would also count ICU and ventilator care given at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, toward the existing ICU and ventilator tests. Finally, it extends a payment reduction that applies to the site-neutral rate. The extension runs through fiscal year 2032 instead of ending in 2026. The text doesn't give cost estimates.
does: Adds a new 'high acuity' exemption from the lower site-neutral Medicare rate for LTCH stays that follow a hospital or critical access hospital stay and meet a diagnosis-weight test (0.8 or higher, not ventilator-based).

Limits the new exemption to LTCHs that were enrolled, in their qualifying period, mid-construction (with a binding contract and spending of at least 10% or $2.5 million), or had state certificate-of-need approval before enactment.
Requires mid-build hospitals to send a written certification from their CEO or COO to the Secretary within 60 days of enactment.
Lets ICU and ventilator care at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, count toward the existing ICU and ventilator exemptions for discharges on or after October 1, 2026.
Extends an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral payment rate by changing the end date from 2026 to 2032.
Applies the new exemptions to discharges on or after October 1, 2026.
who: Medicare patients who are critically or chronically ill and need long-term hospital care
Long-term care hospitals and their owners
Critical access hospitals (small rural hospitals) that transfer patients
Regular acute-care hospitals that transfer patients to LTCHs
Medicare program and taxpayers who fund it
Developers planning new LTCHs, who would be excluded from the new exemption

benefits: More LTCH stays may qualify for the higher specialized payment rate, which could help LTCHs that treat high-acuity patients.
Patients with complex, costly conditions may have more LTCH options, since the exemption may support continued care for very sick patients.
Critical access hospitals may see their ICU and ventilator care count toward LTCH qualification, which could matter for small rural facilities.
concerns: Higher payments for some LTCH stays could raise Medicare spending, depending on how many stays qualify.
The payment reduction extension keeps the lower site-neutral rate in place longer, which may affect LTCH finances.
The limit on new LTCHs may give an advantage to facilities already operating or approved before the bill became law.
imp.cost: ["The bill text does not include cost estimates. The overall effect on Medicare spending is not stated in the material provided."]
unknowns: How many LTCH stays would qualify under the new high-acuity test is not stated.
The total cost or savings to Medicare is not given.
The material does not say how the 0.8 relative weight threshold compares with current patient groups.
The size of the payment reduction being extended, and its effect on LTCHs, is not described.
Whether access to LTCH care for patients in rural areas would change is not stated.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to secure access to care for seniors in critical condition, the "Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025." According to the CRS summary, it would exempt certain long-term care hospital (LTCH) stays from the lower Medicare site-neutral payment rate when the patient meets specified high-acuity criteria, and it would extend an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral rate through FY2032.

oppose: The bill would pay more Medicare money to some LTCH stays that would otherwise get the lower site-neutral rate, which could raise federal spending depending on how many stays qualify. The text does not give cost estimates.

The new exemption covers LTCH stays that follow a hospital or critical access hospital stay and meet a diagnosis-weight test of 0.8 or higher. Some constituents may worry this test is too broad and could reward costly stays without clear quality gains.

The bill limits the new exemption to LTCHs already enrolled, in a qualifying period, under construction, or approved before enactment. Constituents may view this as giving an advantage to existing facilities and shutting out new competitors.
support: The bill would help LTCHs that treat very sick patients with long hospital needs by letting more of their stays qualify for the higher specialized Medicare rate instead of the lower site-neutral rate.
Patients with complex, costly conditions may keep more options for long-term hospital care, which supporters say matters for seniors in critical condition.

The bill would let ICU and ventilator care at a critical access hospital, a small rural facility, count toward LTCH qualification, which supporters say could help rural communities keep access to care.

crs:
Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025
This bill exempts additional types of hospital stays from the Medicare site-neutral payment rate for long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) and extends certain adjustments to the payment rate. (The site-neutral rate is the lower of Medicare’s acute care hospital payment rate under the inpatient prospective payment system or 100% of the cost of the stay. LTCH stays that do not qualify for the specialized LTCH payment rate under Medicare are instead paid at the lower, site-neutral rate.)
Specifically, the bill exempts discharges from LTCHs from the site-neutral payment rate if the discharge meets specified high acuity criteria. It also allows discharges to qualify for the exemption if certain intensive care or ventilator services were furnished by a critical access hospital immediately prior to the LTCH stay. These exemptions apply to discharges that occur on or after October 1, 2026.
The bill additionally extends an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral payment rate through FY2032.

life.reason: Expands access to specialized LTCH care for very sick patients with high-acuity needs who transfer from hospitals, which may help protect their lives and health.

people_over_profit.reason: Raises Medicare payments to LTCH owners by exempting more stays from the lower site-neutral rate, benefiting facility owners' revenue more than taxpayers or patients.

no_bailouts.reason: Keeps higher Medicare payments flowing to LTCHs by exempting stays from site-neutral pricing and extending a payment reduction tied to it, which functions as a federally funded subsidy to specific providers; the mid-construction grandfathering also protects projects already in progress.

label: S. 1254
title: A bill to amend the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to clarify a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes.
one: The bill would let holders of existing federal land water-conveyance permits (like ditches and canals) use them to refill underground aquifers, for themselves or for public bodies, without new federal approval, after giving 30 days' notice to the Bureau of Land Management.
summary: Many ditches, canals, and pipelines cross federal land under permits, easements, or rights-of-way. A earlier law, the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, said holders could move water to refill underground water supplies (aquifers) without extra federal approval, as long as the use did not expand or change the operation. This bill would clarify and widen that rule. The holder could use the existing authorization for aquifer recharge, acting for itself or for a state, local government, Indian Tribe, or other public entity. It would not need new approval from the Interior Secretary, and this use would not count as an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation from the original permit. The holder would have to tell the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) at least 30 days ahead. The notice must name who will use it, identify the permit, describe the planned use, and include a copy of the agreement between the parties. The bill also says the law does not excuse anyone from following all other applicable federal laws and BLM policies, and it does not allow building, changing, or expanding infrastructure. The Senate committee's amended version replaced the first draft. The first draft would have had a rent exemption and named specific laws, and it would have said these uses are not "major Federal action." The amended text drops those parts. CRS has not yet published a summary, so this is based on the bill text alone.
does: items below
who: Holders of federal rights-of-way, easements, and permits for ditches and canals (irrigation districts, water companies)
States, local governments, Indian Tribes, and public entities that want to recharge aquifers
Bureau of Land Management, which would receive notices
Farmers and communities that depend on groundwater
Nearby residents, downstream water users, and wildlife that depend on affected waterways

benefits: Could speed up and lower the cost of aquifer recharge projects, helping groundwater supplies in dry regions.
The 30-day notice gives BLM and the public record some visibility into planned uses.
Clearly keeps all federal laws and BLM policies in force and bars new construction or expansion under this authority.
Public entities and Tribes can use existing infrastructure rather than building new.
concerns: Treating recharge as not an expansion or modification could bypass new federal review of local environmental effects, and the notice does not give the public a chance to comment.
The notice goes only to BLM; the bill does not require public posting or input from nearby residents, which could limit local say and transparency.
Water quality could be affected if recharged water carries pollutants; the bill relies on existing laws for this.
The text says 'acting ... on behalf of' a public entity but does not clearly bar for-profit involvement, since the rent exemption and for-profit carve-out were dropped in the amended version.
The amended 'all applicable Federal laws' language is broader than the original draft, but it is unclear how it interacts with the 'not a substantial deviation' language.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is provided in the text. BLM would have to process notices, which could add small administrative costs. No new spending is authorized.
unknowns: Whether BLM can object to or block a use after receiving notice.
How the changes affect water rights under state law.
Whether and how environmental review (like NEPA) would apply in practice, since the bill no longer states 'major Federal action' wording.
What BLM does if the notice is incomplete.
No CRS summary or cost estimate was available.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify and widen an earlier law, the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, which lets holders of permits, easements, or rights-of-way on federal land move water through existing ditches, canals, and pipelines to refill underground water supplies without extra federal approval. The amended bill says this use is allowed when it is for aquifer recharge, whether the holder acts for itself or for a public entity, and that it does not need new Interior Secretary approval, as long as the holder gives BLM at least 30 days' notice. The bill states that other federal laws and BLM policies still apply and that it does not allow building or expanding infrastructure. The official title describes the bill only as clarifying a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes. No CRS summary is available yet, so this is based on the bill text alone.

oppose: The bill says recharge use is not an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation of an existing permit, so it may avoid new federal review of possible local environmental effects of the water movement.
The only required step is a 30-day notice to the Bureau of Land Management. The bill does not require public posting or a chance for nearby residents to comment, which could limit local input.
Water quality is not addressed in the bill itself. It depends on existing laws, and the bill does not add new safeguards if recharged water carries pollutants.
support: The bill could make aquifer recharge projects faster and less costly by using infrastructure that already exists, which may help groundwater supplies in dry regions.
The 30-day notice gives BLM a written record of who will use the water, which permit is involved, what the use is, and a copy of the agreement between the parties.

The bill keeps all other federal laws and BLM policies in force and states that it does not allow new construction or expansion of infrastructure. Public entities and Tribes could use existing facilities instead of building new ones.

life.reason: The bill mainly changes administrative approval for aquifer recharge; it keeps all other federal laws in force, so effects on human, animal, and plant life are unclear and likely neutral.

water.reason: Facilitating aquifer recharge helps replenish groundwater supplies, though the bill does not add water quality protections and relies on existing law for pollutant concerns.

air.reason: The bill does not address air quality or emissions.

transparency.reason: The 30-day notice goes only to BLM with no public posting or comment opportunity, and it removes the need for new federal approval, which reduces public visibility into these uses.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill could benefit for-profit water companies, but it also serves public entities and the effect on corporate margins versus public interest is unclear from the text.

local_say.reason: Projects that previously might have received federal review for local effects can proceed on notice alone, with no public input from nearby residents.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves no direct subsidies, bailouts, or ratepayer-funded tax breaks, and the rent exemption was removed in the amended text.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not bear directly on honesty or kindness toward people.

label: S. 1262
title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to release a reversionary interest in certain land in the Black River State Forest in Millston, Wisconsin, and for other purposes.
short_title: Black River State Forest Land Swap (Deli, Inc.) Release Bill
one: The bill would have the federal government give up its legal claim requiring about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest in Wisconsin to stay in public use, so Wisconsin can trade that land to a moss-producing company, Deli, Inc., for about 37.27 acres that would be added to the forest.
summary: Some of the land in Wisconsin's Black River State Forest, near Millston, came with a federal strings-attached rule. Under an older farm law, the United States keeps a "reversionary interest." This means the land must always be used for public purposes. If it isn't, the federal government could claim it back. This bill would remove that rule from about 31.83 acres. The release would happen only if the State of Wisconsin offers, in a written agreement, to trade that land to Deli, Inc. Deli is a sphagnum moss (a bog plant used in gardening) business in Millston. In return, Deli would give the state about 37.27 acres in two separate parcels, and those acres would be added to the state forest. After the release, the Secretary of Agriculture (through the Forest Service) must provide a quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed is a paper that passes along whatever federal interest exists, at no charge. It must be recorded before the swap deeds. The Secretary may fix mistakes in the land descriptions, working with the state. The bill's land definition says the swap is subject to approval by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, the Natural Resources Board, and the Governor. The bill text does not mention appraisals, environmental review, or public comment.
does: Removes the federal 'public purposes' reversionary interest on about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest land.
Triggers the release only if Wisconsin makes a written offer to trade that land to Deli, Inc. for about 37.27 acres of Deli land.
Says the Deli land would be added to Black River State Forest after the swap.
Requires the Agriculture Secretary to provide a free quitclaim deed 'as expeditiously as practicable', to be recorded before the swap deeds.
Lets the Secretary, working with the state, correct the legal descriptions of the state land.
Describes the Deli land as subject to existing public water use or easements on Lee Lake, plus existing roads, zoning rules, and the railroad right-of-way.
who: Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss producer in Millston, Wisconsin, which would get the state forest parcels
The State of Wisconsin, including the Department of Natural Resources, Natural Resources Board, and Governor, who must approve the exchange
Visitors and nearby residents of Jackson County and the Town of Millston who use or live near the forest
The U.S. Forest Service / Department of Agriculture, which gives up its claim and issues the deed
Wisconsin taxpayers and the public, who own the state forest

benefits: The state would gain about 37.27 acres that would be added to the state forest, if the exchange goes through.
The swap could give the state forest land in exchange for land of similar or different use, which may simplify ownership of the area.
Deli, Inc. would receive the release of the federal restriction on its trade-off parcel, which may make the land more useful to the business.
concerns: The bill text does not mention appraisals, so it is not stated whether the two parcels are of equal value.
The bill does not mention environmental review or public comment before the exchange.
Because the release depends on a state offer and state approvals, the final terms would be set outside this bill.
Removing the public-use requirement from about 31.83 acres could allow those acres to be used differently in the future, depending on later state decisions.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state any cost, appropriation, or funding amount. The quitclaim deed is described as being provided at no charge."]
unknowns: It is not stated whether the land values in the exchange are equal.
It is not stated what environmental, appraisal, or public review steps would apply before the swap.
It is not stated how the 37.27 acres would be managed once added to the state forest.
It is not stated what uses Deli, Inc. might make of the released land, or what happens if the state does not make an offer.

stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the Secretary of Agriculture release a federal reversionary interest on about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest land near Millston, Wisconsin, so that land can be exchanged with Deli, Inc. for about 37.27 acres that would be added to the state forest. The bill describes the release as conditional on Wisconsin offering that trade in writing. The bill's text does not state a broader problem beyond this land exchange.

The bill does not require environmental review or public comment before the exchange. Ask whether local residents and neighbors should have a chance to weigh in before federal restrictions are removed.

support: The bill would let Wisconsin add about 37.27 acres to Black River State Forest, which would expand public forest land if the exchange goes through.
The land swap could simplify land ownership in the area by trading parcels between the state and a private business, which may make the forest easier to manage.

crs:
This bill directs the Forest Service to release its reversionary interest in approximately 31.83 acres in the Black River State Forest if the State of Wisconsin offers to exchange those acres for approximately 37.27 acres of land owned by Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss production business located in Millston, Wisconsin. The Forest Service's reversionary interest requires the state forest land to be used for public purposes. 
After the release, the Forest Service must provide a quitclaim deed of the release as expeditiously as practicable.

people_over_profit.reason: It frees about 31.83 acres of public forest land for a private moss business, with no stated appraisal or fair-value requirement, which tilts toward a private company's interests.
