label: S. 4709
title: UNLOCK AUKUS Act
one: The bill makes a one-line change to the Arms Export Control Act so that three specific exclusions no longer limit the license-free export of certain defense items to Australia and the United Kingdom under the AUKUS security partnership.
summary:
AUKUS is a security partnership among Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Under current law, some U.S. defense items and services can be sent to Australia and the UK without the usual individual export license. That shortcut has limits. This bill changes one of those limits.

The limit sits in Section 38(l)(4)(B) of the Arms Export Control Act. It refers to another part of the law, subsection (j)(1)(C)(ii). The bill adds the words "excluding subclauses (I), (II), and (III)" after that reference. In effect, three listed items in that other part would no longer count toward the limit.

The bill text does not say what those three items are. It also doesn't say how much easier or harder exports would become. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. I could not see the text of the section being referenced, so I can't say exactly which items or technologies are affected. The bill's title suggests the goal is to speed up licensing and technology sharing among the three countries. That is an inference from the name, not something the text says.

The bill has 10 cosponsors from both parties. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee reported it without changes, and it is now on the Senate calendar. The text sets no start date, no new spending, and no new reporting rules.

Narrows a limit on AUKUS license-free defense exports and transfers, so three listed items would no longer count toward that limit.
Gives the bill its short name, the UNLOCK AUKUS Act.
Adds no new funding, no new reporting rules, and no new penalties in the text provided.

concerns: Because the bill does not name the three items, it is hard to tell which technologies could move with less review.
Less licensing oversight for some items could raise questions about how sensitive technology is controlled, though the text does not say this will happen.

label: S. 4846
title: TAAP Act
short_title: TAAP Act (Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Program Act)
one: Renews and extends a federal program that studies groundwater shared between the U.S. and Mexico, adds Arizona aquifers to the study list (with one exception), and authorizes funding through fiscal year 2036.
summary:
Some underground water supplies, called aquifers, sit under both the United States and Mexico. A 2006 law set up a program to study these shared aquifers, working with states, universities, and Mexico. The program's funding permission ran out after 2016. This bill would renew it.

The bill does three things. First, it widens the list of states where "priority" aquifers can be picked for study. The current law covers New Mexico and Texas. The bill would add Arizona, but not the shared aquifer that is partly in the Yuma groundwater basin, which is excluded. Second, it says Congress may spend money on the program for fiscal years 2026 through 2036. Third, it resets the program's end date so the clock starts from when this new law is enacted instead of from 2006.

The bill does not set a dollar amount or change the other parts of the 2006 law. "Authorizing" funding only allows Congress to pay for the program. A separate spending bill would still have to provide the money. The bill text does not say why the Yuma-area aquifer is left out. The bill text does not give the new end date, because it refers to the existing law's timeline, which I could not see.

The bill covers only study and assessment. It does not itself change water quality rules or limit pumping, so some people may see it as an expansion of federal research without direct protections.
support: Shared aquifers under the U.S. and Mexico need better data. Renewing the program could give border communities and local governments clearer information about the water they depend on.
Adding Arizona to the list of eligible states lets the program study priority aquifers in another border state, which could help with planning for drinking water supplies.

The program works with states, universities, and Mexico. Continued study could improve cooperation with Mexico on water that crosses the border, and the research results are meant to be public and transparent.

cost_flag: The bill authorizes appropriations for fiscal years 2026 through 2036. It gives no dollar figure in this text; the amount is set in the 2006 law, which I could not see. No Congressional Budget Office estimate was provided.

life.reason: Better data on shared aquifers can support protection of drinking water and ecosystems, though the bill itself only authorizes studies.

water.reason: Renews a program studying shared groundwater in border regions, improving information about water supplies, but does not itself protect water quality or limit pumping.

transparency.reason: The program produces public, research-based data on shared aquifers that communities and governments can use.

label: S. 4870
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (a USGS-led effort to map underground resources) for five more years (2027–2031), adds newer mapping technologies, and links it to the 3D Hydrography Program.
summary:
This bill would keep alive a federal program called the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, or Earth MRI. It was created in the 2021 infrastructure law and is run through the U.S. Geological Survey. The program collects maps and data about what is under the ground, with a focus on critical minerals, which are materials used in things like batteries and electronics. Its current authorization runs from 2022 through 2026. The bill changes that to 2027 through 2031.

The bill also updates the program's mapping purpose. It says the data may come from newer tools, such as airborne gravity gradiometry (measuring tiny changes in gravity from aircraft), digital geochemistry, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis. These could help describe critical minerals, geothermal energy, geologic hydrogen, and other underground resources.

Finally, the bill adds the 3D Hydrography Program, a federal water-mapping effort, to the list of data sources the Earth MRI must combine with its own data.

The bill text we have does not give a dollar amount. It only extends the time period. Any money would depend on later spending decisions by Congress. The bill also does not add rules on environmental review, public input, or mining permits.

Says the program's mapping data may come from newer technologies, including airborne gravity gradiometry, digital geochemistry, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis.
Adds geothermal, geologic hydrogen, and other underground resource systems to the resources the data may help describe, alongside critical minerals.
Adds the 3D Hydrography Program to the data sources the program must integrate.
Replaces the original bill text with a committee amendment; the main change is wording on the technology list and on adding "geologic hydrogen."

Communities near areas that may be explored or developed for minerals
Researchers, planners, and the public who use open geologic and water data
Federal taxpayers, who fund the program

Newer mapping tools may produce more detailed information about critical minerals and other underground resources.
Combining Earth MRI data with the 3D Hydrography Program could make geologic and water data work together more closely.
concerns: The bill text does not give a dollar amount, so it is unclear whether the program would receive enough funding to use the extended time period fully.
The bill does not add rules on environmental review, public input, or mining permits, so the mapping data alone would not change those processes.
Mapping data could be used to support future mineral or energy development, which may raise environmental or land-use questions that the bill does not address.

label: S. 4950
title: ITS Codification Act
one: The bill writes the Commerce Department's Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (a federal radio and wireless test lab) into law and creates an initiative to develop technology for locating people trapped in mines, collapsed buildings, and similar places where radios don't work well.
summary: The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) is a federal lab that already exists inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the part of the Commerce Department that advises on telecom and manages federal use of radio airwaves. This bill would put ITS into permanent law instead of leaving it to agency decisions alone. The law would say ITS serves as a lab for the executive branch. It would study radio signals, how they travel, and how they cause interference. It would also test technology that lets federal and non-federal users share airwaves, and it would study how well federal systems tolerate interference. ITS could also take on other tasks the NTIA head assigns. The bill lets ITS make agreements with companies, universities, and other agencies under existing laws on technology partnerships, interagency work, and patents and licensing. The second part requires ITS to start an initiative for emergency communication and tracking tools. These would help find people trapped in places such as underground mines, tall buildings, or collapsed structures. ITS would work with private companies and federal agencies to assess needs and help develop technical standards. Within 18 months, NTIA must send Congress a public report on that needs assessment. The bill does not state a dollar amount or new funding.

Could speed development of tools to find trapped miners and disaster victims, which could save lives.
Requires a public report on needs, which adds transparency.
Spectrum sharing research could help use airwaves more efficiently.

Spectrum sharing work between federal and commercial users could favor commercial interests, depending on how it is carried out.

label: S. 5352
title: Desalination Reauthorization Act
one: Extends and adjusts federal programs that help fund and research turning seawater, salty groundwater, and wastewater into usable water, including a new pilot-project research track and a higher university grant cap.
summary:
This bill renews and updates federal desalination programs. Desalination means removing salt and other minerals from ocean water, salty groundwater, or wastewater so people can use it. The bill restarts the clock on the authority for these programs from the date the bill becomes law. It sets the Bureau of Reclamation's desalination project program to expire 15 years after enactment.

For construction projects, the bill defines which projects can get help. They must be in a western "Reclamation State" or mainly benefit one, and they must involve an ocean or brackish water plant run or backed by a state, Tribe, or water district. It lets the Interior Secretary pay up to 25 percent of a project's total cost, with no dollar limit.

The bill also adds "advanced pilots" to the research program. These are real-world tests of new or first-of-a-kind technologies, including ways to treat or dispose of brine, the very salty leftover waste. Pilot projects fall under the existing cost-sharing rules. Finally, it raises the cap on grants to colleges and universities from $1 million to $2.5 million.

The text I was given does not include a new dollar amount of funding, and no CRS summary was available. The Senate committee replaced the original text with a version that adds the university grant increase and changes how the pilot program is defined.
does: Restarts the authority period for the desalination programs from the date this bill becomes law.
who: Water districts, states, and Tribes in western "Reclamation States" seeking desalination funding

benefits: Continued federal support could help communities in drought-prone western areas develop new water sources.
Real-world pilot testing may help show whether new technologies and brine management methods work at scale.
A higher university grant cap may allow larger research awards.
concerns: Because the 25 percent federal share has no dollar limit, total federal costs could grow as more projects qualify.
Limiting eligible projects to western Reclamation States may leave other regions without access to these programs.
Brine disposal is a known environmental concern, and the pilot program may test disposal methods whose effects are not described in the material.

label: S. 5359
title: Pennington County Land Conveyance Act
one: The bill would give about 9 acres of Black Hills National Forest land, plus any buildings on it, to Pennington County, South Dakota, for public uses such as a highway maintenance and public works facility, with the land returning to the federal government if it is misused.
summary: This bill would require the U.S. Department of Agriculture, through the Forest Service, to hand over a small piece of the Black Hills National Forest to Pennington County, South Dakota. The parcel is about 8.97 acres, and any buildings or other improvements on it go along with it. The map title, "Pennington County (SD) Highway Maintenance Facility Land Conveyance," suggests the land is tied to a county highway maintenance site. The county would not pay anything for the land. The Forest Service may attach any conditions it considers appropriate. The county must use the land for public purposes, including a public works facility. After the transfer, the national forest boundary would be redrawn to leave out the parcel. The Senate committee changed the bill's wording so the land may be used for "public purposes, including a public works facility." The original version said "a public works facility or any other uses determined to be necessary by the County." The committee version also adds a reversion rule. If the Forest Service, after consulting South Dakota, finds the county is using the land in a way the bill does not allow, the land could go back to the United States. Before that, the Forest Service must notify the county, hold a hearing if the county asks, and take public comment. It must also give the county a reasonable chance to fix the problem. The bill text does not say how much the land is worth, and I could not see the map or any environmental review.

label: S. 5526
title: Agricultural Act of 2026
one: A very large five-year farm bill that renews and changes USDA programs for crop and dairy supports, conservation, trade and food aid, SNAP and nutrition, rural development, research, and forestry, with a mix of strong water and conservation investments and several environmental-review waivers and subsidy increases.
summary:
This is the farm bill. It extends most farm programs through 2031 and rewrites many of them. I could read Titles I through VIII and part of Title VIII's last sections. The text I was given stops partway through Section 8609. I did not see the remaining parts, which by the CRS summary cover horticulture, crop insurance, energy, livestock, foreign ownership of farmland, and year-round E15 fuel and the Renewable Fuel Standard. I can't judge those parts.

Title I (Commodities) keeps price-support laws suspended through 2031. It lets farm-storage loans cover propane and fertilizer storage. It raises the cap on extra "base acres" (the acres that set payments) to 31.5 million. It requires twice-yearly public budget books and quarterly reports from the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC), the USDA's funding arm. For dairy, it ends the margin-coverage fee and gives free coverage on the first 6 million pounds of milk. It also requires processors to report production costs. Disaster aid widens for livestock, trees, and community irrigation ditches. A new specialty-crop aid framework would allow payments of at least $900,000 per large farm entity once money is appropriated. The bill also allows disaster block grants to states.

Title II (Conservation) extends the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) with a 27-million-acre cap. It raises the payment limit from $50,000 to $125,000 and allows emergency haying and grazing, exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). It authorizes higher funding for the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP, up to $3.255 billion by 2031) and the Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP). It adds public comment and five-year reviews for conservation standards and expands the use of private technical providers. It creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program and repeals the Healthy Forests Reserve Program. It raises cost-share for farmland easements, expands the watershed program, and adds a $150 million feral swine program and a $50 million per year state conservation grant program.

Title III (Trade) renews Food for Peace and moves it from the State Department to USDA. It adds protections for "common names" such as parmesan and feta in trade talks. It sets trade promotion funding at $515–533 million per year and adds several trade reports.

Title IV (Nutrition) adds hot rotisserie chicken to SNAP-eligible foods. It delays state SNAP cost-sharing by a year and ties a share of costs to state error rates starting in 2031. It makes online SNAP purchasing permanent. It adds cybersecurity rules, chip cards, and fast, free replacement of stolen cards. It tightens which retailers may take SNAP and allows contractors to help with staffing under safeguards. It switches dietary guidelines to a 10-year cycle, with conflict-of-interest disclosure and a ban on certain topics, including food labeling and production practices. It sets a 95 percent Buy American target for school food. It raises dairy and food-incentive funding.

Title V (Credit) fixes outdated language and rules for USDA farm loans. Title VI (Rural Development) rebrands and expands the ReConnect broadband program, adds a "Last Acre" farm broadband program, and boosts rural water, wastewater, and cybersecurity aid. It adds the "Healthy H2O" program for filtration at private wells and homes, rural hospital zero-interest loans, childcare and healthcare priorities, a meat-processing grant program, and a rural development innovation center. It also lets the USDA set loan guarantee fees up to 3 percent after 30 days' public notice.

Title VII (Research) extends dozens of programs and raises funding for 1890 land-grant colleges, veterinary programs, farmworker automation, aquaculture, AI, biochar, PFAS and tick-borne disease research. It also moves $200 million from the CCC to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research.

Title VIII (Forestry) extends forest health programs and raises project size limits from 3,000 to 10,000 acres. It creates new NEPA shortcuts for hazard-tree removal, utility rights-of-way, and communications sites. It relieves agencies from re-consulting under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) on land plans. It raises the stewardship contract limit to 20 years, widens Good Neighbor Authority, and funds wood innovation and white oak restoration. It designates several wilderness and scenic areas, makes land conveyances, creates Civilian Conservation Centers for youth, and directs prairie dog control near private land.

Overall the bill funds many things this reader values, especially clean drinking water, conservation, and rural services. It also reduces environmental and public review in several places, raises some subsidies and payment limits, and sends money to private groups.
does: Title I: Extends the suspension of permanent price-support law (so the old 1938/1949 farm laws don't take effect) through 2031, and treats USDA loan servicing as an excepted activity during a government shutdown.
Lets enrolled agents certify adjusted gross income for farm-payment eligibility.
Requires the Commodity Credit Corporation to file quarterly as well as annual reports, post a twice-yearly searchable 'Commodity Estimate Book,' and categorize spending by authority.
Expands farm storage facility loans to cover propane and fertilizer storage, with rules due in 180 days.

Makes protecting domestic production of key food-ingredient commodities a 'priority objective of the President' in covered commodity policy, orders a dry edible bean safety-net study, and authorizes 'such sums as necessary' for a dry bean stocks mitigation program.
Replaces the 30 million cap on additional base acres with a cap of the lesser of eligible acres or 31.5 million.

Dairy: reauthorizes indemnity and promotion programs to 2031, repeals the forward pricing program, and requires dairy processors to report production costs and yields, with a public report every two years.
Dairy margin coverage: eliminates the administrative fee and gives free coverage on the first 6 million pounds of milk, with optional paid tier II coverage above that.

Disaster aid: broadens noninsured crop aid for community ditches/acequias; adds unweaned livestock, Mexican gray wolves and panthers, and more loss causes to livestock programs; widens the Tree Assistance Program through September 30, 2035.

Creates a specialty crop emergency payment framework (payments floor of at least $900,000 for farm-dependent entities) and a state block grant authority for covered disaster losses, both dependent on later appropriations.

Title II: Extends CRP to 2031 with a 27 million acre cap, raises the CRP payment limit from $50,000 to $125,000, allows emergency haying/grazing exempt from NEPA, and expands grazing and water infrastructure cost-share.
Updates CREP agreements, adds seasonal flooded working-lands habitat agreements, and extends the farmable wetland program.

EQIP: allows irrigation-history waivers only if no aquifer depletion or stream flow reduction would result; adds wildlife corridor payments; caps water conservation payments at $2 million and organic payments at $140,000; bars required soil testing or whole-farm plans beyond practice needs; defines precision agriculture.

Authorizes EQIP at $2.5 billion (2027) rising to $3.255 billion (2031), CSP at about $1.275–1.325 billion, $100 million a year for non-CRP water and grazing infrastructure, and $25–65 million for the Forest Conservation Easement Program.

Requires five-year rolling reviews of conservation practice standards with public comment, a streamlined process for new practices, and expanded third-party technical providers and farmer-to-farmer networks.
Caps CRP and wetland easement enrollment at 25 percent of a county's cropland; lets USDA bar conservation payments that benefit entities tied to 'foreign countries of concern.'

Easements: raises the federal cost-share for agricultural land easements to 60 percent, creates a lower cost-share option, streamlines entity certification, adds wetland easement stewardship, de minimis adjustments, and an AGI exemption for easement income.
RCPP: restates purposes, adds agricultural retailers as partners, allows advance payments, caps federal share at $15 million per project, and adds big-game migration corridor projects.

Creates the Forest Conservation Easement Program (up to 75 percent federal share, $500,000 restoration cap, minerals allowed under conditions) and repeals the Healthy Forests Reserve Program while keeping existing contracts.

Rewrites the Watershed Protection and Flood Prevention Act (250,000-acre limit, 45-day decisions, congressional approval for plans over $50 million), expands emergency conservation and watershed programs to public-land permit holders, and waives NEPA comment periods on certain BLM land.
Creates a $150 million feral swine program (2027–2031), a $50 million per year state conservation grant program, and an NRCS white oak initiative.

Title III: Reauthorizes Food for Peace to 2031, allows cash or commodities for nonemergency aid, repeals minimum aid levels, requires $15 million a year for the international food relief partnership, and transfers Food for Peace to USDA through a plan due in 180 days.

Trade: defines and protects 'common names' of foods in trade talks, funds trade promotion ($515M in 2027, $533M a year after), adds specialty crop and domestic competitiveness reports, a perishable produce working group, a shrimp trade report, an exchange program ($10M a year), and adjusts Food for Progress, McGovern-Dole, and the Global Crop Diversity Trust.
Title IV: Adds hot rotisserie chicken to SNAP-eligible foods; delays state SNAP cost-share to FY2029 and sets a 20 percent state share for states with error rates of 10 percent or more from FY2031.

Makes SNAP online purchasing permanent, and in the Enhanced Cybersecurity for SNAP Act requires chip cards, transaction alerts, replacement cards within 5 business days, no replacement fees for fraud, retailer chip terminals, GAO and Puerto Rico security reports, and full state reimbursement for upgrades for five years.

Requires SNAP retailers to own food inventory, bars inventory-less aggregators, allows contractors for temporary SNAP staffing with conflict-of-interest limits and public notice, and requires reporting of all payment errors regardless of size.

Nutrition programs: extends TEFAP, commodity programs, Seniors Farmers' Market and others to 2031; ties TEFAP's $525 million base to inflation; raises the dairy nutrition incentive ceiling from $20M to $80M; sets a $10M a year rural senior home-delivery pilot; and reauthorizes GusNIP and studies moving produce prescriptions to HHS.

Sets a 95 percent Buy American standard for school food purchases and moves dietary guidelines to a 10-year cycle with notice-and-comment, an independent board, conflict-of-interest disclosures, and exclusion of topics such as labeling and production practices.

Title V: Cleans up USDA farm credit law (agency names, notices, interest-rate caps at 5 percent on certain loans, obsolete reports and appeals provisions) and extends time for sales of inventory property.

Title VI: Renames and expands ReConnect broadband ($100M a year), raises speed targets, adds a Last Acre farm broadband program ($25M a year), bars rate regulation of broadband, and adds cybersecurity and transparency features.

Rural water and community aid: expands grants, loans, technical assistance, a cyber circuit rider ($10M), disaster-response help ($20M), distressed-system consolidation, private-well and septic aid, and the 'Healthy H2O' filtration grant program.

Rural economy: rural hospital zero-interest loans, expanded health facility refinancing, childcare and mental health priorities, meat processing grants ($25M a year, including humane handling infrastructure), loan guarantee fees up to 3 percent with 30 days' public notice, a Rural Development Innovation Center, and an efficiency report.

Title VII: Extends and expands research and extension, including 1890 and 1994 institutions, vet loan repayment and rural vet grants, a $30M a year specialty crop automation program, biochar network, PFAS and tick research, AGARDA, farmer stress network, 4-H name authority, and a $200M CCC transfer to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research.

Title VIII: Expands forest inventory (adds carbon), raises forest project size limits from 3,000 to 10,000 acres, and creates NEPA categorical exclusions for hazard trees, utility rights-of-way, and communications sites; relieves ESA re-consultation on land plans; extends stewardship contracts to 20 years; widens Good Neighbor Authority; and grows water source protection and wood programs.

Forestry land and workforce: designates wilderness, scenic area, and special management areas in Virginia, Illinois, and Arkansas; authorizes land conveyances and exchanges in several states; orders prairie dog limits and control near private land; adds white oak programs; and creates Civilian Conservation Center workforce and wildland firefighter hiring programs.

Unseen: the text ends in Section 8609 (rural fire prevention); I could not see the remaining sections, which presumably include Titles IX–XII (horticulture, crop insurance, energy/E15/RFS, foreign land investment, and miscellaneous).

label: S. 632
title: IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2025
one: Lets health workers who got Indian Health Service scholarships or loan repayment help pay back their service commitment by working half-time, for twice as long.
summary: Today, doctors, nurses and other health workers who accept Indian Health Service (IHS) scholarships or loan repayment help must "pay back" that help by working full-time in Native health care settings. This bill adds a half-time option. Scholarship recipients could work half-time if they agree in writing to serve twice as long. For the loan repayment program, a participant could choose full-time service for 2 years, half-time service for 4 years, or half-time service for 2 years with loan payments cut to 50 percent of the full-time amount. The bill also says what happens if someone breaks the contract. Half-time service would be converted to its full-time equivalent when figuring out how much money the person owes back. The places where people can serve stay the same. They include IHS facilities, tribal programs, urban Indian programs, and some private practices in shortage areas that serve many Native patients. The bill doesn't add new money in its text. It was reported out of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee without changes and is waiting for a Senate floor vote.
does: Lets Indian Health Scholarship recipients meet their service obligation through half-time practice if they agree to double the length of service.
Lets loan repayment participants choose full-time (2 years), half-time (4 years), or half-time for 2 years with 50 percent loan payments.
Keeps approved service sites the same: IHS, tribal programs, urban Indian programs, and qualifying private practice in shortage areas serving many Native patients.
Requires half-time service to be converted to full-time equivalents when calculating damages owed for breaking a contract.
Requires half-time participants to agree in writing to the terms (for scholarships).
who: Health professionals with IHS scholarships or loan repayment contracts
Native patients and communities served by IHS, tribal, and urban Indian health programs
IHS and tribal health facilities that struggle to recruit and keep staff
Health professionals who want part-time work for family, caregiving, or other reasons
Federal taxpayers, as the program's administrators

benefits: Could give health workers more flexibility, such as working part-time while meeting their obligation, which may make the programs more appealing.
Could help Native health facilities keep or recruit clinicians who might otherwise not join a full-time commitment.
Could expand the number of clinicians available to serve Native communities, though the bill text does not provide an estimate.
concerns: Half-time service over a longer period could mean fewer clinical hours per year at a given site than full-time service would provide.
Participants who choose half-time options may take longer to finish their service obligations, which could affect their career timelines.
Allowing half-time service could reduce the total hours of care provided per commitment, depending on how many people choose it.
imp.cost: ["The bill text does not add new money, according to the summary provided. The material does not state any cost estimate or budget effect. The half-time loan option that cuts payments to 50 percent could change how loan repayment dollars are spent, but the amount is not stated."]
unknowns: The material does not say how many people would choose the half-time options.
The material does not give a cost estimate or say whether the program would need more funding to operate.
The material does not explain how the buyback or repayment calculations would work in detail beyond converting half-time service to full-time equivalent.
The material does not say whether IHS can meet staffing needs under the new options or how the change would affect recruitment.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give Indian Health Service scholarship recipients and loan repayment participants a half-time option for meeting their service obligations, so they can fulfill those commitments in Native health care settings under a different schedule. According to the CRS summary, the bill allows recipients of Indian Health Professions Scholarships or participants in the Indian Health Service Loan Repayment Program to fulfill their service obligations through half-time clinical practice.

oppose: Half-time service spread over a longer period may mean fewer clinical hours per year at a given site than full-time service would provide, which could reduce care for Native patients who already face shortages.
Under the bill, a scholarship recipient who picks half-time must serve twice as long, so a career timeline could stretch out, and the bill does not estimate how many people would choose this option.

The bill does not add new funding in its text, so a half-time option could reduce total care hours per commitment without any added resources to make up the difference. Constituents could ask how the Senate plans to measure whether Native communities receive enough care.
support: The bill gives scholarship and loan repayment participants a half-time option, which may make these programs more appealing to health workers who cannot or do not want a full-time commitment.

Half-time options could help Native health facilities keep or recruit clinicians who might otherwise not join a full-time service obligation, according to possible benefits identified in the bill summary.

The bill keeps the approved service sites the same, including IHS facilities, tribal programs, urban Indian programs, and qualifying private practices in shortage areas, so service would stay in Native health care settings. It also converts half-time service to full-time equivalents when calculating what a person owes if they break a contract.

transparency.reason: The bill sets written-agreement requirements for participants but does not meaningfully change public transparency of government operations.

local_say.reason: Tribal and urban Indian programs remain approved service sites and can keep recruiting staff, which supports community-serving health care in Native areas.

honesty_kindness.reason: Written agreements and clear conversion rules for half-time service make the terms of the obligation explicit and fair to participants.

label: S. 638
title: A bill to amend the Act of June 22, 1948.
short_title: Boundary Waters County Payments Appraisal Fix (Thye-Blatnik Act amendment)
one: The bill changes how federal payments to three Minnesota counties for Boundary Waters wilderness land are calculated, so the payments are based on the highest appraised value, including past values, instead of the current appraised value, preventing payment decreases.
summary:
Much of the land in Minnesota's Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness is owned by the federal government, so it doesn't pay local property taxes. To make up for that, the federal government makes yearly payments to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties. Under a 1948 law called the Thye-Blatnik Act, the size of those payments depends on the "fair appraised value" of the land, as figured by the Department of Agriculture.

This bill makes a one-line change to that law. Instead of using the current fair appraised value, payments would be based on the highest fair appraised value, including past (historical) values. In practice, that means that if land appraisals drop, the counties' payments would not drop with them. The Congressional Research Service says the goal is to prevent decreases in these annual payments.

The bill does not change the size of the wilderness, add new land protections, or change rules about recreation, mining, or logging. It does not say how much extra money, if any, the change would cost. The Senate committee reported it without changes, and it is waiting on the Senate calendar for a floor vote.
does: Amends Section 5 of the Thye-Blatnik Act (16 U.S.C. 577g).
Replaces 'fair appraised value' with 'highest fair appraised value, including historical fair appraised values' as the basis for payments.
Keeps the Secretary of Agriculture as the one who determines the appraised value under that section.
Prevents annual payments to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties from falling if appraisals go down.
Does not change land boundaries, wilderness protections, or land-use rules.
who: Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota, which would get steadier or possibly higher payments
Local residents and local governments that rely on these payments for schools, roads, and services
Federal taxpayers, who fund the payments
The U.S. Forest Service / Department of Agriculture, which determines appraised values
Visitors and communities near the Boundary Waters, indirectly, because the payments help offset the tax-free federal land

benefits: Counties may receive more stable payments, since a drop in current land appraisals would not automatically reduce payments.
Local budgets that rely on these payments may be easier to plan for if payment amounts stay steady.
concerns: Because payments would be based on the highest past value, counties could receive more than the current land value would support, which some may see as unfair to other taxpayers or programs.
Federal spending could rise if appraisal values fall, since payments would not decline with them.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not say how much extra money, if any, the change would cost. The material does not provide a cost estimate."]
unknowns: The material does not state how much the payments would change under the new formula.
It is not stated how many past appraisal years would be considered or how far back the 'highest' value would reach.
It is not stated whether the change would affect other counties or payment programs.
The material does not say whether the bill is likely to pass the full Senate or the House.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to prevent decreases in the annual payments made to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota for national forest land within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. It does this by changing the Thye-Blatnik Act formula so payments are based on the highest fair appraised value, including historical values, instead of the current fair appraised value.

oppose: The bill changes the payment formula so counties are paid based on the highest past appraised value, not the current value. Payments could be higher than today's land values would normally support.

Federal payments could rise over time if appraisals fall, because the bill is designed so payments do not go down. This could add to federal spending, and the bill does not state how much it would cost.
The payments come from federal funds that support other taxpayers and programs. You may want to ask your member of Congress whether this change is fair to other places that receive similar payments.
support: The bill helps Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties plan their budgets. Because the federal government owns much of the Boundary Waters land, these counties cannot collect local property taxes on it, and the payments help make up the difference.
Under the bill, a drop in land appraisals would not automatically lower the counties' payments. This gives local governments more predictable funding year to year.
The bill makes only a narrow change to the Thye-Blatnik Act. It does not change the wilderness boundaries, protections, or rules for recreation, mining, or logging.

crs: This bill prevents decreases in annual payments provided to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota for national forest lands in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. Specifically, the bill modifies the formula created under the Thye-Blatnik Act that the Department of the Treasury uses to determine the amount of the payments. Treasury must base the payments on the highest fair appraised value, including historical fair appraised values, rather than on the fair appraised value of the land.

no_bailouts.reason: It locks in federal payments to three counties at the highest historical appraisal, so they cannot decline even when land values fall, which is a federal payment guarantee that is not tied to current conditions and has no stated cost estimate.

news.overall: Evidence is limited: each perspective group has only one headline-level article, and neither mentions the bill itself or the Act of June 22, 1948. The Lean Left piece frames the story around a state's federal funding dispute, while the Center piece frames it around mining development versus wilderness protection, so the two groups are covering different aspects of Minnesota with no visible overlap. Without full article text, these descriptions reflect only the headlines and cannot show how either outlet treats the bill.

label: S. 769
title: United States Research Protection Act of 2025
short_title: United States Research Protection Act of 2025
one: Narrows and clarifies a federal ban on researchers taking part in "malign foreign talent recruitment programs" so it applies to programs tied to foreign countries of concern (such as China, Iran, North Korea and Russia), whether the benefits come directly or indirectly.
summary: Under current law (part of the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act), researchers who get federal research money cannot take part in "malign foreign talent recruitment programs." These are programs where a foreign government offers pay or other perks in exchange for activities that create a conflict of interest or that aren't authorized, such as sharing sensitive information without permission. This bill changes the wording of that definition in two main ways. First, it ties the definition to a "foreign country of concern," a term already defined in federal law that includes China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The older text said just "foreign country," and the bill removes a separate part of the definition (subparagraph B) that I could not see in full because the bill only lists the edits. Second, it says the pay or benefits can be given "directly or indirectly." That could cover money sent through a university, company, or middleman. The bill adds no new money, penalties or agencies. It only edits the definition. The result is that the ban would more clearly target programs backed by the named countries, and would also reach programs that route benefits through other parties. Researchers working with allied or other countries could be less likely to be caught by the rule.
does: Adds 'of concern' after 'foreign country' in the definition of a malign foreign talent recruitment program.
Removes an older part of the definition (subparagraph B), whose content is not shown in the bill text provided.
Says the compensation or incentive can be provided 'directly or indirectly.'
Reorganizes the list of qualifying activities (nine items) into lettered subparagraphs.
Adds no new funding, penalties, or reporting rules on its face.
who: University and national lab researchers who receive federal grants
Universities and research institutions that must comply with the ban
Federal research funding agencies
Foreign-born and international researchers, especially those with ties to China, Iran, North Korea or Russia
Researchers collaborating with allied countries

benefits: Could make the ban more clearly focused on programs backed by named countries of concern.
The "directly or indirectly" wording could cover payments routed through universities, companies, or middlemen, which may make the rule harder to get around.
concerns: Narrowing the definition to countries of concern could leave some programs from other countries outside the rule, which may matter if those programs raise similar research-security risks.
Removing subparagraph B could change which programs are covered in ways the summary does not explain.
Researchers may find it harder to tell which arrangements are covered, especially with indirect payments, which could lead to uncertainty or unintended violations.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state any cost or funding amounts. The bill is described as adding no new money, penalties, or agencies."]
unknowns: The full text of subparagraph B, which the bill removes, is not included in the material, so its exact effect is unclear.
It is not stated how "directly or indirectly" would be applied in practice or how agencies would enforce it.
It is not stated whether the change would affect how many researchers or programs are covered.
The bill's current status is listed only as out of committee and on the Senate calendar; no vote timing is given.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Reported by Senator Cruz without amendment. With written report No. 119-45.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify the definition of a "malign foreign talent recruitment program" in the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which is part of the CHIPS and Science Act. It states that the research-funding ban on these programs should apply to programs sponsored by a "foreign country of concern" (such as China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia) and that compensation or incentives may be provided directly or indirectly.

oppose: The bill narrows the ban to programs sponsored by countries of concern. Programs from other countries that raise similar research-security risks could fall outside the rule, so a constituent could ask whether that gap is intended.

The bill removes subparagraph (B) of the existing definition, and the bill text provided does not show what that subparagraph covered. A constituent could ask the member to explain which programs would no longer be covered and why.

Adding 'directly or indirectly' may make it harder for researchers to know whether a particular arrangement is covered. Constituents could ask for clear guidance so honest researchers do not face accidental violations.
support: The bill ties the ban to 'foreign countries of concern,' a term already defined in federal law, which may focus enforcement on the countries that research-security officials see as the greatest risk.

The 'directly or indirectly' wording could stop foreign governments from avoiding the ban by routing payments through universities, companies, or middlemen, which may better protect federally funded research.
The bill adds no new spending, penalties, or agencies. It only edits an existing definition, so it could clarify current rules without creating a large new burden.

crs:
United States Research Protection Act of 2025
This bill clarifies the definition of a 
malign foreign talent recruitment program
 under the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act.

The Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which was included in the CHIPS and Science Act, prohibits researchers who receive federal funds from participating in malign foreign talent recruitment programs, in which foreign countries incentivize or compensate researchers for activities that present a conflict of interest for the researcher or that are otherwise unauthorized (e.g., sharing proprietary information without proper authorization).
The bill clarifies that these restrictions apply to programs that are sponsored by a foreign country of concern, including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia. The bill also clarifies that malign foreign talent recruitment programs may involve direct or indirect compensation or incentives from such countries.

transparency.reason: The bill edits a research-security definition without adding any disclosure, reporting, or public-access requirements.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not address honesty or kindness; it narrows the ban's coverage to certain countries and adds indirect compensation, which is a security-policy change with no clear bearing on these values.

label: S. 789
title: Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
one: Directs the Interior Department to report on who controls the world's critical minerals and rare earths, help U.S. owners sell foreign mining stakes to buyers outside China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, and plan technology and IP sharing with allies.
summary: This bill is mostly about gathering information and making plans. It does not open new mines, give out money, or change environmental rules. It tells the Interior Department to do three things. First, it must send Congress a report within one year, and then every two years, on critical minerals and rare earth elements around the world. These are materials used in electronics, batteries, and defense equipment. The report would cover who controls them, which mines produce them, how much is left, who the real owners are, and which companies are involved. It would also list cases where companies were forced to sell mining stakes under the rules of countries like China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. Second, within a year, Interior must set up a process for U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and U.S. companies to tell the government when they plan to sell stock in foreign mining, processing, or recycling operations. Interior may then help them find a buyer that is not controlled by those four countries. Third, Interior must develop a plan to work with allies on advanced mining, refining, and recycling technology. It must also develop a way to share the intellectual property from that work so allies can license it and develop their own resources. Interior must report on progress each year. The text we saw has "struck out" markings, which may mean it was amended, so the final wording could differ.
does: Requires Interior, working with Energy and other agencies, to report to Congress within 1 year and every 2 years on global critical mineral and rare earth resources.
The report must show who controls resources, mine output, remaining volumes, operators, and ultimate beneficial owners.
The report must list forced divestments and takeovers tied to governments of covered nations such as China and Russia.
The report must be unclassified, though it may have a classified annex.
Requires a process for U.S. persons to notify Interior of plans to sell foreign mining stock, with optional help finding buyers outside covered-nation control.
Requires a strategy to work with allies on advanced mining, refining, and recycling technology.
Requires a method for sharing resulting intellectual property with allied governments so they can license it.
Requires annual progress reports on the strategy and IP-sharing method.
who: Department of the Interior, Energy, State, and Commerce staff who would do the work
U.S. mining, processing, and recycling companies and investors with foreign stakes
Allied and partner governments and their mining sectors
Manufacturers and defense and tech industries that rely on rare earths
Communities near current or future mines, indirectly
Congress and the public, as readers of the reports

benefits: Could give Congress and the public a clearer picture of who owns the world's critical minerals, including ultimate beneficial owners.
Could reduce reliance on supply chains controlled by countries seen as adversaries.
Could encourage recycling technology, which can reduce the need for new mining.
Does not create new spending programs, subsidies, or bailouts.
concerns: Could indirectly speed up mining and processing worldwide, which can harm water, air, wildlife, and local communities.
Has no environmental or community-consent safeguards.
Classified annexes could limit what the public sees.
The IP-sharing method is vague and could favor private companies over the public.
Helping private investors sell stakes could be seen as a government benefit to companies.
imp.cost: The bill provides no funding and gives no cost estimate in the text provided. Costs would be Interior staff time and money, likely covered by existing budgets. Any added spending would need separate appropriations.
unknowns: The cost of the reports and programs.
The text has "struck out" markings, so it is unclear whether the final wording changed.
How IP from federally funded work would be shared, and who would profit.
How much help Interior would actually give sellers, since assistance is optional ("may").
Whether the work would lead to more mining and where.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to secure U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth elements by requiring the Department of the Interior to report on global supply and ownership, help U.S. persons find non-adversary buyers when selling stakes in foreign mining operations, and develop allied strategies and an intellectual property sharing method for advanced mining, refining, and recycling technology. The official title and CRS summary describe these steps as aimed at reducing reliance on supply chains tied to countries such as China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

oppose: The bill does not create new mines or new permits, but a global report on supply and ownership could still lead to policy pressure that speeds up mining and processing abroad, which can harm water, air, wildlife, and nearby communities.
The bill contains no environmental review, community consent, or local-impact safeguards, and I would like to see those added before any push to expand critical mineral development.
Parts of the required reporting could be placed in a classified annex, which would limit what the public and local communities can see about who controls these resources.
The intellectual property sharing method is described only in general terms, and I am concerned it could favor private companies over taxpayers and the public interest.

Helping private investors find buyers for foreign mining stakes could be seen as a government service that benefits companies, and I would like to know what costs and conflicts of interest that involves.
support: The bill would give Congress and the public a clearer, regularly updated picture of who owns and supplies the world's critical minerals, including ultimate beneficial owners, every two years.
Reducing reliance on supply chains controlled by countries seen as adversaries, such as China and Russia, is a goal that supporters say matters for electronics, batteries, and defense equipment.
The bill focuses on recycling and advanced processing technology, which supporters say could reduce the need for new mining over time.
The bill does not create new spending programs, subsidies, or bailouts, and it is mainly a reporting and planning measure, which supporters may see as a low-cost step.

crs:
Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
This bill establishes requirements for the Department of the Interior related to securing U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth element (REE) resources. 
Critical minerals
 mean any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey. 
REEs
 mean cerium, dysprosium, erbium, europium, gadolinium, holmium, lanthanum, lutetium, neodymium, praseodymium, promethium, samarium, scandium, terbium, thulium, ytterbium, and yttrium. 
First, Interior must report on the critical mineral and REE resources, including recyclable or recycled materials containing those resources, around the world. Among other information, the report must include an assessment of the global ownership and supply of critical mineral and REE resources. Interior must submit the report within a year and every two years thereafter.
Next, Interior must establish a process to assist a U.S. person—a U.S. citizen, a non-U.S. National (alien under federal law) lawfully admitted for permanent residence, or an entity organized under U.S. laws—seeking to divest stock in mining, processing, or recycling operations for critical minerals and REEs in a foreign country with finding a purchaser that is not under the control of North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran.
Finally, Interior must develop (1) a strategy to collaborate with U.S. allies and partners to develop advanced mining, refining, separation, processing, and recycling technologies; and (2) a method for sharing related intellectual property with U.S. allies and partners to enable those countries to license those technologies and develop their resources.

transparency.reason: It requires recurring reports on mine ownership, including ultimate beneficial owners, though a classified annex is allowed and the reports go to Congress.

label: S. 81
title: Guidance Clarity Act of 2025
one: Requires federal agencies to put a standard notice on the first page of their guidance documents saying the document is not law and doesn't bind the public or the agency.
summary: Federal agencies often publish "guidance" documents. These explain how an agency reads a law or how it plans to handle something. They aren't formal rules, and they skip the public comment process that formal rules go through. This bill would make agencies put a set statement on the first page of that kind of guidance. The statement says the document does not have the force and effect of law, does not by itself bind the public or the agency, and is meant only to give the public clarity about existing legal requirements or agency policies. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB, the White House office that oversees agency management) would have 90 days after enactment to write instructions for carrying out the law. Agencies would have to start using the statement 30 days after OMB issues those instructions. The Senate committee rewrote the bill and changed which part of the Administrative Procedure Act (the main law on how agencies make rules) it points to. The text does not describe any penalty for agencies that skip the statement. It also doesn't say how the statement would be enforced or how it would be handled in court. The bill doesn't change what guidance can legally do. It only requires the label.

Requires the statement to appear prominently on the first page.

Directs OMB to issue implementing guidance within 90 days of enactment.

Applies to guidance under a specific part of the Administrative Procedure Act, apparently the section that exempts certain documents from public notice and comment. The committee amendment changed the cross-reference from 553(b)(3)(A) to 553(b)(4)(A).

OMB, which must write the implementing instructions
Businesses and industries that follow agency guidance

The bill may help readers tell apart guidance documents from binding regulations.
Because the bill changes only the labeling requirement, it would not directly add new burdens on the public's rights.
concerns: The bill text does not describe any penalty for agencies that skip the required statement, so compliance may be uneven.
The bill does not say how the statement would be enforced or how courts would treat it, leaving open questions.
Some readers may find that a disclaimer on guidance could reduce how much weight agencies or the public give to guidance, though the bill does not say this directly.

label: S. 90
title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
one: The bill would bar the Bureau of Land Management from spending money to carry out or finish certain Utah road and trail (travel management) plans until Utah's long-running "historic road" lawsuits are resolved, and in six areas it would put older pre-2017 plans back in force.
summary:
This bill deals with which roads and trails are open on federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in Utah. Utah and many of its counties have sued the federal government for years. They say they own old rights-of-way (legal claims to use old roads across federal land) under a law from 1866 called R.S. 2477. Congress repealed that law in 1976 but kept rights that already existed.

While those lawsuits are pending, the bill would stop BLM from spending federal money on certain travel management plans. These are plans that decide which routes stay open to vehicles. The bill covers 11 named areas, including the San Rafael Swell, Nine Mile Canyon, Dolores River, Book Cliffs and Henry Mountains. In all 11 areas, BLM could not carry out plans finished after a January 2017 legal settlement with conservation groups. In six of them, BLM could not finish new plans. Those six areas would go back to the plans in effect before the settlement.

The ban would last until the Interior Secretary tells Congress that every listed lawsuit has been decided or otherwise resolved. It applies "notwithstanding any other law," meaning it overrides other laws that might conflict. The Senate committee rewrote the bill. The summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS, Congress's neutral research office) describes the earlier version, so some details here differ from it.
does: see items
who: Bureau of Land Management staff and offices in Utah
Utah state government and the counties in the R.S. 2477 lawsuits
Off-road vehicle riders, ranchers, hunters, and others who use backcountry routes
Conservation groups, including the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, that were part of the 2017 settlement
Hikers, campers, and visitors to the named areas
Local residents and Tribes near the affected public lands
Wildlife, plants, water sources, and cultural sites in the named areas

Could give Utah counties and the state more certainty while their court cases continue.
Could prevent route closures that might later be found to violate the counties' legal claims.
concerns: Could freeze or undo travel plans that were written to protect land, water, wildlife, plants, and cultural sites from vehicle damage.
Congress would be overriding a negotiated legal settlement and a public planning process, which may reduce public input and transparency.
The 'notwithstanding any other law' language could override other legal duties, though the bill doesn't spell out which ones.

The Interior Secretary decides when the cases count as resolved. The text doesn't say how 'otherwise resolved' is judged.
The bill puts the claims of state and county governments ahead of the views of other people who use or care about these public lands, which belong to all Americans.
imp.cost: No cost estimate was provided. The bill does not appropriate (set aside) any new money. It only blocks BLM from spending money on certain plans. It could still have indirect costs, such as ongoing litigation or resource damage.
unknowns: The text doesn't say which specific routes would be open or closed under the older plans, so the on-the-ground effect is unclear.
I could not see the older (pre-2017) plans or the 2017 settlement terms, so I can't compare how protective each one is.
The CRS summary describes the earlier version of the bill, so it may not match the amended text.
It is unclear when the lawsuits will end, so the length of the ban is unknown.
It is unclear how the bill would interact with other environmental and public-lands laws.

purpose: The bill says it addresses long-running lawsuits by Utah and 22 counties over old rights-of-way for historic roads on BLM land under R.S. 2477, a law repealed in 1976 that FLPMA partly preserved. crs:
Historic Roadways Protection Act
This bill prohibits the Bureau for Land Management (BLM) from closing historical roads on public lands in certain areas of Utah until the Federal District Court for Utah makes a decision on each of the R.S. 2477 cases, which are cases brought by Utah and counties to keep historical roads on BLM land in Utah open for public use.
By way of background, a provision of the Mining Law of 1866, commonly known as R.S. 2477, granted rights-of-way to states and counties across public lands for the construction of roads for public use in order to promote settlement of the American West. In 1976, Congress repealed R.S. 2477 when it enacted the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), but FLPMA preserved rights-of-way that had been established under R.S. 2477. After the BLM released travel management plans that closed some historical roads, Utah and 22 counties filed lawsuits about their rights-of-way across public lands for historical roads.
Until the BLM certifies that those cases have been decided, the bill prohibits the BLM from obligating or expending federal funds to (1) finalize or implement a new travel management plan for certain travel management areas in Utah; or (2) implement, with respect to land within the boundary of Utah, the Indian Creek (Canyon Rims) Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Desert Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Swell Travel Management Plan, or the Labyrinth/Gemini Bridges Travel Management Plan.

life.reason: Blocking travel plans written to limit vehicle damage could expose wildlife, plants, and cultural sites in the named areas to more disturbance, though the effect is indirect.

water.reason: Freezing plans that restrict routes near water sources could allow more vehicle impacts on streams and springs in the affected areas.

transparency.reason: The bill overrides a negotiated settlement and public planning process and applies 'notwithstanding any other law,' which reduces public visibility into and input on land decisions.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill favors state and county claims and some user groups over the broader public interest in land protection, though it does not directly involve corporate profits.

local_say.reason: It advances the wishes of Utah and its counties, who are seeking to keep routes they consider historic and locally important open.

Lean Left coverage is a single Politico headline focused on a Utah GOP governor's views on Trump and 2028, while Center coverage is three Deseret News pieces centered on the governor's dealmaking stance, data center transparency, and Utah's new politics. label: H.R. 2385
title: CREATE AI Act of 2025
short_title: CREATE AI Act (National AI Research Resource)
one: Sets up a national program, run through the National Science Foundation and a outside operator, to give U.S. researchers and students access to AI computing power, data, training, and testing tools.
summary:
This bill would create the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), a shared national toolbox for AI research. Today, the computing power and large datasets needed for advanced AI work are mostly held by very large tech companies. The bill aims to open access to university researchers, students, educators, nonprofits, some small businesses that have federal funding, and federal employees with a job need.

The National Science Foundation (NSF) would have one year after enactment to set up the program, with a program office of at least three full-time staff. A White House–led steering group of federal agencies would oversee the plan and budget. NSF would pick a nongovernmental organization through a competitive, transparent process to run day-to-day operations, and could replace it if it performs poorly.

NAIRR would offer computing, data, an open data commons, training, and AI testing tools. A significant share of computing time must go to projects on AI privacy, ethics, safety, security, and trustworthiness. Users would face minimum security rules, and people tied to certain foreign adversary governments would be barred. The operator could charge fees, but must offer a free tier. The program could also accept donations of cash, services, and property from private companies. Many resources depend on Congress providing money; the bill text itself does not set a dollar amount.

crs:
Creating Resources for Every American To Experiment with Artificial Intelligence Act of 2025 or the CREATE AI Act of 2025
This bill establishes a national program to provide U.S. researchers, educators, and students with access to artificial intelligence (AI) data, computational resources, educational tools and services, and testbeds.
The program, to be known as the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), must be established by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to improve U.S. AI research capacity and spur the strategic development of AI capabilities. NAIRR may accept and use donated resources from the private sector and federal agencies.
Those eligible to use NAIRR resources are (1) researchers, educators, and students based in the United States and affiliated with a U.S. institution of higher education, nonprofit, executive agency, or other specified entity; and (2) employees of U.S. executive agencies or federally funded research and development centers with a demonstrable mission need.
NSF must select a nongovernmental organization to operate NAIRR (i.e., an 
operating entity
) through a competitive and transparent process. The operating entity must ensure that a significant percentage of the annual allotment of computational resources is provided to projects primarily focused on AI privacy, ethics, safety, security, risk mitigation, or trustworthiness. The operating entity must also establish minimum security requirements for all individuals interacting with NAIRR.
The operating entity may establish a fee schedule for access to NAIRR, which must include a free tier of access and must ensure that the primary purpose of NAIRR is to support research.

label: H.R. 3087
title: Civil Rights Cold Case Records Collection Reauthorization Act
short_title: Civil Rights Cold Case Records Collection Reauthorization Act
one: The bill extends the Civil Rights Cold Case Records Review Board's life from 7 to 11 years, helps state and local governments pay to send old civil rights case records to the National Archives, and limits a privacy exemption for records created in 1990 or earlier.
summary: A 2018 law created a Review Board and a collection at the National Archives for records about unsolved civil rights–era crimes, called "cold cases." This bill would make that system stronger and keep it going longer. First, it says Congress believes federal, state, and local records on these cases should be presumed open to the public right away and eventually released. This is only a statement of opinion, not a binding rule. Second, it lets the Board repay state and local governments in full for the cost of scanning, copying, or mailing records to the National Archives. Third, it removes the wording that excused state and local governments from the requirement to send their records to the Archives. Fourth, it changes the privacy exemption in the law so that personal information in records created on or before January 1, 1990 can no longer be withheld under the Freedom of Information Act privacy exemption (section 552(b)(6)). Finally, it extends the Board's lifespan from 7 years to 11 years. The bill does not give a dollar amount. The text does not say how reimbursements would be funded, and I could not see the committee's amendments. The House committee voted 36–4 to report an amended version.

label: H.R. 3108
title: RPM Access Act
short_title: RPM Access Act (Rural Patient Monitoring Access Act)
one: Sets a minimum geographic payment level for Medicare remote patient monitoring, requires providers to meet care-quality and data-reporting conditions to be paid, and orders a report on savings and costs.
summary:
This bill changes how Medicare pays for remote patient monitoring (RPM). RPM means using devices, like blood pressure cuffs or glucose monitors, that send a patient's health readings to a care team while the patient is at home.

First, Medicare adjusts what it pays doctors by location using "geographic indices," which are numbers that reflect local costs. Right now, some areas, often rural, have indices below 1.00, so they get paid less. Starting January 1, 2026, the bill would raise any practice expense or malpractice index to 1.00 for RPM payments. It would not offset this with cuts elsewhere, so total Medicare spending on RPM could go up.

Second, starting in 2026, Medicare would only pay for RPM if three things are true. A physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant must be available in real time to respond to any unusual reading. The system must be able to send data in a form that works with electronic health records. And the provider must report data that the Health Secretary requires so savings can be measured. The Secretary can excuse a provider if reporting would cause unreasonable hardship.

Third, within five years, the Health Department must report to Congress on savings from earlier care and fewer hospital days, savings from patients taking medicines as prescribed, and the practice costs of RPM, over 2026 to 2029.

The bill's findings say RPM pays least in states with high rates of heart failure, high blood pressure, and diabetes. The committee advanced it 39-0.
does: Raises practice expense and malpractice geographic payment indices to at least 1.00 for Medicare remote patient monitoring starting January 1, 2026.
Says this floor is not 'budget neutral,' meaning it is not paid for by cutting other Medicare payments, so it could raise federal spending.
Bars Medicare payment for RPM from 2026 unless a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant can respond in real time to abnormal readings.
Requires RPM systems to send data in a format compatible with electronic health records, as needed.
Requires providers to collect and report data the Health Secretary requires to measure Medicare savings, with a hardship exemption available.
Requires a report to Congress within 5 years covering 2026-2029 on savings from fewer hospital days, better medication adherence, and RPM practice costs.

label: H.R. 3514
title: Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act of 2025
short_title: Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act of 2025
one: Requires Medicare Advantage insurance plans to use secure electronic systems for prior authorization, publicly report how often they approve, deny, and delay requests (including when AI is used), and lets the government set faster response deadlines.
summary: Prior authorization is when an insurance plan must approve a treatment, test, or service before it will pay for it. This bill would add rules for private Medicare Advantage plans, which are the private-insurer versions of Medicare. Starting in 2027, plans that use prior authorization would have to report data each year to the government, which would post it publicly for each individual plan. The data includes how many requests were approved or denied, how many denials were appealed and overturned, how long decisions took, and how often computer tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) were used to decide. Plans must also share their approval criteria with doctors and, on request, with patients. Starting in 2028, plans must set up secure electronic systems to send and answer prior authorization requests, instead of using fax or certain private portals. They must also build their programs with input from patients and providers, review which services need approval each year, and may ease the rules for providers with good track records. The bill lets the Health and Human Services Secretary set response deadlines, such as 24 hours, including for "real-time" decisions on routine items. It also orders reports: one from CMS (the Medicare agency) on real-time decisions and AI's effect on access, including for rural and low-income people, plus reports from MedPAC (an advisory commission) and the GAO (a congressional watchdog agency).

Requires reporting of how many requests were approved or denied using AI, machine learning, or other decision-support tools, and a description of those tools.
Requires reporting of average and median decision times, and how many requests were left out of that math for missing documentation.
Requires reporting of cases where a provider found extra or different care was needed during a procedure that had been approved, and the number of prior-authorization-related grievances.
Requires CMS to publish this data on a public website at the individual plan level.
Requires plans to give providers and patients (on request) access to their approval criteria and required documentation.

Sets patient protection standards: programs developed with enrollee and provider input, possible waivers for providers who follow evidence-based guidelines, and annual reviews of which services need approval.

Lets the HHS Secretary set response deadlines (for example 24 hours) for expedited, real-time, and other prior authorization requests, applying to requests starting in the third plan year after enactment.
Orders a CMS/ONC report by January 1, 2028 on defining real-time decisions and the effect of AI-only decisions on access, including for rural and low-income people.
Orders MedPAC, HHS, and GAO reports to Congress (GAO by January 1, 2032; HHS every two years).

Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act of 
2025
This bill establishes several requirements and standards relating to prior authorization processes under Medicare Advantage (MA) plans.
Specifically, MA plans must (1) establish an electronic prior authorization program that meets specified standards; (2) annually submit to the CMS for publication specified prior authorization information, including the percentage of requests approved and the average response time; and (3) meet other standards, as set by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), relating to the quality and timeliness of prior authorization determinations.

label: H.R. 4140
title: Burma GAP Act
short_title: Burma GAP Act (Burma Genocide Accountability and Protection Act)
one: The bill sets U.S. policy to protect Rohingya people, send them humanitarian aid, and push for accountability for genocide committed by Burma's military, with yearly public reports to Congress.
summary:
This bill is about the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority group in Burma (also called Myanmar). The U.S. State Department has officially determined that Burma's military committed genocide and crimes against humanity against them. Many Rohingya now live in crowded refugee camps in Bangladesh, where food is short and violence is a risk.

The bill states U.S. policy to prevent more atrocities, hold the guilty accountable, and isolate Burma's military government diplomatically and economically until civilian rule returns. It lets the Secretary of State name a senior career diplomat as Special Representative for Burma for five years if there is no U.S. ambassador. It says the State Department should help protect Rohingya refugees, support their access to asylum, legal help, and safe rescue at sea, and work toward their safe, voluntary return with full citizenship rights when conditions allow.

It says aid should continue for food, health care, water, sanitation, shelter, education, protection from gender-based violence and trafficking, and job training. It supports collecting and preserving evidence of atrocities for future trials. It also asks for a report within 180 days and once a year for five years. The public part of each report must be posted on the State Department website. It authorizes spending of "such sums as necessary" plus $5 million and $4 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 for investigations and evidence work. "Authorizes" means it permits the spending, but Congress must still pass a separate funding law.
