title: Stop DC CAMERA Act
one: Congress would repeal Washington, D.C.'s legal authority to use traffic cameras (speed, red-light and other automated enforcement) and to post "no right turn on red" signs.
summary:
This bill would overrule local law in Washington, D.C. by removing the city's power to run automated traffic enforcement. That means the cameras that catch speeding, red-light running and similar violations would lose their legal basis. The bill does this by repealing Title IX of a 1996 D.C. budget law, which is the part that set up the automated enforcement program. It also repeals a section of a 2012 D.C. law that required a plan to expand the camera program. Separately, it repeals a section of the 1925 D.C. Traffic Act that lets the city put up signs banning right turns on red lights.

The bill's full name, "Stop DC Capital Authoritarian Motorvehicle Enforcement and Restoration of Autonomy Act," shows the sponsors' view that the cameras are an overreach by the D.C. government. The bill text does not say what happens to existing cameras, pending tickets, fines already issued, or the money the program brings in. It also does not say what would replace the cameras. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. The House Oversight Committee reported the bill with an amendment that replaced the original text, and it is now on the House calendar. It has not passed the House.

label: H.R. 5688
title: Non-Domiciled CDL Integrity Act
one: Sets federal rules for when states may issue commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) to people who live outside the state or in a foreign country, requiring proof of lawful status, a work-related visa, short license terms, and records kept for federal review.
summary:
This bill changes the federal law that tells states who they can give a commercial driver's license (CDL) to. A CDL is the license needed to drive big trucks and buses. Under the bill, a state could issue a CDL only to someone who lives in that state, or in a state that does not issue CDLs. There is one narrow exception for people who live in a foreign country.

For a foreign resident to get a CDL, they must be lawfully in the United States and hold a visa the Secretary of Transportation decides is directly tied to a real job that needs a CDL. The state must check their lawful status each time it issues, transfers, renews, or upgrades the license. The license can last at most one year, or until the person's authorized stay ends, whichever is sooner. The state must keep its records for at least two years, and hand them to the federal government within 48 hours if asked.

People who live in U.S. territories (Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands) have a separate path. They must show proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful permanent residence (a green card). The state must confirm it and keep the same records.

The text does not say when the rules start or what happens to states that do not follow them. It also does not say which visas the Secretary would approve.

label: H.R. 8801
title: DC ROADS Act
short_title: DC ROADS Act (Ban on DC Congestion Tolls)
one: Bars the District of Columbia's Council and Mayor from creating or enforcing any congestion toll, meaning a charge to enter or drive through roads in DC.
summary: This bill would stop the District of Columbia's local government from charging drivers a "congestion toll." The bill defines that as any charge for entering or passing through roads, bridges, tunnels, approaches, or ramps located in or leading into DC. The DC Council would not be allowed to pass a law, resolution, or rule that sets up such a toll. The Mayor would not be allowed to enforce one. label: H.R. 9250
title: Great American Outdoors Act 250
one: Renews and renames a fund that pays to fix the repair backlog on national parks, forests, wildlife refuges, other public lands and Indian schools, paid for by energy revenue and new fees on foreign visitors, while speeding up environmental review and contracting.
summary: This bill continues a program that pays for long-delayed repairs on federal lands. It renames the existing fund the "America's Legacy Restoration Fund." Money goes in from three sources: new fees on foreign visitors, donations, and half of the federal government's oil, gas, coal, and renewable energy revenue from federal land. Deposits from fees and energy revenue are capped at $1.9 billion a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. The money can be spent without a yearly vote in Congress. Of that money, 70% goes to the National Park Service, 15% to the Forest Service, and 5% each to Fish and Wildlife, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Education schools. It can't be used to buy land, tear out roads, or pay bonuses. Up to 15% can go to outdoor recreation and hunting and fishing access projects. Agencies must publish project-picking criteria, run a public online project tracker, ask governors for ideas, and report to Congress. The bill pushes private donations and matching, and nonprofit partners. It also tells agencies to build a shortcut environmental review (a "categorical exclusion"), allows emergency-style contracting rules, caps architect fees, and requires disposing of unneeded buildings and other assets. Foreign visitors would pay at least $100 per person to enter fee-charged federal sites, or at least $250 for an annual pass.

label: H.R. 9607

short_title: Less Bureaucracy, Better Workforce Development Act
one: Moves the federal office that runs career, technical, and adult education programs from the Department of Education to the Department of Labor, with its staff and money, within six months of enactment.
summary:
This bill would move the programs run by the Education Department's Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education over to the Department of Labor. These programs include career and technical education (job-focused classes in high schools and colleges) under the Perkins Act. They also include adult education and family literacy programs, such as help for adults to learn to read, earn a high school diploma, or move on to more training, under Title II of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. Two sections of the Perkins Act (sections 116 and 117) would stay out of the transfer.

The staff, property, records, and unspent money tied to these programs would move to Labor, and the money could only be used for the purposes it was first approved for. The White House budget office (OMB) would settle any questions about which functions move. It must also make sure the move does not add to the total number of federal employees at the agencies involved. It must tell the House and Senate education committees that the bill is being followed. Existing rules, grants, contracts, lawsuits, and pending applications would continue as before. The change would start six months after enactment, though the transfer could begin earlier. The bill does not say how much it would cost or save, and it does not change what the programs are required to do. The CRS summary notes that Education and Labor already signed an agreement in July 2025 for Labor to help run these programs.

label: H.R. 9641
title: Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
one: Requires nursing homes and certain other long-term care facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid to let each resident name two essential caregivers who can still visit in person when regular visits are suspended.
summary:
During emergencies like disease outbreaks, nursing homes have sometimes shut their doors to visitors. This bill would stop families from being fully cut off from loved ones in those times. Facilities covered by Medicare or Medicaid would have to let each resident pick two "essential caregivers." Residents could change their picks at any time. If a resident can't decide because of dementia or a mental disability, their legal representative can choose for them. Caregivers must agree to follow the facility's written safety and infection rules. Those rules can't be stricter than the ones for the facility's staff.

There are limits. Federal guidance could let a facility bar in-person visits for the first 7 days of a visitation shutdown, but only if it offers video calls in that time. Only one caregiver can be in the room at a time. A facility could turn away a caregiver who has symptoms of a serious contagious disease until a negative test, or who breaks safety rules. Roommates' rights must be reasonably protected. For residents in hospice-style end-of-life care, access can't be denied or time-limited. State inspectors must put caregiver-access complaints first and tell the person who complained the outcome within 3 days. Emergency waivers couldn't set these rules aside. The rules would start one year after enactment, and federal regulations are due within 18 months.

Requires caregiver safety rules to be written down and no stricter than those for staff.
Requires state inspectors to prioritize caregiver-access complaints and notify the complainant within 3 days.
Stops emergency waivers from setting aside these requirements.
Requires HHS to write regulations within 18 months; the law applies 1 year after enactment.

Facilities may find it hard to balance caregiver access with infection control, especially during outbreaks.

Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
This bill requires certain nursing and long-term care facilities to ensure residents have access to their designated essential caregivers during periods of restricted visitation.
Specifically, the bill requires Medicare skilled nursing facilities, long-term care hospitals, and inpatient rehabilitation facilities, as well as Medicaid nursing facilities and intermediate care facilities for individuals with intellectual disabilities, to allow residents to designate two essential caregivers and to allow these caregivers in-person access to residents even when visitation is otherwise restricted. 
Facilities may limit access of essential caregivers only in accordance with guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, as specified. Essential caregivers must agree to follow all safety protocols established by the facility, which may be no more restrictive than the protocols for staff.

title: Moab UMTRA Project Transition Act of 2025
one: When the federal cleanup of the Moab uranium mill tailings site is finished, the Department of Energy would give the land, and some water pipeline infrastructure and water rights, to local Utah governments at no cost.
summary: For years the federal government has been cleaning up a large pile of radioactive waste (uranium mill tailings) left by an old uranium mill about three miles from Moab, Utah. This bill sets up what happens to the land afterward. Once the Energy Department decides the cleanup is far enough along, it would give the Moab site to Grand County, Utah, for free. Any safety limits on how the land can be used, set by the Energy Department or the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, would still apply. The federal government would keep the water rights it needs to finish its cleanup duties, including access to wells if groundwater cleanup is still going on. The county could not pass the land to a private company or nonprofit. A bracketed section in the text, which may be an added or proposed amendment, would also give the Grand County Water Conservancy District the Green River water pipeline, pump stations, diesel pumps, easements, a holding pond at Crescent Junction, and the Crescent Junction water right. The district would have to use these to address the water shortage in the communities it serves, and it could not pass them to private or nonprofit groups. The Energy Department could keep water rights strictly needed to finish groundwater cleanup. The bill gives no dates and no dollar amounts.

label: S. 1885
title: Stop the Scroll Act
one: Requires social media and anonymous content-sharing platforms to show a mental health warning label, with a link to resources like the 988 Lifeline, each time a U.S. user accesses them, and again after each hour of continuous use.
summary:
This bill would make social media companies show a mental health warning to people in the United States every time they open the platform. The label would warn that using the platform could harm mental health. It would also point users to federal help, including the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. A user could not turn the label off. It would go away only if the person leaves the platform or clicks to say they understand the risk and want to continue. If they continue, the label would appear again after every hour of nonstop use. The label could not be hidden only in a link or in the fine print, and it could not be crowded out by extra information.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), with approval from the Health and Human Services Secretary acting through the Surgeon General, would write detailed rules within 180 days of the bill becoming law. The rules would be reviewed at least every five years. The requirements would start one year after enactment. The FTC could enforce the law, treating violations like unfair or deceptive business practices, and it could also reach nonprofits and common carriers. State attorneys general and other state consumer protection officers could also sue for civil penalties. The law would cover violations that involve people in the U.S., even if the company is based elsewhere. The bill covers "social media platforms" as defined in an existing law, plus websites or apps that let people share content without registering.

Forcing a label on every access might raise questions about how platforms determine a user's location, with possible privacy implications.

How 'clearly and conspicuously' and 'hour of continuous use' will be defined and measured.

Whether courts would uphold the label requirement.

label: S. 298
title: Returning SBA to Main Street Act
short_title: Returning SBA to Main Street Act
one: As introduced, the bill would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to move at least 30% of its Washington-area headquarters staff to offices outside the D.C. region, end full-time telework for those staff, and cut headquarters office space by at least 30%.
summary:
Every section of the text I was given is marked "struck out." That usually means a committee amendment replaced the original wording. The replacement wording was not included, so this analysis covers the original text only. The final version could differ.

As introduced, the bill would push the SBA to shift some of its workforce away from Washington, D.C. Within one year of enactment, the SBA would have to move the permanent work location of at least 30% of its headquarters employees to SBA offices outside the D.C. area. Those employees would be paid by the pay scale of their new location, which is often lower than D.C. pay. They could no longer work from home full time. Employees who work from home full time but stay in the D.C. area would also lose that option. Workers who have a full-time telework accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act would not be moved, but they would still count toward the 30%.

The SBA would also have to cut its headquarters office space by at least 30% within two years. It would have to send Congress a report within 180 days and add staffing numbers to its yearly budget requests. Employees who must relocate would get no relocation bonuses. The bill would override union contracts and other laws. It would not let anyone sue over how it is carried out.

label: S. 371
title: SBA Disaster Transparency Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to post on its public website the disaster assistance reports it already must send to Congress.
summary:
When a disaster hits, the Small Business Administration (SBA) offers loans to small businesses, homeowners, and renters to help them recover. A 2008 law already requires the SBA to send several kinds of reports about this work to Congress. Those reports cover things like how the disaster loan program is performing. Right now, the law only requires them to go to congressional committees, so the public may have a hard time finding them.

This bill makes a small change. It adds the words "and publish on the website of the Administration" to four reporting requirements in the 2008 law. It also says the information in those reports must be "submitted and published." That means the SBA would have to put the same reports on its own website where anyone can read them.

The bill does not create new reports, change who can get disaster loans, or add money to any program. It does not set a deadline for posting or say how easy the reports must be to find. The text does not list what each report covers. I could only see the amendments, not the full 2008 law. Because of that, I can't describe the content of each report in detail. No Congressional Research Service summary is available yet.

label: S. 3791
title: Regional Ocean Partnerships Reauthorization Act
one: Extends federal authorization for state-led Regional Ocean Partnerships through fiscal year 2031, bars them from enforcement and regulatory work, and requires a new NOAA effectiveness report.
summary: Regional Ocean Partnerships are groups led by state governors. They work with federal agencies, states, tribes and others on shared ocean and coastal issues, such as protecting resources, collecting data and public outreach. This bill keeps them authorized through fiscal year 2031. Their current authorization ends after 2027. The bill text lists yearly funding limits for 2028 through 2031. These run from about $11.6 million in 2028 to about $11.9 million in 2031. Authorizing money means Congress allows it to be spent. A separate spending bill must still provide the actual money. The CRS summary says the bill also bars partnership funds from being used to write regulatory proposals, model regulations or compliance programs. It says the partnerships may not have an enforcement role. Current law only bans regulatory functions. It also renews the requirement that NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) report to Congress on how well the partnerships work. The first report was already required, and a new one would be due within 5 years of enactment. The CRS summary says the bill removes Vermont from the Northeast Regional Ocean Council. I could not see that provision in the text provided, because the text was marked up with struck-out sections. The bill does not create new regulations or change any environmental standard.

Regional Ocean Partnerships Reauthorization Act
This bill reauthorizes Regional Ocean Partnerships (ROPs) through FY2031 with certain funding restrictions and removes Vermont from the Northeast Regional Ocean Council (an existing ROP). 
As background, ROPs are regional organizations that are convened by state governors and work in collaboration with federal agencies, state governments, tribal governments, and other stakeholders to address ocean and coastal issues of common concern in the region. ROPs conduct projects involving resource conservation, data collection, outreach, and related activities. They are overseen at the federal level by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The bill provides that ROP funding may not be used to develop any regulatory proposal, model regulation, or compliance program. It also specifies that ROPs may not have an enforcement function. (Under current law, regulatory functions are prohibited.)

label: S. 68
title: Complete COVID Collections Act
one: The bill extends the pandemic-fraud watchdog to 2030, gives prosecutors 10 years to bring COVID relief fraud cases, requires collection of small COVID business loans, and requires regular public reports on recoveries.
summary: This bill is about getting back money that was lost to fraud or improper payments in COVID-19 relief programs, mainly Small Business Administration (SBA) loans and grants. First, it keeps the Special Inspector General for Pandemic Recovery (a watchdog office) going until September 30, 2030, and widens its reach to cover SBA programs such as Paycheck Protection Program loans, COVID disaster loans, restaurant grants, and shuttered venue grants. Second, it sets a 10-year deadline for bringing criminal or civil fraud cases tied to certain relief programs. Third, it tells the SBA to send unpaid COVID loan claims under $100,000 to the Treasury Department, which decides whether to collect, pause, or end collection. The SBA head must brief Congress every 30 days and testify every year about collections and improper payments. Fourth, the Justice Department must send Congress monthly reports on COVID program prosecutions, money recovered, referrals, and declined cases with reasons. Fifth, the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee must post real-time data on recovered COVID funds on its website. Finally, any money collected because of fraud in these programs must go only toward reducing the federal debt. The text does not give a cost estimate.

label: H.R. 3194
title: LOCOMOTIVES Act
short_title: LOCOMOTIVES Act (ban on state limits on existing train emissions)
one: The bill would bar states from setting their own air pollution rules for existing locomotives used by freight and passenger railroads, leaving that power to the federal government.
summary: Under the Clean Air Act, states are already blocked from setting their own emission standards for new locomotives and new locomotive engines. That leaves states some room to regulate older trains already running on their tracks. This bill would close that gap. It adds a new category to the Clean Air Act's list of things states cannot regulate: locomotives and locomotive engines that are "engaged in commerce." The bill says this covers every locomotive that provides common carrier railroad transportation for pay, which means ordinary freight and passenger railroads. In practice, a state such as California could no longer require older, dirtier trains to meet its own limits, run less, or be upgraded. Only federal rules, set by the EPA, would apply. The bill also makes small wording changes to the existing rules. Those changes clarify that the current bans on state rules for new construction/farm engines under 175 horsepower and for new locomotives apply to engines that are subject to federal regulation. Supporters say a patchwork of state rules burdens railroads that cross state lines. Critics say it removes a tool that states and communities near rail yards use to cut diesel pollution. The bill has no funding provisions, and the text does not set a start date beyond becoming law. The House committee advanced it, as amended, on a 26–23 vote.

Reaches existing (not only new) locomotives, since the new category covers those not already covered by the 'new locomotive' ban.

Leaves federal EPA locomotive emission rules in place; it creates no new federal standards.

Could leave a regulatory gap if federal rules for in-use locomotives are weak or slow to change.
Narrow committee vote (26–23) suggests significant disagreement.
imp.cost: The text contains no spending or funding provisions. No cost estimate was provided in the material I was given. Costs would fall mostly on communities (health effects) or railroads (compliance), depending on how it plays out.
unknowns: Exactly which state rules or pending programs would be blocked; the text does not name any.
How strong federal rules for existing locomotives are or will be going forward.

label: H.R. 6130
title: ASAP Act
short_title: ASAP Act (Alzheimer's Screening and Prevention Act)
one: Starting in 2028, Medicare would cover FDA-cleared or approved blood tests (and similar equivalent tests) that screen for early-stage or pre-symptom Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
summary: This bill would add a new Medicare benefit: coverage of early-detection screening tests for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. The tests must be given on or after January 1, 2028, and must be cleared or approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The main type covered is a genomic sequencing blood test, which reads genetic material in a blood sample. The bill also lets the Health and Human Services Secretary cover "equivalent" tests that give comparable results. The bill's list of examples includes single-marker tests, panels of several markers, whole genome sequencing, protein tests, and medical imaging. These can be based on blood, tissue, urine, or other samples. The bill also adds these tests to the Medicare rules that set payment for lab tests, so they would be paid like other covered clinical lab tests. The bill does not say what Medicare would pay, whether patients would owe copays, who is eligible for screening, or how often. It also gives no cost estimate in the text provided. Supporters would say earlier detection could help people and families plan and get care sooner. Open questions include the cost to Medicare, what patients would be charged, test accuracy, and what happens after a positive result, since treatment options are limited.

label: H.R. 7651
title: Chloe Cole Act of 2026
one: Lets people who received puberty blockers, hormones, or surgery as minors for gender transition (or their parents) sue the doctors, hospitals, and clinics involved, including for care given before the law passes.
summary:
This bill creates a new way to sue in federal court. Anyone who, as a child under 18, got puberty blockers, sex hormones, or surgery meant to delay puberty or change their body so it no longer matches their sex could sue later. Their parents or guardians could sue too. The defendants could be doctors, hospitals, or clinics that took part. The bill defines "sex" as a fixed male or female classification set at conception.

Winners could get money for medical costs, including treatment to reverse or fix the effects (called detransition care). They could also get money for pain and emotional distress. Punitive damages (extra money meant to punish) are possible if the plaintiff proves bad conduct by "clear and convincing evidence." For care after the law passes, providers would be "strictly liable," meaning they could owe damages without proof of carelessness. Providers cannot use a signed waiver to avoid liability. Doubts in the law are resolved against the provider.

The law would reach back to care given before it passed. In those cases, courts would give only "limited deference" to medical standards that were in serious dispute. People would have 25 years after turning 18 to sue, or 4 years after paying for detransition care, whichever is later. Exceptions cover intersex conditions, injuries, and certain organ conditions, but providers must prove they apply. Doctors may still discuss options and risks.
does: Creates a federal right to sue providers, hospitals, and clinics over puberty blockers, sex hormones, or surgery given to minors for gender transition.
Allows suits over care given before, on, or after the date the law passes.
Allows compensatory damages, pain and suffering damages, and punitive damages.
Makes providers strictly liable for care given after enactment, proven by clear and convincing evidence.
Bars waivers of liability and resolves ambiguities against providers.
Gives limited deference to older standards of care that were in serious scientific dispute.
Sets a deadline of 25 years after the person turns 18, or 4 years after detransition costs are incurred, whichever is later.
Excludes care for intersex (disorders of sexual development) conditions, injuries, and certain organ conditions, with providers bearing the burden of proving the exclusion.
Defines sex as an immutable male or female classification determined at conception.
Lets providers still share information about options, risks, and benefits.
who: Transgender and gender-diverse minors and their families
Detransitioners and people who regret treatment received as minors
Doctors, nurses, and other licensed health professionals
Hospitals and clinics, including their insurers
Federal courts that would hear the cases
States with their own laws on this care

May push providers toward more careful evaluation and informed consent.
Long filing window helps people who realize harm only years later.
Providers may still discuss options, risks, and benefits.
Exceptions protect care for intersex conditions, injuries, and certain organ conditions.

Providers must prove exceptions by clear and convincing evidence, a high bar.
No waivers, so parental consent is no defense; this could cut into parents' decision-making.
Could cause hospitals and clinics to stop care, reducing access for minors who want it and whose families consent, with possible mental health effects that are debated.
Federal rule may override states that allow this care.
The sex definition is rigid and could affect how other laws are read.

unknowns: How many lawsuits would be filed and how much providers would owe.

How it interacts with state laws and malpractice insurance.

purpose: The bill says it creates a federal right to sue doctors, hospitals, and clinics over puberty blockers, sex hormones, or surgery given to minors to change their body so it no longer matches their sex. It aims to give people harmed by such care, and their parents or guardians, a way to seek compensation, including for the cost of reversing or treating the effects. The CRS summary was not available, so this description relies on the bill's title and the plain-English summary provided.

oppose: Strict liability for care given after the law passes would let providers owe damages without a finding that they were careless or broke the medical standards of the time, which could be seen as an unusually high legal burden for doctors.

The bill applies to care already given before the law passed, and gives only "limited deference" to medical standards that were legal and widely used at the time, which some may see as judging past care by new rules.

Some worry that the liability risk could lead hospitals and clinics to stop offering this care, which could reduce access for minors whose families want it, and the mental health effects of such changes are debated.
support: The bill gives detransitioners and families a clear path to compensation, including the costs of reversing or treating effects of treatment they received as minors.
A 25-year filing window, or 4 years after detransition costs are paid, gives people time to recognize harm that may only become clear years later.
Making providers liable without proof of carelessness and barring waivers may push doctors toward more careful evaluation and more thorough informed consent before treatment.
The bill keeps exceptions for intersex conditions, injuries, and certain organ conditions, and lets doctors still discuss options, risks, and benefits with patients.

label: H.R. 8705
title: CHARLIE Act
short_title: CHARLIE Act (American History and Civics Funding Limits)
one: Bars money from the federal American History and Civics Education grant program from being used for "discriminatory equity ideology" or "gender ideology" (as defined in two 2025 executive orders) and bars the Education Department from giving grant priority based on race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status.
summary: This bill changes one federal education grant program: the American History and Civics Education program, which gives money to groups that teach U.S. history and civics. It adds two rules. First, none of the program's money may be used for what the bill calls "discriminatory equity ideology" or "gender ideology." The bill does not write its own definitions. It points to two executive orders from January 2025 (orders signed by the president, not laws passed by Congress). Order 14190 describes "discriminatory equity ideology" as treating people as members of preferred or disfavored groups instead of as individuals. That includes the idea that one race or sex is superior, or that a person is inherently racist or oppressive because of their race or sex. Order 14168 describes "gender ideology" as replacing categories of biological sex with gender identity. Second, when the Education Secretary picks grant winners, the Secretary may not give a group extra priority because of race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status. This covers the group's identity or purpose, who runs, works for, or is served by the group, and what the group plans to do. The bill does not add money or create a new program. Because the definitions come from executive orders, a future president could change those orders. The bill text doesn't say whether the definitions would stay fixed as written in 2025 or change with later orders. It also doesn't say how violations would be found or enforced.

Bars any funds in this grant program from being used for 'discriminatory equity ideology' or 'gender ideology.'
Bars the Education Secretary from giving grant priority based on race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status.
Applies the priority ban to the applicant's identity or purpose, to who controls, works for, or is served by the applicant, and to the proposed activities.
Defines the two key terms by pointing to Executive Orders 14190 and 14168 instead of writing definitions into the bill.

K-12 teachers and students who take part in funded programs
LGBTQ+ students, educators, and groups
Immigrant and minority-serving organizations that might have received priority
The Department of Education, which runs the grants

Supporters say it keeps federal civics money focused on teaching history and civics, not contested ideological content.
Applies to one grant program and adds no new spending.
concerns: The terms are vague and come from executive orders, so applicants could be unsure what is allowed.
Applicants might avoid topics like racism, slavery's legacy, or gender identity out of fear of losing funds, which could limit honest teaching of history.
Groups serving LGBTQ+ or immigrant communities might be disadvantaged or discouraged from applying.
The definitions rest on executive orders, not on laws passed by Congress.
The title language ('radical indoctrination') is loaded and could affect how the rules are applied.
imp.cost: No new spending. It limits how existing money in the American History and Civics Education program can be used. No cost estimate was provided in the material I was given.
unknowns: Whether the executive order definitions are locked in as of 2025 or change if the orders are changed or revoked.
How the Department of Education would enforce the ban or decide that a grantee broke it.
How many current or past grantees would be affected.
Whether the priority ban would change how grants are scored now, since the bill doesn't say what priorities exist today.
The program's funding level, which isn't in the bill text.

label: H.R. 9317
title: BUSES Act
one: The bill would stop states and cities from enforcing bus idling limits shorter than 15 minutes through their Clean Air Act plans, block citizen lawsuits over those limits, and end programs that pay private people for reporting idling intercity buses.
summary: This bill changes the Clean Air Act to set a national floor for how long certain buses can sit with their engines running. Under it, a state's clean air plan could not include, and no state or local government could enforce through that plan, any idling rule that applies to school buses or "over-the-road" buses (the tall coach buses used for intercity and tour travel) for periods under 15 minutes. In effect, a state or city could not penalize these buses for idling unless they idle 15 minutes or more. The bill also bars people from filing citizen lawsuits against owners or operators of these buses for breaking those idling rules. Finally, it bans any state or local program that pays private individuals a reward for reporting or helping enforce idling violations by over-the-road buses. Programs already running would have to end within 180 days of the bill becoming law. The bounty ban names only over-the-road buses, not school buses. The bill has no new spending. It was ordered reported out of committee on a 26–22 vote. Some details are unclear from the text, such as how it would affect local idling rules that are not part of a state's clean air plan, and how the 15-minute threshold would be measured.
does: Bars state clean air plans from including idling limits under 15 minutes for school buses and over-the-road buses.
Bars states and local governments from enforcing such shorter limits through those plans.
Blocks citizen lawsuits against owners or operators of these buses over those idling rules.
Bans state and local programs that pay private individuals for reporting or enforcing idling violations by over-the-road buses.
Requires existing bounty-style programs to end within 180 days of enactment.
Defines over-the-road bus using the Americans with Disabilities Act definition.
who: Intercity, tour, and charter bus operators
School districts and school bus contractors
Children, drivers, and people living near bus stops, terminals, and schools
State and local governments with idling rules, such as New York City
People who earn rewards by reporting idling under local programs
Residents and groups who might otherwise bring citizen suits

Operators could avoid fines for short idling, for example while keeping heat or air conditioning on for passengers.
It ends reward programs that critics say may encourage over-reporting or harassment of drivers.
A 15-minute limit still remains possible, so some idling rules would still be allowed.
concerns: Buses could idle up to 15 minutes without penalty under state clean air plans, which could add exhaust near schools, terminals, and homes.
School bus exhaust could affect children's health, including asthma.
States and cities would lose power to set stricter local idling rules through their clean air plans.
Citizen suits over bus idling would be blocked, reducing public enforcement.
Existing reward programs, such as those that let residents report idling and share in fines, would have to shut down within 180 days.
imp.cost: The bill has no spending or funding provisions. Possible effects include lost fine revenue for state and local governments, but the text gives no estimates.
unknowns: No CRS summary or cost estimate was available.
It is unclear how it would apply to local idling rules that are not part of a state's clean air plan.
The bounty ban covers only over-the-road buses, so its effect on school bus reporting programs is unclear.
The text does not say how idling time would be measured or how exceptions such as extreme weather would work.
The size of the air quality effect depends on how much bus idling currently happens under short limits, which the text does not say.

purpose: The bill says it sets a national floor for how long school buses and over-the-road buses may idle before idling rules can apply under the Clean Air Act. The official title is the BUSES Act. The text does not state the sponsor's reasons beyond these provisions.

oppose: Under this bill, school and over-the-road buses could idle up to 15 minutes before a state clean air plan could penalize them, which may add exhaust near schools, bus terminals, and homes.
Exhaust from school buses can affect children's health, including asthma. I would like to know how the bill protects students who wait near idling buses.
The bill would limit states and cities from setting stricter idling rules through their clean air plans, which takes away local choice on air quality.

life.reason: Allowing more bus idling, including school buses, could increase exhaust exposure that harms children's and neighbors' health.

transparency.reason: It removes the public's ability to bring citizen suits and ends public reporting reward programs, which reduces public accountability for enforcement.

people_over_profit.reason: It lessens enforcement against bus operators' idling, which could favor operators' convenience over residents' air quality, though it also eases compliance costs for operators.

local_say.reason: It overrides state and local choices about idling limits and forces cities to end their own reporting programs.

label: H.R. 9381
title: AWARE Act
short_title: AWARE Act (AI Workforce Assessment and Research Enhancement Act)
one: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to start collecting and reporting data on how artificial intelligence is being used in workplaces within 18 months of enactment.
summary: This bill would add artificial intelligence (AI) to the list of things the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) must track. The BLS is the federal agency that counts jobs, wages, and working conditions. The bill does this by changing the 1913 law that created the Department of Labor, so that its required statistics on labor conditions, products, and hours of employment also cover how AI is used. Within 18 months after the bill becomes law, the BLS must begin collecting this information. The bill's findings explain why: current surveys were not built to measure how many employers use AI, how workers use it on the job, how tasks and job duties are changing, what AI-related training is happening, or how AI affects hiring, hours, wages, and employment. The bill does not ban or regulate AI, does not require employers to do anything specific, and does not set aside money. It does not spell out how the data will be collected, such as through new surveys or changes to existing ones. It also does not describe privacy rules or whether employers would be required to respond. Those details would be left to the BLS and existing law. The goal is better information so that workers, employers, schools, trainers, and lawmakers can respond to changes in work caused by AI.
does: Amends the 1913 Department of Labor law (29 U.S.C. 2) to add statistics on AI usage to the labor statistics the department must collect.
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to begin collecting AI usage statistics no later than 18 months after enactment.
Uses the definition of AI from the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020.
Includes findings that current BLS data do not measure AI adoption, worker use, task changes, training, or effects on hiring and wages well.
Does not create new penalties, regulations on AI use, or a specific funding amount.

Educators and job training providers
Researchers and policymakers who use labor data
Congress, which gets better data for oversight and lawmaking

benefits: Could give workers, educators, and policymakers timely facts on how AI affects jobs, pay, hiring, and training.
Could help target retraining and support to workers most affected.
Could improve government job projections and oversight.
Creates public, neutral data rather than relying on industry or private estimates.
concerns: Collecting data alone does not protect workers from job loss or unsafe or unfair AI use.
Employers could face added survey burden, though the bill does not say if responses are mandatory.
Worker-level data collection may raise privacy questions that the bill does not address.
No dedicated funding is provided, so BLS could need to shift resources from other work.
imp.cost: The bill provides no specific funding. Costs to BLS for new or expanded surveys are not estimated in the text and no CBO estimate was provided.
unknowns: How the data would be collected (new surveys or changes to existing ones).
Whether employer participation would be required.
How individual worker and business privacy would be protected.
How much it would cost and where the money would come from.
How often results would be published.

label: H.R. 9624
title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
one: The yearly bill that sets spending and rules for U.S. intelligence agencies, with the dollar amounts mostly secret and a mix of new oversight tools and new secrecy-related powers.
summary:
This is the yearly bill that authorizes money and sets rules for U.S. spy agencies, including the CIA, NSA and others. Most of the spending is in a classified (secret) schedule, so the public cannot see the total. The public figures include about $602.5 million for the Director of National Intelligence's management account and $514 million for the CIA retirement fund.

The bill adds several oversight and ethics measures. Congress's intelligence committees would get fuller budget documentation. Some inspectors general (internal watchdogs) would be protected from budget cuts. Whistleblowers would get faster guidance on how to reach Congress safely. Intelligence employees could not use secret information to bet on prediction markets. Senior intelligence officials could not lobby for foreign-adversary-controlled entities for 10 years after leaving. It also withholds 5% of Director of National Intelligence office funds until overdue election-threat reports are delivered.

It also gives agencies new powers. The Defense Department could create "cover" pay, retirement and health arrangements for a few undercover members, and courts could not review those decisions. The CIA could buy commercial technology through open competitions using fixed-price contracts. The CIA's drone authority would be extended to 2030. The bill orders reviews and reports on DeepSeek, Unitree and other named Chinese companies, and on Iran. I could not see every section, including Sections 324 through 405 and 423 through 514, so this analysis is incomplete.

label: S. 3573
title: A bill to amend the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act to modify a provision relating to the extension of certain dates for the completion of the Regional Water System, and for other purposes.
short_title: Aamodt Settlement Water System Deadline Extension
one: The bill lets the parties to the Aamodt water rights settlement in New Mexico agree to push back the deadlines for finishing the Regional Water System.
summary:
In 2010, Congress approved the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act. It settled a long court fight over water rights in the Pojoaque Basin near Santa Fe, New Mexico. The settlement involves four Pueblos (Nambé, Pojoaque, San Ildefonso and Tesuque), the United States, the State of New Mexico, Santa Fe County and the City of Santa Fe. It calls for building a Regional Water System to deliver water to Pueblo and non-Pueblo residents. The law sets dates by which the system must be finished. If those dates are missed, the settlement could fall apart.

This bill makes a small change to Section 623(g) of that law. It says the deadlines in subsection (e) may be extended if the Pueblos, the United States (acting through the Secretary of the Interior), the State, the City and the County all agree that an extension is reasonably necessary. Without this change, the dates would be harder to move. The bill doesn't add money. It doesn't change who gets water or how much. It doesn't say how long an extension may last. I did not have a CRS summary. The bill text only amends the earlier law, and I could not see the full text of Section 623 in the material provided. The effect depends on what that section says.
does: Amends Section 623(g) of the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act (Public Law 111-291).
Lets the completion dates in subsection (e) be extended if the Pueblos, the U.S. (through the Secretary), the State, the City and the County all agree an extension is reasonably necessary.
Relabels the existing text as 'Conditions precedent; expiration date' and adds a new paragraph on 'Determination of substantial completion'.
Adds no new funding and sets no maximum length for an extension.

Non-Pueblo residents and water users in the Pojoaque Basin
Santa Fe County and the City of Santa Fe
State of New Mexico
U.S. Department of the Interior (Bureau of Reclamation)

benefits: May keep the water rights settlement from expiring because of construction delays.
May help ensure the Regional Water System is completed and delivers clean drinking water.
Requires agreement from all parties, including the Pueblos, for any extension.
Gives flexibility without a new law each time a delay happens.
concerns: The bill sets no limit on how long or how many times dates can be extended.
Unanimity means any single party could block an extension and could put the settlement at risk.
Delays could keep residents without reliable water longer.
Delays could raise project costs, and the bill does not say who pays.
imp.cost: The bill authorizes no new money. A Congressional Budget Office estimate was not provided. Delays could raise costs of the underlying project, but the bill text doesn't address this.
unknowns: Exact wording of Section 623(e) and what happens if the dates are missed.
How long an extension might be and what the current project schedule is.
Whether delays would raise costs and who would pay.
How the new 'substantial completion' heading relates to the rest of the section.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to amend the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act so that the deadlines for finishing the Regional Water System can be extended if all the parties agree an extension is reasonably necessary. The settlement covers a long-running water rights dispute in the Pojoaque Basin near Santa Fe, New Mexico, and the law says the settlement could fall apart if the completion dates are missed. The bill does not add funding, and the materials provided do not include a CRS summary or the full text of Section 623.

oppose: The bill sets no limit on how long or how many times the completion deadlines can be extended, so a project could be delayed for many years without a new law.
Extensions need agreement from all five parties, which means any one party could block a change. Some people may see that as a risk if the settlement could expire.
The bill does not say who would pay for added costs caused by delays, so taxpayers or local governments could end up covering higher project costs without clear rules.
Longer delays could mean residents who need reliable water wait longer for the system, and the bill does not include new money or firm timelines to prevent that.
support: The bill lets the deadlines be extended if the Pueblos, the federal government, New Mexico, the City of Santa Fe and Santa Fe County all agree, so it adds flexibility without requiring a new law for every delay.
Without this change, the settlement could expire if construction runs late, which could put the water rights agreement at risk for everyone involved.
Because every party must agree, no extension can happen without the Pueblos' consent, which protects the tribes' interests in the settlement.
The goal of the project is to deliver water to Pueblo and non-Pueblo residents, and keeping the settlement in place helps move that goal forward.

life.reason: Helping finish a drinking water system supports the health of the people who will use it.

water.reason: It helps keep the settlement alive so a regional drinking water system can be completed for Pueblo and non-Pueblo residents.

local_say.reason: Extensions need agreement from the Pueblos, the State, the City and the County, so local governments and Tribes decide together.

honesty_kindness.reason: It helps the government keep a negotiated commitment to Tribal communities rather than letting it lapse on a technicality.

label: S. 4053
title: A bill to take certain land in the State of California into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians, and for other purposes.
short_title: Pechanga Band Land Into Trust Bill
one: Moves about 860 acres of federal land in Riverside County, California, into trust for the Pechanga Band of Indians, to be kept as open space with no gaming.
summary: This bill would move about 860 acres of land in Riverside County, California, from the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to the U.S. government to hold "in trust" for the Pechanga Band of Indians. Trust means the federal government holds the legal title for the tribe's benefit. The land would become part of the tribe's reservation and be managed under the usual rules for tribal trust land. The bill sets firm limits on how the land can be used. It must stay open space. It can be used only for purposes consistent with open space and for protecting and maintaining the archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources there. Utilities or structures are allowed only if they fit with open space and serve that protection purpose. Casino-style gaming (Class II and Class III under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act) is banned on the land. Existing rights, such as easements, rights-of-way, leases, permits, and licenses, stay in place. Existing water rights and service agreements are not changed. The map of the land must be kept on file for public inspection at BLM offices. The bill text does not include a cost estimate, and I could not see the map itself.

label: H.R. 1031
title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Establishment Act
short_title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Act
one: Creates a new national park unit at Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York, to preserve the story of 982 World War II Holocaust refugees sheltered there in 1944–46, once enough land has been acquired.
summary: This bill would create the Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park in New York as part of the National Park System. Its purpose is to protect and teach about the 982 World War II refugees who were housed at Fort Ontario from August 1944 to February 1946. The park would not officially exist right away. First, the Secretary of the Interior must decide that enough land inside a mapped "Proposed Boundary" has been acquired to make a manageable park. Then, within 30 days, the Secretary must announce the park in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice publication. The National Park Service could get land by donation, by purchase using donated or appropriated (Congress-approved) money, or by land swap. Land owned by New York State or local governments could only be donated, not bought. The Park Service could sign agreements with the state and with public or private groups to offer education and interpretation, and to restore historic resources on nearby non-federal land. If the Park Service helps with non-federal land, the public must have reasonable access. Within three fiscal years after money is provided, the Park Service must finish a general management plan, working with the state. The bill does not say how much money would be needed. The map is to be available for public inspection.

label: H.R. 6869
title: To amend the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act to modify a provision relating to the extension of certain dates for the completion of the Regional Water System, and for other purposes.
short_title: Aamodt Settlement Water System Deadline Extension Bill
one: The bill lets the parties to the Aamodt water settlement in northern New Mexico agree to push back the deadlines for finishing the Regional Water System if they all agree an extension is reasonably necessary.
summary:
This bill changes a 2010 law, the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act. That law ended a decades-long court fight over water rights in the Pojoaque Basin near Santa Fe, New Mexico. Part of the deal was building a Regional Water System. The system would deliver clean water to four Pueblos (Nambé, Pojoaque, San Ildefonso and Tesuque) and to nearby non-Pueblo residents. The 2010 law sets dates by which the system must be substantially finished. If those dates are missed, parts of the settlement could expire or fall apart.

H.R. 6869 would add a new paragraph to the section about those deadlines. It says the dates in subsection (e) may be extended if five parties all agree an extension is reasonably necessary. Those parties are the Pueblos, the United States (through the Secretary of the Interior), the State of New Mexico, the City of Santa Fe, and Santa Fe County. The bill also relabels the existing text in that section. It does not add money, and it does not say how long an extension could last. The bill text does not say what the current deadlines are or how the section would work in detail. I could only see the bill's short amendment, not the full underlying law, and no Congressional Research Service summary is available yet.

one: The bill lets private groups, chosen by the Interior Secretary, raise money to put up Wisconsin regiment memorials at Antietam and Manassas battlefields, with the National Park Service handling upkeep afterward.
summary: This bill would allow two memorials to be built on National Park Service land. One would honor soldiers from five Wisconsin infantry regiments (the 2nd, 3rd, 5th, 6th, and 7th) who fought at the Battle of Antietam in 1862. It would go inside Antietam National Battlefield in Maryland. The other would honor soldiers from three Wisconsin regiments (the 2nd, 6th, and 7th) who fought in the Second Battle of Bull Run in 1862. It would go inside Manassas National Battlefield Park in Virginia. The Secretary of the Interior would pick the groups or people who build each memorial. The Secretary would also approve the location, size, design, and inscriptions. No federal money could be used to design, buy, prepare a site for, or install the memorials, so private donations would have to cover those costs. If fundraisers falsely claim ties to the memorials or the federal government, the Secretary could suspend their authority. Until a memorial is installed, its builders must send the Secretary a yearly report on fundraising and progress. After installation, the National Park Service would take over upkeep. It could accept donations for maintenance, which would be held in a separate account with the National Park Foundation.

label: H.R. 8276
title: Quindaro Townsite National Historic Landmark Act
short_title: Quindaro Townsite National Historic Landmark Act
one: Designates the Quindaro Townsite in Kansas City, Kansas, a Free-State and Underground Railroad site, as a National Historic Landmark and lets the Interior Secretary partner with and fund local groups to protect and interpret it, without limiting what property owners can do.
summary:
This bill would officially name the Quindaro Townsite in Kansas City, Kansas, a National Historic Landmark. Quindaro was founded in 1857 to help the Free-State side in the fight over whether Kansas would allow slavery. It served as a Missouri River port for people opposed to slavery and as a stop on the Underground Railroad, where people escaping slavery could reach freedom. Archaeologists have found many artifacts there, and more may be found.

After the designation, the Secretary of the Interior could sign cooperative agreements with public or private groups. These agreements would aim to protect historic resources at the site and provide education and interpretation programs for the public. The Secretary would talk with the State of Kansas, Kansas City, Kansas, and nearby local governments first. The Secretary could also give technical and financial help to those partners. The bill does not say how much money, and it does not set a budget.

The bill says the designation would not stop property owners, including owners of the landmark, from doing what they could otherwise do with their property. It also says that Kansas City, Kansas, and the State would keep running the site as they do now. In other words, there is no federal takeover and no new federal land ownership in the text. The bill was introduced by a Republican with a Democratic cosponsor from Missouri and one from Kansas, and had a subcommittee hearing in September 2026.

label: H.R. 8546
title: Pechanga Band of Indians Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act
short_title: Pechanga Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act
one: Makes technical fixes to a 2016 water rights settlement with the Pechanga Band in Southern California: it clarifies what land counts as the reservation and lets a water quality fund pay for more than just desalination.
summary: In 2016, Congress approved a settlement of water rights claims involving the Pechanga Band of Luiseño Mission Indians in Southern California. This bill makes small fixes to that law. First, it rewrites the definition of the Band's "Reservation" so it lists the specific 1882 and 1907 executive orders and the dates when land was later added (from 1893 through 2008). It also says the Reservation includes land next to it that the U.S. holds in trust for the Band on the settlement's enforceability date. It also includes nearby land placed in trust later, if that land lies inside the Santa Margarita River Watershed. Second, it changes how the Pechanga Water Quality Account can be used. Today the money is tied to groundwater desalination in the Wolf Valley Basin. The bill would let it pay for any activities that address water quality problems in that basin. Third, it tells the Secretary of the Interior to promptly sign matching changes to the settlement agreement, which Congress says the parties already agreed to. The bill says it does not change the settlement's legal start conditions, the Secretary's 2020 finding that those conditions were met, or any existing water right. The text does not give a cost estimate, and no CRS summary was available.

title: Geese House Site Conveyance Act
one: The bill would transfer about 21,578 acres of federal land in the Denali National Park and Preserve to the Alaska Native corporation Doyon, Limited, ban mining and sale of that land, and shrink the preserve's boundary.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of the Interior give about 21,578 acres of federal land inside the preserve part of Denali National Park and Preserve to Doyon, Limited. Doyon is an Alaska Native regional corporation. The land is what Doyon chose in 1978 under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), a 1971 law that settled Alaska Native land claims. The transfer must happen within one year of the bill becoming law. It is subject to valid existing rights, and the government must keep the public access easements that ANCSA requires. Some lots and two lakes are left out.

The land includes the Geese House, a site with cultural importance. The bill says Doyon could not sell or transfer the land to anyone except the United States. Doyon also could not allow any mining or mineral activity, or any development that would harm the Geese House's cultural value. The bill says the transfer would not have to follow the usual federal conveyance regulations or any past land withdrawals (earlier federal protections). It would also redraw the park boundary to leave out the transferred land. The bill text does not explain why this site is being transferred or how the Geese House is used. It has no cost estimate, and no CRS summary is available yet.

label: H.R. 9590
title: SAFE for Manatees Act
one: Directs the Interior Department (through the Fish and Wildlife Service) to study where manatees could find new warm-water habitat, natural or man-made, as Florida power plants and similar industrial sites that warm the water are shut down, and to publish a report within 180 days.
summary:
Many Florida manatees spend cold winters in warm water that flows out of coastal industrial sites, such as power plants. Some of these sites are being shut down, which will make the water cooler. Manatees can get sick or die from cold stress, so losing these warm spots is a concern.

This bill does not build anything. It tells the Secretary of the Interior, working through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to study the problem. The study must find and assess places that could work as habitat. These include natural warm-water spots manatees do not use now, and places where people could build artificial warm-water refuges. The Secretary must also work with the Army Corps of Engineers to develop possible ways to build such refuges, along with construction plans. The Secretary must coordinate with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the Secretary must make a report on the results public. The bill only covers the species Trichechus manatus (the West Indian manatee). It does not give money for construction and does not say how much the study would cost. Any building would need separate approval and funding later.

label: H.R. 6213
title: Heat Workforce Standards Act of 2026
one: Bars the Labor Department from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing OSHA's proposed workplace heat safety rule, or any similar rule.
summary: This bill would stop the U.S. Department of Labor from finishing or enforcing a workplace heat safety rule that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) proposed in August 2024. That proposal, called "Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings," would require many employers to write a plan to find and reduce heat dangers. It would apply to outdoor and indoor work in general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture. According to the Congressional Research Service, the proposal would kick in when the heat index reaches 80°F (an initial trigger) or 90°F (a high-heat trigger). The bill also blocks any "substantially similar standard," so OSHA could not simply write a close copy later. The bill does not set up any new heat protections of its own. Right now, OSHA has no specific heat rule. It can still cite employers for dangerous heat under the general duty to provide a workplace free of recognized hazards. It also runs a National Emphasis Program on heat. This bill does not mention either of those, so they appear to be left as they are. The text does not say how much "substantially similar" would cover, and a court or agency would have to decide that.

crs:
Heat Workforce Standards Act of 2025
This bill prohibits the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing a safety standard requiring certain employers to create a heat injury and illness prevention plan to evaluate and control heat hazards in their workplaces.
Specifically, OSHA is prohibited from finalizing the proposed rule titled 
Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings,
 which was published on August 30, 2024, or any substantially similar standard. The proposed standard generally applies to employers conducting outdoor and indoor work in all general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture sectors where OSHA has jurisdiction. Employers must develop plans in accordance with the specified standards to address employee exposures to heat indexes at or above 80 degrees (initial heat trigger) or 90 degrees (high heat trigger) Fahrenheit.
As background, the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 generally requires employers to provide their employees with a place of employment that is free from recognized hazards that are causing or likely to cause death or serious harm to employees. OSHA conducts workplace inspections and cites employers that fail to satisfy these requirements. Currently, OSHA does not have specific heat exposure standards; however, OSHA has historically used its general authority to cite employers for violations involving excessive heat, including through a National Emphasis Program that focuses on indoor and outdoor heat exposure in industries that have the highest risks.

Lean Left outlets (mostly New York Times) focus on climate urgency, COP31, and climate-related economic effects, with one Wisconsin Public Radio piece touching on worker safety that is the closest link to the bill's subject. The Center view rests on a single CSM article about the summit's modest goals, so the evidence for comparison is thin and mostly indirect.

label: S. 2586
title: MARA Act of 2025
short_title: MARA Act of 2025 (Marine Aquaculture Research for America Act)
one: Sets up a NOAA office and a permit-based demonstration program for fish and seafood farming in federal ocean waters, plus grants, workforce training, and required studies.
summary: This bill would let the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) create a program to test large-scale seafood farming in federal ocean waters (from the state boundary out to 200 nautical miles). It creates an Office of Aquaculture inside NOAA's fisheries service, with a coordinator in each regional office. Within 180 days, NOAA must start an assessment program. NOAA would then issue 10-year, renewable permits for "demonstration projects." These projects may raise only native or historically naturalized species. They must limit escapes, whale and sea turtle entanglement, pollution, and antibiotic use. They must follow the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, and National Environmental Policy Act, and partner with a university. The public can comment, and affected Governors and Tribal leaders can object. If NOAA misses its deadline and no one objects, a permit can be treated as approved. NOAA can modify, end, or remove projects for violations or safety harms after a warning. The bill also funds grants: $25 million a year for Aquaculture Centers of Excellence at minority-serving and Tribal colleges, and $20 million a year for working waterfront grants, both for 2026–2030. It sets up marketing grants, workforce grants, and a database. NOAA must also run outreach promoting offshore aquaculture. Finally, the National Academies must study offshore aquaculture and the Government Accountability Office must report on it, each within 5 years.

label: S. 5718
title: Trucker Bathroom Access Act
one: Requires many businesses to let delivering or waiting truck drivers use their restrooms, and requires port terminal operators to provide restrooms and parking for port truck drivers.
summary: This bill would make businesses let truck drivers use the bathroom. First, if a commercial truck driver delivers goods to a business, or is waiting there to be loaded, that business would have to let the driver use a restroom meant for its customers or employees. This covers stores open to the public and also shippers, receivers, factories, warehouses, and distribution centers. There are limits. The restroom can be refused if letting the driver in would create an obvious health, safety, or security risk. Very small structures of 800 square feet or less (such as a small filling station or restaurant) with an employee-only restroom are excluded. Businesses would not have to remodel a restroom to comply. Second, the bill deals with "drayage" drivers, who haul cargo in large trucks (over 33,000 pounds) at ports and rail yards. Marine terminal operators, including port authorities that run terminals, would have to provide enough restrooms or portable toilets where these drivers usually go. They would let drivers use existing restrooms when it is safe, add more where the need is greatest, and provide parking near the restrooms. The text does not name a penalty, an enforcement agency, or a start date, and no cost estimate or CRS summary was available. The Senate Commerce Committee has approved the bill with a substitute amendment, which I could not see, so the final wording may differ.

label: H.R. 1390
title: Ocean Pollution Reduction Act II
one: Lets the EPA issue a permit that allows San Diego's Point Loma sewage plant to keep using a reduced level of treatment, instead of full "secondary" treatment, if it meets set pollution limits and builds enough recycled drinking water capacity by 2039.
summary:
The Point Loma Wastewater Treatment Plant in San Diego sends treated sewage through a long pipe into the Pacific Ocean. Under the Clean Water Act, most plants must give sewage "secondary treatment," a more thorough cleaning. Point Loma has long run on a temporary waiver (a "variance") from those standards. The city has applied for a new waiver. If it doesn't get one, it would have to build a full secondary treatment plant.

This bill creates a third path. It lets the EPA give the plant a regular discharge permit with special conditions, without the city having to ask for another waiver. The plant would have to keep its deep ocean pipe (at least 300 feet deep and 4 miles out). It would also have to cut the yearly amount of solid waste it releases in steps: 12,000 metric tons now, 11,500 from the end of 2029, and 9,942 from the end of 2031. It would have to remove at least 80% of suspended solids each month and 58% of a measure of oxygen-depleting waste each year. It would have to meet the other secondary treatment limits, run a pretreatment program and an ocean monitoring program, give the EPA 10 years of ocean data, and get California's sign-off. Finally, if state and federal rules allow it, the city would have to show it will make 83 million gallons a day of water clean enough to recycle into drinking water by the end of 2039. The city can still choose to apply for full secondary treatment instead.

purpose: The bill says it creates an alternative permit path for the Point Loma Wastewater Treatment Plant in San Diego. Under the bill, the plant could get a Clean Water Act discharge permit with set conditions, instead of repeatedly applying for a temporary waiver from secondary treatment standards. The bill's stated aim, as described in its summary, is to put firm, written limits on solids discharged, tie the permit to producing recycled drinking water, and give the city an option other than building a full secondary treatment plant.

oppose: The bill lets the plant keep a deep ocean discharge while meeting only 80% solids removal and 58% oxygen-demand removal, instead of full secondary treatment. You could ask your representative how much pollution would still reach the ocean under these limits.

The bill uses the phrase "notwithstanding any provision" of the Clean Water Act to create a special rule for one plant. You could ask whether this could encourage other utilities to seek similar exceptions to federal standards.

The recycled drinking water requirement applies only "to the extent potable reuse is permitted" by regulators, and the deadline is 2039. You could ask what happens if the city misses that target or a milestone, and how the bill would be enforced.
support: The bill sets firm, written limits in law on solids discharged, including cuts in 2029 and 2031, rather than relying on repeated waivers. You could ask your representative how these written limits would be enforced.

The bill may help the city avoid the cost of building a full secondary treatment plant, which could protect ratepayers from a large bill. You could ask how the bill addresses the costs of the recycled water work.

The bill ties the permit to producing 83 million gallons per day of water suitable for recycling into drinking water, which could add a local water supply. It also keeps California's sign-off, ocean monitoring, and pretreatment requirements in place.

life.reason: Allowing partly treated sewage (80% solids, 58% oxygen-demand removal) to continue into the ocean instead of full secondary treatment could still harm marine life, though deep outfall and solids caps limit the harm.

water.reason: Ocean discharge of partly treated sewage continues under a permit that falls short of full secondary treatment, though the solids caps and recycled-water goal partly offset this.

air.reason: The bill does not meaningfully address air quality.

transparency.reason: Replacing the periodic waiver process with a permit may reduce or leave unclear the public comment steps, and the bill does not spell out public review requirements.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly concerns a public city utility, so it does not clearly favor corporate profit over people or the reverse.

local_say.reason: A special federal permit path for one city, with EPA discretion over milestones and an unspecified public comment process, reduces the local and public role compared with the existing waiver process.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill avoids a full secondary plant, which may lower ratepayer costs, but it creates no tax break or bailout and the cost and funding of the recycled water buildout are unspecified.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not bear on honesty or kindness in a clear way.

news.overall: Only one Lean Left article (a New York Times headline) was provided, so the evidence is very limited and no cross-perspective comparison is possible. The sole framing is industry safety claims set against a pending Texas test, and the headline gives no description of the bill's text, so this reflects only that single headline and should not be taken as representative of Lean Left coverage generally.

label: H.R. 2518
title: Fishing Industry Credit Enhancement Act of 2025
one: Lets Farm Credit System lenders make loans and offer financial services to businesses that provide services to commercial fishermen and other harvesters or producers of aquatic products.
summary: The Farm Credit System is a network of lending institutions that make loans to farmers, ranchers, and some related businesses. Under current law, the Farm Credit Act already covers certain fishing and aquatic producers. This bill would widen who can borrow. It would let Farm Credit Banks and Production Credit Associations lend to "persons furnishing" services directly related to the operating needs of producers or harvesters of aquatic products. In practice, that could mean businesses that serve fishing operations, though the bill does not list examples or define the term. The bill changes three spots in the Farm Credit Act: the section on who is eligible for credit at Farm Credit Banks, the section on the purposes of those loans, and the section on who can borrow from Production Credit Associations. It does not give out any new money, grants, or tax breaks. It does not create a new program or change environmental or fishing rules. Loans would still be made by Farm Credit lenders under their normal business practices. The bill is short and technical. It was introduced March 31, 2025, with bipartisan cosponsors, and sent to a House Agriculture subcommittee. No hearing or vote has been reported.

Makes no new appropriations and creates no new program, subsidy, or regulation in the text provided.

purpose: The bill's official title is the Fishing Industry Credit Enhancement Act of 2025. Based on its title and the summary provided, it aims to widen access to Farm Credit System loans for businesses that provide services directly related to the operating needs of aquatic product producers or harvesters, by adding those providers to the eligible borrowers and loan purposes in the Farm Credit Act.
