label: H.R. 4987
title: Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
one: Sets one national standard for the wording of voluntary "best by" and "use by" dates on food labels, and blocks states and localities from requiring different wording.
summary: Today, food makers use many different phrases for dates on packages, such as "sell by," "best before," "use by," and "expires on." Shoppers often don't know which ones mean the food is unsafe and which only mean the quality may slip. This bill would create two standard phrases. If a company chooses to print a quality date, it must put "BEST If Used By" in front of it. If it chooses to print a date after which the food should be thrown away, it must use "USE By." Short forms, "BB" and "UB," are allowed only when the package is too small. Companies may add "or freeze by." Dates must be easy to read and easy to find. Putting a date on a package stays optional. The bill covers foods overseen by the FDA and the USDA (meat, poultry, and eggs), but not infant formula. Within two years, the agencies must write rules and start a consumer education campaign. The rules would apply to foods labeled two years after the bill becomes law. The agencies could later pick different standard phrases. Labels that break the rules would count as "misbranded" under federal food laws. The bill also overrides state and local rules about date wording. It bars states and cities from banning the sale or donation of food after its quality date. States may still ban sales or donations after a discard date. People's ability to sue under existing state or federal law is preserved.

Requires 'USE By' (or 'UB' on tiny packages) before any discard date.

Lets companies add 'or freeze by' and use QR codes or smart labels in addition.

Excludes infant formula and keeps existing rights to sue under other laws.

crs:
Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
This bill establishes uniform requirements for quality and discard date phrases (e.g., 
best by
 and 
use by
) placed voluntarily on food labels.
Specifically, if a food is labeled with a quality date (i.e., the date after which the quality of the item may deteriorate), the label must include the phrase 
BEST If Used By
 or the abbreviation 
BB
. Similarly, if a food is labeled with a discard date (i.e., the date after which the item should not be consumed), the label must include the phrase 
USE By
 or the abbreviation 
UB
. Abbreviations may be used only if an item’s packaging is too small to fit the full phrase.
Quality and discard dates must be written in a single, easy-to-read font and placed in a prominent location on an item’s label or package. The phrase 
or freeze by
 may be added after a quality or discard date phrase where appropriate.
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA) must promulgate regulations to carry out these provisions and ensure that the uniform phrases are standardized across all food products. HHS and USDA may specify alternative quality and discard date phrases through regulations.
The bill specifies that no state or local government may enforce a requirement related to quality and discard date phrases that differs from the requirements of the bill. The bill does not apply to infant formula, which is subject to separate labeling requirements under current law.

label: H.R. 5935
title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
short_title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
one: Ratifies a settlement of long-running water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band, two Coachella Valley water agencies, and the U.S., confirming a 20,000 acre-feet-per-year groundwater right, spending $500 million in federal money, and moving about 2,700 acres of federal land into trust for the Tribe.
summary:
This bill would approve a deal, signed May 19, 2025, that ends water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and two local water agencies, the Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD) and the Desert Water Agency (DWA). The Tribe's right to pump up to 20,000 acre-feet of groundwater a year from the Indio Subbasin (the aquifer under the Palm Springs area) would be confirmed. That right dates to 1876–77 and would take priority over the agencies' claims to native groundwater. The Tribe would also keep its rights to certain creeks.

The federal government would put $500 million into a trust fund for the Tribe: $300 million for water projects, $100 million to reimburse the water agencies for groundwater-recharge projects, $50 million for water management, and $50 million for operations and upkeep. Amounts would be adjusted for construction cost inflation. In exchange, the Tribe and the U.S. would give up many past and some future water claims. They keep claims under the Clean Water Act, the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Superfund law (CERCLA), and claims over misconduct.

The bill moves about 2,700 acres of Bureau of Land Management land into trust for the Tribe, bars gaming on it, and lets CVWD buy about 842 acres at fair market value. It sets up a Tribal possessory-interest tax that replaces the county property tax on those interests, with payments to other local agencies. It also adds protections for Native cultural resources. It takes effect only after several conditions are met, and expires if they aren't met by the end of 2035.

Honors a senior Tribal water right and adds cultural resource and burial protections at the CVWD facility; bars gaming on transferred land.
Allottees get a tribal process with appeals, then federal recourse; the tax deal requires the Tribe to pay other local agencies at least what they would have received, enforceable in federal court.
Public notice: the Secretary must publish findings in the Federal Register before the deal takes effect, and the Tribe must file annual expenditure reports.
concerns: Costs U.S. taxpayers $500 million in mandatory spending, with automatic inflation adjustments that could raise the total.
Waives many damage claims, including past overdraft, subsidence, and water-quality claims where water meets standards; some of these releases are broad and cover unknown claims.
The Tribal water right is not subject to state law or the replenishment charge, and can't be lost through non-use. This could shift aquifer management costs to other pumpers or ratepayers.

The Tribal tax preempts county property tax, which could reduce local government oversight; the Tribe need not pay other agencies more than they'd otherwise get.
Off-reservation leasing of water for up to 99 years, with Secretary approval, could affect neighboring communities.
Some expenditure details and tribal rate-setting for reservation customers are in the Agreement, which I could not see.

label: H.R. 6182
title: Find It Early Act
one: Requires private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and VA care to cover extra breast cancer imaging (like ultrasound and MRI) with no out-of-pocket costs for people at higher risk or with dense breasts, and for others whose doctor says they need it.
summary:
This bill would make breast cancer screening and follow-up imaging free to patients in more cases. Today, a standard mammogram is often covered at no cost, but extra tests, like ultrasounds, MRIs, or other advanced imaging, can leave patients with big bills. Under this bill, people at higher risk of breast cancer, or with dense breast tissue, could get these tests with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. Higher risk would be judged using guidelines from the American College of Radiology and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network. People not in those groups would also get free imaging if their health care provider decides they need it, based on things like age, race, ethnicity, or personal or family medical history. The tests would be covered as often as the cancer network's guidelines recommend.

The rule would apply to job-based and individual health plans, including older "grandfathered" plans. It would also apply to Medicare (including Medicare Advantage), Medicaid, military TRICARE coverage, and Veterans Affairs care. Veterans would qualify even if they are not enrolled in VA health care. Most parts would start January 1, 2026, a date that has already passed or is close, since the bill was introduced in November 2025. States could get extra time for Medicaid if they need to pass new state laws. The bill text does not include a cost estimate or funding plan.

label: H.R. 6806
title: Antisemitism Response and Prevention Act of 2025
short_title: Antisemitism Response and Prevention Act of 2025
one: Creates a permanent, nonpartisan DOJ office to coordinate efforts against antisemitism, builds a new FBI hate crime reporting center, adds campus civil rights duties, protects the Education Dept. civil rights office, and bars political conditions on nonprofit security grants.
summary:
This bill is aimed at fighting antisemitism (hostility toward Jewish people) while also limiting what its authors call political misuse of that fight. It would set up a Justice Department office, led by a non-political career official with a four-year term, to coordinate federal work against antisemitism using the 2023 national strategy. It would also create an FBI Hate Crime Reporting Center to collect and publish data on hate crimes against all groups, and run a public awareness campaign.

Colleges that take federal student aid would have to name a staff member to handle Title VI (federal anti-discrimination law) complaints, run an awareness campaign, publish yearly reports, and tell apart illegal discrimination from protected political speech. The bill would authorize $280 million a year for the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights, require it to reopen regional offices closed since January 2025, and bar moving or closing it without new law. It would raise the Nonprofit Security Grant Program to $500 million a year and bar conditions tied to diversity programs, immigration, or political views. It also requires reports on extremism in prisons and law enforcement and on domestic terrorism. The findings and a "sense of Congress" section sharply criticize the current administration's antisemitism policies and say the IHRA definition shouldn't be used in deportation or criminal cases. These sections are statements of opinion and carry no legal force.

label: H.R. 6809
title: Alyssa’s Act of 2025
short_title: Alyssa's Act of 2025 (School Safety Clearinghouse Expansion)
one: The bill expands a Department of Homeland Security school safety information center to offer training, research on wearable panic alarms, a national school safety data hub, and standards for school emergency maps that federal money can buy.
summary: This bill would build up the Federal Clearinghouse on School Safety Evidence-based Practices, which sits inside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). It would have DHS run public education on preventing and responding to school emergencies, including school shootings. It would also have DHS give training and one-on-one consulting to schools and states, and hire experts. DHS would run a program to develop and test wearable "panic alarm" devices that connect to emergency services. It would also set up a National School Safety Data Center on SchoolSafety.gov within one year. The center would collect and publish data on school violence, injuries, deaths, safety plans, and other issues such as fights and truancy. A Director of the Clearinghouse would be named within 120 days, and the Secret Service would be brought into the process. The bill also bars any federal money from buying emergency response maps of school buildings unless they meet technical rules, including that the school owns the data, it is stored in the U.S., and it is checked every year by a walk-through. DHS must send Congress a strategy within a year and yearly reports on its work. A later report on "master plans" for school shooting prevention would be due in four years. The bill says it gives the Clearinghouse no power to make rules. It does not set a dollar amount.

label: H.R. 7976
title: Moral Injury Recognition and Restitution Act
short_title: Moral Injury Recognition and Restitution Act
one: Requires the VA to backdate disability compensation for veterans whose approved claims are based on military sexual trauma to the day after they left military service, with back pay.
summary: Today, when a veteran gets approved for VA disability pay, the start date usually depends on when the claim was filed or other timing rules. That means many veterans who waited years to speak up about sexual assault or harassment during service only get paid from a later date. This bill would change that for one group: veterans whose claims are approved because of military sexual trauma (MST). For these veterans, the VA would have to treat the start date of the benefit as the day after they were discharged. The VA would then pay the money owed from that date forward, as a lump of back pay. The bill covers mental health conditions tied to MST, using a definition already in federal law, and also any physical injury or disease caused or made worse by MST. It does not change how a claim is decided. A veteran still has to be approved first. The bill does not say how much it would cost or when it would start, and no official cost estimate or CRS summary is available yet. The bill was sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee.

label: H.R. 9017
title: Restore Florida Water Independence Act of 2026
short_title: Restore Florida Water Independence Act of 2026
one: The bill would declare that a 2020 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wildlife-protection review already satisfies the Endangered Species Act for the EPA's approval of Florida taking over federal wetland dredge-and-fill permitting, and would bar any further wildlife consultation on it.
summary:
Under the Clean Water Act, anyone who wants to dredge or fill wetlands and certain waters needs a "Section 404" permit, which is normally issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. A state can ask the EPA for permission to run that program itself. In December 2020, the EPA approved Florida's request. Before that approval, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wrote a "biological opinion," which is an expert review of how the action could harm endangered species. It included an "incidental take statement," which says how much harm to protected species is allowed.

This bill would say two things by law. First, that the 2020 biological opinion meets the requirements of the Endangered Species Act, and that following it counts as following the Act, for the EPA's approval of Florida's program. Second, that no more consultation with wildlife agencies is needed under section 7(a) of the Act. The bill also says the "Agency Action" covers "other activities," a phrase it defines only by pointing to the glossary of the biological opinion. That glossary was not provided, so the full reach is unclear. The bill does not change the text of the Endangered Species Act or the Clean Water Act. It does limit how the Act applies to this one approval. The bill text does not say why it is needed. It does not mention any court case or other background.

label: H.R. 9104
title: Rock Creek National Park Act of 2026
short_title: Rock Creek National Park Act of 2026
one: Renames Rock Creek Park in Washington, D.C. as "Rock Creek National Park" and updates legal references to match.
summary: This bill changes the official name of Rock Creek Park, a large park in Washington, D.C. that Congress created in 1890, to "Rock Creek National Park." The bill says the change recognizes the park's important natural, cultural, and historical resources and its recreation opportunities. It also fixes two spots in Title 40 of the U.S. Code (the part of federal law about public buildings and property) so they use the new name. Finally, it says that any other law, map, rule, or record that mentions "Rock Creek Park" will be read as meaning "Rock Creek National Park." The bill text does not add money, change park boundaries, change who manages the park, add new rules, or give the park new protections. It only changes the name and references. Rock Creek Park is already run by the National Park Service as part of the national park system, so what the new "National Park" label would change in practice is not spelled out in the bill. Other effects, such as signs, maps, or visitor interest, would depend on later decisions by the park service and Congress.

label: H.R. 9221
title: Outdoor Americans with Disabilities Act
one: The bill would make it much harder for the Forest Service and Interior Department to close roads on federal public land, using disability access as the stated reason, and would speed up road changes by skipping some environmental review.
summary:
This bill covers National Forest land and land managed by the Interior Department, such as Bureau of Land Management land. It tells the agencies to make updating their travel and motor vehicle use plans a priority. It also sets rules for deciding which roads stay open to cars, off-road vehicles, e-bikes, and snow vehicles.

Any square mile of public land that has at least 2.5 miles of authorized motor-vehicle road is called "disability-accessible land." On that land, agencies could not close roads if the closure would drop the land below that threshold. There are narrow exceptions: a temporary or emergency road less than a year old, or a road that is a direct safety threat.

On other public land, agencies would have to consider reopening roads closed in the last 10 years. They could not close more roads except for a direct safety threat. They could never close roads they find useful for wildfire work, fuel reduction, or search and rescue.

Any closure would need public notice and a hearing, though these can come after the closure in an emergency. Each closure would require a new road to be built within a year. Closures and new roads would skip full National Environmental Policy Act review (the law that requires environmental studies) unless extraordinary circumstances exist. Roads would be presumed open unless "clear and compelling evidence" shows a closure is needed. Roads with unresolved old right-of-way claims (called RS 2477 claims) would stay open until those claims are settled. The bill does not create new roads in wilderness areas, inventoried roadless areas, primitive areas, or most national parks.

label: S. 2042
title: Roadless Area Conservation Act of 2025
one: Writes the existing 2001 Roadless Rule's bans on road building and logging in national forest roadless areas into federal law, so a future administration couldn't simply repeal them by changing the regulation.
summary: This bill would turn a long-standing Forest Service rule into law. The 2001 "Roadless Rule" limits building new roads, rebuilding roads, and logging in certain undeveloped parts of national forests, called inventoried roadless areas. Right now it is only a regulation, so a president's administration can change or cancel it. Under this bill, the Secretary of Agriculture, working through the Forest Service, could not allow road building, road rebuilding, or logging in those areas wherever the Roadless Rule already bans them. The bill uses the rule as it stands, including the changes made for Idaho (2008) and Colorado (2012 and 2016). It does not create new restrictions beyond the rule, and Congress says in its findings that it keeps the "multiple use" approach, so uses the rule already allows would continue. The findings say these areas protect drinking water for tens of millions of people, shelter wildlife, offer recreation, contain sacred Native sites, and have fewer wildfires than roaded areas. They also say the Forest Service already has a $5.98 billion road maintenance backlog. The bill is short, has no new spending, and has had a Senate subcommittee hearing. The findings are Congress's statements, and some of the claims, such as wildfire rates, may be debated.

label: S. 2662
title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2025
short_title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act
one: The bill changes the SBA's 504 small business loan program to make it easier and cheaper for small manufacturers to get financing, speeds up loan closings, and adds goals like job training and energy efficiency.
summary: The 504 loan program is run by the Small Business Administration (SBA). It helps small businesses buy buildings and equipment, using loans from private lenders paired with loans from nonprofit "certified development companies." This bill would change several rules, with a special focus on small manufacturers. It would raise the maximum loan for certain manufacturing projects from $5.5 million to $10 million. It would lower the down payment small manufacturers must put in, in most cases to 5% of the project cost. It would stop the SBA from requiring extra collateral from small manufacturers. It would also let them refinance up to 100% of an expansion's cost. The bill would let some lenders fix paperwork errors and make small changes at closing without new approvals. It would move loan file reviews from SBA district lawyers to the SBA's Office of Credit Risk Management. It would also make development company attorneys responsible for certifying closing documents. The bill would add program goals: job training of at least 12 weeks, energy-efficient products and renewable energy, disaster-area revitalization, and help for businesses with 10 or fewer employees. It would require each SBA district office to partner with groups like Small Business Development Centers to train manufacturers on the program. It would also change the rules on how much of a building owners can lease to others, and require a report to Congress within 5 years. The text does not give a cost estimate.

label: S. 3395
title: Mammography Access for Veterans Act of 2025
short_title: Mammography Access for Veterans Act of 2025
one: Makes the VA's telescreening mammography pilot permanent and requires the VA to offer breast cancer screening options in every state and Puerto Rico within two years.
summary:
This bill would change a 2022 law that created a small test program (a "pilot") at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). The pilot lets veterans get breast cancer screening (mammograms) through telescreening, where a mammogram is taken at one site and read by a specialist somewhere else. The bill removes the word "pilot," so the program would become an ongoing one instead of a temporary test. It also changes a reporting deadline in the old law to May 1, 2027.

The bill would also require the VA, within two years of the bill becoming law, to offer at least one of three things in each state and Puerto Rico: the telescreening program, a full mammography program inside a VA facility, or a mobile mammography unit (a vehicle that travels to patients). The VA must make sure these programs can be used by veterans with paralysis, spinal cord injuries, or other disabilities, following existing accessibility rules.

Finally, the bill says it does not stop the VA from spreading telescreening to other VA facilities beyond the pilot sites or beyond states that lack VA breast imaging. The text does not give a cost estimate or set a funding amount.

label: H.R. 3184
title: PFAS Alternatives Act
short_title: PFAS Alternatives Act (Protecting Firefighters and Advancing State-of-the-Art Alternatives Act)
one: The bill would create federal grants to research and test PFAS-free firefighter protective gear, fund training on safely using and cleaning that gear, and require a progress report to Congress.
summary:
This bill is about the protective clothing firefighters wear, called turnout gear. Much of today's gear uses PFAS, a family of long-lasting chemicals that have been linked to health problems, including some cancers. Firefighters can be exposed to these chemicals through their gear.

The bill would direct the Department of Health and Human Services, working through the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), to set up a grant program within 180 days of becoming law. Grants would go to qualified nonprofits, universities, and national fire service or fire safety groups. They would use the money to research, develop, and test PFAS-free turnout gear. Applicants must explain how they will partner with firefighting groups, including groups that represent rank-and-file firefighters, so the results reach real use.

Starting in fiscal year 2027, the bill would also fund grants or contracts to create guidance and training on safely wearing, cleaning, and caring for the new gear. Within two years, HHS must send Congress a progress report.

The bill authorizes $25 million a year for 2025–2029 for research and $2 million a year for 2027–2031 for training. "Authorizes" means Congress would still need to pass separate spending laws to provide the money. The bill does not ban PFAS in gear or require fire departments to buy anything.

label: H.R. 4509
title: NOPAIN for Veterans Act
one: Requires the VA to add FDA-approved non-opioid post-surgery pain drugs to its national formulary (its standard drug list) within a year of those drugs becoming eligible for certain Medicare extra-payment status.
summary:
This bill would change how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) picks drugs for its national formulary, which is the VA's standard list of medicines it buys and offers. It focuses on non-opioid pain drugs: medicines approved by the FDA to reduce pain after surgery, or to numb a region of the body after surgery, without acting on the body's opioid receptors.

Under the bill, once one of these drugs becomes eligible for extra Medicare payment in outpatient surgery settings (a "temporary additional payment" or separate payment), the VA would have one year to add it to its national formulary. The VA would also have to put these drugs on its "drug standardization list," which is the list of drugs the VA tells its facilities to prefer for purchasing. The VA Secretary would have 90 days after the law passes to put these changes into effect.

The bill also says money from the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund, a fund set aside for veterans harmed by toxic exposure such as burn pits, cannot be used to pay for this. The bill does not say where the money would come from instead, and it does not give a cost estimate. The goal is to give veterans more options for pain control after surgery, which could reduce the need for opioid painkillers and the risk of addiction.

label: H.R. 5995
title: Have You Served Act
one: Creates a VA grant program that helps states and tribes train social service workers and local providers to ask people whether they or a loved one has served in the military, so veterans can be connected to suicide prevention and other resources.
summary: This bill would have the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) give grants to states, territories, D.C., and American Indian and Alaska Native tribes. The money pays for "Ask the Question" campaigns. These campaigns train social service workers, state and local governments, and community providers to politely ask the people they serve, "Have you or a loved one served in the military?" If the answer is yes, the worker can point the person to help from the VA and other groups. To qualify, a state or tribe must first write a veteran suicide prevention plan (for states, called a Governors Challenge Action Plan) and send the VA a proposal for carrying it out. The VA would give up to 25 grants a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, each capped at $200,000. The VA must also offer technical help, such as best practices, local veteran resource information, and information on how it screens for suicide risk. Grant recipients must report on how well their training works. The VA must report to Congress within one year and then every year. The VA must also write a plan, with the White House budget office, for bringing similar campaigns to other federal agencies that serve the public. Congress would authorize $6 million a year for five years. Authorizing money does not guarantee it will be spent. A later spending bill would have to provide it.

label: H.R. 7942
title: DEATH BETS Act
one: Bars regulated U.S. trading platforms from listing or clearing event-based contracts (like prediction market bets) tied to terrorism, assassination, war, or an individual's death.
summary: This bill changes the Commodity Exchange Act, the law that governs regulated futures and event-trading markets. It adds a new rule for "registered entities," meaning exchanges and similar platforms overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Those platforms would not be allowed to list for trading, or accept for clearing (processing and guaranteeing), certain contracts based on an "excluded commodity." That is a legal term that covers things like events or outcomes that are outside anyone's control and that have economic consequences. The banned contracts fall in two groups. First are contracts that involve, relate to, or reference terrorism, assassination, war, or similar activity, as the CFTC decides. Second are contracts that involve or reference a person's death, or that could be read as closely tied to a person's death. In practice, this would stop prediction-market style bets on things like whether a leader is killed, whether a war breaks out, or whether a named person dies. The bill does not set penalties itself, does not say when it takes effect, and does not define "war" or "similar activity" beyond leaving the CFTC to decide. It also does not appear to cover unregulated or offshore platforms. The text has no funding provisions.

Does not appear to cover unregulated or offshore platforms, so bets could move elsewhere.
Gives the CFTC discretion over what counts as war-related or similar, which could change with leadership.
imp.cost: No funding or cost figures are given in the text. Costs would likely be limited to CFTC oversight and enforcement, which the bill does not fund separately.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to stop regulated futures and event-trading platforms from listing or clearing contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, war, or similar activity, and contracts that reference a person's death. people_over_profit.reason: It limits platforms' ability to earn fees and profit from contracts on death, war, and terrorism.

honesty_kindness.reason: It discourages treating human tragedy and death as a betting opportunity, which is a matter of basic decency.

label: H.R. 8041
title: Supporting VA Families Act
one: Gives Department of Veterans Affairs employees, including many clinical staff, four extra weeks of unpaid leave to bond with a new birth, adopted, or foster child.
summary: This bill would let employees of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) take four extra weeks of leave without pay after a child is born or placed with them for adoption or foster care. It covers all VA employees. That includes doctors, nurses, and other health care workers hired under a special part of federal law (Title 38, chapter 74) who are often left out of the usual leave rules. The four weeks can be used within any 12-month period, and the right to use them ends 12 months after the birth or placement. The leave is added on top of any leave the employee already has under the regular federal family leave rules (Title 5) or, for certain VA health workers, under section 7425(c) of Title 38. It does not replace that leave. The leave is unpaid, so the bill does not directly raise worker pay. The text does not say how the VA would cover the work of employees who are out, and it does not give a cost estimate. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. The bill passed a House subcommittee by voice vote on April 15, 2026, and now goes to the full committee. It has 96 cosponsors.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give Department of Veterans Affairs employees, including health care workers hired under Title 38 chapter 74, up to four additional weeks of unpaid leave after a birth, adoption, or foster placement, so they can spend time with a new child without losing their job. label: S. 3475
title: A bill to authorize, ratify, and confirm the Agreement of Settlement and Compromise to Resolve the Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim in the State of New York, and for other purposes.
short_title: Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim Settlement Act
one: Congress would approve a negotiated settlement of a decades-old Mohawk land claim in northern New York and treat certain tribe-owned land as "Indian country."
summary: This bill would put Congress's approval on an agreement that settles a long-running land claim by the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe in northern New York. The agreement was signed by the tribe, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne, New York State, Franklin and Saint Lawrence Counties, the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay, and the New York Power Authority. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the agreement restores land rights and access to land for the tribe, gives tuition help to tribal members at certain colleges, and requires the Power Authority to make yearly payments to the tribe. The bill text itself does not list these terms. They are in the settlement agreement, which was not included in the material I reviewed. The bill also approves any land, right-of-way, or easement transfer that is the subject of three named federal court cases, which are the lawsuits the settlement resolves. Finally, it says land the tribe owns now, or buys later, inside the "Settlement Acquisition Areas" would count as "Indian country," a legal term for land under tribal and federal jurisdiction. This applies subject to the settlement's terms and limits. The Senate Committee on Indian Affairs has ordered the bill reported favorably without changes.
does: Authorizes, ratifies, and confirms the Akwesasne Mohawk Land Claim settlement agreement.
Approves any land, right-of-way, or easement transfer that is the subject of three named federal lawsuits.
Declares land the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe owns, or later acquires, in the Settlement Acquisition Areas to be Indian country under 18 U.S.C. 1151(a), subject to the settlement's terms.
Per CRS, the underlying agreement restores land rights and access, provides tuition aid for tribal members, and requires annual New York Power Authority payments to the tribe.
who: Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and its members
Mohawk Council of Akwesasne
State of New York
Franklin and Saint Lawrence Counties and the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay
New York Power Authority and, possibly, its customers
Landowners and residents near the settlement areas

benefits: Ends long-running litigation and uncertainty through a negotiated deal that all the parties signed.
Restores land rights and access to the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe.
Provides tuition assistance for tribal members.
Gives the tribe clear jurisdiction over land it owns in the settlement areas, subject to the settlement's limits.
concerns: Annual New York Power Authority payments could be paid for by electricity customers, though the bill does not say so.
Nearby non-tribal residents could be affected by the jurisdiction change, and the bill text does not describe their protections.
Environmental, water, and land-use rules for newly designated Indian country are not described in the bill.
imp.cost: The bill text includes no appropriation. The Power Authority pays the tribe each year under the settlement, per CRS. The state and others may have other obligations. The amounts were not provided, and no CBO cost estimate was in the material.
unknowns: Dollar amounts of the Power Authority payments and who ultimately pays for them.
Size and location of the Settlement Acquisition Areas.
Land that would be transferred or restored, and what happens to current private owners.
Environmental protections and local-government roles under the settlement.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to approve, or "ratify and confirm," a settlement agreement that resolves the Akwesasne Mohawk land claim in northern New York. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the settlement restores land rights and access for the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe, provides tuition help for tribal members, and requires annual payments from the New York Power Authority. The bill also approves related land transfers tied to three named federal court cases and recognizes certain tribal land in the settlement areas as Indian country.

oppose: The settlement terms (land, payments, tuition, and access) are in the settlement agreement, not the bill text, so a constituent may want to ask for the full agreement before Congress approves it.

The bill would designate tribal land in the Settlement Acquisition Areas as Indian country, which changes which governments have jurisdiction there. Ask how nearby non-tribal residents' rights and protections would be handled.

The bill does not describe environmental, water, or land-use rules for newly designated Indian country. Ask how those rules would be enforced and who pays for any related costs, including whether the Power Authority payments would be passed on to electricity customers.

crs:
This bill recognizes and settles the Akwesasne land claim in northern New York. (Akwesasne is a Mohawk territory that extends into the United States and Canada, specifically New York, Ontario, and Quebec.)
The bill authorizes, ratifies, and confirms a specified settlement agreement entered into by the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe (SRMT), the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne, the State of New York, Franklin and Saint Lawrence Counties in New York, the towns of Fort Covington and Bombay in New York, and the New York Power Authority. (Among its provisions, the settlement agreement restores land rights and provides access to land to SRMT, provides tuition assistance for tribal members to certain postsecondary institutions, and requires the New York Power Authority to make annual payments to SRMT.)
Additionally, the bill authorizes, ratifies, and confirms any transfer of land, right-of-way, or easement that is the subject of claims in specified court cases.
The bill also recognizes as 
Indian country

Indian country
, for purposes of criminal jurisdiction, generally refers to all lands within a tribal reservation, dependent Indian communities, and tribal allotments.)

honesty_kindness.reason: It honors a negotiated resolution of a long-standing grievance and restores land rights to the Mohawk people.

label: S. 3859
title: A bill to amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 with respect to future membership in the Catawba Indian Nation.
one: Removes a 1993 federal limit on who can join the Catawba Indian Nation so the tribe itself decides its future membership rules.
summary: In 1993, Congress passed a law settling a land claim for the Catawba Indian Tribe in South Carolina. One part of that law said new tribal members had to be direct descendants of someone on the tribe's final base membership roll (the official list of original members) and had to have kept up political relations with the tribe. This bill deletes that federal restriction from the 1993 law. The change is very short: it strikes one clause from Section 7(d). After that, the tribe would decide for itself who can be a member. According to the Congressional Research Service, the tribe uses three base rolls, and anyone who wants to enroll must show direct descent from someone on one of those rolls. The bill does not itself say what the tribe's rules must be, and it does not spend money or change land rights. It was introduced by Sen. Lindsey Graham with two cosponsors in February 2026. The Senate Committee on Indian Affairs voted to send it to the full Senate favorably without changes in November 2026. The text does not say when the change would start beyond becoming law, and it does not say whether the tribe plans to change its current rules.
does: Strikes the clause in Section 7(d) of the 1993 Catawba settlement act that limited enrollment to lineal descendants of people on the final base roll who maintained political relations with the tribe.
Leaves membership decisions to the Catawba Indian Nation under its own rules.
Does not set new membership criteria, and does not add spending or change land provisions.
who: Catawba Indian Nation and its government
People who may want to enroll in the tribe, including those who don't meet the 1993 federal criteria
Current tribal members, whose tribe would control the rules for new members
Federal and South Carolina officials who deal with the 1993 settlement

benefits: Gives the Catawba Indian Nation control over its own enrollment.
Removes an outside federal restriction that dates to 1993.
Could let the tribe adapt its rules over time to its community's needs.
Costs nothing directly.
concerns: Without the federal limit, the tribe's rules could change in ways that affect who gets tribal benefits or voting rights, though the tribe would decide this.
Membership changes could lead to internal disputes over enrollment.
The bill text does not explain why the change is requested or how the tribe's members feel about it.
imp.cost: No spending or funding is in the bill text. No cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: Whether the tribe plans to change its current membership rules after the bill passes.
Whether tribal members broadly support the change.
Whether the change could affect settlement-related benefits or any related state agreements, which the text does not address.
Whether a cost estimate or committee report exists.

stage.last_action: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 so that future membership in the Catawba Indian Nation is no longer limited by federal law. The 1993 law limited future enrollment to lineal descendants of people on the final base membership roll who maintained continuous political relations with the tribe. By removing that limit, the bill would let the tribe decide its own membership.

oppose: The 1993 law set a federal standard for who can join the Catawba Nation. Removing it means a federal restriction is gone and the tribe alone sets the rules, which some constituents may feel should stay in place.

Changes to membership can affect who receives tribal benefits and who can vote in tribal matters. The bill does not say what new rules the tribe would adopt, so constituents may want more details before supporting it.

The bill text does not explain why the tribe requested the change or how tribal members feel about it. Constituents may ask the senator to share the tribe's reasons and to confirm that its members were consulted.
support: The bill gives the Catawba Indian Nation control over its own enrollment, which many people see as a basic matter of tribal self-government.
The restriction dates to 1993 and was written by Congress. Removing it lets the tribe adapt its membership rules over time to meet its community's needs.
The bill costs nothing directly, does not spend federal money, and does not change land provisions in the 1993 settlement.

crs:
This bill revises tribal membership requirements for the Catawba Indian Nation (a tribe in South Carolina).
The Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 explicitly restricted the tribe’s future membership to lineal descendants of people on the final base membership roll who maintained continuous political relations with the tribe. This bill removes these membership criteria and allows the tribe to determine its membership. (The tribe uses three base membership rolls and anyone who wants to be enrolled must prove lineal descent from someone listed on one of these base membership rolls.)

label: H.R. 10956
title: IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2026
one: The bill lets health workers who got Indian Health Service scholarships or loan repayment help pay back their service commitment by working half-time instead of full-time, for a longer period.
summary:
The Indian Health Service (IHS) helps pay for health training and student loans. In return, the health worker agrees to work for a set time in Native American health care. Right now, the scholarship rules require full-time work to meet that promise. This bill would add a half-time option.

For scholarship recipients, half-time work would be allowed at the same kinds of sites as full-time work: the IHS, tribal programs, urban Indian programs funded under title V, or certain private practices in shortage areas that serve many Native Americans. The catch is that the person must agree in writing to serve twice as long. If they fail to start or finish, the damages for breaking the contract would be figured by converting their half-time service into its full-time equivalent.

For the loan repayment program, a person could choose full-time service for 2 years, half-time service for 4 years, or half-time service for 2 years with a loan payment of 50 percent of the full-time amount. The same full-time conversion would be used if someone breaks the contract.

The bill does not add money by itself. It changes service rules. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to a subcommittee. The text does not give a start date.
does: Lets IHS scholarship recipients meet their service obligation through half-time clinical work.
Requires half-time scholarship recipients to agree in writing to double the length of service.
Gives IHS loan repayment participants three options: 2 years full-time, 4 years half-time, or 2 years half-time with 50 percent of the loan payment.
Says half-time service must be converted to full-time equivalents when calculating damages for breaking a contract.
Uses the Public Health Service Act definition of "full-time" and "half-time."

American Indian and Alaska Native patients who use IHS, tribal and urban Indian health programs
Tribal and urban Indian health programs that hire these workers
The Indian Health Service and the Department of Health and Human Services, which run the programs

benefits: Could give scholarship and loan repayment recipients more flexibility, such as working part-time while meeting their service obligation.
Could make it easier for some health workers to join or stay in IHS and tribal health programs, which may help fill staffing gaps.
The loan repayment option with half-time pay could let some workers choose a path that fits their needs.
concerns: Half-time service may mean a longer total commitment (4 years instead of 2 for the half-time loan option, or twice as long for scholarships), which some workers may find burdensome.

Because half-time service counts toward the full-time equivalent, the number of full-time staff hours delivered per worker could be lower than under current rules, which may matter in understaffed facilities.
The text does not say how damages would be calculated in dollars, so the financial risk of breaking a contract is unclear.

label: H.R. 10828
title: Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act
short_title: Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act
one: The bill would cancel U.S. permissions that let Russian oil and diesel be sold, require sanctions on Russian oil and gas companies, bar U.S. development-bank deals tied to Russian-owned energy, and require regular reports to Congress.
summary: This bill is aimed at cutting the money Russia earns from oil and gas while its war in Ukraine continues. First, it stops the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC, a government agency that backs overseas investments) from supporting or joining any deal involving energy owned by a Russian foreign person, even if the assets are outside Russia. Second, it cancels five Treasury "general licenses" (blanket permissions) that allowed certain Russian crude oil, petroleum products, and diesel to be delivered and sold, including to India. It also bars the Treasury Secretary from issuing new permissions of this kind for Russian oil, fuel, or natural gas. This ban lasts three years. Third, it expands Congress's power to review sanctions-related actions on Russia, including any licensing actions that help Russian energy sales, until the State Department certifies that Russia has ended its war and committed to a just peace that includes paying Ukraine for war damages. Fourth, within 30 days it calls for sanctions on any Russian person involved in oil and gas extraction, refining, production, or shipping. These include freezing U.S.-linked assets and denying or revoking visas. There are exceptions for humanitarian aid, food, medicine, U.N. obligations, and U.S. intelligence or law enforcement work. Finally, it requires reports to Congress on how the licenses affected Russian oil sales and revenue, and on whether Russian energy companies took part in abducting or deporting Ukrainian civilians, including children.
does: Bars the DFC from supporting or joining any deal involving energy owned by a Russian foreign person, even outside Russia, with criminal and civil penalties borrowed from the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
Makes OFAC General Licenses 133, 134A, 134B, 134C, and 135 (permitting certain Russian oil and diesel sales) have no effect starting on the day the bill becomes law.

Bars Treasury from issuing new general licenses or other authorizations for buying, selling, delivering, or offloading Russian crude oil, petroleum products, diesel, or natural gas; this expires after 3 years.

Expands congressional review under the CAATSA sanctions law to cover executive orders under the Russia national emergency (EO 14024) and licensing actions that help Russian energy sales, until the State Department certifies Russia has ended its war and committed to a just peace including compensation to Ukraine.

Within 30 days, directs the President to impose sanctions on Russian persons involved in oil and gas extraction, refining or production, or maritime transport of oil and gas. These include blocking property in U.S. jurisdiction and denying or revoking visas.

Exempts food, agricultural goods, medicine, medical devices, humanitarian assistance, U.N. headquarters obligations, and authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities.

Lets courts see classified evidence behind sanctions decisions privately (ex parte and in camera, meaning without the sanctioned party seeing it), and says this does not create a right to judicial review.
Requires reports to Congress within 30 days and every 60 days for 3 years on the effects of the licenses, including Russian export volumes, prices, government revenue, and production.

Requires reports within 30 days and every 180 days for 2 years on Russian state-owned or state-affiliated energy companies' role in abducting, deporting, or indoctrinating Ukrainian civilians, including children.
who: Russian oil, gas, refining, and shipping companies and their executives
Buyers of Russian oil and diesel abroad, such as India and other importers
U.S. companies, banks, and shippers that deal with Russian energy
U.S. fuel consumers and ratepayers, if global energy prices shift
Ukrainian civilians, including children who were deported or abducted
The DFC, the Treasury Department (OFAC), and the State Department
Congress, which gains more review authority and information

benefits: Supporters may see the bill as reducing Russian revenue from oil and gas while the war in Ukraine continues.
Limiting DFC involvement could keep U.S. public money from supporting deals tied to Russian-owned energy.
Added congressional review could give lawmakers more oversight of Russia-related licensing decisions.
Required reports could give Congress information on oil revenue and alleged civilian abductions or deportations.
concerns: Canceling licenses and banning new ones could raise fuel prices or disrupt supply in some markets, though the bill's text does not analyze this.
Countries such as India that buy Russian oil could face supply changes, and the bill does not describe how they would adjust.
The broad definition of energy involvement and the mandatory sanctions could reach companies that have limited connection to the war, and the bill does not describe how such cases would be handled.
The bill's wording on the 30-day sanctions and the expanded congressional review may create uncertainty for businesses and agencies that must follow it.
imp.cost: ["The bill's text, as summarized, does not state a cost estimate or specific funding amounts. No Congressional Budget Office estimate is provided in the material."]
unknowns: The material does not state whether a Congressional Budget Office cost estimate exists.
The effect on global oil prices, fuel supply, and buyers in India is not stated.
How the 30-day sanctions requirement would be carried out, and how it would apply to specific Russian persons, is not described.
The specific terms of the five canceled general licenses and their past sales volumes are not given.
The bill's status beyond introduction and referral to a House committee is not stated, and no CRS summary was provided.
What 'just peace' and war-damage payments would require in practice is not defined in the material.

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

purpose: The bill says its goal is to cut the money Russia earns from oil and gas while its war in Ukraine continues. It would do this by limiting U.S. development finance support for Russian-owned energy deals, canceling five Treasury general licenses that allowed certain Russian oil and diesel sales, barring new licenses for Russian oil, fuel, or natural gas for three years, expanding congressional review of Russia sanctions actions, and requiring new sanctions and reports to Congress.

oppose: The bill cancels five existing Treasury licenses and bars new ones for Russian oil, petroleum products, diesel, and natural gas for three years. Someone opposing it could ask the member how this would affect fuel prices and supply, since the bill's text does not analyze those effects.

Countries such as India buy Russian oil under these licenses. Someone opposing the bill could ask how allied and partner countries would adjust their supplies, because the bill does not describe a plan for that.

The bill requires sanctions on any Russian person involved in oil and gas extraction, refining, production, or shipping within 30 days. Someone opposing it could ask how companies with limited connection to the war would be identified and handled, since the bill does not say.
support: The bill aims to reduce Russian revenue from oil and gas while the war in Ukraine continues. A supporter could tell the member that this is a direct way to limit funding for the war.

The bill would stop the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation from supporting or joining deals involving Russian-owned energy, even outside Russia. A supporter could say this keeps U.S. public money out of deals tied to Russian energy.

The bill requires reports to Congress on the effects of the licenses and on whether Russian energy companies took part in abducting or deporting Ukrainian civilians, including children. A supporter could say this gives lawmakers information they need for oversight.

transparency.reason: Expands congressional review of sanctions and licensing actions and requires multiple reports to Congress, though court ex parte classified review cuts somewhat against openness.

people_over_profit.reason: Cuts off licenses and government support that help Russian energy firms earn profits and restricts DFC deals with Russian-owned energy, though it may raise global fuel prices for consumers.

no_bailouts.reason: Bars DFC financing and support for deals involving Russian-owned energy, limiting government-backed investment subsidies to those companies.

honesty_kindness.reason: Requires reporting on whether Russian energy companies took part in abducting and deporting Ukrainian civilians including children, and humanitarian exemptions protect aid and medicine.

news.overall: Lean Left headlines frame the issue around Trump's personal engagement with Putin, the war's continuation, and energy-price politics, while Center headlines treat it as a set of events and congressional process questions, such as the Crimea strike, peace-talk expectations, and oversight tools. Neither group's headlines mention the bill by name, so the evidence on how either perspective covers this specific legislation is very limited (five and three headlines respectively, with only descriptions missing from all of them). The shared gap is that no headline connects the bill's anti-corruption oil-deal focus to the coverage.

label: H.R. 10961
title: To direct the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to report on the Warrior Training Advancement Course of the Veterans Benefits Administration.
one: Requires the VA Secretary to report to Congress on the Warrior Training Advancement Course, which trains transitioning service members for Veterans Benefits Administration jobs, including participation, cost savings, and hiring results.
summary: This bill does not create a new program or change who can get benefits. It asks the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to report on an existing training program called the Warrior Training Advancement Course (WARTAC). WARTAC trains service members who are leaving the military, through the military's Transition Assistance Program (TAP), so they can qualify for certain jobs in the Veterans Benefits Administration. Within two years after the bill becomes law, the VA Secretary must send a first report to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees. After that, a yearly report is due. The reports must say how many service members applied, took part in, and finished the course, and how the VA trains them during TAP. They must also say how much money the VA estimates the course saves each year and since it began, and whether other agencies could save money with a similar program. Finally, they must describe how the VA finds jobs these graduates can fill, what pay grades those jobs have, and how many graduates the VA has hired. The first report must also be sent to the head of every federal agency within 30 days. The bill gives no new money and sets no new rules for the program itself.

label: H.R. 10966
title: Supporting Veteran Mothers Act of 2026
one: The bill would require VA medical facilities to staff enough dedicated maternity care coordinators for pregnant and postpartum veterans, check staffing every two years, fix shortfalls with action plans, and report publicly on the results.
summary: This bill is about veterans who are pregnant or have recently had a baby and get care through the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Maternity care coordinators are VA staff who help line up that care, from the time a pregnancy is confirmed through the postpartum period (the months after birth). The bill would require larger VA medical facilities to have enough of these coordinators. Each coordinator counted would have to work only on maternity coordination, not on unrelated tasks. Every two years, each facility would have to count its coordinators and its pregnant and postpartum patients and check whether it meets the minimum. If it falls short, the facility head would have 45 days to send a plan to the VA Secretary and Congress explaining how and when it will fix the gap, and then carry out the plan. The Secretary could grant a waiver in extraordinary cases, such as a local worker shortage. The VA would write guidance within 180 days of enactment, and the first reviews would be due about 240 days after that. The VA would report to Congress each year for five years and post a public summary online. The bill text does not say how much money it would cost or provide new funding. The staffing ratio wording is also unclear, because it lists two overlapping ratios.

label: H.R. 10968
title: No Veteran Left Behind: Housing Retention Act of 2026
short_title: No Veteran Left Behind: Housing Retention Act of 2026
one: The bill would create a VA grant program that pays nonprofits, co-ops, and certain government/tribal entities to provide support services (health, food, transportation, eviction prevention) to lower-income veterans so they can stay in permanent housing and avoid homelessness.
summary:
This bill would add a new section to federal veterans' law. It tells the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to give grants to approved groups that help certain veterans keep their homes. The money would go to private nonprofits, consumer cooperatives (member-owned housing groups), and state, local, or tribal housing agencies. The groups would use it for things like mental health and substance use counseling, food assistance, rides to appointments and job interviews, help with medications, money management, eviction prevention, home accessibility changes, and help finding health care.

To qualify, a veteran must have income at or below 80 percent of the area median (not counting VA disability or pension pay). The veteran must live in permanent housing or be moving into it. The veteran must also be formerly homeless or at risk of homelessness. In addition, the veteran must be 55 or older, terminally or chronically ill, have a chronic substance use disorder, or have a significant medical need.

The VA would favor groups serving veterans leaving homelessness or at risk of returning to it. It must try to spread money fairly across regions, including rural areas and tribal lands. Grantees must tell veterans the VA is paying for services, report each year on what they did, and join case conferences with VA, health providers, and housing providers, following privacy laws. The bill does not state a dollar amount.

label: H.R. 10972
title: NEW HORIZON Act
short_title: NEW HORIZON Act (Orbital Data Center Pilot Program)
one: Requires the Defense Department, through the Defense Innovation Unit, to run a pilot program of up to five years testing commercial orbital data centers and space-based cloud computing for military and intelligence uses.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of Defense, working through the Defense Innovation Unit, start a pilot program within one year of the bill becoming law. The pilot would test whether commercially built "orbital data centers" (computers, storage, and networking placed in space) and space-based cloud computing can help with national security missions. These could include intelligence, tracking objects in space, command and control, and moving data. The idea is that processing data in orbit could cut delays and make systems harder to knock out than relying only on ground facilities.

The bill tells the Pentagon to encourage competition from newer, non-traditional defense companies and commercial space firms. It requires strong cybersecurity and supply-chain protections for any service handling sensitive or classified information, including protections against foreign ownership or influence. It also asks the Pentagon to study how to defend these assets from attacks. The Pentagon must consult with the Space Force, the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and others. A briefing to Congress's defense committees is due by December 31, 2028. The authority ends five years after enactment. The bill does not set a dollar amount, and it does not mention environmental review, public reporting, or rules for debris and launches.

label: H.R. 10984
title: INNOVATE Act
one: Creates an Office of Innovation inside the Veterans Health Administration with new flexible deal-making powers, a purchase-guarantee tool, and a mixed-source funding account to bring in outside technology and partners.
summary: This bill would set up a permanent Office of Innovation inside the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), the VA's health care system. The office would work with outside companies, nonprofits, and universities to develop and roll out new health technologies and services for veterans. It would also get new powers that normally apply only to a few agencies. First, it could make "other transactional" deals. These are agreements that are not regular contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements, and they would usually be capped at $10 million unless a senior VA official writes a justification. Partners would have to be U.S.-based and not tied to a foreign adversary. Second, it could make "advance market commitments," which are promises to buy a product at a set price if it meets a defined health need. Third, it would create an Innovation Flexibility Account that could take money from VA sources and from outside donors such as companies, nonprofits, and individuals. It could not use money meant for direct veteran care, and it could not take money from foreign governments. Inventions made under these deals would be exempt from some federal patent rules. VA-linked nonprofit research corporations could keep royalties. The bill also requires conflict-of-interest checks, public reporting, Government Accountability Office (GAO) access to records, and audits every two years. The VA would have 120 days after enactment to carry it out.

one: The bill extends the authorization of the USDA Intermediary Relending Program, which funds local lenders that make loans in rural areas, through fiscal years 2027–2031.
summary: This bill is very short. It changes one date range in an existing federal law. The law covers the Intermediary Relending Program, run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). In this program, the federal government makes low-interest loans to "intermediaries," such as local nonprofits, cooperatives, or public groups. The intermediaries then lend that money to businesses and community projects in rural areas. Right now the law's authorization period reads "2014 through 2023." That period has ended. The bill replaces it with "2027 through 2031." In practical terms, this gives Congress's permission to keep funding the program for those five years. The bill does not set a dollar amount. It also does not change who can borrow, the loan terms, or the rules of the program, at least in the text provided. Whether money is actually spent depends on separate spending decisions, called appropriations, that Congress makes each year. The bill has only been introduced and sent to the House Agriculture Committee. No cost estimate or Congressional Research Service summary was available yet.

label: H.R. 11002
title: Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act of 2026
short_title: Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act of 2026
one: The bill would ban building data centers on National Forest and Interior Department-managed federal land, and require that any federal land sold or transferred in the future return to the government if it is used for a data center.
summary: This bill would stop anyone from building a data center on certain federal public lands. Data centers are large buildings full of computers that store and process online information, and they often use a lot of electricity and water. The ban would cover National Forest System land and land managed by the Secretary of the Interior (which includes agencies like the Bureau of Land Management and National Park Service). The ban applies "notwithstanding any other provision of law," so it would override other laws that might allow such projects. Tribal lands are left out of the ban. That includes reservations, pueblos, rancherias, and land held in trust or with restrictions for Tribes or individual Indians. The bill also deals with land the government sells or gives away. Any transfer of federal land after the bill becomes law would need a "reversionary clause." That is a legal term meaning the land goes back to the United States if it is used for a data center. The only exception is when Congress passes a specific law allowing a data center on that land. The bill does not create new spending or programs, and it does not set penalties or name an agency to enforce the rules. It has been introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees. It has not yet been voted on. Land managed by other agencies, such as the Defense or Energy Departments, does not appear to be covered by the definition.

label: H.R. 11005
title: Corey Adams Searchlight Act
short_title: Corey Adams Searchlight Act (Green Alert for Missing Veterans)
one: Creates a voluntary national "Green Alert" network, run through the Department of Justice, to help states and tribes issue alerts and organize searches for missing veterans, with $3 million authorized.
summary: This bill would have the U.S. Attorney General set up a national "Green Alert" network, similar in spirit to AMBER Alerts for missing children, but for missing veterans. It covers people who are currently serving or who served in the armed forces, including the National Guard and Reserves. The Justice Department would name a national coordinator. That person would work with states, tribes, local police, broadcasters, and the Department of Veterans Affairs to encourage states to set up their own Green Alert plans. The coordinator would write voluntary guidelines. These would cover when an alert is warranted (including a veteran's mental or physical condition and whether the person reporting is credible), how to avoid overusing alerts, and how to protect missing veterans' privacy and medical information. Alerts would be aimed at the areas a missing veteran could reasonably reach. The coordinator would also offer training and materials. They could fund a full-time state coordinator and help states connect Green Alerts to their existing alert systems. An advisory board would be created, and the coordinator would send Congress yearly reports on how states are doing, including costs and results. Participation by states is voluntary, and the coordinator may not interfere with existing voluntary arrangements between local broadcasters and law enforcement. The bill authorizes $3 million, but the money would still need to be approved separately.

label: H.R. 1394
title: CURD Act
one: Creates a federal legal definition of "natural cheese" and makes it illegal to sell a food labeled "natural cheese" if it does not meet that definition, while setting a single national standard for this label term.
summary:
This bill would add a legal definition of "natural cheese" to the federal food safety law. Natural cheese would mean cheese made by curdling the protein in milk, cream, buttermilk, or similar dairy ingredients (using rennet or other suitable agents) and draining off some of the whey. It can be soft, semi-soft, or hard, ripened or not, and may have a coating. It can also include safe, suitable non-milk ingredients of the kind already allowed in existing federal cheese standards. Milk from animals other than cows counts. Cheese made under most existing federal cheese standards also qualifies.

The definition leaves out process cheeses, process cheese foods, cheese spreads, blended cheeses, cold pack cheeses, grated American cheese food, similar products, and anything else the FDA Secretary designates as process cheese.

If a product's label uses "natural cheese" to describe a kind of cheese but it doesn't meet the definition, it would be "misbranded" (illegally labeled) and could not be sold. The bill says companies can still use "natural" or "all-natural" in ways that follow current FDA rules. Finally, the bill would add this new rule to the list of labeling rules where states cannot set different requirements. Congress's stated goal is to help shoppers tell natural cheese from process cheese. The bill was just introduced and sent to committee.

label: H.R. 1924
title: Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025
short_title: Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act
one: The bill would let long-term care hospitals get Medicare's higher, specialized payment rate for very sick patients whose diagnosis group has a relative weight of 0.8 or more, for discharges starting October 1, 2026.
summary: Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) treat patients with serious, long-lasting illnesses, often after an intensive care stay. Medicare pays LTCHs a higher, specialized rate only for stays that meet certain rules. Stays that don't meet those rules are paid a lower "site-neutral" rate. That rate is the lower of two amounts: what a regular acute care hospital would be paid, or 100% of the cost of the stay. Today, a stay can avoid the lower rate if it follows an ICU or hospital stay of a certain type, or if the patient needed a ventilator for a long time. This bill adds a third way to qualify. A discharge would get the higher LTCH rate if the patient's case falls into a Medicare diagnosis group (a billing category for an illness and its severity) with a "relative weight" of 0.8 or higher. The relative weight is a number that reflects how costly a case usually is. The change would apply to discharges on or after October 1, 2026. The bill does not name specific diseases, and it does not say how much it would cost. The text does not include a cost estimate. Whether more LTCH stays would be paid at the higher rate depends on how many cases fall in those diagnosis groups.

label: H.R. 2203
title: Innovative FEED Act of 2025
one: Creates a new legal category for animal feed additives that act only in the gut (such as ones that change digestion byproducts, cut human-pathogen germs, or alter gut bacteria) and regulates them through the FDA's food additive process instead of the animal drug process.
summary:
Right now, if a feed ingredient is meant to change how an animal's body works, such as by shifting gut bacteria or lowering methane from digestion, the FDA may treat it as an animal drug. Drug review can be slower and more costly. This bill creates a new category called "zootechnical animal food substances." These are things added to animal feed or water that work only inside the digestive tract. They may be meant to change the byproducts of digestion, reduce germs in food animals that could make people sick, or change the animal's gut microbiome (the community of microbes in the gut).

Under the bill, these substances would be reviewed as food additives. The company would file a petition with the FDA. It would have to include data showing the substance works as intended and full reports of its studies. The FDA would set the conditions of use, and could deny the petition if the company fails to show the substance achieves its intended effect. The bill keeps the usual food additive process, which centers on safety.

Labels would have to say the product is not for diagnosing, curing, treating, or preventing disease in animals. They could also state the intended effect on the animal's body. Disease treatments, hormones, ionophores (a type of antimicrobial feed additive), and certain ingredients already in approved or studied animal drugs are excluded. The FDA could exclude other substances by rule. The bill does not let the government force anyone to use these substances.

as a substance that is added to the food or drinking water of animals and that affects only the animal's gastrointestinal tract, with the intended purpose of affecting the byproducts of the animal's digestion, reducing foodborne pathogens, or altering the animal's gastrointestinal biome.
The definition does not include substances that are used to treat or prevent diseases in animals, hormones, or active ingredients of animal drugs. Labels for zootechnical animal food substances must include a disclaimer that the substance may not be used to treat or prevent diseases in animals.

air.reason: Substances meant to change the byproducts of animal digestion, such as methane, could reduce air emissions from livestock, though the bill does not require any emissions reduction and effects are speculative.

transparency.reason: The bill moves these substances into the food additive pathway and requires studies to be filed with FDA, but the full study reports may be kept from public view and the review is less rigorous than drug approval, which reduces public visibility.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill speeds up and lowers the cost of approval for companies by replacing drug review with a food additive petition, which mainly benefits manufacturers' commercial interests.

honesty_kindness.reason: Labels must carry a disclaimer that the product is not for treating or preventing disease, and the bill does not force use, which is neutral to mildly positive on honesty, but the overall effect on honesty is unclear.

label: H.R. 2731
title: Great Lakes Mapping Act of 2025
one: Directs NOAA to create a high-resolution public map of the floors of all five Great Lakes by the end of 2030, working with Great Lakes states and regional groups, and authorizes $50 million per year for five years.
summary: This bill tells the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to survey and map the bottoms of the Great Lakes in high detail by December 31, 2030. Right now, much of the lakebed is not mapped at high resolution. The work would include collecting depth data (called bathymetric data), building a full map, and storing the data and related background information (metadata). NOAA would have to work with the governors and relevant agencies of the states that border the lakes, a national ocean mapping council, the Great Lakes Observing System's Lakebed 2030 initiative, other regional observing groups, and anyone else NOAA thinks is relevant. NOAA must release finished pieces of the map to the public within a "reasonable time" it decides, and release the full map and any legally required data, where practical, within 180 days after finishing. The data would also be added to products like nautical charts and tools for resource mapping and habitat studies. The bill does not change how NOAA runs two existing mapping laws. It authorizes up to $50 million each year for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, available through fiscal year 2030. "Authorizes" means Congress allows the spending, but a separate spending bill must actually provide the money. The bill is at the start of the process and has been sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.
