label: H.R. 2740
title: To modify the boundaries of the Talladega National Forest, and for other purposes.
one: The bill expands the official boundary of Alabama's Talladega National Forest to include land on a specific map, and lets the Forest Service acquire land inside that area only from willing sellers.
summary:
This bill would change the official boundary of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama. The new boundary would include land shown on a Forest Service map titled "Talladega National Forest Proposed Proclamation Boundary Addition," dated September 6, 2024. The map must be kept on file where the public can look at it.

Inside the new boundary area, the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) could use existing national forest land-buying powers, including the 1911 Weeks Law, to acquire land, water, and related interests. Any private land or water would have to come from a willing seller. The land could be donated, swapped for other land, or bought with donated or appropriated money (money Congress sets aside). The government is asked to do this without undue delay when practical.

Land acquired this way would be managed under the same rules as other national forest land bought under the Weeks Law. Drawing the boundary does not by itself make anyone sell, and the bill does not say that land already in private hands becomes federal. The bill text does not give the size of the area, name the landowners, or set a dollar amount. I could not see the map itself.

label: H.R. 3212
title: LAST ACRE Act of 2025
short_title: LAST ACRE Act of 2025 (Farm Broadband Grants)
one: Creates a USDA grant-and-loan program, funded at $20 million a year for 2026–2030, to bring high-speed internet and wireless connections to farmland that lacks it. It also adds broadband questions to USDA farm surveys and repeals two existing USDA broadband programs.
summary:
This bill would set up a new "Last Acre Program" at the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The program would help internet and wireless companies connect farms and ranches that have little or no high-speed internet. The money could pay for service to tractors, irrigation systems, drones, soil sensors, barns, and farm offices. It could also pay for towers and poles, or for adding equipment to existing structures such as water towers and grain elevators.

Companies would bid for money. Once one company bids on a piece of land, nearby registered companies get a chance to submit competing bids. Other companies can also challenge a bid if they already serve the land or are already committed to serving it. USDA must pick the bid with the lowest cost to the government that can also reliably meet the farm's needs. The federal government could pay up to 80% of a project's cost, or 90% for low-income, small-sales farmers. Remote, unserved land gets priority. Companies must meet basic cybersecurity rules and finish building within 4 years, or face penalties.

The bill would authorize $20 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, which is $100 million in total. Authorizing money does not guarantee it, because Congress must still appropriate it. The bill also requires farm surveys to ask about broadband use. It repeals two existing USDA broadband programs: the innovative broadband program and the middle-mile program. USDA must report on outcomes each year, and the reports would be public.

Linking Access to Spur Technology for Agriculture Connectivity in Rural Environments Act of 2025 or the LAST ACRE Act of 2025
This bill requires the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make grants and loans to facilitate broadband and wireless connectivity projects on active agricultural land.
To be eligible for support, projects must involve (1) the provision of broadband service to structures and devices, including tractors, irrigation systems, and drones; (2) the provision of wireless connectivity to facilitate data transmission between structures and devices; or (3) activities that support the construction of wireless infrastructure. Projects must involve agricultural land that is used for the active production of agricultural commodities or livestock and that lacks broadband service at specified minimum speeds.
To apply for funding, a broadband or wireless connectivity provider must submit an initial bid to USDA relating to a project on eligible agricultural land. The application must include information on the provider’s engagement with the relevant farmer or rancher and a description of how the grant or loan assistance would be used to establish connectivity on the land. Once an initial bid is received, USDA must allow other providers that operate on or near the relevant land to submit competing bids.
Separately, the bill requires USDA to include in certain surveys of U.S. farmers questions related to whether and how respondents use broadband service at farm sites.
Finally, the bill repeals two USDA loan and grant programs that support innovative broadband projects and middle mile broadband infrastructure, respectively.

local_say.reason: Farmers and rural communities gain better connectivity on their own land, and the bid process lets nearby providers compete and lets the farm's needs drive which bid wins, which somewhat strengthens farmers' voice in what gets built.

label: H.R. 3584
title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
short_title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
one: Lets the Secretary of Agriculture allow a memorial for 9 Air Force crew members killed in a 1982 crash to be moved from private land onto a rest area in Nantahala National Forest, with no federal money used.
summary: This bill deals with a memorial for the nine Air Force crew members who died when their C-141B transport plane crashed over the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests in North Carolina on August 31, 1982. The memorial now sits on private land next to the Cherohala Skyway, a scenic road. If the private landowner agrees, the bill lets the Secretary of Agriculture (whose department oversees the U.S. Forest Service) approve moving it to the Stratton Ridge rest area at mile marker 2 of the Skyway in Graham County, inside the Nantahala National Forest. The move would be done through a "special use authorization," which is a permit the Forest Service gives to use national forest land for a specific purpose. The exact spot must be approved by the Secretary along with the North Carolina Department of Transportation. If the site is next to a federal-aid highway, the Federal Highway Administration must also agree. No federal money may be used to move, install, or maintain the memorial. Whoever asks for the move must pay all costs, including processing the application, any environmental review, and the move and upkeep. The Secretary can set conditions on the permit, including a ban on making the memorial bigger.

label: H.R. 382
title: Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
short_title: Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
one: Requires the EPA to publish a yearly public report on carbon dioxide and methane emissions from U.S. fossil fuel use at home and from U.S. fossil fuels that are exported and burned or leaked abroad.
summary: This bill would make the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) track and publish how much carbon dioxide and methane comes from fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) tied to the United States. The first report would be due within 180 days after the bill becomes law, and new ones would come out every year. Each report would cover the previous ten calendar years. It would include two numbers. The first is emissions released inside the U.S. and its territories from digging up, processing, moving, burning, and otherwise using fossil fuels. The second is emissions released outside the U.S. from leaks and burning of fossil fuels that were produced or refined in the U.S. and then exported. The EPA would have to use the best available science, such as direct measurements and data that other governments publish about their own emissions. It would also be guided by international accounting standards, including the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. The EPA would have to consult the Energy Information Administration and the International Energy Agency. The results would be posted on the EPA's website for anyone to see. The bill does not limit emissions, create fees or taxes, or change any rules for energy companies. It only requires measuring and publishing information. It does not state a dollar amount for the work.

Exported Carbon Emissions Report Act of 2025
This bill directs the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to annually collect, calculate, and publish information on certain emissions of carbon dioxide and methane from fossil fuels. Specifically, the EPA must publish information, for each of the previous 10 years, on the total emissions of carbon dioxide and methane that are released (1) within the boundaries of the United States that are the result of the extraction, processing, transportation, combustion, and other use of fossil fuels; and (2) outside the boundaries of the United States that are the result of leakage and combustion of fossil fuels produced or refined in the United States and subsequently exported.

summary:
This bill renews the Farm and Ranch Stress Assistance Network, a U.S. Department of Agriculture program. The program gives competitive grants (money groups must apply for and win) to states, Indian tribes, and qualified nonprofit groups. The bill makes three changes. First, it says money for farm helplines and websites can also be used for crisis lines. Second, it raises yearly funding authorized for the program from $10 million to $15 million for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030. Those providers are certified community behavioral health clinics, health centers, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and critical access hospitals. The word "may" means referrals are optional, not required. The bill was introduced July 15, 2025, and sent to the House Agriculture Committee. It has not advanced further.

label: H.R. 4991
title: Disarming Felons Act
one: Adults who, at ages 15 to 17, were found to have committed an act that would be a felony for an adult would be barred from owning or possessing a firearm, and it would be illegal to sell or give them one.
summary:
Federal law already bans certain groups from having guns, such as people convicted of felonies, and bans selling guns to them. This bill adds one more group. It covers adults who, when they were 15, 16, or 17, were found to have committed "juvenile delinquency" (a youth court finding of wrongdoing) for an act that would have been a felony if an adult had done it.

If the bill became law, two things would change. First, those adults could not legally possess a firearm. Second, anyone selling or giving a gun to them would be breaking the law if they knew or had reasonable cause to believe the person fell in this group. That second part comes from how the existing sale rule is written.

The bill is short and only adds these two lines to the law. It does not set an end date for the ban. It also does not say how it would treat sealed or expunged (erased) youth records, and it does not create a way to get gun rights back. It does not name a start date, so it would likely take effect when signed. Penalties are not written in this bill. Existing penalty rules for these gun laws would probably apply, but the bill text itself does not say so. Youth records are often confidential, so it is unclear how a seller or the background-check system would find out about them.

label: H.R. 5041
title: Smith River National Recreation Area Expansion Act
short_title: Smith River National Recreation Area Expansion Act
one: The bill would extend the Smith River National Recreation Area into southwest Oregon and protect about 24 creek segments there as Wild and Scenic Rivers, while requiring a study of the added area's waters, plants and animals.
summary:
This bill would grow the Smith River National Recreation Area, now in California's Six Rivers National Forest, into Oregon. A new map dated January 23, 2023 would set the added land. The bill would also give 24 stream segments in the North Fork Smith River watershed in Oregon "wild river" status under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act. That status is the most protective river class. It generally blocks dams and keeps the rivers free-flowing. The bill also changes how part of the Smith River in California and Oregon is described and classed.

Within 5 years, the Forest Service would have to study the new area. The study would cover streams, wetlands, lakes, plants (including Port-Orford-cedar), animals, fungi and algae. It would then have to change its management plans to fully protect what it finds. Parts of the Oregon area would be managed as roadless, meaning no new roads. The Kalmiopsis Wilderness would stay under wilderness rules.

The bill would let the government buy land, not only accept donations. It would direct the government to acquire the 555-acre Cedar Creek Parcel, but only if Oregon's State Land Board approves and money is available. It keeps firefighting and forest-health thinning allowed. It says nothing in the bill reduces tribal rights. The Forest Service would also seek agreements giving tribes access for cultural activities. Oregon's state and local governments would get the same roles that California's now have. The bill gives no cost estimate.

who: Residents and communities in southwest Oregon (Curry County area) and northern California near the Smith River

Land purchases could remove land from local tax rolls, though the bill does not say how this would be handled.
Requiring plan changes to "fully protect" resources could limit how managers respond to future conditions.

label: H.R. 5054
title: Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
short_title: Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
one: Rewrites the federal Hobbs Act so that violence or threats of violence used to obtain property count as extortion even during labor disputes, while exempting minor, non-patterned incidents tied to peaceful picketing.
summary:
This bill changes a federal crime law called the Hobbs Act, which bans robbery and extortion that affect interstate commerce. In 1973, the Supreme Court (United States v. Enmons) ruled that violence by union members during a strike was not Hobbs Act extortion when it aimed at legitimate union goals, such as higher wages. This bill would undo that ruling. It does so by removing the requirement that force, violence, or fear of violence be "wrongful" for it to count as extortion. Fear that does not involve force or violence must still be wrongful. The penalty stays the same: up to $100,000 in fines, up to 20 years in prison, or both.

The bill also adds an exemption. Conduct is not covered if it is incidental to otherwise peaceful picketing during a labor dispute, consists only of minor injury, minor property damage, or threats of those, and is not part of a pattern of violence or coordinated violent activity. Those cases can be prosecuted only by state and local authorities. The bill says it does not change major labor laws, including the National Labor Relations Act, the Norris-LaGuardia Act, the Railway Labor Act, and certain Clayton Act sections. It also says federal jurisdiction is not blocked just because the conduct also broke state law or happened during a labor dispute. Critics and supporters may disagree on whether it protects people from violence or exposes strikers to heavy federal charges.
does: Replaces Section 1951 of Title 18 (the Hobbs Act) with a new version covering interference with commerce by threats or violence; penalties stay at up to $100,000 fine, up to 20 years in prison, or both.

Redefines extortion as obtaining property with the person's consent when that consent is induced by actual or threatened force or violence (no longer needing to be 'wrongful'), by wrongful use of fear without violence, or under color of official right.
Effectively reverses the Supreme Court's 1973 Enmons decision, so violence during a strike aimed at legitimate union goals could be prosecuted as extortion.

Exempts conduct that is incidental to otherwise peaceful picketing in a labor dispute, involves only minor bodily injury, minor property damage or threats of them, and is not part of a pattern or coordinated violent activity.
Limits prosecution of that exempted conduct to state and local authorities.
Defines 'labor dispute' by reference to the National Labor Relations Act.
States that the bill does not repeal or change the Clayton Act sections 6 and 20, the Norris-LaGuardia Act, the National Labor Relations Act, or the Railway Labor Act.

Includes an exemption and a state-only prosecution route for minor, isolated incidents during peaceful picketing.
Explicitly preserves existing labor-protection statutes such as the NLRA and Norris-LaGuardia Act.

Removing 'wrongful' from violence-based extortion could sweep in conduct in ordinary, legitimate bargaining disputes.
Could shift the balance of power in labor disputes toward employers, which may work against workers' interests.
State and local authorities already can prosecute violence, so federal duplication may be unnecessary.

crs:
Freedom From Union Violence Act of 2025
This bill broadens the scope of conduct that constitutes extortion under the federal criminal statute commonly known as the Hobbs Act. The Hobbs Act prohibits robbery or extortion affecting interstate commerce.
Currently, an extortion offense includes obtaining property of another through the wrongful use of force, violence, or fear. Typically, Hobbs Act violations are investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney's Office.
In 1973, in 
United States v. Enmons
, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the use of violence by union members during a strike did not constitute extortion under the Hobbs Act because its purpose —to achieve legitimate union objectives—was not wrongful.
This bill eliminates the requirement that the use of force, violence, or fear of force or violence to obtain property must be wrongful. The bill specifies that the use of fear not involving force or violence must still be wrongful.
Finally, the bill exempts from the Hobbs Act prohibition conduct that (1) is incidental to peaceful picketing during a labor dispute, (2) consists solely of minor bodily injury or property damage, and (3) is not part of a pattern of violent conduct or of coordinated violent activity. A violation involving exempted conduct is subject to prosecution by state and local authorities.

people_over_profit.reason: Expanding federal felony exposure for strike-related conduct could weaken workers' leverage against employers, though it also protects people from violence.

honesty_kindness.reason: Discouraging violence and intimidation during labor disputes promotes safer, more humane conduct.

equality.reason: It singles out labor-dispute conduct by reversing a union-related precedent, which could tilt bargaining power away from workers.

personal_freedom.reason: Vague terms and heavy federal penalties could chill lawful striking and picketing, though violence itself is not protected.

label: H.R. 5069
title: Peter J. McGuire Labor Day Landmark Act
short_title: Peter J. McGuire Labor Day Landmark Act
one: Designates the Peter J. McGuire Memorial and Gravesite in Pennsauken, New Jersey, as a National Commemorative Site and lets the Interior Department partner with and fund groups that run education programs there.
summary: This bill would honor Peter J. McGuire, a 19th-century labor leader who helped found the American Federation of Labor and the carpenters' union, and who proposed Labor Day. It would name his memorial and gravesite in Pennsauken, New Jersey, the "Peter J. McGuire Memorial National Commemorative Site." The bill's long title says "National Historic Landmark," but the text itself creates a "National Commemorative Site." The site would not become part of the National Park System. The Secretary of the Interior would be allowed, but not required, to make cooperative agreements with public or private groups to provide educational and interpretive displays and programs at the site. The Secretary could also give those partners technical help and money. The bill does not set a dollar amount or say where funds would come from. The bill also says the designation does not block property owners from doing what they could already do with their property. That includes the owners of the site itself. The bill has a long list of findings about McGuire's life, the memorial built in 1952, and the site's listing on state and national historic registers in 2018 and 2019. It was introduced August 29, 2025, and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.

label: H.R. 5070
title: Federal Police Camera and Accountability Act
short_title: Federal Police Camera and Accountability Act
one: Requires federal law enforcement officers to wear and use body cameras and put video cameras in patrol cars, with rules on when to record, how long to keep footage, who can see it, and a ban on facial recognition.
summary:
This bill would make federal law enforcement officers wear body cameras. They would have to turn on both video and audio when responding to a call or starting a stop with a member of the public. They could not turn the camera off until the stop ends and they leave. Officers would have to tell people they are being recorded. In a home without a warrant or in non-emergency situations, officers would have to ask the occupant if they want the camera off. Crime victims and anonymous tipsters would get the same offer. There are exceptions, including for undercover work, risks to informants, national security, military police, protective details, and school grounds.

Footage would be kept 6 months and then deleted. Footage involving force or a complaint would be kept at least 3 years. People filmed could view footage. The public could request footage, with limits, and it could not be withheld just because it is a law enforcement record when an officer's conduct is under review. Cameras could not use facial recognition. Patrol cars would get in-car cameras, with recordings kept at least 90 days. Officers who break the rules could face discipline, and courts would presume in favor of defendants or plaintiffs when evidence was not captured or was destroyed. The Government Accountability Office (GAO, a congressional watchdog) would study training, pursuits, and use of force. The Attorney General would write the rules within 6 months. The text does not give a cost or a start date for the requirements.
does: Requires federal law enforcement officers to wear body cameras with a wide field of view.
Requires video and audio recording when responding to a call or starting an enforcement or investigative stop, until the stop ends and the officer leaves.
Requires officers to tell people they are being recorded.

Requires officers to offer to turn off the camera for occupants of private homes (without a warrant or in non-emergencies), crime victims, and anonymous reporters. The offer and answer must be recorded first.
Bans using body cameras to gather intelligence on First Amendment speech, association, or religion, to record unrelated activity, or to use facial recognition or biometric surveillance.

Requires agencies to post their body camera policies online.

label: H.R. 509
title: Western Hemisphere Nearshoring Act
one: Offers cheaper government loans, moving-cost financing, 15 years of duty-free trade treatment, and a special tax break to companies that move factories from China to Latin America or the Caribbean, and tells the U.S. to pursue trade and nuclear-reactor-sale talks with those countries.
summary:
This bill tries to get companies to move their factories out of China and into Latin America and the Caribbean. It does this with several kinds of help. First, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC, a government development bank) must put at least 10% of its financing money toward paying moving, worker-training, and building costs for these companies. It must also cut the interest rates on their loans. Second, the President must give these companies duty-free (no import tax) or similar treatment for goods they make in the region, for 15 years. Third, the bill creates a special tax rule letting these companies write off 75% of the cost of new equipment and buildings right away, for property placed in service before 2038.

Companies must create jobs in the new country, must not be controlled by China, Russia, or another adversary, and must keep their assets in the region. State-owned companies can't qualify. The Commerce Secretary must find the help won't hurt U.S. jobs. Tariffs collected on Chinese goods go into a trust fund to cover the lost revenue.

The bill also tells the U.S. Trade Representative to start trade talks with countries in the region that lack a trade deal, if they curb migration, reduce reliance on China, and allow a Taiwan commercial office. It allows talks on selling nuclear reactors on the same terms. Cuba and Venezuela are excluded unless the State Department certifies major democratic and human rights steps.

crs:
Western Hemisphere Nearshoring Act
This bill provides assistance for corporations to relocate operations from China to Latin America or Caribbean (LAC) countries and specifies actions to expand trade and nuclear energy agreements with LAC countries. 
Specifically, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation must use at least 10% of its funding to finance moving, workforce development, and facility construction costs associated with such relocations. Tariffs collected by the United States on goods manufactured in China shall be used to fund such assistance. The President must provide duty-free or other preferential treatment for goods and services produced in a LAC country by a corporation that received relocation assistance under this bill.
A corporation must meet certain conditions to receive these benefits, including creating sufficient jobs in the LAC country and guaranteeing that the corporation will not be controlled by China, Russia, or other foreign adversary government. State-owned enterprises are not eligible. 
Additionally, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative must start trade negotiations with each LAC country that does not have a free trade agreement with the United States if the country meets certain conditions (such as reducing economic reliance on China). The President is authorized to start negotiations with a LAC country for the sale of nuclear reactors if these same conditions are met and the sale does not threaten U.S. national security. 
Neither Cuba nor Venezuela qualify as a LAC country unless the Department of State certifies that the country has taken certain actions, including holding free and fair elections.

people_over_profit.reason: Large subsidies, interest-rate cuts, duty-free treatment, and a 75% expensing tax write-off mainly benefit corporations' bottom lines, with worker protections limited to job-creation conditions.

no_bailouts.reason: It directs DFC financing at reduced interest rates, duty-free treatment, and accelerated tax write-offs to specific companies, which are targeted corporate subsidies and tax breaks paid for by taxpayers and tariff revenue.

Both groups instead cover adjacent trade topics: U.S.-China tensions, tariffs, and North American trade relations, with Lean Left leaning toward global economic fragility and Center toward tariff and export-control policy. label: H.R. 5092
title: District of Columbia Police Home Rule Act
short_title: District of Columbia Police Home Rule Act
one: The bill would remove the President's power under the DC Home Rule Act to take emergency control of Washington, DC's police department.
summary: Under the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, passed in 1973, DC residents elect a mayor and council to run local affairs. One part of that law, section 740, lets the President take over control of the city's Metropolitan Police Department in certain emergencies. This bill would delete that section entirely. It would also remove the matching line from the law's table of contents. Nothing else in the Home Rule Act would change. If the bill became law, the President would no longer have this specific emergency power over DC police, and the city's elected government would keep control of its police. The bill text does not say what the section 740 power currently requires, such as time limits or reporting rules. It also does not say whether the President could use other legal powers, such as the National Guard, in an emergency. Those powers are outside this bill and would stay as they are. The bill was introduced on September 2, 2025 by Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton, who represents DC in the House but cannot vote on final passage. It has been referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. No start date is given, so it would take effect when signed into law.

Some people may disagree with removing a federal emergency power over the capital's police force.

label: H.R. 5093
title: District of Columbia National Guard Home Rule Act
short_title: DC National Guard Home Rule Act
one: The bill would move command of the District of Columbia National Guard from the President to the Mayor of DC, giving DC the same kind of control over its Guard that governors have in the states.
summary: Today, the President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the DC National Guard. Every state's Guard is led by its governor, but DC has no governor, and its elected mayor has no command role. This bill would change that. It would replace "President" with "Mayor of the District of Columbia" in the old 1889 law that sets up the DC militia. That includes the power to appoint and retire officers, call the Guard out for duty, and convene courts-martial (military trials). The bill also edits many places in federal law (Titles 10 and 32 of the U.S. Code) where a "commanding general" of the DC Guard now gives consent or makes decisions. In those places the Mayor would take over, for example on active-duty orders, moving units, appointing the adjutant general (the Guard's top administrative officer) and the fiscal officer, and running programs like the National Guard Challenge Program. It would also treat DC as a "State" for one federal assistance provision. Finally, it removes the National Guard from a section of the DC Home Rule Act that limits the DC government's authority over certain federal matters. The bill does not say whether the President could still call the DC Guard into federal service in the way presidents can with state Guards. The text does not set a start date or a cost.

label: H.R. 51
title: Washington, D.C. Admission Act
one: The bill would make most of Washington, D.C. the 51st state, "Washington, Douglass Commonwealth," with two Senators and one House member, while keeping a small federal "Capital" district around the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court and National Mall.
summary:
This bill would turn most of the District of Columbia into a new state called the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth. A small area would stay under direct federal control as "the Capital." It would hold the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the Supreme Court, the national monuments, and nearby federal office buildings.

Once the President certifies the law, the D.C. Mayor would call elections for two U.S. Senators and one U.S. Representative. The current non-voting D.C. Delegate job would end. The House would permanently grow to 436 members. The new state would use D.C.'s existing laws, its 2016 proposed state constitution, and its current officials. It could not tax federal property unless Congress allows it.

Many federal duties would continue for a while. These include judges' pensions, the public defender service, prosecutors, parole supervision, courts funding, and an enhanced Medicaid match rate. Each would end only after the state certifies that it has its own laws and funding in place. An 18-member commission would advise on the transition for two years after admission. People living in the Capital could vote by absentee ballot in the state where they last lived. The bill also sets fast-track rules for Congress to consider a constitutional amendment repealing the 23rd Amendment, which gives D.C. presidential electors. It would not repeal that amendment on its own.

crs:
Washington, D.C. Admission Act
This bill provides for the establishment of the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, and its admission into the United States.
The state is composed of most of the territory of the District of Columbia (DC), excluding a specified area that encompasses the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the U.S. Supreme Court building, federal monuments, and federal office buildings adjacent to the National Mall and the U.S. Capitol. The excluded territory shall be known as the Capital and serve as the seat of the government of the United States, as provided for in Article I of the Constitution. The state may not impose taxes on federal property except as Congress permits.
The bill provides for the DC Mayor to issue a proclamation for the first elections to Congress of two Senators and one Representative of the state. The bill eliminates the office of Delegate to the House of Representatives.
The bill applies current DC laws to the state. DC judicial proceedings and contractual obligations shall continue under the state’s authority. The bill also provides for specified federal obligations to transfer to the state upon its certification that it has funds and laws in place to assume the obligations. These include maintaining a retirement fund for judges and operating public defender services. 
The bill establishes a commission that is generally comprised of members who are appointed by DC and federal government officials to advise on an orderly transition to statehood.

transparency.reason: Giving residents their own voting representatives could make government more accountable to them, though the bill adds no new disclosure rules.

local_say.reason: It would give D.C. residents voting seats in Congress and end Congress's power to override their local laws and budget.

title: Regulatory Cooling Off Act of 2025
one: Requires most final federal agency rules to wait 6 months (instead of 30 days) before taking effect, lengthens public comment to at least 60 days, adds posting and notice requirements, and makes it easier to sue agencies in more courts.
summary:
When a federal agency, such as the EPA or the FDA, writes a new rule, it usually must let the public comment first. After the rule is final, it normally can't take effect for at least 30 days. This bill would change that in several ways.

First, the public would get at least 60 days to comment on a proposed rule. Second, the waiting period before a final rule takes effect would grow from 30 days to 6 months. Third, agencies would have to send each final rule to the congressional committees that oversee the issue at least 6 months before it takes effect. They would also have to post final and proposed rules on their own websites at least 24 hours before publishing them in the Federal Register (the government's daily journal of rules), and publish a notice on the day a rule actually takes effect.

The bill also changes where people can sue an agency over a rule. A lawsuit could be filed in the plaintiff's home district or in any district where the agency has an office. Finally, it changes the Congressional Review Act, the law that lets Congress cancel new rules. Big rules that now wait 60 days would wait 6 months, unless Congress passes a measure approving them.

The bill does not say whether existing exceptions to the waiting period, such as emergencies, would still apply. It does not edit those parts of the law.

label: H.R. 5112
title: Tipped Worker Protection Act
one: The bill would phase out the lower "tipped" minimum wage so tipped workers get the full federal minimum wage, and it adds new rules to stop employers from keeping tips, hiding service charges, or imposing tip pools without worker votes.
summary:
Right now, employers can pay tipped workers a lower cash wage (the federal floor is $2.13 an hour) as long as tips bring them up to the regular minimum wage. This bill would end that system in steps. In the first year after enactment, the minimum cash wage for tipped workers would be $3.60 an hour. Each year after, it would rise by $1.50 until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage (currently $7.25). At that point, tipped workers would be paid the full minimum wage by the employer, and tips would be extra.

The bill also sets new tip rules. Employers could not keep tips, and managers and supervisors could not take any part of them. Employers could not use tips to pay credit card processing fees. Tip pools (where tips are shared) would only be allowed if at least 51 percent of non-supervisory workers vote for them, after at least 30 percent ask for a vote. Joining a pool would have to be voluntary, and workers could not be punished for how they vote.

Mandatory service charges would have to be explained to customers and workers, including how much goes directly to workers. Any part promised to workers must be paid to them promptly. A charge described as optional could not be added unless the customer asks. Those worker-directed charges would also count as tips for an employer Social Security tax credit. Penalties for misusing tips would be expanded. The bill's text does not include cost estimates.

label: H.R. 5122
title: NASA Talent Exchange Program Act
one: Lets NASA swap employees with private companies for 3 months to 3 years, with ethics, conflict-of-interest, and reporting rules attached.
summary:
This bill would let NASA set up a program to temporarily trade workers with private companies. A NASA employee could work at a company, or a company's employee could work at NASA. Both the company and the worker must agree. Each assignment would last at least three months and normally no more than two years. It could run up to three years if NASA decides the mission needs it. A single NASA employee could not spend more than three years total on these assignments.

A written agreement would cover each assignment. NASA employees would have to return to government service for twice as long as their assignment, or repay the costs. Company workers sent to NASA would stay on their company's payroll. They would be treated as federal employees for many ethics, conflict-of-interest, and liability laws. They could not see the home company's trade secrets. They also could not do "inherently governmental" work, meaning core decisions that only the government should make. The company could not bill the government for those workers' pay. No more than 2% of NASA's civil service workforce could be on assignment at once.

NASA would have to build a system to manage conflicts of interest. It would also have to send Congress yearly reports. These would name the companies, positions, and pay grades involved. The Government Accountability Office (GAO, Congress's watchdog) would review the program within three years. The bill does not say who pays the salary of NASA workers sent to a company.

label: H.R. 5147
title: WIRELESS Leadership Act
one: Sets national deadlines for local and state governments to decide on cell tower and small-cell applications, automatically approves applications that miss the deadline, limits fees and local rules, and bars local regulation based on radio-frequency health or environmental concerns.
summary:
This bill changes federal communications law to speed up approval of cell towers, antennas, and small cell equipment. It keeps the basic idea that cities, counties, and states decide where wireless facilities go. But it adds strict rules on how they decide.

Local governments would have firm deadlines. These run from 60 days for small equipment on an existing structure to 150 days for other large facilities. The clock covers all local proceedings together. A local moratorium (a pause on new applications) would not stop the clock. If a government misses the deadline, the company can send written notice, and the request is then treated as approved with no further local action.

Any denial would have to be in writing, backed by substantial evidence, and made public the same day it is issued. Local governments could not treat providers differently, and could not block or effectively block wireless service. They could still set objective, reasonable engineering, safety, and appearance rules. They could not regulate based on the environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions if the facility meets Federal Communications Commission (FCC) limits.

Fees would have to be set in advance, made public, and based on actual, reasonable costs. Anyone harmed by a local decision or delay could sue within 30 days, or ask the FCC to review it. The FCC would have 120 days to rule. The bill text does not say how environmental, historic, or community review would fit into these deadlines.

crs:
Winning the International Race for Economic Leadership and Expanding Service to Support Leadership Act or the WIRELESS Leadership Act
This bill imposes limits on state and local review and regulation of requests to construct wireless telecommunication facilities.
Specifically, states and localities must grant or deny requests to place, modify, or construct personal wireless service (PWS) facilities by a specified deadline. This deadline varies based on the nature of the request and the proposed facility. If a state or locality fails to act on a request within that timeframe, the request is deemed granted. On the day a decision to deny a request is made, the state or locality must publish the decision and provide it to the requesting party.
Further, the bill expands an existing prohibition on unreasonable discrimination in the regulation of such requests. Under the bill, any discrimination among PWS facilities or communications service providers is prohibited. For example, a state or locality may not grant preferential or exclusive use of facilities to a particular provider or class of providers. However, states and localities may establish objective, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory engineering standards, safety requirements, or aesthetic requirements.
Finally, the bill establishes requirements for fees imposed by states and localities for consideration of a request. For example, such fees must be (1) competitively neutral, technology neutral, and nondiscriminatory; (2) established in advance and publicly disclosed; and (3) based on actual and direct costs to the state or locality.

life.reason: Shortened review clocks and deemed-approval rules may leave little time for environmental, historic, or community review, and RF-emission concerns are largely removed from local consideration.

transparency.reason: Denials must be in writing, backed by substantial evidence, and published the same day, and fees must be published in advance.

people_over_profit.reason: Deemed-approval and binding deadlines give wireless providers faster approvals and limit local leverage over company-proposed facilities, favoring provider speed over community review.

local_say.reason: Local governments lose much of their power over siting: deadlines are firm, moratoria do not stop the clock, missed deadlines mean automatic approval, and RF-based objections are barred.

label: H.R. 5151
title: Quiet Communities Act of 2025
one: The bill would bring back the EPA's Office of Noise Abatement and Control to research noise pollution, help states and towns fight it, and study aircraft noise, with $25 million a year authorized for five years.
summary:
This bill would restart an office inside the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that deals with noise pollution. That office, called the Office of Noise Abatement and Control, has not had funding since 1982. Congress says that has left noise programs across the country dormant, even though the EPA is still legally responsible for enforcing the noise rules already on the books.

The restarted office would give states technical help and grants to build noise control programs. Those grants could cover equipment for local communities. The office would also research how noise affects mental and physical health, track noise levels over time, and create public education materials, training, and workshops. It would set up regional help centers that work with colleges and private groups. It would also review how well the 1972 Noise Control Act has worked.

The EPA would also run a special study of aircraft noise. Outside scientists would look at how the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) measures noise, at what noise level health problems begin, and at whether airport noise programs work. A report with recommendations would be due to Congress within 2 years.

The bill also updates the grant section of the 1972 Noise Control Act and repeals a 1970 noise law. It says the office should favor approaches that rely on state and local action, market incentives, and teamwork with other agencies. It authorizes $25 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. "Authorizes" means Congress would still have to actually provide the money in a separate spending bill.

label: H.R. 5152
title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
short_title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
one: Requires the federal Bureau of Prisons to give departing U.S.-citizen prisoners a REAL ID-standard photo ID card valid at least 18 months, to be accepted for many federal benefit programs and to help them get state IDs.
summary:
This bill would require the Bureau of Prisons (BOP), which runs federal prisons, to hand a photo ID card to each U.S. citizen leaving federal custody. The card would have to meet the federal REAL ID security standards. The BOP would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start issuing the cards. Each card would stay valid for at least 18 months after the person is released.

The bill would also make many federal agencies and programs accept the card as proof of identity. These include Social Security, Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP (food assistance), TANF (cash assistance), and programs at the Education, Housing and Urban Development, and Veterans Affairs departments. It would also cover federal probation and pretrial services, the D.C. offender supervision agency, and entry into federal buildings.

The BOP director would have to negotiate with each state so the card can be used to get a state ID. The director would report on that progress to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees each year, starting one year after enactment. Within one year, the Attorney General would also issue guidance to states that want to issue similar release cards to people leaving state prisons. The bill does not say how much this would cost, and it does not replace the BOP's existing duty to plan for prisoners' release. It does not cover non-citizens.

label: H.R. 5157
title: Streamlining American Manufacturing Strategy Act
one: Changes how often the Manufacturing USA program must update its strategic plan from every 3 years to every 4 years, so it lines up with the National Strategy for Advanced Manufacturing.
summary:
Manufacturing USA is a network of institutes where government, companies, and universities work together on new manufacturing technology. Under current law, the program's strategic plan (a planning document that sets goals and priorities) must be updated at least every 3 years. label: H.R. 5159
title: Nationwide Right to Unionize Act
one: The bill would repeal the part of federal labor law that lets states ban contracts requiring workers to join or pay a union, which would end state "right-to-work" laws.
summary: Federal labor law lets employers and unions agree to a contract rule that workers covered by the union contract must support the union, usually by paying dues or fees, to keep their jobs. These are called "union security" agreements. Right now, Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act lets each state ban those agreements. About half the states have used that power to pass "right-to-work" laws. This bill is just one operative sentence. It repeals Section 14(b). If it became law, states could no longer ban union security agreements for workplaces covered by that Act, which covers most private-sector employers. Employers and unions in those states could then negotiate these agreements, as they already can in other states. The bill does not force any employer or union to adopt such an agreement. It only removes the state ban. The bill text does not say when it would start, and it does not add other rules, funding, or penalties. The title talks about a "right to unionize," but the bill does not change the right to form or join a union. It only changes whether states can bar union-security clauses. Outside the bill text, existing court rulings limit what unions can require of workers who object to joining. Those rulings are not changed by this bill. Because there is no CRS summary yet, this reading relies on the short bill text.

title: Go Pack Go Act of 2025
one: Lets TV subscribers in 13 northwestern Wisconsin counties, who now get Minnesota-market stations, choose to receive Wisconsin network stations instead of, or in addition to, their assigned local stations.
summary: Some Wisconsin counties near the Minnesota border are placed in TV markets based in another state, so cable and satellite customers there often see Minnesota news, weather, and sports instead of Wisconsin programming. This bill would let customers in 13 named Wisconsin counties (Ashland, Barron, Bayfield, Burnett, Douglas, Dunn, Florence, Iron, Pierce, Polk, Sawyer, St. Croix, and Washburn) pick what they get for each TV network. They could choose the local-market station their provider must already carry, a Wisconsin station from a neighboring TV market, or both. The bill applies to counties that have no same-network station of their own in Wisconsin. If a customer picks only the Wisconsin station, that counts as meeting the provider's duty to carry a local station. The bill also changes some copyright and broadcast-rule details so these Wisconsin signals do not use up satellite limits, do not need the usual cable permission deal, and are treated as "significantly viewed" (a rule that lets certain out-of-market stations be carried). Satellite companies only have to do this where it is technically feasible, as decided by the FCC. The bill does not say when it would start or what it would cost, and the text does not describe how it affects local stations' finances.

label: H.R. 5170
title: CABLE Leadership Act
one: Requires local cable franchising authorities to approve or deny a new cable franchise request within 120 days, or the request is automatically approved.
summary: Today, a cable company that wants to offer service in a town or county usually needs a "franchise," which is a permission agreement from the local government (the "franchising authority"). This bill would put a strict clock on that process for new franchise requests (not renewals). The local government would have 120 days after getting a complete request to say yes or no. If it misses the deadline, the request is automatically treated as approved. The clock covers all local steps combined, and a local moratorium (a pause on considering requests), whether official or informal, cannot stop the clock. If a local government says no, it must do so in writing, back the decision with substantial evidence in a written record, and release it publicly and to the applicant the same day. The bill also defines a "complete" request. A request counts as complete once the applicant takes the first step the locality requires, unless the locality sends a written notice within 30 days naming the missing information and citing a public rule that requires it. If no such notice arrives, the request is treated as complete and received the day after that 30-day period ends. The bill does not mention broadband build-out terms, community service requirements, or fees, so how those would interact with automatic approval is not addressed in the text.

label: H.R. 663
title: To oppose the permitting of deep seabed mining and exploration for deep seabed mining, and for other purposes.
short_title: Oppose Deep Seabed Mining Permitting Act
one: The bill would direct the President to have U.S. representatives at international bodies push for a pause on deep seabed mining permits and exploration, and oppose funding for it, until international rules are in place and certified as protective of the ocean.
summary: This bill is about mining the deep ocean floor for minerals. It starts with a list of findings from Congress. These say scientists think deep seabed mining poses major risks, such as killing unique species, creating large clouds of sediment, adding noise pollution, possibly contaminating food fish, and harming the ocean's ability to store carbon. It also says we don't yet know enough about the deep sea to judge the full risks. The bill then states the "sense of Congress," which is a non-binding opinion. That opinion is that no deep seabed mining should happen in international waters until the International Seabed Authority (the UN-linked body that oversees the international seabed) adopts a full, binding set of rules based on solid science. The one binding part is an instruction to the President. The President must tell U.S. representatives at international organizations the U.S. belongs to or observes to use the country's voice, vote, and influence to call for a moratorium (a pause) on permitting deep seabed mining and exploration. They must also oppose investment, financing, or other support for it. This continues until the President certifies to Congress that the International Seabed Authority has issued regulations that are based on scientific consensus and effectively protect the marine environment. The President must also send Congress a report describing those regulations. The bill does not create a domestic ban or change U.S. law on permits.

label: H.R. 664
title: American Seabed Protection Act
one: Bans new federal permits for deep seabed mining and for hardrock mining on the Outer Continental Shelf (except scientific research) and orders a National Academies study of the environmental effects of such mining.
summary:
This bill would stop the U.S. government from issuing licenses, permits, or other approvals for two kinds of ocean mining. The first is exploring for or commercially recovering minerals from the deep seabed, which is the ocean floor beyond national boundaries that current law lets U.S. companies seek permits for. The second is exploring for, developing, or producing hardrock minerals (such as metals) on the Outer Continental Shelf, the underwater lands off U.S. coasts that the federal government manages. Permits for scientific research would still be allowed.

The bill also tells the Commerce Secretary, working through NOAA, to try to make a deal within 90 days with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. The Academies would do a broad study of how this mining could affect ocean life, habitats, sediment clouds, the ocean's ability to store greenhouse gases, fishing, recreation, fish farms, undersea cables, and Indigenous peoples and cultures. The study would also estimate greenhouse gas emissions from mining and look at alternatives, like recycling, substitute materials, and cleaner land-based mining. label: H.R. 8424
title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
short_title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
one: Directs USDA to create a single application (or shared-information system) and standard technology so small direct-selling farmers and ranchers can more easily accept SNAP, WIC, senior farmers market, and GusNIP benefits.
summary:
Farmers who sell directly to shoppers, such as at farmers markets, often have to fill out separate applications for each federal food assistance program they want to accept. They also may need different equipment for each one. This bill would tell the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make that easier.

First, USDA would build either a single application farmers and ranchers could use to apply to SNAP (food stamps), WIC (nutrition aid for women, infants, and children), the Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program, and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (which helps people buy more fruits and vegetables). Or, USDA would build a system that shares a farmer's information between programs, so approval in one program automatically counts as pre-qualified for the others.

Second, USDA would set up a streamlined way for these farmers to process benefits with standard technology, such as one device or one mobile app.

Third, the bill changes the SNAP law so USDA must make sure equipment and systems that states or their partners provide are right for the seller. For farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets, that includes wireless or mobile equipment.

USDA must report to Congress on progress within one year. The bill gives no dollar amounts for funding.

crs:
Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
This bill directs the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to establish a streamlined process for farmers and ranchers to provide benefits under certain federal nutrition programs. These programs include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP); the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program (SFMNP); the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC); and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (GusNIP).
Specifically, USDA must establish a streamlined application process for farmers and ranchers to apply to be vendors under the nutrition programs, including by developing a single application for the programs or an information sharing system. USDA must also develop a streamlined process for these vendors to use standardized technology to process program benefits (such as a single piece of equipment or a mobile application).
Further, USDA must ensure that the program benefit processing equipment and systems made available by a state agency are appropriate for the entity. For example, this includes ensuring wireless or mobile processing equipment and technology systems are appropriate for farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets.

people_over_profit.reason: Streamlined applications and standardized payment tools reduce paperwork and cost burdens for small direct-sale farmers relative to large vendors' compliance capacity, modestly favoring independent producers.

honesty_kindness.reason: Making it easier for low-income shoppers and seniors to use benefits at farmers markets and for small farmers to participate supports fair, accessible access to nutrition programs.

label: H.R. 9968
title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
short_title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
one: Requires the USDA to study and publicly report on barriers that organic and organic-transitioning farms face in USDA programs, then give three yearly progress updates.
summary: This bill does not create new programs or hand out money. It orders the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to study why certified organic farms, and farms thinking about switching to organic, have trouble using USDA programs. The USDA would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to send a report to the House and Senate agriculture committees and post it on its website. The report would look at programs for conservation, loans, disaster aid, crop insurance, exports, marketing, technical help, rural development, data collection, buying food for government use, and organic certification cost-sharing. It would include data where possible on how many organic farms apply, are approved or denied, how much funding they get, where they are, and why they are denied or don't take part. It would also look at specific problems such as eligibility rules, payment rates, paperwork, crop insurance prices, how disaster losses are valued, and whether USDA staff know enough about organic farming. It would assess the need for organic training for field staff. The USDA must describe the steps it plans to take and suggest any law changes Congress should consider. For three years after, it must post yearly updates on progress and remaining barriers.

label: H.R. 11039
title: Ahmad Butler Pediatric Cancer Hope for a Cure Act
short_title: Ahmad Butler Pediatric Cancer Hope for a Cure Act
one: The bill would put $2 billion over 10 years into childhood cancer research and help families pay for clinical trial costs, and it would create a voluntary donation fund, including a tax-return checkoff, for the same work.
summary: This bill aims to fight childhood cancer. It tells the Department of Health and Human Services to step up research, especially on rare and high-risk tumors, brain cancers, cancers that come back or resist treatment, and the long-term health of survivors. It also tells the National Institutes of Health to start a research effort on holistic, nutritional, and alternative therapies. That research must be evidence-based and focused on safety and effectiveness. The bill creates grants for families in pediatric cancer clinical trials. These can cover travel, lodging, meals, childcare, and unpaid leave. Other grants go to groups that run trials, to open sites in underserved areas. Congress would appropriate $2 billion for fiscal years 2027 through 2036. That money could not be shifted to adult cancer programs. The bill also sets up the "One Lunch 4 Cure" fund at the Treasury. People, employers, and groups could donate voluntarily, including by payroll deduction and by a line on federal tax returns that lets filers send an overpayment to the fund. The fund could not pay agency administrative costs, and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) would audit it every year. HHS would send Congress yearly reports on spending, results, trial enrollment, and gaps. The bill says it should not reduce existing pediatric cancer programs.

label: H.R. 11042
title: Public Shipyard Workforce Protection Act of 2026
short_title: Public Shipyard Workforce Protection Act of 2026
one: Bars the Defense Department from using fiscal year 2027 funds to freeze hiring, cut staff through layoffs, or needlessly delay filling civilian jobs at public (government-owned) shipyards.
summary: This bill is short. It says that for fiscal year 2027, money given to the Department of Defense cannot be used to do three things at a public shipyard. A public shipyard is a government-owned yard, such as the Navy yards that repair ships and submarines. First, the department cannot freeze hiring there. Second, it cannot carry out a "reduction in force," which is the formal name for layoffs or job cuts. Third, it cannot delay filling an open federal civilian job there without a good reason. The bill does not define "public shipyard" or "without cause," and the text we have doesn't say who decides what counts as a good reason. It does not add new money, create new jobs, or set hiring targets. It only limits how existing funds may be used for one year. The bill was introduced November 17, 2026, and sent to the House Armed Services Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee. It has not yet had a vote or hearing. There is no Congressional Research Service summary yet.

Applies only to fiscal year 2027.

label: H.R. 11047

one: Requires companies seeking or holding Defense Department aerospace contracts to disclose ties to Chinese entities on U.S. government military-concern lists, and requires the Pentagon to assess those ties, without banning them.
summary: This bill would make companies that bid on or hold certain Defense Department (DoD) aerospace contracts tell the Pentagon about business ties to Chinese companies the U.S. government has already flagged as helping China's military. Covered contracts, grants, and other agreements involve software, technology, or intellectual property used to design, build, or maintain military aircraft, spacecraft, launch vehicles, propulsion, avionics, and related systems. Ties that must be reported include joint ventures, technology or intellectual property licenses, co-production deals, any stock ownership (even partial), and other arrangements that give recurring access to the company's controlled technology, people, or facilities. Parent companies and affiliates count. The Defense Secretary would issue guidance within 90 days. Current contractors would have 180 days after that guidance to report existing ties. New ties and ties with newly listed entities would have to be reported within 90 days. The Pentagon must review each disclosure for security, supply chain, and technology-transfer risks. It may require fixes or weigh the disclosure, or a failure to disclose, when deciding whether to renew a contract. It is not required to act, and the bill does not ban any relationship. The Pentagon would also send Congress an annual report, unclassified but possibly with a classified annex, giving the number and general nature of disclosed ties and actions taken.

support: The bill would give the Pentagon better visibility into ties between defense aerospace contractors and Chinese entities the government has already flagged as helping China's military.
Disclosure of joint ventures, technology licenses, and co-production deals could help the Pentagon spot security, supply chain, and technology-transfer risks earlier.
The Pentagon could use disclosures when deciding whether to renew contracts, giving it leverage to require fixes for risks it finds.
The annual report to Congress would give lawmakers unclassified information, with a possible classified annex, on how many ties exist and what actions were taken.

transparency.reason: Contractors must tell the Pentagon about ties to flagged Chinese entities, and the Pentagon must report to Congress each year, though not in detail to the public.

people_over_profit.reason: It lets the Pentagon weigh national security risks against contractors' commercial deals, and failure to disclose can affect contract renewal.

honesty_kindness.reason: It encourages honest reporting by tying disclosure, or failure to disclose, to contract decisions.

label: S. 5608
title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends by three years the federal program that sends payments to rural counties and schools near national forests and other federal land, and fixes a few typos.
summary: Many rural counties contain large amounts of national forest land that cannot be taxed. Since 2000, the Secure Rural Schools program has sent these counties payments to help pay for schools, roads, and other services. The program's authority is set to run out after 2026. This bill pushes the key dates back three years, from 2026 to 2029, so the payments can continue. It also moves back by three years the dates for the local advisory committees and for the special projects they can recommend on federal land. These projects are paid for with a share of the payments. Counties would also get three more years to spend certain project money, with the dates moving from 2028 and 2029 to 2031 and 2032. A pilot program for the advisory committees is also extended to 2029. Finally, the bill makes three tiny wording fixes, such as adding the word "of" before "acres" and removing stray commas. The bill does not set a dollar amount itself. It changes dates in the existing law, so payment amounts would follow the formulas already in that law. We could not see those formulas in the text provided, so the cost is not stated here.
does: Extends the Secure Rural Schools payment authority from 2026 to 2029.
Extends the deadline for distributing payments to eligible counties to 2029.
Extends the committee composition waiver authority to 2029.
Extends authority for special projects on federal land by three years (to 2031 and 2032).
Extends the time counties may spend project funds by three years (to 2031 and 2032).
Extends the resource advisory committee pilot program to 2029.
Makes three minor wording corrections to the existing law.
who: Rural counties and school districts containing national forest or other federal land
Residents who rely on county-funded schools, roads and services in those areas
Local resource advisory committee members who review project proposals
The Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, which work with the committees
Federal taxpayers, who fund the payments

benefits: Gives rural counties and schools predictable funding for three more years.
Keeps local advisory committees active so residents can weigh in on projects.
Corrects small typos for clarity.
concerns: Adds federal spending, but the amount is not stated in the bill.
Special projects on federal land could affect forests, water or wildlife depending on how they are chosen.
Continues a payment system that is not tied to how much timber is harvested, which some may see as a long-term subsidy.
imp.cost: The bill gives no dollar figure. It changes dates in existing law, so costs depend on the existing payment formulas, which are not shown. No Congressional Budget Office estimate was provided.
unknowns: Total cost to taxpayers over the three years.
Which counties would receive how much.
What kinds of special projects will be approved and their environmental effects.
Whether the bill will be changed in committee or pass.

stage.last_action: Introduced in Senate

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep the Secure Rural Schools program running by extending its key deadlines from 2026 to 2029, so rural counties with large amounts of untaxable national forest land can keep receiving payments for schools, roads, and other services. It also extends related deadlines for local advisory committees, special projects on federal land, and the time counties have to spend project funds, and makes three small wording corrections. The bill does not set a dollar amount; payments would follow the formulas already in existing law.

oppose: The bill adds federal spending for three more years, yet it does not state a total cost, so taxpayers cannot see the full price from the bill text alone.
Payments under this program are not tied to how much timber is harvested, so you could argue it is a long-term subsidy that should be reviewed rather than simply extended.
Special projects on federal land are funded by these payments; you could ask that project selection include strong safeguards for forests, water, and wildlife.
support: The bill gives rural counties and schools three more years of predictable funding, which helps them plan budgets for schools, roads, and services.
Counties with large amounts of national forest land cannot collect property tax on that land, and these payments help make up for that lost revenue.
Local advisory committees stay active for three more years, so residents keep a voice in choosing special projects on federal land.

people_over_profit.reason: It directs public money to rural schools, roads and community services rather than to private companies.

local_say.reason: It extends local advisory committees that let residents recommend projects on nearby federal land.
